Optimal patient management-including accurate radiologic diagnosis, early detection of malignancies, differential diagnosis, assessment of disease extent, and posttreatment surveillance-can be achieved through comprehensive radiologic evaluation. ©RSNA, 2026 Supplemental material is available for this article.
42848606: MR neurography (MRN) is a powerful tool for evaluating peripheral nerve disorders, traditionally focused on larger nerves like the sciatic nerve, lumbosacral plexus, and brachial plexus. With advances in hardware and software and improved vascular signal suppression, MRN enables reliable assessment of fine-caliber nerves-defined as those with a diameter of up to 6 mm. The small size, variable anatomy, and proximity to vessels and soft-tissue lesions make imaging of such nerves particularly challenging at routine MRI. The authors focus on MRN of fine-caliber nerves throughout the body, offering technical guidance and case-based examples for practical applications. The MRN protocol should include high-resolution two-dimensional and three-dimensional (3D) isotropic acquisitions, with a tailored field of view and appropriate coil selection. Vascular signal suppression is critical and can be achieved using noncontrast or contrast-enhanced techniques, such as postcontrast short τ inversion-recovery (STIR) or steady-state sequences. Sequence optimization, considering parameters like echo time, fat suppression, spatial resolution, and echo train length, is essential to improve nerve conspicuity. A structured approach to imaging and reporting the most clinically relevant fine-caliber peripheral nerves is presented, highlighting protocol suggestions, key anatomic landmarks, and common lesion sites. By applying dedicated imaging protocols with advanced 3D techniques, radiologists can enhance detection of fine-caliber nerve lesions and provide more confident imaging guidance for clinical decision making and treatment planning. ©RSNA, 2026 Supplemental material is available for this article.
42849797:
BACKGROUND: Recent randomized trials have reported conflicting results regarding the clinical benefit of intravascular imaging (IVI) in complex percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). The aim of this research was to evaluate whether IVI guidance reduces target vessel failure (TVF) in complex PCI.
METHODS: PubMed, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library were searched through June 2026 for randomized trials comparing IVI-guided with angiography-guided PCI in trial-defined complex PCI or extractable complex-lesion cohorts. Risk ratios (RRs) were pooled using random-effects models. Prespecified analyses evaluated left main, chronic total occlusion, bifurcation, and moderate-to-severely calcified lesions, with a sensitivity analysis excluding IVUS-CHIP. Secondary clinical outcomes and potential effect modification by imaging modality were evaluated in exploratory analyses.
RESULTS: Fifteen trials, including 11,557 patients were analyzed. IVI reduced TVF (RR, 0.70; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.56-0.86; number needed to treat, 26 [95% CI, 18-55]). Lesion-specific estimates consistently favored IVI but were not significant; all became significant after excluding IVUS-CHIP. IVI reduced target vessel revascularization (RR, 0.68; 95% CI, 0.53-0.87), target lesion revascularization (RR, 0.67; 95% CI, 0.52-0.85), and stent thrombosis (RR, 0.42; 95% CI, 0.24-0.73). All-cause mortality was not reduced, whereas IVI guidance showed a borderline association with 26% lower cardiovascular mortality (RR, 0.74; 95% CI, 0.54-1.00; p = 0.05). Effects were similar for intravascular ultrasound and optical coherence tomography (interaction p = 0.93).
CONCLUSIONS: IVI guidance reduced TVF, repeat revascularization, and stent thrombosis in complex PCI, with consistent but exploratory effects across major lesion subsets and a borderline association with lower cardiovascular mortality.
42849887: Vibe coding is a workflow in which users describe the desired software behavior in natural language, following which large language models (LLMs) generate the code. It is increasingly being used by non-developer clinicians without any formal programming training to create tools that support the clinical workflow. This development is both timely and consequential for radiology, one of the specialties both most exposed to artificial intelligence (AI)-driven automation and best positioned to adopt it owing to its longstanding engagement with imaging AI, digital infrastructure, and information system workflows. Therefore, radiologists may become not merely passive AI users, but also clinical workflow orchestrators. This opportunity is illustrated by a structured prostate magnetic resonance imaging reporting tool, vibe-coded by a non-developer radiologist in approximately four hours, with an institution-based voluntary, radiologist-led coding community. This investigation highlighted four cautions: erosion of domain expertise, risks to security and patient data, absence of peer feedback, and uncoordinated proliferation of tools. A minimum safeguard set for clinician-built tools was proposed. As previously framed, LLMs represent a "fire of Prometheus" for non-native English-speaking researchers. Similarly, vibe coding may warm and burn radiologists equally, with its impact determined less by technology than by how responsibly the specialty adopts it.
42849889: Voice change is an uncommon but clinically important complication of thyroid radiofrequency ablation (RFA), because it may indicate injury to the recurrent laryngeal nerve or, less commonly, the vagus nerve. Early recognition and appropriate intervention are important, because neural dysfunction may remain reversible before the occurrence of irreversible structural nerve injury. Thermal nerve injury during thyroid RFA is not always a single instantaneous event. Rather, it may involve direct thermal exposure of the nerves, leading to acute endoneurial or perineural edema, microvascular compromise, and delayed inflammation or fibrosis. Therefore, a practical approach to the management of voice changes during thyroid RFA should emphasize prevention, frequent intraprocedural voice assessment, immediate cessation of ablation, and prompt bolus injection of cold 5% dextrose in water. After adequate cooling, local dexamethasone injections and a short course of oral corticosteroid therapy may be considered. In conclusion, a mechanism-based framework may improve operator preparedness and reduce the risk of persistent nerve dysfunction.
42850761:
PURPOSE: To develop a vessel wall imaging (VWI)-dedicated image restoration model enabling high-resolution whole-brain VWI in under 6 min.
METHODS: A transformer-based 2.5D model was trained in a supervised manner to enhance the image quality of CAIPIRINHA 2 × 2-accelerated VWI acquisitions to a level comparable to that of GRAPPA twofold-accelerated scans. The majority of k-space data used for training and testing were acquired on a Siemens 3 T system equipped with a standard 20-channel head-neck coil. Region-of-interest fine-tuning and slice-to-volume reconstruction were devised to balance global structural fidelity with local vascular precision and 3D continuity. Model performance was evaluated both quantitatively and qualitatively through single-center retrospective testing and prospective testing in multi-center, generalized settings. Integration of the model into the vendor's inline image reconstruction pipeline was also investigated.
RESULTS: Compared with the input images, model outputs improved peak SNR by more than 7 dB and structural similarity index measure by 0.19 in the retrospective test set. When applied to CAIPIRINHA fourfold-accelerated data that otherwise underwent offline or inline GRAPPA reconstruction, the model significantly enhanced vessel wall SNR, wall-to-lumen CNR, wall-to-cerebrospinal fluid CNR, and image quality scores. These improvements were sustained in an independent cohort from different institutions and reproduced in a dataset acquired with smaller field of view and a 64-channel coil, supporting the model's robustness and generalizability.
CONCLUSION: The proposed inline-integrable image restoration model enables clinically viable whole-brain VWI in under 6 min using standard 20-channel coils, offering a practical approach to improve patient throughput without compromising diagnostic quality.
42851072: ObjectivesThe American College of Radiology Thyroid Imaging Reporting and Data System (ACR TI-RADS) provides a standardized framework for thyroid nodule risk stratification based on predefined ultrasound features. This study aimed to evaluate the accuracy and robustness of ChatGPT-5.6 Sol in extracting and scoring ACR TI-RADS features and classifying thyroid nodules from synthetic free-text ultrasound reports.MethodsA primary dataset of 100 synthetic thyroid ultrasound reports was constructed, with each report describing 1 nodule and the 5 ACR TI-RADS feature categories. ChatGPT-5.6 Sol was evaluated using a structured prompting strategy for feature identification, feature scoring, total score calculation, and final Thyroid Imaging Reporting and Data System classification. A less-directive prompt was also tested for total score calculation and final classification. Robustness was further assessed using a 30-case synthetic challenge set balanced across TR1 to TR5. Outputs were compared with reference annotations based on the 2017 ACR TI-RADS criteria. Accuracy was reported with Wilson 95% confidence intervals, and final-category agreement was assessed using Cohen's kappa.ResultsIn the primary dataset, accuracy for both feature identification and scoring was 100.0% for each ACR TI-RADS feature category (100/100; 95% confidence interval: 96.3%-100.0%). Total score calculation and final classification were also correct in all cases (100/100; 95% confidence interval: 96.3%-100.0%), with a Cohen's κ of 1.000. In the challenge set, feature identification, feature scoring, total score calculation, and final classification were correct in all 30 cases (30/30; 95% confidence interval: 88.6%-100.0%), with a Cohen's κ of 1.000. The less-directive prompt produced identical total score and classification accuracy in both datasets, with no discordant cases.ConclusionsChatGPT-5.6 Sol demonstrated high accuracy and consistent ACR TI-RADS-based classification across both synthetic datasets. Large language models may have potential for standardized Thyroid Imaging Reporting and Data System interpretation of free-text ultrasound reports; however, further validation in larger and more diverse settings is needed to establish generalizability.
42852505:
BACKGROUND: Hypothermia reduces ischemic injury in preclinical stroke models, yet translation into the clinical setting remains challenging. We aimed to assess the feasibility of inducing adjuvant systemic hypothermia among patients with large-vessel occlusion stroke during mechanical thrombectomy.
METHODS: This was a phase II randomized feasibility-controlled trial involving 10 sites in the United States, conducted between May 2019 and May 2024. All eligible patients had confirmed proximal middle cerebral artery or internal carotid artery occlusions, an Alberta Stroke Program Early Computed Tomography Score of 6 to 10, and symptom onset within 24 hours. Patients underwent mechanical thrombectomy and were randomly assigned to either treatment with adjuvant hypothermia using a novel intravascular cooling catheter or standard of care. The primary feasibility end points were the ability to achieve a target temperature of <34 °C within 1 hour of arterial puncture and overall door-to-reperfusion times. The primary safety end point was core-laboratory-adjudicated hemorrhagic conversion within 36 hours, and secondary end points included final infarct volume and serious adverse events.
RESULTS: A total of 95 patients were enrolled (29 in the roll-in phase and 66 randomized). The mean age of the randomized cohort was 65±12 years, with a median National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale score of 15. Among patients in the treatment arm, 30 of 33 (91%) achieved hypothermia within 1 hour of arterial puncture during thrombectomy, and 23 of 33 (70%) patients were at target temperature (<34 °C) before reperfusion. The median time to hypothermia was 10 minutes (interquartile range [IQR], 7-22) from arterial puncture. There were no significant differences in door-to-reperfusion times (hypothermia: 95 minutes [IQR, 54-116] versus control: 94 minutes [IQR, 77-121]; P=0.70). Final infarct volumes were numerically lower in the hypothermia treatment arm (hypothermia: 11 cm3 [IQR, 5-42] versus control: 30 cm3 [IQR, 6-80]; P=0.13), with no significant differences in the rates of hemorrhagic conversion or pneumonia. There was a higher number of serious adverse events in the hypothermia arm (45.5% versus 24.2%; P=0.12), although the trial was not powered for differences in serious adverse events or clinical efficacy.
CONCLUSIONS: This is the first clinical trial to demonstrate the feasibility of early and rapid systemic hypothermia as an adjunct therapy during mechanical thrombectomy without delaying time to reperfusion. The potential impact on infarct volumes and serious adverse events, however, warrants further investigation.
REGISTRATION: URL: https://www.clinicaltrials.gov; Unique identifier: NCT03804060.
42852923: Myocardial strain imaging enables quantification of cardiac deformation. Cardiovascular magnetic resonance imaging (CMR) is well suited for strain assessment due to the ability to image in any given plane with high spatial and contrast resolution. CMR strain measures have incremental diagnostic and prognostic utility over conventional clinical imaging parameters across disease states. Routine integration of CMR strain assessment in clinical practice has been hindered by the lack of agreement on imaging protocols and analysis methods, variability due to noise sensitivity, and a paucity of robust normative age-, sex- and ethnicity-specific reference ranges. In recognition of the expanding applications of strain techniques in clinical and research CMR, this joint SCMR/RSNA/EACVI scientific statement integrates data from original research studies, guidelines, and opinions from experts across the field to guide responsible and evidence-based utilization of CMR strain. © 2026 The Author(s). BACKGROUND: Fibrinolytic phenotypes have been implicated in postinjury pathophysiology and outcomes. While prehospital tranexamic acid (TXA) administration has demonstrated survival benefits, the interaction between TXA administration and distinct fibrinolytic profiles remains poorly defined.
METHODS: We analyzed data from a harmonized dataset combining 2 prospective trials evaluating prehospital TXA use in trauma (Prehospital Tranexamic Acid Use for Traumatic Brain Injury and the Study of Tranexamic Acid During Air and Ground Medical Prehospital Transport Trial). Patients were stratified by initial thromboelastographic (TEG) LY30 into fibrinolytic shutdown (<0.9%), hyperfibrinolysis (>3%), and physiological fibrinolysis (0.9-3%). The primary outcome was 30-day mortality. Secondary outcomes included 24-hour mortality and adverse events. Multivariable regression adjusted for TXA administration, fibrinolysis phenotypes, age, mechanism of injury, injury severity score, and shock index on presentation to the hospital.
RESULTS: Among 1,249 patients, 30-day mortality was 14.5% in the fibrinolytic shutdown group, 6.7% in the hyperfibrinolysis group, and 6.5% in the physiological fibrinolysis group. After multivariable regression, hyperfibrinolysis was associated with increased risk of death (HR 2.87; 95% CI: 1.10-7.53; p 0.03). Patients with fibrinolytic shutdown who were randomized to TXA had decreased risk of death (HR 0.32; 95% CI: 0.11-0.91; p =0.03).
CONCLUSIONS: This multitrial analysis revealed greater statistically significant differences between fibrinolytic phenotypes than analysis of each trial alone. Fibrinolytic phenotypes were independently associated with mortality. Fibrinolytic shutdown in patients randomized to receive TXA was associated with lower risk of death. These findings support the relevance of fibrinolysis profiling during early trauma care and underscore the need for larger studies to further elucidate the prognostic and therapeutic implications in trauma.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Prognostic and Epidemiological; Level III.
42853595:
BACKGROUND: Radiofrequency ablation (RFA) is a minimally invasive treatment for low-risk papillary thyroid microcarcinoma (PTMC). Although intratumoral calcification is a common feature of papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC), its impact on RFA efficacy remains unclear. We aimed to evaluate the technical feasibility, clinical outcomes, and pattern-specific course of calcification resolution with RFA for PTMC.
METHODS: This retrospective study included 258 consecutive patients with low-risk, unifocal PTMC who underwent RFA between November 2017 and August 2022. Intratumoral calcification was classified on ultrasonography as microcalcification, macrocalcification, rim calcification, or mixed calcification. The primary outcomes were technical success and calcification disappearance rates by calcification pattern. Secondary outcomes included serial volume reduction ratio (VRR), cumulative disease progression, local tumor recurrence, and complications.
RESULTS: Among 258 PTMCs, 94 had calcifications (68 microcalcifications, 12 macrocalcifications, 14 rim calcifications) and 164 had none. Mean follow-up was 53.5 ± 16.7 months. Technical success was achieved in all patients in both groups. By 18 months, mean VRR exceeded 90% in both groups, and all tumors achieved 100% VRR at the final follow-up (≥36 months). Cumulative disease progression occurred in one patient (0.4%, lymph node metastases at ipsilateral neck level IV and VI), and 15 patients (5.8%) developed new PTC in the remaining thyroid; the rates did not differ between groups. Among PTMCs with calcifications, complete disappearance of calcification occurred in 90 cases (90/94, 95.7%) after 14.2 ± 12.3 months. Disappearance rates were highest for microcalcifications (100%), followed by rim calcifications (92.9%) and macrocalcifications (75.0%). Microcalcifications were resolved significantly faster (mean, 12.0 months), whereas rim calcifications were resolved the slowest (mean, 24.8 months; p < 0.001). The solid component and calcification resolved concurrently in 75.5% of tumors. One minor complication (transient hoarseness, 0.4%) occurred, and no major or delayed complications were observed.
CONCLUSIONS: In this retrospective cohort, RFA achieved complete resolution of the viable soft-tissue component with a low complication rate in low-risk PTMC, both with and without intratumoral calcification. Technical success was achieved in 100% of tumors regardless of calcification status, and no significant difference in outcomes was observed between the calcified and noncalcified groups. These findings suggest that intratumoral calcification does not preclude effective ablation.
42855273:
BACKGROUND: Intratumoral susceptibility signals on susceptibility-weighted imaging have emerged as a potential biomarker for glioma grading and molecular characterization.
PURPOSE: To evaluate the diagnostic performance of intratumoral susceptibility signals for glioma grading using harmonized World Health Organization grade contrasts.
DATA SOURCES: PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane were searched from inception through December 18, 2025.
STUDY SELECTION: Studies reporting preoperative semiquantitative assessment of intratumoral susceptibility signals in histologically confirmed gliomas were included; grading reference standards ranged from histology-based to integrated 2021 World Health Organization histomolecular diagnosis.
DATA ANALYSIS: The primary analysis compared World Health Organization grades III-IV with grade II. Alternative contrasts were analyzed separately. Threshold-specific sensitivity and specificity were pooled when at least 3 comparable studies were available. Observed-only and leave-one-out analyses assessed robustness.
DATA SYNTHESIS: Nineteen studies including 1383 patients were included; 10 contributed to quantitative grading analyses. For World Health Organization grade III-IV versus II, pooled sensitivity and specificity were 0.96 (95% CI, 0.86-0.99) and 0.48 (0.22-0.75) at an intratumoral susceptibility signal threshold ≥1, 0.85 (0.74-0.91) and 0.93 (0.84-0.97) at threshold ≥2, and 0.72 (0.59-0.82) and 0.97 (0.93-0.99) at threshold ≥3. Molecular findings were heterogeneous and summarized descriptively, with higher intratumoral susceptibility signal burden most consistently associated with isocitrate dehydrogenase wild-type status.
LIMITATIONS: Studies were predominantly retrospective and single-center, with heterogeneous intratumoral susceptibility signal scoring, imaging protocols, and World Health Organization reference standards. Some contingency tables required reconstruction.
CONCLUSIONS: Intratumoral susceptibility signals showed threshold-dependent performance for distinguishing World Health Organization grade III-IV from grade II gliomas. Among the prespecified ordinal thresholds, a threshold ≥2 provided the most balanced sensitivity-specificity profile. Molecular evidence remains exploratory.
42855974:
OBJECTIVE: To determine the efficacy and safety of different pharmacological and non-pharmacological methods of feticide to induce fetal asystole prior to termination of pregnancy (TOP).
METHODS: MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, SCOPUS, PubMed and Cochrane Library databases were searched electronically from January 1991 to June 2025. Observational and randomized studies of feticides using pharmacological or non-pharmacological methods prior to TOP in the second or third trimester were included. The primary outcome was failure to achieve fetal asystole prior to TOP. Secondary outcomes included the total dose of feticidal agent, maternal complications and influence of feticide method on feasibility and quality of postmortem evaluation. Quality assessment of the included studies was performed using the Risk Of Bias In Non-randomized Studies of Interventions tool, Revised Cochrane Risk-of-Bias-2 tool and National Institutes of Health Quality Assessment Tools. A meta-analysis of the proportions of failed procedures was conducted using random-effects models.
RESULTS: Twenty-five studies with a total of 10 683 cases were included in the systematic review. Pooled proportions of failed procedures were 0.4% (95% CI, 0.1-2.4%) (I2 = 0%) for intracardiac potassium chloride (KCl), 3.2% (95% CI, 1.2-8.2%) (I2 = 0%) for intrafunic KCl, 4.8% (95% CI, 3.9-5.9%) (I2 = 19.0%) for intrafetal digoxin and 10.6% (95% CI, 6.4-17.1%) (I2 = 0%) for intra-amniotic digoxin. A range of doses were reported for KCl, lidocaine and digoxin by all routes of injection. There were four cases of postprocedure chorioamnionitis across all studies, but no other significant adverse events related directly to feticidal procedures. There was limited assessment of the impact of feticidal agent on postmortem examinations, but fetal intravascular lidocaine and KCl were associated consistently with cell lysis.
CONCLUSIONS: Feticide is an important procedure to induce asystole prior to TOP. Point estimates from the meta-analysis indicate that the most effective feticidal method is intracardiac KCl. Effectiveness should be considered alongside safety and feasibility when deciding on appropriate methods for different settings. © 2026 The Author(s). 42857857: A 40-year-old woman with no personal or family history of breast cancer had a right breast mass first characterized as a probable fibroadenoma on an outside MRI evaluation. A repeat MRI performed years later again described a well-circumscribed, benign-pattern (type 1) enhancing nodule assessed as Breast Imaging Reporting and Data System (BI-RADS) 3. Targeted ultrasound showed an oval, parallel-oriented, circumscribed hypoechoic mass, and an integrated artificial intelligence (AI) lesion-characterization tool returned a categorical output of benign (BI-RADS 2) based on the shape and orientation descriptors displayed on screen. However, shear-wave elastography of the same lesion showed markedly elevated stiffness (maximum elasticity 135.48 kPa), prompting the radiologist to revise the overall assessment to BI-RADS 4 and pursue ultrasound-guided tru-cut biopsy, which revealed solid, cribriform, and comedo-type high-grade (nuclear grade 3) ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) arising within a fibroadenoma. Whole-body 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG) PET/CT subsequently showed FDG uptake at the known primary site with no other avid disease, while histopathology established the diagnosis and stage. The patient underwent segmental mastectomy with sentinel lymph node biopsy; final pathology confirmed a 1.5 × 1 cm focus of high-grade DCIS entirely confined to the fibroadenoma, with clear surgical margins and no nodal involvement (pTisN0(i-,sn)). This case demonstrates that malignancy, including high-grade DCIS, can arise within an otherwise typical, long-stable fibroadenoma and can retain a benign morphological profile on B-mode ultrasound and AI-assisted shape-based classification. Quantitative elastographic stiffness discordant with a benign shape classification should not be dismissed and warrants biopsy. Multiparametric correlation, combining morphologic assessment with quantitative elastography, remains essential and should not be superseded by a single shape-based descriptor, human or algorithmic. Ultimately, in this case, only tissue sampling provided a clear and definitive diagnosis, underscoring that biopsy should not be deferred when a breast mass is reassessed after a long interval or shows any feature discordant with a straightforward fibroadenoma.
42858633:
PURPOSE: To systematically review MRI-derived radiomic and artificial intelligence models predicting outcomes in men on or eligible for active surveillance (AS) for prostate cancer, and whether reported endpoints permit quantitative synthesis.
METHOD: Following PRISMA 2020, we searched PubMed, Scopus, Embase, and Web of Science (2000-September 2026). Two reviewers independently screened, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias (QUADAS-2, PROBAST) and methodological quality (METRICS). Three subgroups were defined: AS selection at diagnosis, baseline detection of clinically significant cancer, and progression during follow-up. Pooling was pre-specified for subgroups with at least four independent cohorts; endpoint equivalence was assessed.
RESULTS: Seventeen studies across 12 unique cohorts were included. Seven publications derived from two cohorts; 12 independent cohort-level estimates (n = 2703) remained after overlap resolution. Nine publications (four independent cohorts) addressed progression (AUC 0.70 to 0.95), but progression was defined in five non-equivalent ways, from any grade-group increase to composite core-count criteria, precluding quantitative synthesis. Risk of bias was high or unclear in 16 of 17 studies; the median METRICS score was 32.3 % (range 18.9-52.3 %). No study reported external validation or calibration for progression.
CONCLUSIONS: Progression endpoints were heterogeneous and several were of limited clinical relevance. A core outcome set for AS (at least ISUP grade group ≥3 and/or unequivocal radiological progression), followed by multi-centre external validation with a head-to-head comparison against the PRECISE v2 (Prostate Cancer Radiological Estimation of Change in Sequential Evaluation) score, is the priority before clinical use can be considered.
42858876:
OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the association between uterine synechiae identified on ultrasound and adverse pregnancy outcomes through a systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies.
DATA SOURCES: A systematic search of PubMed, Cochrane Library, CINAHL and ScienceDirect was performed from database inception to July 2025 in accordance with MOOSE guidelines.
STUDY ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA: Cohort and case-control studies reporting pregnancy outcomes among women with versus without uterine synechiae were eligible.
STUDY APPRAISAL AND SYNTHESIS METHODS: Two reviewers independently screened studies, extracted data and assessed quality using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. Random-effects models were used to calculate pooled odds ratios and mean differences for maternal and neonatal outcomes.
RESULTS: Four studies met inclusion criteria, comprising 628 pregnancies with uterine synechiae and 65,959 controls. Uterine synechiae were associated with an increased risk of preterm birth <37 weeks (odds ratio 1.80; 95% CI: 1.35-2.39), preterm premature rupture of membranes (odds ratio 3.58; 95% CI: 1.13-11.36), placental abruption (odds ratio 3.34; 95% CI: 1.57-7.13) and placenta previa (odds ratio 3.19; 95% CI: 1.07-9.57). Mean birth weight was significantly lower among affected pregnancies (mean difference -154.29 g; 95% CI: -259.20 to -49.38). No significant differences were observed for preterm birth <34 weeks, overall cesarean delivery, fetal growth restriction, stillbirth or NICU admission. A subgroup analysis demonstrated higher odds of cesarean delivery for fetal malpresentation in pregnancies with synechiae (odds ratio 1.97; 95% CI: 1.23-3.13).
CONCLUSIONS: Uterine synechiae identified on ultrasound are associated with increased risks of preterm birth, PPROM, placental abruption, placenta previa and fetal malpresentation, as well as lower birth weight. These findings indicate that synechiae are not incidental findings and support their association with adverse outcomes in pregnancy.
42860134: The DNA code represents a genetic instruction as to how the human body develops and works. A 'spelling mistake' in the DNA code of the developing fetus can lead to a single gene condition. Examples of single-gene conditions include cystic fibrosis, sickle cell disease and Huntington's disease. Single gene conditions collectively affect 1 in 100 births and can be inherited from one or both parents, or can occur without any family history, arising spontaneously out of a one-off change (pathogenic variant) in a known gene. Sometimes there can be specific anomalies seen on the ultrasound scan that suggest this. Autosomal dominant inheritance is where a parent has the spelling mistake in their DNA and there is then a 1 in 2 (50%) chance that the baby will inherit the condition. Alternatively, both parents may be carriers of the spelling mistake within their DNA code but do not themselves have the condition (autosomal recessive inheritance), in which case there is then a 1 in 4 (25%) chance of having a baby with that condition. There are also X-linked (sex-linked) conditions where usually only boys can inherit the condition, while girls can be carriers. Traditionally, when embarking on a pregnancy where there is a risk of a baby being affected with a genetic condition, invasive testing using amniocentesis (via a needle through the mother's abdomen to take a sample of amniotic fluid from around the baby) or chorionic villus sampling (via a needle through the mother's abdomen to take a sample from the placenta) is offered to the parents to obtain a sample of DNA from the baby to test for the condition. However, these tests are invasive involving a needle going into the womb and can carry a small miscarriage risk of around 1 in 200. It is now known that DNA from the placenta (which represents the DNA in the baby) circulates in the mother's blood from early pregnancy. This is known as cell-free fetal DNA (cffDNA) and so is a potential source of genetic material that can be used to test the baby for selected genetic conditions. Discovery of cffDNA in the mother's blood now allows for testing for genetic conditions as early as the 8th week of pregnancy, commonly referred to as non-invasive prenatal diagnosis (NIPD). Its use has evolved in clinical practice from 2011 when it was originally developed to screen for common chromosome differences such as Down, Edwards and Patau syndromes and for this purpose is referred to as non-invasive prenatal screening or testing (NIPS/T). While the acronym of 'NIPD' is similar to 'NIPS/T' it is important to be clear that these test for different things, can be a screening or a diagnostic test and use different technological approaches. The mother's own cell-free DNA (cfDNA) will also be present in the sample and must be distinguished from that of her developing fetus. NIPD is currently available in the UK through the National Health Service (NHS) for some limited scenarios, for example, where parent(s) have already had a baby affected by a condition, or to test for specific conditions where there are differences detected on an ultrasound scan that suggest certain conditions. This testing can be performed on a blood sample taken from the mother any time from 8 weeks of gestation, i.e. earlier than invasive testing and with no risk. If the condition being tested for is already known because of family history, this test is considered diagnostic and no further testing for confirmation is required.
42860463:
PURPOSE: Iodine-131 (I-131) thyroid ablation is strictly contraindicated during pregnancy due to the risk of fetal thyroid damage after 10 weeks of gestation. Current society guidelines lack consistency regarding the best timing and method for pregnancy testing. This review aims to consolidate current recommendations and propose a standardized testing algorithm.
METHODS: A literature review was conducted using the PubMed/MEDLINE database over a 55-year period to identify peer-reviewed publications on professional society guidelines for pre-radioiodine therapy pregnancy testing, as well as performance characteristics of serum and urine pregnancy tests.
RESULTS: Fetal susceptibility to radioiodine begins around 8-10 weeks of gestation. While serum hCG tests are approximately 2.5 times more sensitive than standard urine tests, they still have a "biological window" during which early pregnancy might be undetectable. Current guidelines differ on testing timelines, ranging from 24 to 72 h before therapy.
CONCLUSION: Patients should be advised to abstain from sexual activity for at least two weeks before therapy and provide a written attestation on the day of treatment confirming they completed this abstinence period. Serum pregnancy testing is preferred because of its higher sensitivity and should be performed within 72 h prior to therapy, ideally within 24 h.
42861192:
BACKGROUND: Preoperative assessment of muscle invasion in bladder cancer using the Vesical Imaging-Reporting and Data System (VI-RADS) relies heavily on diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI), but conventional single-shot echo-planar imaging diffusion-weighted imaging (ss-EPI-DWI) may be limited by image distortion and artifacts, potentially affecting interobserver agreement. Zoomed diffusion-weighted imaging without parallel transmission technology (non-pTx zoomed-DWI) may improve image quality. This study aimed to compare the interobserver agreement of non-pTx zoomed-DWI versus conventional ss-EPI-DWI for ordinal biparametric VI-RADS-based scoring in bladder cancer lesions ≥1 cm across different morphological types among radiologists with varying levels of experience.
METHODS: This retrospective single-center study included patients with pathologically confirmed bladder cancer who underwent preoperative biparametric magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), including T2-weighted imaging (T2WI), conventional ss-EPI-DWI, and non-pTx zoomed-DWI, before transurethral resection of bladder tumor or radical cystectomy. Three radiologists independently assigned ordinal biparametric VI-RADS-based F-scores from 1 to 5 for each eligible lesion using ss-EPI-DWI and non-pTx zoomed-DWI datasets separately. T2WI was used for lesion localization and morphological classification, whereas the corresponding DWI sequence, including high-b-value DWI images and apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) maps, was used to assign ordinal biparametric VI-RADS-based F-scores according to the standard VI-RADS scoring criteria. Subjective image quality was rated on a 4-point scale. Interobserver agreement was assessed using linear weighted kappa statistics with 95% confidence intervals.
RESULTS: A total of 162 patients (138 males, 24 females; median age 67 years) with 214 eligible bladder cancer lesions were included. Non-pTx zoomed-DWI provided significantly higher subjective image quality scores than ss-EPI-DWI for both readers (P<0.001). Based on the original ordinal VI-RADS-based F-scores, overall pairwise interobserver agreement was good with ss-EPI-DWI (linear weighted κ=0.708-0.761) and excellent with non-pTx zoomed-DWI (linear weighted κ=0.851-0.870). In morphology-specific analyses, agreement also improved with non-pTx zoomed-DWI across lesion subgroups. The improvement was particularly evident in broad-based nodules, for which agreement increased from good with ss-EPI-DWI (κ=0.700-0.752) to excellent with non-pTx zoomed-DWI (κ=0.892-0.919), and in nodules with pedicles, for which agreement improved from moderate-to-good (κ=0.535-0.640) to good-to-excellent (κ=0.786-0.847).
CONCLUSIONS: Non-pTx zoomed-DWI improved subjective image quality and interobserver agreement for ordinal biparametric VI-RADS-based scoring in bladder cancer lesions ≥1 cm compared with conventional ss-EPI-DWI. These findings suggest that non-pTx zoomed-DWI may support more consistent MRI-based assessment of muscle invasion risk, particularly in morphologically complex lesions. Further prospective studies with lesion-level pathological correlation are needed to determine whether improved agreement translates into improved diagnostic accuracy.
42861924:
BACKGROUND: The operational definition and imaging assessment of the no-reflow phenomenon, a potential contributor to poor clinical outcome despite successful thrombectomy, remains debated. We aimed to develop expert-based international consensus on the definition, assessment, and reporting standard of cerebral no-reflow post-thrombectomy.
METHODS: Three-rounds of a modified Delphi web-based survey was conducted among corresponding authors of peer-reviewed clinical studies on cerebral no-reflow between 2020 and 2025. Responses at each round were used to develop structured questionnaires for subsequent rounds. Consensus was predefined as ≥65% agreement.
RESULTS: Among 27 panelists, the response rate was 70%, 74%, and 74% over all rounds. There was broad agreement to conceptualize no-reflow as macrovascular recanalization with impaired microvascular reperfusion. Consensus was reached that macrovascular recanalization is ideally assessed as (1) digital subtraction angiography with expanded thrombolysis in cerebral infarction (eTICI) grades 2c without clear distal vessel occlusions and/or eTICI 3 only, and (2) absence of a wedge-shaped time-to-maximum (Tmax) or time-to-peak (TTP) delay on post-recanalization perfusion computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Regarding impaired microvascular reperfusion assessment, cerebral blood flow, and/or volume were preferred over time-based perfusion parameters (Tmax/TTP). The panel expressed a preference that no-reflow should ideally be assessed ≤6 hours post-recanalization. Pending formal validation, histopathological-radiological correlation in animal models would sufficiently validate the use of imaging-based definitions in humans.
INTERPRETATION: Based on currently available literature and expert opinions, this Delphi study provides a framework for systematically reporting cerebral no-reflow after endovascular treatment (EVT). The variability in opinions regarding quantitative thresholds highlights priorities for future methodological standardization and validation studies. ANN NEUROL 2026.
42862319: Periprosthetic sarcomas associated with total hip arthroplasty (THA) are exceedingly rare, and most reported cases represent undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma or osteosarcoma. Primary leiomyosarcoma of bone is also an uncommon malignancy, accounting for less than 1% of primary malignant bone tumors. The occurrence of primary leiomyosarcoma adjacent to an orthopedic implant is therefore exceptionally rare. A 69-year-old woman presented with progressive left thigh pain 13 years after THA. Radiographs demonstrated osteolysis and cortical thinning at the distal femoral stem. Computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed an intramedullary lesion with cortical thinning and contrast enhancement. 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography-CT showed increased uptake at the lesion (SUV max, 11.9), without evidence of other primary tumors. The differential diagnoses included implant-related osteolysis, infection, metastatic tumor, and primary bone tumor. An open biopsy was performed, and a diagnosis of pleomorphic sarcoma was made. Wide resection with proximal femoral replacement was performed. Histopathological examination established the diagnosis of primary leiomyosarcoma of bone. Prominent lymphocytic infiltration and immunohistochemical findings, including p53 overexpression and partial loss of Rb expression, within the tumor, raise the possibility of chronic inflammation and associated molecular alterations as theoretical contributing factors to tumorigenesis. Periprosthetic sarcomas can mimic more common postoperative complications, making diagnosis challenging. Delayed diagnosis may adversely affect prognosis. This case highlights the importance of considering malignancy in atypical periprosthetic lesions and underscores the role of multimodality imaging and biopsy in achieving an accurate diagnosis.
42862457: This systematic review evaluates evidence on artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) models for prediction and diagnosis of fetal growth restriction (FGR). The authors searched PubMed, Scopus, Embase, Web of Science, and Google Scholar, through June 2026 following PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Studies on AI/ML-based prediction or diagnosis techniques for FGR, Intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) or Small for gestational age (SGA) fetuses. The prediction model risk of bias assessment Tool (PROBAST) was used to perform data extraction and risk of bias assessment. Twenty-seven studies were eligible for inclusion. AI applications were biophysical (n = 10), Doppler-based (n = 10), clinical (n = 7), ultrasound (n = 7), MRI (n = 7), radiomics imaging (n = 10), cardiotocography (n = 10), genomics (n = 10), and metabolomics-based biomarker models (n = 10). The model performance was good, with area under the receiver operating characteristic curves (AUC) of 0.71-0.91 and classification accuracies of 78.9-93.3%. Imaging and multimodal data-based models showed the highest predictive performance. The PROBAST assessment showed that the risk of bias was low for the participant, predictor and outcome domains, but the analytical domain raised methodological concerns; nine studies were low risk, 14 moderate and 4 high. The AI and ML models for FGR detection performed promisingly. Multimodal approaches that combine clinical, imaging and molecular data consistently outperform single modality models and constitute a major advance in precision obstetrics. However, there remains substantial heterogeneity, limited external validation and methodological issues. Future prospective multicenter studies, standardized reporting, and real-world implementation research are needed for routine clinical adoption.
42863451:
BACKGROUND: Computed tomography (CT) is vital in diagnostic imaging but involves ionizing radiation, requiring careful dose management. Diagnostic Reference Levels (DRLs), recommended by the International Commission on Radiological Protection (ICRP), serve as benchmarks for optimizing radiation doses and improving patient safety. While many DRL studies exist, most focus on individual countries, anatomical regions, or clinical indications, limiting broader applicability. This systematic review addresses this gap by analyzing adult CT DRLs across continents and major anatomical areas. It compares international benchmarks, highlights methodological inconsistencies, and explores drivers of regional variability to inform global dose optimization.
METHODS: Following PRISMA-S guidelines, a systematic search of PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and Embase identified studies published in English from 2018 to 2025. Keywords related to DRLs and CT imaging were used. Studies reporting DRLs for adult CT using standardized dose metrics were included. Pediatric studies, narrative reviews, Phantom studies, case reports, pilot studies, and gray literature were excluded.
RESULTS: Of 2719 identified articles, 63 met the inclusion criteria. Local DRLs were reported in 48 % of studies, and national DRLs in 52 %. Substantial variability was observed across examination types and geographical regions. For head CT, CTDIvol values ranged from 38.2 to 117.6 mGy, while DLP values ranged from 512 to 1943 mGy·cm across the included studies. Similar variability was observed for other examination categories, which may reflect differences in patient characteristics, equipment, and imaging protocols.
CONCLUSION: This systematic review identified substantial international variability in DRLs for adult CT examinations, associated with differences in imaging practices, patient characteristics, available technology, and methodological approaches to DRL establishment. The 75th percentile was the most commonly used method for defining DRLs across the included studies. These findings support regular DRL review and greater methodological standardization to improve comparability across regions and strengthen CT dose optimization practices.
42864519:
OBJECTIVE: We wanted to investigate and compare the reliability of two measuring methods for glenoid bone loss, one linear- and one surface area method, in acute glenoid fractures after dislocation. This was an experimental study.
METHOD: Thirty CT-shoulder scans in patients with an acute glenoid rim fracture were measured in a lateral"en face" view in 2D and 3D by two independent assessors. In 10 of 30 patients contralateral shoulder CT-scan was obtained for reference circle placement. Intra- and interrater reliability was analysed by Intra Class Correlation. Wilcoxon signed rank test was performed for comparison of bone loss estimates between methods.
RESULTS: The reliability ranged from 0.85 to 0.97 for the two methods in both 2D and 3D, which is considered good to excellent. The bone loss estimates were significantly larger with linear method than area method. Drawing of a best-fitting-circle had a good reliability between assessors.
CONCLUSIONS: Linear- and surface area methods demonstrated comparable reliability in assessing glenoid bone loss in acute fractures and we found no difference between 2D- and 3D-modalities. However, linear methods may overestimate defect in cases with irregular fracture lines, suggesting area method may be preferable in acute fractures.
42864584: The increased utility of quantitative metrics in medical imaging has prompted the use of colour representation of the data. Colour schemes for image display can highlight pathology and distinguish normal anatomy, thus potentially aiding image interpretation. Adding colour schemes to images may serve the sole purpose of visualising an abnormality or may seek to represent and meaningfully convey a quantitative metric. An early use of colour representation is exemplified by colour Doppler in ultrasound (US), where a two-sided linear scale is commonly applied. More recently, many schemes have arisen, ranging from a single colour to depict a segmented region to a range of colours that embrace the entire colour spectrum. These may be applied as continuous or discrete palettes, depending on the software vendor or even on individual user settings. The lack of standardisation of colour schemes across the medical community, especially in medical imaging, risks misinterpretation of quantitative data and potential unintended negative clinical consequences. The purpose of this article is to review the colour schemes used for quantitative imaging across US, computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and positron emission tomography (PET), the way in which they are applied, the clinical applications where their use is desirable for enhanced interpretation, and the pitfalls where standardisation is lacking in a variety of clinical applications. Finally, we discuss some solutions that could be employed to enable standardisation and augment the use of colour in image interpretation. KEY POINTS: Question Colour schemes in medical imaging can highlight pathology, but standardisation is lacking for most imaging modalities, thus risking misinterpretation of quantitative data. Findings For T1, T2, and T2* maps and their inverses, colour map recommendations have recently been proposed, but are mostly lacking for other quantitative data. Critical relevance statement Standardised colour maps can enhance data analyses across scanners and institutions, which is important for multicentre studies and handling big data. Furthermore, standardised and harmonised colour maps could improve lesion conspicuity, cross-platform comparability, and longitudinal reliability.
42865020:
OBJECTIVES: Prophylactic inguinal node irradiation (PINI) is standard in chemoradiotherapy for anal squamous cell carcinoma. However, PINI increases toxicity, including bowel and sexual dysfunction, bone marrow suppression, and lymphoedema. Evidence on inguinal node relapse risk without PINI remains limited, warranting systematic review.
METHODS: A systematic literature review was performed in accordance with the PRISMA standards using Scopus, Embase, Cochrane Library, and Pubmed for relevant studies between 1980 and 2025. Studies of >10 patients treated with chemoradiotherapy without PINI and a minimum FU of 24 months were included. Data on stage, recurrence, staging investigations, and radiotherapy technique was extracted and analyzed.
RESULTS: Nine articles were identified satisfying predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria, included 727 patients. All 9 reported individual outcomes for stages grouped as T1/2 and T3/4, 6 articles detailed outcomes for individual stages. The pooled estimated risk of lymph node relapse in T1/2 patients is 8.0% (95% CI, 6.0-10.6). The pooled analysis for T1 and T2 tumors, respectively, were 2.20% (95% CI, 0.5-8.3) and 8.7 (95% CI, 5.4-13.7).
CONCLUSIONS: The quantification of inguinal relapse rates supports existing clinical practice that in selected patients, with T1 tumors or the frail and co-morbid population, it may be appropriate to omit PINI.
ADVANCES IN KNOWLEDGE: Following the recently published ACT4 study, suggesting that reduction of dose does not reduce morbidity, this research suggests that exclusion of inguinal nodes in early-stage tumors may be an alternative strategy and should be investigated further in clinical trials.
42867374: Women with extremely dense breasts have an increased risk of breast cancer but also a decreased sensitivity of mammography. The Dense Tissue and Early Breast Neoplasm Screening (DENSE) trial, initiated in 2011, showed that supplemental full-protocol MRI screening reduced the number of interval cancers in women with extremely dense breasts. Cost-effective screening scenarios have been described, but imaging costs and capacity remain barriers to implementing full-protocol MRI in population-based breast cancer screening programs. Therefore, the DENSE-2 trial was set up to investigate two alternate screening techniques, contrast-enhanced mammography (CEM) or abbreviated MRI (AB-MRI), that are expected to be cheaper and to make more efficient use of the available capacity while potentially achieving similar results to full-protocol MRI. DENSE-2 is a multicenter randomized controlled trial embedded in the Dutch screening program. It comprises two consecutive screening rounds in which women receive the same breast imaging technique both times. The trial investigates the value of supplemental screening with CEM or AB-MRI in women with extremely dense breasts with a negative screening mammogram. The primary aim is to determine whether these methods will lead to a reduction of interval cancers compared with mammography. The DENSE-2 trial results will provide insights into the performance, feasibility, and acceptability of both screening modalities, enable long-term outcome modeling, and support decision-making on the most appropriate screening strategy for women with extremely dense breasts. ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT06636370 © RSNA, 2026 Supplemental material is available for this article. See also the editorial by Bahl in this issue.
42867514:
OBJECTIVES: The introduction of improved multi-agent systemic therapies has made restaging and treatment response assessment in patients with localized pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) increasingly complex. This scoping review aims to assess and compare methods for local disease restaging and treatment response assessment in localized PDAC, with a focus on their association with resectability, overall survival (OS), and R0-resection rates.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: This scoping review included studies on restaging in patients with PDAC following systemic therapy using CT and PET/CT from MEDLINE, Embase, and CENTRAL.
RESULTS: Among 4680 identified studies, 20 fulfilled the eligibility criteria. Most (n = 15) studies analyzed CT, and 5 analyzed PET/CT. Groups of restaging methods included new response categories, size-based metrics, volume, vascular contact, tumor attenuation, fluorine-18 fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG) PET/CT derived metabolic parameters, and resectability criteria. Dual-energy CT-derived extracellular volume (DECT-ECV) was evaluated as a baseline predictive biomarker. Associations between restaging methods and outcomes were reported inconsistently: some studies found significant associations for specific methods, whereas others did not. No restaging method showed a consistent association with both R0-resection and survival across all studies.
CONCLUSION: Restaging of localized PDAC after systemic treatment remains challenging due to the limited accuracy of RECIST 1.1, particularly for the classifications partial response and stable disease. The current evidence suggests that integrating additional imaging features, alternative imaging modalities, and the biomarker carbohydrate antigen (CA)19-9 may improve the assessment of resectability and prognosis. These findings support a future version of RECIST 1.1 to alert clinicians to this issue.
KEY POINTS: Question How effective are current (PET/)CT-based restaging methods in assessing local disease resectability and prognosis in localized PDAC after modern multi-agent systemic therapy? Findings Current restaging methods show inconsistent association with R0-resection and survival; RECIST 1.1 is particularly limited for the assessment of partial response and stable disease. Clinical relevance Current evidence confirms a need to integrate additional imaging features and the biomarker CA19-9, during restaging in patients with localized pancreatic cancer after modern systemic therapy to improve accuracy and reduce the risk of missed treatment options.
42867515:
OBJECTIVES: Silent vertebral fractures are common but under-recognised. We aimed to estimate the prevalence in an asymptomatic population and to identify demographic and clinical predictors using the UK Biobank data.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: DXA spine images from 2446 asymptomatic UK Biobank participants aged 40-79 years were analysed retrospectively. Vertebral fractures were defined as moderate or severe deformities (≥ 25% vertebral height loss). Fractures were identified using an artificial-intelligence-assisted six-point morphometric algorithm with manual correction and radiologist confirmation. Associations with age, sex, bone mineral density (BMD), body mass index (BMI), medication, and back pain were analysed.
RESULTS: A total of 2446 participants (mean age 62.0 ± 7.4 years; 1151 men) were analysed. Moderate or severe vertebral fractures were identified in 356 participants (14.6%). Prevalence increased with age, from 9.4% in participants aged 40-49 years to 19.6% in those aged 70-79 years. Fractures were more common in men than women (18.8% vs. 10.8%; adjusted OR 0.51 for women vs. men, 95% CI 0.40-0.66; p < 0.001). BMD and most conventional clinical risk factors had limited predictive value.
CONCLUSIONS: Silent vertebral fractures are common in midlife, frequently occur in individuals with normal bone density, and are more prevalent in men. Conventional clinical risk factors have a limited ability to identify affected individuals.
KEY POINTS: Question Silent vertebral fractures are frequently overlooked in asymptomatic individuals, and their prevalence and demographic distribution in middle-aged adults are not well-characterised. Findings In a large asymptomatic cohort, vertebral fractures were common, showed male predominance, and were frequently present in individuals without low bone mineral density or recognised clinical risk factors. Clinical relevance Silent vertebral fractures are prevalent in asymptomatic adults and are poorly captured by conventional risk assessment, indicating limitations of current approaches to fracture identification.
42869091: This is an update on the European Federation of Societies for Ultrasound in Medicine and Biology (EFSUMB) contrast enhanced ultrasound (CEUS) non-hepatic applications guidelines, which were last updated in 2017. There has been consolidation of some of the previous applications, particularly, renal and urology, which are now part of routine clinical practice. The highest number of publications and areas of research interest have been in the use of CEUS in bowel, endoscopic ultrasound, and neurosonology. A few novel applications have also been tried and show promise, such as in the parathyroids and salivary glands, while there are a few areas that have previously been researched relatively extensively but are yet to find their clinical utility. Nonetheless, the use of CEUS and its applications has been steadily growing. It is timely that there has been another update on these guidelines which come, as usual, with recommendations on CEUS use from an expert panel.
42869316:
BACKGROUND: The glymphatic system, a perivascular pathway supporting cerebrospinal and interstitial fluid exchange and clearance, has been implicated in neurodegenerative and psychiatric disorders. Diffusion tensor imaging along the perivascular space (DTI-ALPS) provides a non-invasive proxy for glymphatic-related processes, yet its role in psychiatric conditions remains uncertain.
METHODS: Following PRISMA guidelines, we systematically searched PubMed, PsycNET, and Embase for articles published up to September 25th, 2025. The protocol was pre-registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251155430). Studies reporting diffusion-based indices of glymphatic function in psychiatric populations were included. Standardised mean differences (Hedges' g) were calculated for patient-control comparisons and pooled using random-effects models. Heterogeneity, methodological moderators, and risk of bias were assessed.
RESULTS: Thirty-two studies met inclusion criteria for the systematic review, covering major psychiatric groups including mood disorders, autism spectrum disorder, ADHD, psychosis, sleep disorders, and substance-related conditions. Twenty-four studies (n = 2855; 1503 patients, 1352 controls) reporting bilateral DTI-ALPS measures were included in the meta-analysis. The pooled random-effects model revealed a significant transdiagnostic reduction in DTI-ALPS index in psychiatric populations compared with healthy controls (Hedges' g = -0.78, 95% CI -1.01 to -0.55, p < 0.0001). Between-study heterogeneity was substantial (I² = 86.3%), and there was evidence of small-study effects.
CONCLUSIONS: Bilateral DTI-ALPS index showed a robust but heterogeneous reduction across psychiatric disorders. These results suggest that impairments of perivascular diffusion, as indexed by DTI-ALPS, may reflect a shared transdiagnostic pattern across psychiatric conditions. Harmonised imaging pipelines and multimodal validation are needed to clarify the biological and clinical significance of these findings.
42870064: Cuboid-navicular coalitions are an exceptionally rare form of tarsal coalitions, representing less than 1% of all tarsal coalitions. Although tarsal coalitions classically become symptomatic during adolescence, cuboid-navicular coalitions may remain clinically silent until adulthood and can present with nonspecific chronic midfoot or hindfoot pain. We present a rare case of bilateral cuboid-navicular coalitions in a 42-year-old man with progressive bilateral midfoot pain, associated degenerative hindfoot and midfoot changes, and bilateral peroneal tendon pathology. Initial management consisted of orthotics, bracing, and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, but symptoms progressed over 8 years. Cross-sectional imaging demonstrated bilateral cuboid-navicular coalitions, progressive degenerative changes, and high-grade right peroneus longus tear. The patient underwent excision of the right cuboid-navicular coalition, excision of the right lateral calcaneal tubercle with inferior peroneal retinacular release, and debridement and repair of the right peroneus longus and brevis tendons. This case highlights the importance of considering rare tarsal coalitions in adults with chronic nonspecific midfoot pain and emphasizes the value of MRI and CT for diagnosis, characterization of associated pathology, and operative planning.
42874424:
BACKGROUND: Recent studies have suggested that intracranial aneurysms (IAs) may be a common arterial manifestation of Loeys-Dietz syndrome (LDS). However, the prevalence, characteristics, and treatment strategies remain unclear because of limited and fragmented evidence.
METHODS: We searched PubMed and Scopus through April 2026. Inclusion criteria were studies reporting epidemiological characteristics or surgical interventions of LDS-associated IAs. Studies with high risk of bias according to an adapted Newcastle-Ottawa Scale were excluded from the meta-analysis. Prevalence and risk factors of harboring IAs in patients with LDS were meta-analyzed using a random-effects model. Between-study heterogeneity was assessed by the I2 statistic. The review protocol was registered with PROSPERO (Registration ID: CRD420261374963).
RESULTS: Nine observational studies were eligible for the meta-analysis. The pooled IA prevalence was 23 % (64/282; 95 % confidence interval, 18-28 %) with low across-study heterogeneity (I2 = 6.4 %). Mean aneurysm size was 3.23 mm, and 78.1 % (50/64) of the aneurysms were saccular. Eighty-five percent (63/74) of IAs were located in the anterior circulation or the posterior communicating artery. The prevalence was significantly higher in women than in men (odds ratio, 2.49; 95 % confidence interval, 1.51-4.10, I2 = 0 %). Current smoking and prior arterial dissection were consistently associated with increased odds of harboring IAs (odds ratio > 4) across two studies. No statistically significant differences in IA prevalence were detected across pathogenic variant groups, although statistical power was limited. No rupture events were reported among 62 IAs during mean or median follow-up periods ranging from 2.0 to 8.9 years. Data about the safety and efficacy of surgical interventions were only available through case reports. A systematic review of 11 case reports, including the case presented herein, identified 16 surgically treated LDS-associated IAs. Angiographic occlusion was achieved in all 16 aneurysms, with no major complications clearly attributable to the underlying connective tissue disorder.
CONCLUSIONS: This study highlights the high prevalence and risk factors of IAs among patients with LDS. The available data do not suggest a high rupture rate in small LDS-associated IAs; however, evidence remains insufficient to define their natural history. Current management strategies are largely extrapolated from sporadic IAs and may not fully reflect LDS-specific vascular pathology.
42875479: The combination of the Internet of Things (IoT), artificial intelligence (AI), and wearable biosensors is transforming healthcare by allowing continuous, real-time monitoring and more intelligent clinical decision-making. This review explores AI-driven monitoring, smart intravenous (IV) infusion automation, and wearable biosensors, and proposes Intelligent IV Automation and Smart Patient Synchronization (INFUSYNC), a conceptual framework synchronizing monitoring, automated fluid delivery, and predictive analytics. The literature shows meaningful progress: wearables increasingly support non-contact monitoring with near clinical-grade accuracy for select parameters, while infusion pumps with dose-error-reduction and AI-assisted decision support are reported to improve delivery precision and safety. Predictive models further support early detection of physiological decline. Progress remains uneven, however: most AI-enabled infusion systems are prototype-stage, closed-loop control remains rare, and interoperability, data security, and privacy remain underdeveloped. Future systems will need compatible, security-by-design, clinically validated, feedback-controlled architectures. Overall, this review outlines a clear but early-stage trajectory toward integrated smart-health environments for IV therapy.
42875997:
BACKGROUND: Subtalar dislocation is a rare injury accounting for 1%-2% of all dislocations. Although prompt closed reduction is the accepted initial treatment, optimal conservative management protocols remain unclear, and no prior systematic review has synthesised outcomes of purely conservatively managed cases across both medial and lateral dislocations. This review aims to systematically assess the rates of post-traumatic osteoarthritis, functional outcomes, subtalar stiffness, avascular necrosis, and need for subsequent surgery following conservative management of acute isolated subtalar dislocations.
METHODS: A systematic review was conducted according to the PRISMA 2020 guidelines. PubMed, Cochrane Library, CINAHL, Web of Science and OVID were searched for studies reporting outcomes of conservatively managed acute isolated subtalar dislocations. Eligible studies included case series and cohort studies reporting radiographic or functional outcomes following closed reduction and immobilisation. Risk of bias was assessed using the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) Critical Appraisal Checklist for case series. Radiographic post-traumatic arthritis rates were pooled using random-effects meta-analysis; functional and other outcomes were synthesised narratively. Given the clinical heterogeneity of the included studies, this review adopted an exploratory descriptive framework.
RESULTS: Ten studies comprising 201 feet were included. All cases were case series (9 retrospective, 1 prospective) with mean follow-up ranging from 12 to 122 months. Medial dislocations predominated (75%-80%). Pooled radiographic post-traumatic arthritis occurred in 36% (95% CI: 18%-53%; I2 = 43%), though many patients remained functionally well despite structural changes. Functional outcomes were generally favourable for closed medial injuries, with the highest scores achieved using early mobilisation protocols. Reduced subtalar range of motion was common, affecting 42.8%-76.6% of patients where reported. Avascular necrosis was rare (0.5%) and subsequent subtalar fusion was required in only 4.2% of cases. Lateral dislocations had significantly worse outcomes than medial injuries.
CONCLUSION: Radiographic post-traumatic arthritis is common following conservative management of subtalar dislocations (36%) but was frequently not associated with functional impairment; favourable functional outcomes were achieved for closed medial injuries, although symptom severity was inconsistently reported across studies. Avascular necrosis is rare. Lateral dislocations consistently have poorer prognoses.
42878808: Prostate-specific antigen (PSA)-based screening for prostate cancer (PCa) remains controversial due to uncertain long-term benefits, overdiagnosis, and overtreatment of indolent disease. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) has transformed the diagnostic pathway of PCa and is increasingly explored as a screening tool. This special report from the ESUR Prostate MRI Working Group provides an overview of current evidence and insights into the potential role of MRI in PCa screening. MRI-based screening strategies appear to improve detection of clinically significant PCa while reducing unnecessary biopsies and diagnoses of non-significant disease, though long-term outcome data, including mortality impact and interval cancer rates, remain limited. Biparametric MRI is particularly suited for screening due to its shorter acquisition time, reduced operational complexity, and lower costs compared with multiparametric MRI. Two main implementation approaches have emerged: MRI-first pathways, which maximise detection but require substantial resources, and risk-stratified strategies, in which MRI is used after initial assessment (e.g. PSA), potentially offering greater feasibility and cost-effectiveness. Evidence from large trials supports integrating MRI into screening pathways, particularly as a reflex test after PSA screening, although uncertainties remain regarding optimal protocols, interpretation thresholds, follow-up strategies, and long-term outcomes. Key barriers include limited MRI capacity, economic considerations, and the need for standardisation and quality assurance. Advances in artificial intelligence may further enhance efficiency. Overall, MRI has the potential to improve the balance between benefits and harms in PCa screening, but further evidence is required to define its optimal implementation. KEY POINTS: Question Can prostate MRI be effectively integrated into population-based prostate cancer screening pathways? Findings MRI-based screening improves detection of csPCa while reducing unnecessary biopsies; biparametric MRI should be the protocol of choice to enhance feasibility, although optimal implementation and long-term outcomes remain uncertain. Clinical relevance MRI may overcome key limitations of PSA-based screening by enhancing the detection of clinically significant prostate cancer while reducing harms such as overdiagnosis and unnecessary biopsies.
42879296: The ureter is an important conduit between the kidney and the bladder and is frequently imaged to rule out cancer in the upper genitourinary tract. However, while malignancy can occur, a spectrum of other pathologic ureteral findings can exist, and these can be divided into congenital, intrinsic, and extrinsic abnormalities that range from postoperative and neoplastic conditions to inflammatory disease. This article provides a comprehensive overview of the ureter, including the ureteral anatomy, ureteral imaging strategies, and various ureteral conditions and their associated imaging features. It is important to identify congenital genitourinary variants, as these are frequently linked to further imaging recommendations, such as nuclear medicine renography and fluoroscopic voiding cystourethrography. Intrinsic abnormalities can be iatrogenic, infectious, inflammatory, or neoplastic. Intrinsic ureteral strictures are most commonly iatrogenic, usually resulting from prior surgery or radiation therapy. Ureteral infections include tuberculosis, schistosomiasis, and Escherichia coli infection, which have varying imaging manifestations. Inflammatory conditions include ureteritis cystica and pseudodiverticulosis. Ureteral masses are rarely benign and are most commonly urothelial carcinomas. Processes in the abdomen and pelvis, including mass effect from pregnancy, ureteral compression from advanced pelvic floor prolapse, and rarely, ureteral obstruction from vaginal devices, also can affect the ureter. The ureter can be injured during pelvic surgery or trauma. It also may be involved by deep pelvic endometriosis, mass effect from extrinsic lesions, or reactive change from inflammatory processes. Radiologists need to have a clear understanding of the patient's history and the range of possible ureteral conditions to establish the optimal differential diagnosis.
42879877:
BACKGROUND: Indocyanine green angiography (ICGA) is frequently used to assess skin viability; however, there is no clear overview of its diagnostic accuracy. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to synthesize evidence on the diagnostic accuracy of ICGA for skin viability assessment, compare quantification methods, and identify clinically relevant cut-off values.
METHODS: A literature search was conducted in the PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library databases up to October 2025. Studies were included if raw diagnostic ICGA data for skin viability assessment were retrievable. Study quality was assessed using the QUADAS-2 tool. Pooled sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, and cut-off values were identified for absolute and relative perfusion using the bivariate random-effects and multiple-threshold models.
RESULTS: Twelve studies were included, of which 10 were pooled in the quantitative synthesis. All 10 studies evaluated post-mastectomy flaps. The reference standard was the postoperative clinical evaluation of skin necrosis. Using multiple-threshold analysis, the pooled sensitivity for absolute perfusion cut-offs (6 studies) was 85.1% (95% CI: 61.9-95.2%) and pooled specificity was 61.4% (95% CI: 43.2-77.0%), with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.77. For relative perfusion (5 studies), the pooled sensitivity was 68.4% (95% CI: 32.2-90.8%) and pooled specificity was 69.1% (95% CI: 45.2-85.8%), with an AUC of 0.74. The pooled negative predictive value was high (94.7-97.1%), whereas the pooled positive predictive value was low (21.3%) at the observed necrosis rate of 10.9%. The identified cut-off values were 18.3 for absolute perfusion and 31.7% for relative perfusion.
CONCLUSIONS: ICGA demonstrated moderate diagnostic accuracy for assessing skin viability of post-mastectomy flaps. Its diagnostic performance for the skin in other locations and procedures is yet to be established.
42880067:
BACKGROUND: To systematically review the diagnostic performance and feasibility of transcranial Doppler (TCD) and optic nerve sheath diameter (ONSD) as noninvasive intracranial pressure (ICP) assessment tools in pediatric traumatic brain injury (TBI).
DATA SOURCES: Ovid MEDLINE, EMBASE, Cochrane CENTRAL, and the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews were searched from inception through February 2025.
STUDY SELECTION: Prospective and retrospective studies evaluating TCD, ONSD, or both against invasive ICP monitoring in children with TBI.
DATA EXTRACTION: Two reviewers independently screened studies, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias using Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies, version 2. Outcomes included ICP correlations and diagnostic accuracy measures (area under the curve [AUC], sensitivity, specificity, and diagnostic thresholds).
DATA SYNTHESIS: Six studies met inclusion criteria: three evaluated TCD, two evaluated ONSD, and one evaluated both. TCD findings were variable; pulsatility index (PI) demonstrated the strongest performance, with PI ≥ 1.3 yielding 100% sensitivity and 82% specificity for ICP >20 mmHg in one study, and PI ≥ 1.065 yielding AUC 0.95 and r = 0.68 in another. End-diastolic velocity showed weaker diagnostic performance. ONSD studies were more consistent, with correlations of r = 0.71-0.74, AUC 0.85-0.93, and optimal thresholds of 5.5-6.1 mm. The single combined-modality study reported r = 0.97 and AUC = 0.99 for ONSD plus PI.
CONCLUSIONS: TCD and ONSD are feasible adjunctive tools for noninvasive ICP assessment in pediatric TBI, though diagnostic performance varied substantially across studies. Evidence supporting combined modality models remains preliminary. Larger multicenter studies are needed to standardize acquisition protocols, establish age-appropriate thresholds, and define clinical utility.
42880521:
BACKGROUND: Atrial fibrillation (AF) recurrence after catheter ablation remains common, with recurrence rates up to 45%. Traditional risk scores demonstrate only modest predictive performance. Machine learning (ML) approaches have shown promise in improving risk stratification by leveraging high-dimensional clinical and imaging data, but direct comparisons with traditional scores remain limited.
OBJECTIVE: To compare the discriminative performance of ML models versus traditional risk scores in predicting AF recurrence following catheter ablation.
METHODS: MEDLINE, EMBASE, Web of Science, and Cochrane databases were searched to 11 June 2026 for studies reporting head-to-head comparisons of ML and traditional risk models predicting AF recurrence after ablation. The primary outcome was model discrimination, measured by the C-statistic. Random-effects meta-analysis was used to pool discrimination estimates, and meta-regression was performed to compare ML and traditional approaches. Subgroup analysis was conducted to explore the effect of ML model architecture. Methodological quality was assessed using the PROBAST tool.
RESULTS: Eleven studies (n = 17,150) were included. ML models demonstrated higher pooled discrimination compared with traditional risk scores (AUC 0.80, 95% CI 0.72-0.86 vs. 0.58, 95% CI 0.53-0.62; QM 18.96, p < 0.001). Subgroup analysis suggested that multimodal fusion models achieved the highest pooled discrimination, followed by neural-network models. Tree-based models did not significantly outperform traditional risk scores in the primary analysis.
CONCLUSIONS: ML models showed higher discrimination compared to traditional risk scores in predicting AF recurrence after ablation. Methodological limitations, lack of calibration reporting, and absence of external validation limit immediate clinical adoption.
42881278: Osteoporosis-related fractures create a large and often preventable burden, yet many individuals undergoing CT for unrelated care do not receive skeletal assessment. This review evaluates artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled use of routine CT for opportunistic case-finding and risk assessment, with emphasis on the boundary between promising retrospective performance and safe clinical implementation. Automated vertebral segmentation and CT-derived bone-density estimation can reduce manual workload, and published diagnostic studies report high discrimination in selected cohorts. However, pooled estimates are heterogeneous because the reference standard, anatomical target, CT acquisition, reconstruction, contrast status, calibration method, prevalence, and validation design differ substantially across studies. These differences preclude a universal CT threshold or a universal minimum detector-row requirement; detector-row configuration should be considered together with the broader acquisition and reconstruction parameters. For implementation, AI should be deployed as a validated triage tool-not as a stand-alone diagnostic replacement for clinical assessment and indicated DXA/QCT.
