Magnetic resonance imaging radiomics predicted pathological complete response in HER2-positive breast cancer with AUC 0.80. No breast cancer-specific perioperative primary study met the eligibility criteria. Deep survival networks achieved concordance index 0.626 versus 0.612 for Cox regression in breast cancer cohorts. Natural language processing identified metastatic recurrence in breast cancer clinical records with sensitivity 83% and specificity 73%. Risk of bias was low to moderate for imaging and pathology studies and high for small sample radiomics studies. Density-stratified performance was reported by only two imaging studies, and receptor status prediction from haematoxylin and eosin staining had not been validated as a safe alternative to immunohistochemistry.
CONCLUSIONS: Artificial intelligence demonstrated clinically meaningful performance across the five domains with eligible primary studies. Breast cancer-specific perioperative and intensive care primary studies were absent, representing the largest evidence gap. External validation, demographic diversity, and prospective clinical integration evidence remained the most consistently identified limitations. Prediction of molecular receptor status without immunohistochemistry requires rigorous prospective safety validation before it can complement standard testing.
42922436:
BACKGROUND: Sleep-disordered breathing (SDB) is common after ischemic stroke and has been associated with adverse outcomes, yet evidence from large stroke cohorts remains limited. We evaluated the association of SDB severity with all-cause mortality, major adverse cardiac and cerebrovascular events (MACCE), and 3-month functional outcome.
METHODS: This retrospective cohort study included consecutive patients with ischemic stroke or transient ischemic attack admitted to Inselspital Bern between 2017 and 2021 who underwent in-hospital respiratory polygraphy. SDB severity was classified according to the apnea-hypopnea index as mild (5-<15 events/h), moderate (15-<30 events/h), or severe (≥30 events/h). Outcomes included all-cause mortality, first postindex MACCE, and modified Rankin Scale scores at 3 months. Multivariable Cox and logistic regression models adjusted for age, sex, body mass index, vascular risk factors, admission National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale, intravenous thrombolysis, and mechanical thrombectomy.
RESULTS: Among 1083 patients (mean age, 66.0±14.5 years; 62.6% men), SDB (apnea-hypopnea index ≥5 events/h) was present in 819 patients (75.6%), including mild (29.8%), moderate (22.9%), and severe (22.9%). Median follow-up was 51.1 months (interquartile range, 39.1-67.8) for mortality and 47.7 months (interquartile range, 36.9-65.5) for first postindex MACCE; 178 deaths and 153 of 880 patients experienced a first postindex MACCE. Severe SDB was independently associated with increased all-cause mortality (adjusted hazard ratio, 1.73 [95% CI, 1.04-2.89]). Mild, moderate, and severe SDB were associated with first postindex MACCE (adjusted hazard ratio, 1.78 [95% CI, 1.03-3.06]; 2.20 [95% CI, 1.26-3.84]; and 2.16 [95% CI, 1.23-3.78], respectively; P for trend=0.009). Moderate and severe SDB were associated with unfavorable 3-month functional outcome (adjusted odds ratio, 1.74 [95% CI, 1.01-3.04] and 2.48 [95% CI, 1.45-4.31], respectively; P for trend <0.001).
CONCLUSIONS: Severe SDB was independently associated with all-cause mortality, whereas SDB severity was associated with first postindex MACCE and unfavorable 3-month functional outcome. Acute-phase SDB assessment may improve prognostic risk stratification.
42925626: Multimodal recommendation integrates auxiliary modalities, such as images and text, to enrich item representations and improve personalized ranking. However, recommendation accuracy can be affected by cross-modal bias, where single-modality signals may dominate multimodal representations and lead to unreliable recommendations. Handling this bias introduces two challenges: (1) Conventional multimodal fusion strategies may dilute misleading single-modality signals during aggregation, resulting in insufficient debiasing penalties. (2) Debiasing without evaluating cross-modal semantic consistency may misidentify semantically consistent items and impose unnecessary penalties. To address these issues, we propose a Consistency-guided Evidential Debiasing framework for multimodal Recommendation (CEDRec). Specifically, CEDRec utilizes an evidential bias network that adopts a simple Dempster-Shafer formulation to represent deceptive evidence and uncertainty for each modality. Subsequently, the network performs evidential fusion over these modality-specific estimates to obtain a reliable cross-modal bias score while alleviating the dilution of strong unimodal signals. Moreover, to prevent misidentifying semantically consistent items, CEDRec employs a semantic bottleneck network based on the variational information bottleneck principle. This network distills shared cross-modal semantics to generate a dynamic gating signal, thus protecting semantically consistent items from unnecessary penalties. Finally, during the joint optimization, gradient projection is employed to resolve conflicts between collaborative preference learning and semantic bottleneck compression, ensuring that shared semantics are distilled without sacrificing ranking performance. Extensive experiments on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that CEDRec effectively mitigates cross-modal bias and achieves a more balanced item exposure distribution while maintaining competitive ranking performance.
42925837:
BACKGROUND: Post-traumatic hydrocephalus (PTH) is a recognized complication following decompressive craniectomy (DC) for traumatic brain injury (TBI). Subdural hygroma has been implicated as a potential risk factor; however, prior studies have been limited by heterogeneous definitions and lack of distinction between hygroma subtypes. The role of interhemispheric hygroma (IHH) as a specific predictor of hydrocephalus remains unclear.
METHODS: We conducted a systematic review in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines. We searched PubMed (MEDLINE), Cochrane, and Scopus from inception to March 2025. We included studies evaluating hydrocephalus following DC for TBI and reporting data on subdural hygroma. We adopted a phenotype-specific approach, focusing on IHH as the primary exposure and clinically significant hydrocephalus (shunt-dependent or clearly defined clinical hydrocephalus) as the outcome. We assessed study quality using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. We performed the meta-analysis using study-level 2 × 2 data, with fixed-effect and random-effects models for primary and sensitivity analyses, respectively.
RESULTS: We included 14 studies comprising 1,621 patients in the qualitative synthesis. We included three studies with comparable definitions in the primary meta-analysis, demonstrating a strong association between IHH and hydrocephalus (pooled OR 6.75, 95% CI 3.4-13.41; I2 = 9.8%). Sensitivity analyses incorporating additional heterogeneous studies confirmed the association, although with a lower effect size and increased heterogeneity. Studies relying on radiological definitions alone were excluded from pooled analysis but showed similar trends. Across studies, incidence of hydrocephalus varied widely depending on outcome definitions.
CONCLUSIONS: Interhemispheric hygroma is strongly associated with the development of clinically significant hydrocephalus following DC. A phenotype-specific analytical approach reduces heterogeneity and improves interpretability compared with prior studies. Recognition of IHH may facilitate early identification of patients at risk for PTH and support more targeted postoperative monitoring and management strategies.
42926303:
BACKGROUND: Malignant bowel obstruction (MBO) is a challenging clinical problem requiring teams to balance complex oncologic disease, limited treatment options, and patient prognosis and values as they approach end of life. Presently, there is limited high-quality evidence to guide decision-making for MBO patients.
OBJECTIVE: A multidisciplinary modified Delphi process was undertaken to create guidance and support clinical decision-making in the medical and surgical care of this patient population.
METHODS: Multidisciplinary experts from all specialties regularly caring for MBO in Canada and the United States were invited for participation, including Acute Care Surgery, Surgical Oncology, Gynecologic Oncology, Gastroenterology, Radiology, Medical Oncology, and Palliative Care. Statements were evaluated through two rounds of surveys and a consensus meeting, with an a priori threshold of 80% agreement for approval.
RESULTS: Forty-nine final evidence-informed statements were included following expert consensus review pertaining to Patient Assessment, Medical Management, Surgical Management, and Palliative Management, in addition to a unifying definition of MBO. Consensus statements address aspects of complex MBO care, including but not limited to, optimal preoperative evaluation and multidisciplinary review; timing and use of steroids, motility, and antisecretory agents; contraindications to surgery; key facets of consent and perioperative decision making; framework for the nuanced use of gastrostomies and IV fluids in the end-of-life setting.
CONCLUSIONS: This Modified Delphi consensus provides multidisciplinary evidence-based recommendations for the care of patients with this challenging problem. These expert approved statements provide much-needed clinical guidance to support best care balanced with patient values and avoidance of undue harm.
42927480:
BACKGROUND: Hospitals use Medicare Severity Diagnosis Related Group (MS-DRG) coding to bill for each admission, with higher payment provided for those with complications or comorbidities (CCs) or major CCs (MCCs). We analyzed variation in MS-DRG coding for carotid endarterectomy (CEA) across Vascular Quality Initiative (VQI) centers to identify opportunities for improvement.
METHODS: We matched CEA cases in the VQI registry with Medicare claims data from 2013 through 2023. A multivariable stepwise logistic regression model was created to identify variables associated with CC or MCC billing (with odds ratios [ORs]). We examined variations in CC or MCC billing percentages among centers and applied a multivariable model to compare observed-to-expected (O:E) CC or MCC billing rates to adjust for patient differences. Billing trends over time were analyzed using linear regression.
RESULTS: Among 75,064 primary CEA admissions for Medicare beneficiaries, 39.5% were billed with CCs or MCCs (31.1% CCs, 8.4% MCCs) and 60.5% without. Eleven VQI clinical variables that indicated CCs were significantly associated with CC or MCC billing: dialysis dependence (OR, 22.30), postoperative neurological events (OR, 5.25), length of stay >2 days (OR, 4.98), pre-existing heart failure (OR, 4.08), any postoperative complication (OR, 3.70), reoperation (OR, 3.65), preoperative neurological event (OR, 1.70), higher American Society of Anesthesiologists class (OR, 1.50), urgent/emergent procedure (OR, 1.28), postoperative intravenous blood pressure management (OR, 1.27), and institutional transfer (OR, 1.16). Across 371 VQI centers, CC or MCC billing rates varied 5.6-fold, ranging from 15% to 84% of admissions. After risk adjustment, observed-to-expected ratios still demonstrated 4.2-fold variation, from 0.45 to 1.90 across centers. The observed rate of CC or MCC billing increased over time, from 35.5% in 2015 to 46.1% in 2023 (P < .001). In contrast, the expected adjusted rates predicted by the model remained stable (P = .269). A discrete inflection point was identified between 2016 and 2017, after which higher billing rates persisted (P < .001).
CONCLUSIONS: Substantial variation exists for MS-DRG billing for CEA across VQI centers. Billing rates for CCs or MCCs increased from 2013 through 2023. These findings suggest potential underbilling at some centers and overbilling at others. Leveraging Medicare-linked VQI registry data and the proposed model could help to improve coding and billing accuracy, optimize reimbursement, and reduce Medicare audit risk.
42927593: Actionable reporting in radiology is a concept that has gained traction since its inception in 2014. The notion is simple: radiology reports should easily translate into clinical action, particularly when the study is abnormal. This is not so simple. But the process of producing an actionable report is as crucial as the report itself. The process should result in a radiology report that consistently results in information being provided to the referrer that results in improved patient care. This review article presents an evidence-based critique of the concept, demonstrates the numerous pitfalls, illustrates points of gold-standard practice (illustrated as 'Rules') and presents a coherent model of the overall process of actionable reporting, which flanks the crucial central element of an actionable report. KEY POINTS: Question The actionable reporting process is highly dependent on cooperation and coordination of many healthcare staff, IT systems, and different departments, with the radiologist at the heart of it; it should be seen as a multistep process where each step is crucial and interdependent with the overall goal of better patient outcomes via better systems of work. Findings The skilful production of an actionable report is central to this process and remains the responsibility of the individual radiologist. Critical relevance statement Fundamentally, actionable reporting represents the current best practice in radiology reporting. It should be the goal of every radiologist to ensure their reports are actionable and their reporting workflow matches that of actionable reporting.
42927686:
BACKGROUND: Intracranial Atherosclerotic Stenosis (ICAS) is one of the leading causes of ischemic stroke worldwide. Endovascular interventions such as drug-coated balloon (DCB) angioplasty and stent angioplasty (SA) have emerged as promising treatment options, particularly for patients with severe stenosis. However, the comparative efficacy and safety of these two approaches remain uncertain. This systematic review aimed to compare the efficacy and safety of DCB versus SA in patients with ICAS.
METHODS: A comprehensive search of PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, and the Cochrane Central was conducted through January 2026. We included randomized clinical trials and comparative cohort studies that compare DCB with SA in patients with ICAS.
RESULTS: Six studies comprising 723 participants (332 DCB, 391 SA) met the inclusion criteria. The mean participant age ranged from 55.3 to 66.33 years. Compared with SA, DCB was associated with a lower overall restenosis rate (RR = 0.28, 95% CI: 0.18 to 0.44, p = 0.0007, I2 = 0.0%, τ2 = 0, PI = 0.16 to 0.48), and recurrent ischemic events (RR = 0.30, 95% CI: 0.22 to 0.42, p = 0.0002, I2 = 0.0%, τ2 = 0, PI = 0.13 to 0.72). No statistically significant difference in periprocedural complications was observed between the two strategies (RR = 0.78, 95% CI: 0.39 to 1.55, p = 0.3878, I2 = 0.0%, τ2 ≤0.0001, PI = 0.35 to 1.73).
CONCLUSION: DCB is associated with greater efficacy than SA in reducing restenosis and recurrent ischemic events in patients with ICAS without increasing procedural complications. However, interpretation of these findings is limited by the predominance of nonrandomized studies and relatively short follow-up durations. More randomized clinical trials with longer follow-up and larger sample sizes are needed.
42928137:
PURPOSE: To compare the patient-level diagnostic accuracy of PSMA-PET with multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging (mpMRI), computed tomography (CT), and bone scintigraphy (BS) for initial T, N, and M staging of newly diagnosed intermediate- to high-risk prostate cancer using paired studies.
METHODS: We searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Scopus from inception to December 1, 2025, for paired studies in which the same patients underwent PSMA-PET and conventional imaging, with histopathology or predefined composite criteria as the reference standard. Risk of bias was assessed with QUADAS-2 and QUADAS-C. Pooled sensitivity and specificity with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated using bivariate composite-likelihood models. Modality effects were tested by meta-regression and likelihood ratio tests, and absolute between-modality differences with 95% CIs were estimated using the delta method.
RESULTS: Forty-three studies including 4,023 patients were analyzed. For local T staging, PSMA-PET did not show uniform superiority over mpMRI. For extraprostatic extension, PSMA-PET/CT did not differ significantly from mpMRI in sensitivity (absolute difference, -7.6 percentage points; 95% CI, -16.1 to 0.9; p = 0.08) or specificity (-7.0 percentage points; 95% CI, -14.7 to 0.8; p = 0.08); no significant differences were observed for seminal vesicle invasion. In an exploratory six-study comparison, PSMA-PET/MRI had higher sensitivity than mpMRI for extraprostatic extension (+ 12.1 percentage points; 95% CI, 1.9 to 22.2; p = 0.02). For regional lymph node staging, PSMA-PET/CT sensitivity was 69.3% (95% CI, 56.6-79.7) versus 45.3% (95% CI, 33.0-58.3) for mpMRI (difference, + 24.1 percentage points; 95% CI, 6.0-40.3; p = 0.009), whereas specificity did not differ (difference, + 3.2 percentage points; 95% CI, -4.6 to 11.8; p = 0.41). For bone metastasis staging, PSMA-PET had greater sensitivity than BS (95.8% [95% CI, 92.8-98.7] versus 76.2% [95% CI, 68.7-83.8]) and greater specificity (92.8% [95% CI, 89.9-95.7] versus 77.4% [95% CI, 71.3-83.5]; both p < 0.001).
CONCLUSIONS: PSMA-PET/CT was more sensitive than mpMRI for regional lymph node staging, while specificity was comparable. PSMA-PET had greater sensitivity and specificity than bone scintigraphy for bone metastasis staging. For local T staging, PSMA-PET did not show uniform superiority over mpMRI.
42928210:
BACKGROUND: The Medical Segment Anything Model (MedSAM) has emerged as a prominent foundation model for medical image segmentation, prompting rapid growth in related research. Despite this proliferation, the literature remains fragmented across multimodal paradigms and lacks rigorous synthesis of methodological innovations, clinical safety evidence, algorithmic bias, and real-world implementation barriers-gaps that limit the field's ability to translate algorithmic progress into clinical impact.
OBJECTIVE: To systematically identify, classify, and synthesize published research on MedSAM and its derivatives, providing a comprehensive overview of methodological developments, evaluation findings, and clinical translation progress.
METHODS: This scoping review followed the PRISMA-ScR guideline. We conducted a systematic search across six major databases (PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library) through June 2025.
RESULTS: From 1,482 initial records, 45 studies met inclusion criteria. Innovation-oriented studies (n = 32) were classified along four methodological axes spanning multimodal paradigms: Architecture Enhancement (encoder/decoder refinements for efficiency and precision), Prompt Strategy (textual, spatial, and multimodal prompting mechanisms), Efficiency and Deployability (quantization, distillation, and system integration), and Pipeline and Application (integration into clinical workflows). Evaluation-oriented studies (n = 13) revealed that MedSAM outperforms general-purpose SAM by 5-20% on structured modalities (CT/MRI) but lags behind task-specific networks for delicate structures. Notably, fairness analyses from two studies (combined n = 1,757 subjects) report Dice disparities of up to 10% across sex, age, and BMI strata, raising concerns about potential demographic bias that warrants further investigation in larger, multi-center cohorts before firm clinical-safety conclusions can be drawn. Real-world deployment is further constrained by prompt sensitivity (5-15% Dice variation), cross-modality domain shift, regulatory compliance gaps (FDA/CE marking, HIPAA, GDPR), and absent multi-center prospective validation, all of which represent principal implementation hurdles for clinical adoption.
CONCLUSIONS: MedSAM represents a significant advancement in medical image segmentation, demonstrating a clear trajectory from large-scale architectures toward lightweight, prompt-aware, and deployable models. This synthesis provides a structured critical appraisal indicating that the evidence base remains at the proof-of-concept stage, with most studies retrospective and single-center, and emerging signals of algorithmic bias, unresolved cross-modality failure modes, and incomplete regulatory pathways represent safety and implementation considerations that should be addressed before multimodal MedSAM-based systems are more broadly deployed in clinical imaging workflows.
42929023:
BACKGROUND: Postoperative hypoparathyroidism remains the most frequent complication after total thyroidectomy. Recently, near-infrared autofluorescence (NIRAF) imaging with or without indocyanine green (ICG) was introduced to evaluate parathyroid glands during surgery. The aim of this paper is to provide recommendations by the European Society of Endocrine Surgeons (ESES) regarding its use in thyroid surgery based on a scoping review and meta-analysis.
METHODS: A working group of experts was created by the ESES. A systematic literature search was performed, using MEDLINE® (PubMed), up to 31 December 2024. Studies were included if a comparative group was used to evaluate short- and long-term postoperative hypoparathyroidism, autotransplantation rates, and/or inadvertent parathyroid gland removal. The results were pooled in a random-effects meta-analysis. Subgroup analyses were performed to assess the impact of NIRAF with or without ICG, as well as central lymph node neck dissection. Recommendations were created among all co-authors and discussed at the 11th ESES conference. A modified Delphi online voting process amongst all members approved all recommendations.
RESULTS: After screening 335 abstracts, there were 34 studies, with a total of 9322 patients, that met the inclusion criteria. These were published between 2017 and 2024 and included 11 RCTs. Meta-analyses showed promising results for NIRAF and ICG with regard to immediate and permanent hypoparathyroidism, inadvertent removal proportions, and autotransplantation proportions. The quality of evidence was rated as 'moderate' for most of the recommendations with good quality of evidence for most questions.
CONCLUSION: These ESES recommendations provide guidance for the use of NIRAF with or without ICG based on a scoping review of the literature, meta-analyses, and expert opinion.
42931483: Low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) is essential for reducing potential radiation-associated risks, but increased noise and artifacts can compromise diagnostic confidence. This review examines how AI is reshaping LDCT by improving reconstruction, denoising, protocol optimization, and workflow integration. It outlines the evolution from FBP to IR and then to deep learning methods that better preserve anatomical detail while reducing noise. The review also considers emerging applications in photon-counting CT (PCCT) and discusses clinical use in screening, pediatric imaging, oncology, cardiac imaging, and emergency care. These developments may support safer imaging, improve consistency across studies, and reduce the need for repeat examinations. However, important challenges remain, including limited generalizability across scanners and patient populations, the potential loss of subtle findings, changes in quantitative imaging features, and the need for careful validation before widespread clinical adoption. Further research should focus on multicenter validation, task-based performance assessment, and integration into routine clinical workflows.
42931489: Background: Infective endocarditis (IE) remains a life-threatening disease associated with substantial morbidity and mortality. Transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography are the first-line imaging modalities, but their diagnostic performance may be reduced in patients with prosthetic valves, intracardiac devices, previous cardiac surgery, extensive calcification, or suspected periannular extension. Cardiac computed tomography (CT) provides complementary high-resolution anatomical information and has gained increasing importance within contemporary multimodality diagnostic pathways. Scope: This Review critically examines the current role of cardiac CT in IE, including acquisition and reconstruction strategies, lesion-specific imaging findings, applications in native, prosthetic, transcatheter, and device-related infection, extracardiac assessment, and preoperative planning. Comparative observations regarding echocardiography and selected multimodality techniques are integrated where directly relevant. Emerging applications of spectral CT, photon-counting detector CT, deep learning reconstruction, radiomics, and artificial intelligence are appraised according to four levels of evidence: clinically validated IE applications, preliminary IE-specific evidence, indirect cardiovascular evidence, and conceptual applications. Main Findings: Cardiac CT is particularly valuable for detecting and anatomically characterizing periannular complications, including abscesses, pseudoaneurysms, fistulous tracts, inflammatory extension, and prosthetic dehiscence. Multiphase electrocardiography (ECG)-gated acquisition improves the assessment of dynamic valvular and prosthetic abnormalities. Transesophageal echocardiography remains more sensitive for small or highly mobile vegetations, leaflet perforation, regurgitant jets, and intracardiac flow abnormalities, demonstrating that the two techniques are complementary rather than interchangeable. Cardiac CT also contributes to coronary assessment, surgical planning, evaluation of previous grafts and reconstructive material, and selected extracardiac complications. Conclusions: Cardiac CT is an important component of contemporary multimodality IE assessment, but it should not be regarded as a replacement for echocardiography. Its clinical value depends on the infected substrate, suspected complication, acquisition protocol, and integration with echocardiographic, microbiological, surgical, and clinical findings. Emerging technologies may improve image quality and quantitative characterization, but most remain supported by preliminary IE-specific, indirect cardiovascular, or conceptual evidence and should not yet be considered established IE-specific diagnostic tools.
42933577:
BACKGROUND: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is increasingly conceptualized as a disorder of distributed neural network dysfunction. The hippocampus comprises functionally distinct subfields, yet evidence on subfield-level functional connectivity (FC) abnormalities in MDD remains heterogeneous, partly because studies use different segmentation approaches.
METHODS: Following PRISMA 2020, we systematically searched PubMed and Scopus for English-language studies published from January 2020 to August 2026 examining FC involving hippocampal subfields or subregions in depression. We summarized segmentation methods, compared atlas-level spatial overlap, performed random-effects meta-analyses where data were comparable, and narratively synthesized case-control and treatment-related findings.
RESULTS: Eighteen studies including 1366 patients with MDD and 935 healthy controls were included. Segmentation approaches differed substantially in hippocampal coverage and granularity. Five studies contributed to exploratory network-specific meta-analyses. FC was lower in MDD for hippocampal subregion-default mode network connections (g = -0.74, 95% CI -0.98 to -0.50) and visual network connections (g = -0.64, 95% CI -0.94 to -0.34). Estimates for salience, limbic, and sensorimotor networks were imprecise and heterogeneous. Narrative findings were bidirectional, while longitudinal studies suggested treatment-related connectivity changes.
CONCLUSIONS: MDD is associated with heterogeneous, subregion-specific hippocampal dysconnectivity. Atlas non-equivalence may contribute to variability across studies, supporting more harmonized and method-aware segmentation approaches.
42933729:
PURPOSE: Management of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is evolving rapidly and decisions regarding locoregional therapy are complex. External beam radiation therapy (EBRT) is a highly effective and safe intervention with an expanding role in HCC, and major guidelines (BCLC 2026, EASL, AASLD, NCCN, ASTRO) now endorse it across defined clinical settings. However, guidelines largely treat EBRT as a single modality, whereas in practice it encompasses multiple delivery techniques and nuanced technical decisions that directly influence safety and efficacy. This review provides radiation oncologists with a practical foundation for selecting patients, planning treatment, and positioning EBRT among contemporary locoregional and systemic therapies.
METHODS AND MATERIALS: We synthesized current consensus guidelines, prospective randomized trials, and key contemporary series evaluating EBRT for HCC, drawing on prior systematic reviews updated to include recent studies. We address liver function assessment and patient selection, practical aspects of treatment delivery (motion management, image guidance, target definition, and adaptive planning), particle therapy, comparative evidence against other locoregional therapies, combinations with systemic therapy, management of high-risk scenarios, bridging to transplant, and post-treatment surveillance.
RESULTS: Mature prospective evidence, including randomized comparisons against chemoembolization, thermal ablation, and systemic therapy, demonstrates that EBRT achieves local control equal or superior to standard locoregional therapies with acceptable toxicity. Advances in motion management, image guidance, functional liver assessment, and adaptive planning have expanded the safe application to high-risk scenarios, such as macrovascular invasion, poor liver function, and re-irradiation, and EBRT is an effective bridging therapy.
CONCLUSIONS: EBRT delivers excellent local control with acceptable toxicity and is now endorsed by major guidelines as an option in selected settings. As imaging, motion management, adaptive strategies, and functional liver assessment continue to evolve, EBRT can be tailored safely to patients with compromised liver reserve, macrovascular invasion, or transplant pathways. Future studies should refine patient selection and optimize combinations of EBRT with other liver-directed and systemic therapies.
42934071:
BACKGROUND: Innovations have improved outcomes in high-risk localised, locally advanced, and biochemically recurrent prostate cancer (PC), yet high-level evidence remains limited for many management decisions. The 2026 Advanced Prostate Cancer Consensus Conference (APCCC) surveyed an international panel on key clinical questions to complement evidence-based guidelines.
OBJECTIVE: Here we present the voting results for the questions on high-risk localised, locally advanced, and biochemically recurrent PC from APCCC 2026.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: Before the conference, a multidisciplinary panel of 144 international PC experts used a modified Delphi process to develop 313 multiple-choice consensus questions, of which 134 covered high-risk localised and locally advanced PC, including prostate-specific antigen (PSA) persistence and PSA recurrence, and side effects of treatment. These questions were administered to the 133 voting panel members "panellists" via a web-based survey prior to the conference.
OUTCOME MEASUREMENTS AND STATISTICAL ANALYSIS: Consensus was defined a priori as ≥75% agreement, with strong consensus defined as ≥90% agreement. Overall, consensus was reached for 44 of the 134 questions (32.8%), with seven questions reaching a strong consensus. Results and limitations The voting results show varying degrees of consensus, as discussed in this article and as detailed in the Supplementary Material. An interactive heat map for the questions can be found at https://apccc.org/APCCC2026-votings-localised-and-locally-advanced-prostate-cancer/. These findings do not include a formal literature review or meta-analysis.
CONCLUSIONS: The voting results can help physicians and patients navigate controversial areas of clinical management for which evidence is scant or conflicting. The findings can also help funders and policymakers in prioritising areas for future research. Importantly, APCCC 2026 once again identified important gaps (areas of no consensus) that merit evaluation in specifically designed trials.
42934295: Arteriovenous malformations (AVMs) are high-flow vascular anomalies traditionally treated as congenital structural lesions with embolization or surgical resection. However, recurrence after embolization alone exceeds 90%, underscoring incomplete understanding of their biology. Next-generation sequencing has identified somatic gain-of-function mutations in KRAS, MAP2K1, BRAF, and HRAS as drivers of sporadic AVMs. Confined to lesional endothelial cells, these mutations activate RAS/MAPK signaling and support a neoplastic-like rather than purely structural disease model. This has therapeutic implications: MEK inhibitors, particularly trametinib, have shown angiographic and clinical responses in refractory AVMs. Interventional radiologists can obtain draining vein liquid-biopsy samples during embolization for molecular genotyping; embolization may increase circulating cell-free DNA yield. This review summarizes the molecular rationale, targeted therapy evidence, and integration of genotyping into embolization workflows to enable combined treatment strategies.Level of Evidence: No level of evidence assigned (Review Article).
42937535: Building agents that perceive and act on their environment with a degree of autonomy has long been a focus of artificial intelligence research. This pursuit has become far more practical with the emergence of large language models (LLMs) capable of using natural language to integrate information, follow instructions, and perform forms of reasoning and planning across a wide range of tasks. With its multimodal data streams and orchestrated workflows spanning multiple systems, radiology is uniquely suited to benefit from agents that can adapt to context and automate complex, repetitive tasks. In radiology, LLMs and their multimodal variants have already demonstrated promising performance for individual tasks such as information extraction and report summarization. However, using LLMs in isolation underutilizes their potential to support complex, multistep workflows where decisions depend on evolving context from multiple information sources. Equipping LLMs with external tools and feedback mechanisms enables them to drive systems that exhibit a spectrum of autonomy, ranging from semiautomated workflows to more adaptive agents capable of managing complex processes. This review article examines the design of LLM-driven agentic systems, explores representative radiology applications, discusses evaluation frameworks, and outlines key challenges, including error cascades, tool-use effectiveness, and integration with health information technology infrastructure.
42937757:
BACKGROUND: Although adjuvant strategies such as systemic chemotherapy, regional nonsystemic chemotherapy, and ablation have been applied, the optimal adjuvant therapeutic strategy for resectable colorectal liver metastases remains uncertain in terms of overall survival and disease-free survival. This network meta-analysis aimed to determine the optimal adjuvant therapeutic strategy for patients with colorectal liver metastases.
METHODS: We searched potentially eligible studies in PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, and China National Knowledge Infrastructure databases until July 2026. Pooled disease-free survival (DFS) and overall survival (OS) were estimated using R software.
RESULTS: Eighteen studies including 18 reports were included. For the DFS, except for adjuvant hepatic arterial infusion chemotherapy (CT, HAIC) concomitant with intravenous CT, adjuvant CT and perioperative CT significantly improved DFS compared with surgery and adjuvant HAIC. There was no statistical difference between all therapeutic strategies for OS. Adjuvant HAIC concomitant with intravenous CT had the highest probability of being the best treatment for improving DFS (85.01%), followed by perioperative CT (11.75%) and adjuvant CT (3.17%); however, adjuvant HAIC concomitant with intravenous CT had the highest probability of being the best adjuvant treatment for improving OS (52.46%), followed by perioperative CT (40.25%) and adjuvant HAIC (5.25%).
CONCLUSION: Adjuvant CT may be the best for improving DFS, but perioperative CT may be the best for improving OS. However, the results should be validated further.
42942361: Background and Objectives: Traumatic intracranial vascular lesions are rare but severe complications of traumatic brain injury (TBI) and include arterial and venous injuries such as arterial dissections, pseudoaneurysms, arterial occlusions, venous sinus thrombosis, arteriovenous fistulas, and carotid-cavernous fistulas. Despite their clinical significance, the available literature remains limited and heterogeneous. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the diagnostic yield of vascular imaging, spectrum, and imaging modalities of traumatic intracranial vascular lesions in adults with TBI. Materials and Methods: A systematic literature search was conducted from database inception to 31 August 2026 in PubMed, Web of Science Core Collection, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library (CENTRAL) according to the PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Cohorts of patients who underwent vascular imaging after TBI were eligible. When the full text was available, the denominator was the number of patients imaged with a modality able to detect the lesion in question and the numerator was reported at patient level for intracranial lesions. The primary analyses were restricted to cohorts with an explicit adult age criterion or a separately reported adult subgroup; cohorts with a pediatric fraction that could not be separated entered a sensitivity analysis only. Data extraction and quality assessment using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale and the Joanna Briggs Institute checklist for prevalence studies were performed independently by two reviewers. Proportions were pooled with a logit-transformed random-effects model with restricted maximum-likelihood estimation and prediction intervals, with Freeman-Tukey and generalized linear mixed models as sensitivity analyses. Results: Nineteen studies with 3542 imaged patients were included, eight of them adult cohorts with 2021 patients. In adult cohorts, the pooled diagnostic yield was 11.0% (95% CI, 2.3-39.8%; four cohorts) for dural venous sinus thrombosis, 4.8% (95% CI, 1.1-18.4%; three cohorts) for pseudoaneurysm, 1.1% (95% CI, 0.0-20.8%; two cohorts) for arteriovenous fistula, and 0.7% (95% CI, 0.2-3.1%; three cohorts) for carotid-cavernous fistula, with I2 between 74.7% and 96.2% and prediction intervals spanning most of the possible range; arterial dissection (7.0%) and arterial occlusion (5.8%) were reported by a single adult cohort and were not pooled. The proportion of patients with any lesion was not pooled, because the seven cohorts that imaged every patient differed in whether and how the venous compartment was assessed; it ranged from 1.5% to 56.9% by cohort. Adding the eleven adult-dominant cohorts gave 17.5% for sinus thrombosis and 4.5% for pseudoaneurysm. In exploratory univariable meta-regressions for sinus thrombosis, trauma mechanism, imaging modality, and study design were each associated with part of the heterogeneity and were confounded with one another in these cohorts. Conclusions: Every estimate describes the yield of vascular imaging in adults selected for it, rests on two-to-four small cohorts, and carries very low certainty; the prediction intervals show that a new cohort may fall far from the pooled value, and none of the estimates can be read as the frequency of these lesions in TBI in general.
42942382: Background and Objective: Body mass index (BMI) is widely used to classify obesity in children and adolescents but does not characterize fat distribution. Visceral adipose tissue (VAT) may provide information on cardiometabolic risk beyond BMI. This systematic review aimed to synthesize evidence on the associations between VAT and cardiometabolic risk in children and adolescents with obesity and to evaluate whether VAT provides additional information beyond BMI. Methods: PubMed and Scopus were searched for English-language studies published between 1 January 2016 and 28 February 2026. Eligible studies included participants aged 6-19 years, assessed VAT using dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), computed tomography (CT), or ultrasonography (USG), and reported at least one cardiometabolic outcome. Two reviewers independently screened the records. Methodological quality was assessed using the appropriate Joanna Briggs Institute Critical Appraisal Tools or the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. Because of methodological and clinical heterogeneity, the findings were synthesized narratively. The review was reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 statement. Results: Twenty studies were included, most of which were cross-sectional. Higher VAT was generally associated with insulin resistance, adverse lipid profiles, elevated blood pressure, inflammatory biomarkers, and early vascular dysfunction, although findings were not uniform across all populations and outcomes. In several studies, associations remained significant after adjustment for BMI or other measures of general adiposity, suggesting that VAT may capture cardiometabolic risk not reflected by BMI alone. DXA was the most frequently used assessment method. Conclusions: VAT may complement BMI in cardiometabolic risk assessment among children and adolescents with obesity. However, predominantly cross-sectional evidence, methodological heterogeneity, and the absence of standardized pediatric thresholds preclude firm conclusions about its incremental predictive value or routine clinical use. Prospective studies directly comparing VAT and BMI are required.
42942421: Background and Objectives: Ultrasound-guided pectointercostal fascial block (USG-PIFB) is increasingly used for post-sternotomy analgesia, but its efficacy remains uncertain. Prior meta-analyses pooled ultrasound-guided blocks with surgeon-performed infiltration, introducing heterogeneity. We aimed to determine the analgesic efficacy of USG-PIFB in adult cardiac surgery by restricting inclusion to ultrasound-guided techniques. Materials and Methods: Six databases were searched through December 2025, with an update search of open sources and trial registries in September 2026, for randomized controlled trials comparing USG-PIFB with control (Comparison 1) or with an alternative regional technique (Comparison 2) in adults undergoing sternotomy. The primary outcome was 24-h opioid consumption in intravenous morphine milligram equivalents. Random-effects meta-analysis (REML, Knapp-Hartung), subgroup, sensitivity and meta-regression analyses, an exploratory trial sequential analysis and GRADE assessment were performed. Results: Twenty-nine trials (2664 participants) were included: 24 in Comparison 1 and eight in Comparison 2. In 13 trials (902 participants), USG-PIFB reduced 24-h opioid consumption (mean difference -6.60 mg; 95% CI, -10.92 to -2.27; I2 = 97.7%), but the 95% prediction interval (-22.24 to 9.04 mg) included no effect and small-study effects could not be excluded. Pain scores were lower by 0.8 to 1.4 points at rest (extubation, 12 and 24 h) and during movement (12 h). Extubation was earlier and intensive care stay shorter, with extreme heterogeneity. No dose-response relationship was detected, and the difference from deep parasternal techniques was near zero. No local anesthetic systemic toxicity or block-attributable pneumothorax was reported; one block-site hematoma occurred in a USG-PIFB recipient. Certainty of evidence was low for rescue analgesic use and block-related complications and very low for all other outcomes. Conclusions: USG-PIFB may modestly reduce 24-h opioid consumption, but the magnitude and reproducibility of this effect across clinical settings remain uncertain. It is best regarded as one component of multimodal analgesia, and adequately powered multicentre trials are needed.
42942553: Background and Objectives: Near-infrared fluorescence cholangiography with indocyanine green (ICG) has been proposed as an adjunct for improving biliary anatomy recognition during laparoscopic cholecystectomy. However, uncertainty remains regarding its comparative efficacy, operative value, safety, and optimal route, dose, and timing. Materials and Methods: A systematic review was conducted to identify randomized comparative and dose-finding studies evaluating ICG fluorescence cholangiography during laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Outcomes included visualization of the cystic duct, common hepatic duct, common bile duct, biliary junctions, operative time, time to critical anatomical identification, conversion or bailout procedures, length of stay, bile duct injury, bile leak, and ICG-related adverse events. Clinical and methodological heterogeneity precluded meta-analysis; findings were synthesized descriptively. Results: Eighteen studies were included. ICG improved visualization of selected biliary structures compared with white-light imaging, particularly before dissection, whereas differences versus radiographic intraoperative cholangiography were less pronounced. Operative effects were inconsistent: several studies reported shorter cholangiography duration or earlier anatomical identification, without consistent reductions in total operative time or length of stay. Bile duct injuries and bile leaks were infrequent, but event numbers were insufficient to establish a protective effect or comparative safety. Selected dose comparisons suggested reduced hepatic background fluorescence with lower doses, although findings depended on administration timing and imaging platform. Interpretation was limited by subjective visualization assessment, risk of bias, and heterogeneous patient populations. Conclusions: ICG fluorescence cholangiography improves visualization of selected biliary structures, but improved visualization should not be equated with demonstrated clinical benefit. Evidence remains insufficient to establish reductions in bile duct injury, conversion, or postoperative morbidity, or a universally optimal route, dose, or timing regimen.
42942963: Background: Nutrition is one of the most modifiable determinants of brain development in preterm infants. Although increasing evidence supports associations between early nutritional exposures and neurodevelopment, studies remain heterogeneous regarding nutritional interventions, imaging biomarkers, and long-term outcomes. This systematic review aimed to summarize contemporary evidence on the relationship between nutrition and brain development in preterm infants using neuroimaging as the primary assessment tool while proposing an integrated translational framework to guide future research. Methods: Following a PECO framework, a systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, and CINAHL: population, infants born before 37 completed weeks of gestation; exposure, any enteral or parenteral nutritional exposure, supplementation strategy, fortification approach, or individualized nutritional intervention; comparator, an alternative nutritional strategy, lower or absent exposure, standard care or, when relevant, a term-born reference group; outcomes, MRI- or CUS-based measures of brain growth, maturation, connectivity, or injury. Studies reporting volumetric, morphometric, diffusion, connectivity, spectroscopy, or quantitative ultrasound outcomes were eligible. The methodology was adapted from the PROSPERO-registered review by Ottolini et al. Original studies published between 2020 and 2026 (1 January 2020-4 September 2026) evaluating nutritional exposures or interventions in preterm infants with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and/or cranial ultrasound (CUS) outcomes were included. Risk of bias was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS), ROBINS-I and RoB 2 according to study design. Quantitative imaging studies were screened for eligibility for ATLAS assessment. Given the substantial heterogeneity in nutritional exposures, imaging protocols, timing of assessments, and neurodevelopmental outcomes, meta-analysis was not performed. Certainty of evidence was assessed at the level of each causal question and neuroimaging outcome domain using the GRADE framework. Randomized intervention evidence and observational exposure evidence were evaluated according to the design and target contrast contributing to each body of evidence. Judgments considered risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, publication bias, and, where applicable, factors that could increase certainty. Statistical significance was not used to determine certainty, and studies arising from shared or partially overlapping parent populations were not counted as independent replication. Results: We found 33 reports that met the inclusion criteria: 4 evaluated randomized treatment contrasts, 5 non-randomized intervention comparisons, and 24 observational nutritional exposure analyses. Greater exposure to human milk and selected strategies involving early protein and lipid provision, docosahexaenoic acid, omega-3 fatty acids, and individualized nutritional support were associated in several studies with favorable MRI measurements, including larger total or regional brain volumes, more advanced white-matter maturation, and differences in structural or functional connectivity. Some studies also reported associations with later neurodevelopment. However, findings were not uniform, and GRADE certainty across outcome-specific nutrition-neuroimaging questions ranged from very low to low, principally because of risk of bias, imprecision, heterogeneous exposure and imaging definitions, and limited independent replication. Although causal inference cannot be directly drawn, neuroimaging may provide quantitative measures of brain development that can be investigated alongside long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes. We propose the Roadmap for Imaging-Guided Enhancement of Neurodevelopment (RIGEL), an integrative research framework combining imaging, molecular biomarkers, standardized neurodevelopmental assessment, and epidemiological evidence across developmental stages. RIGEL should be regarded as a hypothesis-generating research framework that requires prospective validation before any clinical implementation.
42944772:
BACKGROUND/AIM: Iodinated and gadolinium-based contrast agents are indispensable in radiological diagnostics; however, they were previously considered problematic in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) due to potential side effects. Study data from the past 15 years have led to the realization that the nephrotoxic potential of contrast agents has been overstated and that a reassessment is warranted. This consensus paper aims to standardize the intravascular use of contrast agents in the CKD population in a practical manner, based on scientific evidence and international guidelines, enabling both optimal diagnostic yield and maximum patient safety.
METHODS: The Austrian Radiological Society (OERG) and the Austrian Society of Nephrology each nominated four experts in a working group to draft consensus guidelines regarding the safe use of contrast agents in patients with impaired kidney function. Following an initial meeting of this working group a literature search was conducted in various medical databases (PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials) and pertinent guidelines of various international specialist societies were identified. The scientific work and guidelines were evaluated in five further meetings of the working group. The recommendations for the safe use of contrast agents were compiled in a consensus.
RESULTS/CONSENSUS: The recommendations could be summarized in 11 consensus statements. In addition, an algorithm for the administration of iodinated contrast agents in patients with impaired kidney function was created.
CONCLUSION: This consensus paper, endorsed by the OERG and ÖGN provides a standardized approach for the intravascular administration of contrast agents in individuals with CKD. Emphasis is placed on the diagnostic benefits of a contrast agent-assisted investigation in comparison to the potential risk of an associated kidney damage.
42944874: Gadolinium-based contrast agents (GBCA) have been central to magnetic resonance neuroimaging, enhancing diagnostic sensitivity and accuracy, in both adults and children. However, their increasingly widespread use has raised concerns, as evidence exists of gadolinium retention in brain tissue after repeated use. This paper outlines some updated strategies to reduce GBCA administration in pediatric neuroradiology, based on both recent literature and the authors' clinical experience. This paper, therefore, should be considered as a concise review of the main literature data and the opinion of a group of experts in the field, based on their daily practice in large institutions. We mention those most frequent conditions where the usage of GBCA often represents a longstanding, albeit "not strictly evidence-based," common practice which can be critically reconsidered. The use of GBCA in pediatric neuroimaging should be considered carefully based on each case scenario, evaluating if GBCA may provide real and substantial potential benefits to patient management and outcome. KEY POINTS: The use of GBCA in pediatric neuroimaging should be carefully evaluated by the pediatric neuroradiologist on an individual basis, and it should also be supported by specific literature data if present, so as to balance risks and benefits and to improve patient management and outcome. Possible alternative strategies to the use of GBCA may be considered in some cases under a close relationship between pediatric neuroradiologists and clinicians. Prospective development of new sequences is needed to improve unenhanced MR imaging accuracy and expand "Gd-free" examinations.
42946055: Over the past decade, cervical cancer management has evolved substantially, with major changes in surgical approach, surgical radicality, nodal staging, imaging, radiotherapy techniques, brachytherapy and systemic treatments. To harmonize practice and integrate new evidence into clinically applicable recommendations, the French Cervical Cancer Guidelines Group developed national clinical practice guidelines for the management of patients with cervical cancer. The guideline process was conducted under the auspices of the French National College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists and involved a multidisciplinary expert panel representing the French scientific societies involved in cervical cancer care. Clinical questions were formulated using the PICO framework and addressed the full continuum of care, including initial assessment, imaging, diagnostic conization, surgical nodal staging, treatment, fertility preservation, response assessment, follow-up, recurrence and specific clinical situations. Evidence was reviewed and critically appraised according to the GRADE methodology, and all recommendations were based on the 2018 FIGO staging system. External validation was performed through a two-round Delphi process involving 87 independent reviewers. Overall, 130 PICO questions generated 158 recommendations, including 35 strong and 52 weak recommendations, while no recommendation could be issued for 71 questions. Key practice-changing recommendations include the role of diagnostic conization in early-stage assessment, avoidance of minimally invasive hysterectomy from stage IB1 disease, risk-adapted surgical radicality, sentinel lymph node biopsy with ultrastaging, image-guided brachytherapy after chemoradiotherapy, and integration of PEMBROLIZUMAB in selected locally advanced or metastatic settings.
42946126:
PURPOSE: This guideline provides evidence-based recommendations on the use of hypofractionated external beam radiation therapy (EBRT) in patients with localized prostate cancer, including indications for moderate hypofractionation (MHF) and ultrahypofractionation (UHF), appropriate dose-fractionation regimens, target volumes, and treatment planning and delivery techniques.
METHODS: The American Society for Radiation Oncology convened a multidisciplinary task force to address 5 key questions related to hypofractionated EBRT in localized prostate cancer. Recommendations were based on a systematic literature review and developed using a predefined consensus-based methodology with grading of quality of evidence and strength of recommendation.
RESULTS: MHF is recommended over conventional fractionation for patients receiving EBRT across all risk groups, supported by high-quality randomized data demonstrating equivalent oncologic outcomes, toxicity, and quality of life, with shorter treatment duration that may reduce overall treatment burden. UHF is recommended as a standard treatment option for patients with low- and intermediate-risk disease electing for definitive EBRT and may be considered in selected patients with high-risk disease, preferably in the context of clinical trials. Selection of fractionation should generally be independent of patient age, comorbidity, and use of androgen deprivation therapy, although MHF may be preferred over UHF for patients with significant baseline urinary dysfunction. Evidence supports the use of contemporary image-guided, conformal treatment techniques to optimize target coverage and minimize toxicity. Guidance is also provided regarding appropriate dose-fractionation regimens, including commonly used MHF and UHF schedules, as well as target volumes and integration of pelvic nodal irradiation.
CONCLUSIONS: Hypofractionated EBRT has become the predominant form of definitive radiation therapy for localized prostate cancer, supported by mature randomized evidence demonstrating comparable outcomes to conventional fractionation and reduced treatment burden. Ongoing studies will further refine patient selection, the role of UHF in higher-risk disease, and integration of advanced imaging and adaptive technologies. These evidence-based recommendations inform best clinical practices in the use of hypofractionated EBRT for localized prostate cancer.
42946408:
BACKGROUND/AIM: Cranial and neuraxial epithelioid hemangioma (EH) is exceptionally rare and anatomically heterogeneous. We systematically reviewed reported cerebral, cranial osseous, primary non-osseous spinal epidural, and vertebral-origin EH with clinically relevant neuraxial extension and present an illustrative hypervascular calvarial case.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: Electronic searches of MEDLINE via PubMed were supplemented by Google Scholar, Crossref, Semantic Scholar, publisher archives, conference/supplement searches, and backward and forward citation tracking through 19 August 2026. Histologically confirmed EH involving brain parenchyma, cranial bone with relevant intracranial or craniovertebral extension, primary non-osseous spinal epidural space, or vertebral bone with secondary intraspinal/foraminal extension was eligible.
RESULTS: Twenty-two reports were included: 14 (63.6%) vertebral-origin and eight (36.4%) cerebral, combined calvarial-cerebral, cranial osseous, or primary non-osseous spinal epidural. Surgery was reported in 19/22 publications (86.4%), radiotherapy in 10/22 (45.5%), and preoperative embolization in 3/22 (13.6%). Recurrence, progression, or new post-treatment disease was explicitly described in three reports, but heterogeneous follow-up precluded pooled recurrence estimates. The illustrative 32-year-old man had a histomorphologically diagnosed hypervascular parasagittal calvarial EH compressing a patent superior sagittal sinus and underwent Onyx embolization followed by excision and cranioplasty.
CONCLUSION: Cranial and neuraxial EH is rare, with published evidence dominated by vertebral disease. Management should be individualized according to anatomical compartment, neural compression, structural instability, and vascularity. Histological distinction from epithelioid hemangioendothelioma and angiosarcoma is essential, while the available evidence is insufficient to establish comparative efficacy of radiotherapy or embolization.
42946581: Temporomandibular disorders (TMDs) are a common source of persistent orofacial pain and are estimated to affect a substantial proportion of the population. Therapeutic ultrasound is a non-invasive modality frequently used in musculoskeletal rehabilitation, although its clinical effectiveness for TMD-related pain remains debated. This systematic review was designed and reported in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 recommendations. PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched from database inception to April 2026. We included randomized controlled trials, prospective clinical studies, and comparative clinical designs evaluating therapeutic ultrasound for pain management in adults with TMDs. The primary outcomes were pain intensity, assessed using VAS, NRS, or VRS, and mandibular function, assessed mainly by mouth opening. Risk of bias was evaluated using the Cochrane RoB 2.0 tool for randomized trials and ROBINS-I for non-randomized studies. Because of substantial clinical and methodological heterogeneity, findings were synthesized narratively rather than pooled statistically. The search identified 143 records, of which 82 remained after duplicate removal and were screened. Thirty-seven full-text articles were assessed, and 23 studies involving 1256 participants (1226 of them with a temporomandibular disorder) met the eligibility criteria. Twenty-one of 23 studies reported a statistically significant reduction in pain relative to their own baseline; however, these are within-group changes rather than treatment effects, and the certainty of the evidence for pain reduction was very low (GRADE), with low certainty for mandibular function, pressure pain threshold and quality of life/disability. Reported reductions included VAS improvement from 42 to 18 when ultrasound was added to home exercise, compared with 40-26 with exercise alone, and VAS improvement from 4.90 to 1.70 after low-intensity ultrasound therapy in a large randomized trial. Compared with low-level laser therapy or photobiomodulation, four studies favored laser-based treatment, whereas one study favored low-intensity ultrasound combined with exercise. Ultrasound was superior to TENS in two studies, while one study found no meaningful difference among ultrasound, TENS, and LLLT. No consistent difference was observed between continuous and pulsed ultrasound modes. Among randomized trials, 8 studies were judged as low risk of bias, 8 raised some concerns, and 1 was judged as high risk of bias. Adverse events were reported by only 2 of the 23 studies, so the safety of the intervention could not be characterised. Therapeutic ultrasound may reduce pain and improve mandibular function in patients with temporomandibular disorders, particularly as an adjunct to multimodal rehabilitation; however, the certainty of the evidence is very low for pain and low for mandibular function, pressure pain threshold and quality of life/disability, and the optimal treatment parameters remain undetermined. These findings should not be interpreted as establishing clinical efficacy. Although some comparative studies reported greater pain reduction with LLLT/PBM than with ultrasound, this finding should be interpreted cautiously because the number of studies was small and treatment protocols were heterogeneous. Therefore, current evidence does not establish the superiority of LLLT/PBM over therapeutic ultrasound.
42947386:
INTRODUCTION: To compare long-term effectiveness and obstetric outcomes of focused ultrasound (FU) ablation versus loop electrosurgical excision procedure (LEEP) for high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (HSIL) in reproductive-aged women.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: This retrospective cohort included women treated with FU (n = 29) or LEEP (n = 32) for HSIL who subsequently delivered (2017-2023). A control group (n = 61) comprised healthy women with negative preconception HR-HPV/cytology. Outcomes were cumulative HR-HPV clearance, cervical length, pregnancy outcomes.
RESULTS: Both FU and LEEP demonstrated comparable long-term effectiveness: cumulative HR-HPV clearance rates did not differ significantly at any time point (p > 0.05). Post-intervention cervical length was significantly shorter in the LEEP group (24.79 ± 3.98 mm) than in both the FU (27.63 ± 2.80 mm) and control (28.26 ± 3.92 mm) groups (p = 0.003). Cervical insufficiency was more frequent in the LEEP group (15.63%) than in the FU (3.45%) and control (1.64%) groups (p = 0.019). The LEEP group also had higher rates of preterm birth (18.75% vs 3.45% in FU and 4.92% in controls; p = 0.039) and lower rates of vaginal delivery (15.63% vs 44.83% in FU; p = 0.025).
CONCLUSION: In this selected cohort of women with successful live births, FU may have comparable long-term effectiveness to LEEP for HSIL while potentially preserving cervical length and reducing adverse obstetric risks. These preliminary findings suggest FU may be a fertility-sparing option for appropriately selected HSIL women who are planning pregnancy.
42948598: Persistent motor dysfunction in post-stroke spastic hemiplegia may result from impaired voluntary motor control, abnormal muscle overactivity, fixed structural restriction, muscle force imbalance, or their combination. Advances in brain-computer interfaces (BCIs), peripheral nerve surgery, and tendon and soft-tissue reconstruction have expanded therapeutic options, yet optimal indications and sequencing remain unclear. A multidisciplinary expert panel reviewed current evidence, addressed key clinical questions, and developed consensus recommendations for noninvasive BCI, diagnostic motor nerve block (DNB), selective or hyperselective peripheral nerve surgery, and reconstructive procedures. The consensus emphasizes evaluation of four major components: central voluntary motor impairment, dynamic abnormal muscle overactivity, fixed structural limitations, and muscle force imbalance. Treatment should be guided by the patient's functional goals and the primary factor restricting performance. Task-oriented motor training remains fundamental when voluntary motor control is impaired, with BCI-based closed-loop training as a potential adjunct in selected patients. Focal, functionally significant muscle overactivity caused by abnormal neural drive may be considered for selective or hyperselective peripheral nerve surgery, with DNB assisting patient selection. Fixed structural restrictions may require tendon or soft-tissue procedures, while muscle force imbalance may benefit from tendon transfer or other dynamic reconstruction. When multiple impairments coexist, combined reconstruction followed by targeted motor retraining and comprehensive reassessment may be appropriate. Overall, neuro-musculoskeletal functional reconstruction should follow an individualized pathway linking functional goals, dominant pathophysiology, treatment targets, and outcomes. Given the variable evidence quality, no universal treatment sequence or combination strategy is currently supported.
42949009: The current update of the "Recommendations for the Management of Thyroid Cancer in Adult Patients" is based on a critical appraisalof whether the recommendations published in 2022 by the Polish Scientific Societies and the National Oncology Strategy remain valid,and which statements require modification or updating in light of the American Thyroid Association (ATA) Guidelines published in 2025. We have also taken into account the most recent National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) recommendations, as well as guidelines from other international and European scientific societies addressing thyroid cancer, adapting them to the specific epidemiologicaland legal conditions in Poland. We decided that the current Recommendations would not include management of medullary thyroid cancer, as, in our opinion, the Polish Guidelines published in 2022 and 2024 remain up to date. The Recommendations are divided into two sections: "General Principles" and "Clinical Management". The "General Principles" sectionoutlines the key principles of thyroid cancer management, whereas the "Clinical Management" section specifies these principlesaccording to the risk of recurrence, incorporating the well-established and highly accurate ATA 2025 risk stratification system. Thus,the reader will find specific management recommendations depending on whether the patient has low-risk or high-risk thyroid cancer. The "Clinical Management" section includes a dedicated subsection outlining the recommended clinical approach to thyroid noduleswith indeterminate cytology. In these Recommendations, the management of anaplastic thyroid carcinoma and thyroid lymphomas is addressed in a separate subsection. In addition, brief information on other rare histological subtypes of thyroid cancer is also provided.
42949152:
PURPOSE: Patients with recurrent high-grade glioma have poor prognosis and limited treatment options. This pilot study evaluated the feasibility and potential clinical benefit of 177 Lu-PSMA therapy in this patient population.
PATIENTS AND METHODS: Eligible patients were selected for treatment based on positive 68 Ga-PSMA-PET findings. 177 Lu-PSMA (7.4 GBq/200 mCi) was administered at 6-8-week intervals and continued as long as well-tolerated. The safety, tolerability, and efficacy of 177 Lu-PSMA were assessed in each treatment cycle using PET/MRI, SPECT/CT, blood tests, neurological tests, and patient-reported outcome measures.
RESULTS: Ten patients were enrolled (WHO grade 4 glioblastoma, n=6; WHO grade 4 astrocytoma, n=1; WHO grade 3 astrocytoma, n=3). 68 Ga-PSMA-PET before treatment demonstrated tumor uptake in 9 patients (median SUV max : 6.4, IQR: 4.2-9.0). Six patients received treatment (20 cycles total; range: 1-7 per patient). Median absorbed dose per cycle was 0.9 Gy (IQR: 0.8-1.1) for tumors, 2.6 Gy (IQR: 1.9-3.2) for kidneys, and 1.7 Gy (IQR: 1.5-2.2) for parotid glands. No CTCAE grade 3-4 toxicities occurred. The most common patient-reported symptoms were fatigue, transient xerostomia, and nausea. Median survival from treatment initiation was 187 days (range: 87-756) and the median progression-free survival was 45 days (range: 41-335). MRI (RANO 2.0) demonstrated stable disease in half of the patients during all or part of the treatment course.
CONCLUSIONS: 177 Lu-PSMA therapy was feasible and well-tolerated. Radiologic stabilization was observed in a subset of patients, but strategies to increase tumor dose delivery may be needed to improve efficacy.
42949849:
PURPOSE: Robotic-assisted radical prostatectomy (RARP) causes postoperative impairments. Although prehabilitation has shown benefits in surgical populations, data specific to RARP remain limited. We evaluated whether multimodal prehabilitation improves early postoperative health-related quality of life (HRQoL), functional recovery and mental health.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: Prospective, single-center randomized trial including men with prostate cancer scheduled for RARP (May 2022- September 2024). Participants were randomized to a 4-week multimodal prehabilitation program including physical and pelvic floor muscle training, nutritional counselling and psychological support or to usual care. The primary outcome was change in the EORTC QLQ-C30 global health status score from baseline to 1 month after surgery. Secondary endpoints included functional and perioperative outcomes at 1, 3 and 6 months.
RESULTS: Ninety-five of 100 randomized patients were analyzed (53 prehabilitation, 42 control). At 1-month post-operatively, global health status score was higher in the prehabilitation group (adjusted mean difference +15 points, 0-100 scale; 95% confidence interval (CI) 7-22; p<0.001). Improvements at 1-month were also observed in several HRQoL domains, mental health and urinary continence (mean difference in ICIQ-UI SF -2.7; p=0.032). No differences were detected in physical performance or erectile function. Prehabilitation benefits attenuated over time, with the global health status difference decreasing to +4.5 points at 6 months (-1.9 points/month; p = 0.024), whereas improvements in selected HRQoL domains, mental health, and ICIQ-UI SF were maintained throughout follow-up.
CONCLUSIONS: Multimodal prehabilitation before RARP is feasible and should be integrated into clinical practice, as it enhances postoperative recovery and patient-centered outcomes.
42950963: Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) hyperscanning enables the simultaneous measurement of the brain activities of various individuals performing shared or interactive tasks and estimating their interbrain synchrony (IBS). IBS is believed to reflect different mechanisms, including social bonding or mutual prediction, and to be modulated by various factors, such as familiarity or the experimental paradigm. In this systematic review, we assessed fNIRS hyperscanning studies conducted until January 2026, focusing on the experimental protocols and their relation to reported IBS findings. Specifically, we aimed to understand task dependence of IBS results and how they differ between different kinds of dyad compositions. Additionally, we investigated other parameters, including IBS metrics and the association between IBS and psychological, behavioral, and physiological measures. We reviewed a total of 206 studies, revealing a predominance of joint action task paradigms. Our findings suggest that IBS is modulated by the characteristics of dyad composition. IBS is usually higher in dyads with closer bonds, and varies with gender, although a universal pattern could not be identified. Furthermore, the study protocols employed also seem to have an influence on IBS, as participants who engage in face-to-face interactions frequently show higher IBS than those who do not. We also observed that IBS is often associated with behavioral and psychological outcomes, while the association with physiological outcomes is scarcely studied. Future research should consistently include details about dyad familiarity and sex pairings, expand to underrepresented dyads, and investigate IBS across diverse paradigms and contexts in association with other metrics.
42951680:
BACKGROUND: Prostate Imaging Reporting and Data System (PI-RADS) 3 lesions often undergo biopsy despite a low positive predictive value (< 25%) for clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa), defined as International Society of Urological Pathology (ISUP) Grade Group ≥ 2.
PURPOSE: To determine whether mean apparent diffusion coefficient (mADC), alone or with prostate-specific antigen (PSA)-based metrics, improves zone-specific PI-RADS 3 classification for csPCa detection.
STUDY TYPE: Retrospective, single-center.
POPULATION: One hunderd and seventy-one males (71 ± 8 years) with 191 PI-RADS 3 lesions who underwent multiparametric MRI and targeted biopsy.
FIELD STRENGTH/SEQUENCE: 3 T, T2-weighted turbo spin-echo imaging, single-shot echo-planar diffusion-weighted imaging, and fat-suppressed dynamic contrast-enhanced T1-weighted gradient echo sequences.
ASSESSMENT: mADC, PSA, PSA density (PSAD), prostate volume, and body mass index were analyzed.
STATISTICAL TESTS: Logistic regression and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses assessed associations with malignancy and diagnostic performance.
RESULTS: mADC was significantly lower in cancers than non-cancers in 133 PZ lesions (885 ± 165 vs. 1068 ± 168 × 10-6 mm2/s) and 58 TZ lesions (670 ± 127 vs. 832 ± 179 × 10-6 mm2/s). In the PZ, mADC alone, and with PSAD showed no significantly different area under the curve (AUC, 0.79 vs. 0.80, p = 0.28). A combination of mADC and PSAD would result in hypothetical estimated lesion-level biopsy avoidance. In the TZ, combining mADC with PSAD yielded significantly higher AUC than mADC alone (0.88 vs. 0.77, difference: 0.109 [95% CI: 0.010-0.208]). This combination would result in hypothetical estimated lesion-level biopsy avoidance in 58 of 82 non-cancers (71%) while missing one csPCa in the PZ, and 27 of 35 noncancerous lesions while missing one csPCa in TZ.
DATA CONCLUSION: mADC combined with PSAD showed a significant increase in discrimination in the TZ, suggesting improved PI-RADS 3 stratification; independent validation is required before clinical implementation.
EVIDENCE LEVEL: 3.
TECHNICAL EFFICACY: 2.
42951720:
BACKGROUND: Na[¹⁸F]F PET/CT is increasingly used to evaluate treatment responses in metabolic bone diseases (MBDs), where conventional serum biomarkers and structural imaging fail to show local dynamic changes. The performance and utility of Na[¹⁸F]F PET/CT in these diseases, however, has not been fully explored. We systematically evaluated the contemporary use of quantitative Na[¹⁸F]F PET/CT for measuring MBD treatment responses.
METHODS: Current review was prospectively registered on PROSPERO (CRD420261413536) and follows PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Electronic databases were searched for clinical studies using quantitative Na[¹⁸F]F PET/CT in MBDs. Risk of bias was assessed via QUADAS-2, ROBINS-I and QUIPS. Results were synthesized narratively.
RESULTS: Thirteen studies (n=14-72 patients; 358 total cases) met inclusion criteria, focusing on chronic kidney disease-mineral and bone disorder (CKD-MBD, n=9 studies) and fibrous dysplasia/McCune-Albright syndrome (FD/MAS, n=4 studies). Two longitudinal studies evaluated therapeutic response: denosumab in FD/MAS yielded comparable reductions in total lesion metabolic activity across moderate (-64.9%) and high doses (-67.0%), while turnover-guided therapy in CKD-MBD significantly reduced bone kinetic flux (Ki). Remaining literature comprised cross-sectional and observational cohorts. Here, PET kinetic (Ki, FUR) and volumetric metrics (TV, TA, TLF) correlated strongly with bone formation rates and circulating biomarkers. Ki and background-adjusted uptake ratios (SUVR) discriminated bone turnover states with high accuracy (ROC AUC up to 0.98), outperforming serum parathyroid hormone in CKD-MBD. Reporting of reconstruction settings was highly variable; only one study explicitly noted EARL scanner accreditation and none documented compliance with EARL Standard 1 or 2. Risk of bias was primarily driven by small cohort sizes, attrition and unadjusted confounding.
CONCLUSIONS: Quantitative Na[¹⁸F]F PET/CT provides high diagnostic accuracy for tracking regional turnover and treatment response in benign MBDs.
