However, clinical adoption is hindered by a lack of harmonized EARL-compliant protocols, unstandardized outcome metrics and a reliance on small, unadjusted cohorts.
42951722:
PURPOSE: To conduct a systematic review and meta-analysis on the uptake value of fibroblast activation protein (FAP)-targeted PET (FAPI PET) across different histopathological and molecular breast cancer subtypes. As a secondary objective, to perform head-to-head comparisons with [18F]FDG PET.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: This systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. Major medical literature databases were systematically searched to include studies in which biopsy-proven breast cancer patients were recruited, and uptake values for malignant primary tumors and/or metastatic lesions were reported. Meta-analyses were conducted in R (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria) using the meta package.
RESULTS: Thirty-four studies met the inclusion criteria. Pooled average SUVmax in the primary malignancy was 11.74 (95%CI:9.95-13.53) on FAPI PET. In the studies in which SUVmax values were provided for both FAPI PET and [18F]FDG PET, on average, the pooled SUVmax was 6.19 (95%CI:4.26-8.12) higher on FAPI PET compared to [18F]FDG PET. FAPI PET showed rather consistently high uptake across all analyzed breast cancer subtypes (pooled estimates ranged from 10.27 to 19.99). Notably, in studies reporting SUVmax for IDC on both FAPI PET and [18F]FDG PET, FAPI PET showed 11.33 (95%CI:8.36-14.30) higher pooled uptake. Similarly, in studies providing SUVmax for luminal A breast cancer, FAPI PET showed 7.85 (95%CI:5.45-10.25) higher uptake compared to [18F]FDG PET.
CONCLUSION: Our findings suggest that FAPI PET exhibits consistently high semi-quantitative values across breast cancer subtypes and can potentially enhance lesion conspicuity and detection rate, particularly in low-[18F]FDG-avid malignancies.
42952439: Spinal cord injury (SCI) leads to sensorimotor deficits and secondary health complications, such as pain and cognitive impairment. At the brain level, functional reorganization phenomena occur, affecting resting-state (rs) networks devoted to higher-order information processing. However, most studies have focused on changes of the sensorimotor cortex, and current results are partially conflicting. This systematic review aims to synthesize studies on rs networks implicated in SCI and to investigate whether functional connectivity (FC) is affected beyond the somatomotor network, which may be linked to secondary health conditions. Original seed-based whole-brain rs FC (rsFC) studies comparing individuals with SCI and controls were retrieved from Medline, Embase, and Web of Science (last searched on 02.09.2024). Each seed was assigned to a standard rs network, and studies were grouped based on seed network and direction of changed rsFC. Risk of bias was assessed using the quality assessment tool by the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute. The study was registered in Prospero (CRD42024574397). Nine included studies provided 11 datasets (151 SCI individuals, 208 controls). RsFC changes were found between the somatomotor and ventral attentional network, between the ventral attention network and the frontal pole, and between the cerebellum and regions of the attentional and default-mode networks in SCI compared with controls. We propose a model of SCI with widespread network changes that extend beyond the somatomotor network. Our findings call for deeper examination of functional brain changes following SCI in clinical settings and thorough investigations of higher-order cognitive functions.
42952994:
BACKGROUND: Brain imaging is central to the structural, functional, metabolic, and neurophysiological characterization of neurological disease, yet interpretation remains constrained by heterogeneity in acquisition, annotation, expertise, and clinical context.
OBJECTIVE: This systematic literature review evaluates recent artificial intelligence approaches for brain imaging and computer-aided diagnosis, with emphasis on methods, modalities, neurological diseases, diagnostic tasks, datasets, validation practices, and translational limitations.
METHODS: The review followed PRISMA 2020 and covered peer-reviewed English-language studies published from January 2020 through June 2026. Eight information sources were searched using database-specific terms for artificial intelligence, neuroimaging, neurological disease, and diagnostic analysis. The search identified 1,078 records; 236 duplicates were removed, 842 unique records were screened, 258 full texts were assessed, and 123 studies were included after a record-level eligibility re-audit. Heterogeneous evidence was synthesized narratively and by descriptive mapping rather than meta-analysis.
RESULTS: MRI was frequently represented in the included studies and auxiliary mapping data; CT was commonly used in acute stroke and intracranial hemorrhage; PET supported selected molecular and differential-diagnosis studies; fMRI and diffusion imaging were used for network and white-matter analysis; and EEG extended the scope to neurophysiological diagnosis. CNN and three-dimensional networks were commonly reported, while attention, Transformer, graph, self-supervised, generative, multimodal, and foundation-model approaches appeared in selected recent studies. Stroke, dementia, and brain tumors were frequently represented, but heterogeneous populations, outcomes, and incomplete validation extraction precluded ranking diseases, modalities, architectures, or validation strategies.
CONCLUSION: The evidence suggests movement from task-specific pattern recognition toward multimodal and context-rich decision support in selected settings, but it does not establish uniform methodological superiority or clinical maturity. Dependable translation requires patient-level data governance, transparent reporting, uncertainty estimation, independent multicenter testing, prospective workflow evaluation, and clinically meaningful endpoints.
42954286:
BACKGROUND: Placental site trophoblastic tumor (PSTT) is a rare gestational trophoblastic neoplasm characterized by local invasiveness and marked vascularity. Surgical management may be associated with substantial bleeding risk and loss of fertility, particularly when complicated by uterine arteriovenous fistula (UAVF). High-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU) may provide a fertility-preserving adjunctive approach in selected cases.
CASE PRESENTATION: A 23-year-old woman presented with persistently plateaued serum human chorionic gonadotropin levels following hysteroscopic management for suspected incomplete abortion. Imaging revealed a deeply invasive hypervascular uterine lesion with UAVF, raising strong suspicion of gestational trophoblastic neoplasia. Given her strong desire for fertility preservation and high surgical risk, ultrasound-guided HIFU was performed as an initial vascular-modulating intervention. Subsequent expert pathological review confirmed PSTT.
RESULTS: HIFU achieved significant reduction in lesion perfusion and vascular flow, as confirmed by Doppler ultrasound and contrast-enhanced MRI. Although complete tumor ablation was not achieved due to lesion size and deep invasion, subsequent low-dose chemotherapy resulted in complete biochemical remission accompanied by radiologic regression of residual lesions. No major HIFU-related complications were observed, and normal menstrual function resumed during follow-up.
CONCLUSION: HIFU is a technically feasible and safe fertility-preserving adjunct for vascular modulation in hypervascular PSTT complicated by UAVF. While HIFU alone may not achieve definitive oncologic control in large or deeply invasive lesions, it can serve as a bridging strategy to reduce tumor perfusion and vascularity, facilitating subsequent systemic therapy in carefully selected patients. This approach demonstrates the potential role of HIFU as a bridging vascular-modulating strategy within multimodal fertility-preserving management.
42954436:
OBJECTIVES: Fetal ventriculomegaly (VM) is a common prenatal finding with heterogeneous etiology and unpredictable outcome, yet its management remains among the least standardized in fetal medicine. This study aimed to establish expert consensus on key decision points in the prenatal management of fetal VM, and to systematically map the domains of persistent uncertainty as a structured framework for future research priorities.
METHODS: A two-round modified Delphi study was conducted with an international panel of experts in fetal medicine, selected through a systematic review of publications that included more than 50 cases of VM over the preceding decade. Round 1 comprised 39 multiple-choice questions, with consensus achieved when ≥ 75% of panelists selected a single answer option; items that did not reach consensus were reformulated into Likert-scale statements for Round 2, which comprised 60 statements rated on a 9-point Likert scale. In Round 2, consensus was defined by two simultaneous criteria: ≥ 75% of valid respondents scoring in the agreement (score, 7-9) or disagreement (score, 1-3) zone, with an interquartile range of ≤ 2. Non-consensus domains were classified using a post-hoc taxonomic framework into three categories: absent evidence (Type 1), divergent clinical frameworks (Type 2) and undefined construct (Type 3), which could occur independently or in combination.
RESULTS: Of 56 experts who completed Round 1, 45 (80%) also completed Round 2. In Round 1, consensus was reached on 20/39 (51%) questions. In Round 2, 6/60 (10%) statements reached positive consensus and four (7%) reached negative consensus; 50 (83%) did not reach consensus. Over the two rounds, consensus was achieved on standardized measurement technique, three-tier grading, comprehensive neurosonographic and investigative work-up, individualization of the timing of fetal magnetic resonance imaging, stepwise neurosurgical referral and delivery management of fetal VM. Classification of non-consensus domains identified 15/50 (30%) items as Type 1, 16/50 (32%) as Type 2, 4/50 (8%) as Type 3 and 15/50 (30%) as Type 1+3. Ventricular asymmetry, the largest non-consensus cluster with 12 items, was classified as Type 1+3 in 11/12 (92%) statements, reflecting the simultaneous absence of prospective outcome data and of a universally accepted operational definition.
CONCLUSIONS: This Delphi study provides structured expert-derived guidance, primarily applicable to specialist and referral settings, on the prenatal management of fetal VM across key clinical domains. Beyond consensus recommendations, we propose that the original contribution of this study is a hypothesis-generating taxonomic map of persistent uncertainty, classifying unresolved domains by the nature of the underlying evidence gap and identifying the specific prerequisites (definitional, methodological or empirical) required before consensus can be achieved. © 2026 International Society of Ultrasound in Obstetrics and Gynecology.
42954438:
BACKGROUND: Mechanical thrombectomy (MT) is a key intervention for acute ischemic stroke due to large vessel occlusion (LVO). Various MT strategies - stent retriever (SR), aspiration (Asp), and their combination (SR + Asp) - are widely used, but the optimal approach remains unclear.
OBJECTIVES: This network meta-analysis (NMA) aimed to compare the efficacy and safety of these techniques using evidence from randomized controlled trials (RCTs).
MATERIALS AND METHODS: A Bayesian NMA was conducted, including RCTs evaluating different MT techniques in LVO-related stroke. The primary outcome was successful recanalization (thrombolysis in cerebral infarction ≥2b) and good functional outcome (modified Rankin Scale ≤2 at 90 days). Secondary outcomes included all-cause mortality at 90 days and symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage (sICH) within 24 h. Odds ratios (ORs) with 95% credible intervals (CrIs) were calculated using a Bayesian random-effects model.
RESULTS: Twenty-seven RCTs were analyzed. Within the current evidence network, SR demonstrated the highest probability of good functional recovery (OR = 2.27; 95% CrI: 1.72-3.02) and successful recanalization (OR = 13.6; 95% CrI: 3.12-75.0). SR + Asp demonstrated the highest probability of reducing 90-day mortality (OR = 0.771; 95% CrI: 0.638-0.929). Rates of sICH were broadly comparable across thrombectomy strategies, although SR and SR + Asp showed higher estimated odds than standard treatment (ST).
CONCLUSIONS: This NMA suggests that SR thrombectomy has the highest probability of achieving successful recanalization and favourable functional outcomes, whereas combined (SR + Asp) showed the highest probability of reducing mortality within the current evidence network. These probability-based rankings should be interpreted cautiously because they were derived from a heterogeneous network with limited direct head-to-head comparisons. Future adequately powered randomized trials directly comparing thrombectomy strategies are required before definitive recommendations can be made.
42954786: Pulmonary hypertension (PH) is a progressive disease associated with high morbidity and mortality. PH is classified into five groups based on underlying pathophysiology and etiology: pulmonary arterial hypertension (group 1); PH due to left heart disease (group 2); PH secondary to lung disease (group 3); pulmonary artery obstruction, including chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) (group 4); and PH due to unclear or multifactorial mechanisms (group 5). Radiologists play a major role in the multidisciplinary evaluation of patients with PH alongside specialists in pathology, pulmonary medicine, and cardiology. Given the widespread use of CT, imaging may be the first modality to suggest PH and plays a central role in the diagnosis and management of CTEPH. This review describes the pathophysiology of the five PH groups and emphasizes imaging findings that raise suspicion for PH. Discussion includes the roles of CT and MRI in PH evaluation, risk stratification, and assessment of treatment response, as well as the current applications of multienergy CT, echocardiography, and cardiac MRI in PH management. Keywords: CT Angiography, CT-Dual Energy, CT, MR Imaging, Pulmonary Arteries, Pulmonary, Echocardiography, Thorax, Vascular, Pathology, Pulmonary Hypertension, Chronic Thromboembolic Disease, Chronic Thromboembolic Pulmonary Hypertension, Pulmonary Embolism, Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension, Pulmonary Venoocclusive Disease, Pulmonary Capillary Hemangiomatosis, Pulmonary Hypertension Groups, Dual-Energy CT, Photon-counting CT, Spectral CT © RSNA, 2026.
42955037: Biliary tract cancers, comprising gallbladder cancer and intrahepatic and extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, are uncommon but aggressive malignancies that are often diagnosed at an advanced stage. Accurate staging is critical because patients with localized disease may be candidates for curative resection, whereas those with unresectable or metastatic disease are triaged to systemic and palliative therapy. This document reviews the evidence for imaging in five clinical scenarios: locoregional staging of gallbladder cancer, locoregional staging of cholangiocarcinoma, staging of distant metastatic disease, posttreatment evaluation, and surveillance. Contrast-enhanced CT and MRI of the abdomen are the mainstays of locoregional assessment, whereas CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis and FDG-PET are used for distant staging and follow-up. The American College of Radiology Appropriateness Criteria are evidence-based guidelines for specific clinical conditions that are reviewed annually by a multidisciplinary expert panel. The guideline development and revision process support the systematic analysis of the medical literature from peer reviewed journals. Established methodology principles such as Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation or GRADE are adapted to evaluate the evidence. The RAND/UCLA Appropriateness Method User Manual provides the methodology to determine the appropriateness of imaging and treatment procedures for specific clinical scenarios. In those instances where peer reviewed literature is lacking or equivocal, experts may be the primary evidentiary source available to formulate a recommendation.
42955038: Endometrial cancer is the most common gynecologic malignancy in the United States, and accurate pretreatment evaluation is essential for risk stratification, treatment planning, and detection of recurrent disease. This evidence-based review summarizes imaging recommendations for patients with established endometrial cancer undergoing pretreatment assessment, surveillance, or evaluation for suspected recurrence. MRI pelvis without and with intravenous contrast is usually appropriate for assessment of local tumor extension across histologic subtypes and grades. For aggressive histologic tumor types, or when metastatic disease is suspected, CT chest, abdomen, and pelvis with intravenous contrast and FDG-PET/CT are usually appropriate for evaluation of nodal and distant metastases. Routine imaging surveillance is usually not appropriate for asymptomatic patients with treated low- or intermediate-risk disease, whereas CT may be appropriate in selected asymptomatic high-risk patients. MRI pelvis, CT chest, abdomen, and pelvis, and FDG-PET/CT are usually appropriate for suspected recurrence. The American College of Radiology Appropriateness Criteria are evidence-based guidelines for specific clinical conditions that are reviewed annually by a multidisciplinary expert panel. The guideline development and revision process support the systematic analysis of the medical literature from peer reviewed journals. Established methodology principles such as Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation or GRADE are adapted to evaluate the evidence. The RAND/UCLA Appropriateness Method User Manual provides the methodology to determine the appropriateness of imaging and treatment procedures for specific clinical scenarios. In those instances where peer reviewed literature is lacking or equivocal, experts may be the primary evidentiary source available to formulate a recommendation.
42955836: Meckel diverticulum is the most common congenital anomaly of the gastrointestinal tract, yet it is frequently asymptomatic. Meckel diverticulum poses unique diagnostic challenges due to its variable manifestation and infrequent visualization at imaging. The authors review the embryology and anatomy of Meckel diverticulum, its normal radiologic appearances, and its complications and their management. Complications of Meckel diverticulum occur in up to 4%-9% of patients. Symptomatic Meckel diverticulum is more common in children but can also be seen in adults. A giant Meckel diverticulum, presence of ectopic gastric or pancreatic tissue, or adjacent adhesions and bands are associated with a higher likelihood of a symptomatic manifestation. The most common complications include small-bowel obstruction, gastrointestinal bleeding, and diverticulitis. Children more commonly present with gastrointestinal bleeding, while diverticulitis is more common in adults. Small-bowel obstruction can occur at any age and can be secondary to inversion of Meckel diverticulum, intussusception, volvulus, internal or external hernias, neoplasms, enteroliths, congenital bands, or postinflammatory changes. When a patient presents with acute abdomen or gastrointestinal bleeding, the choice of imaging modalities includes CT or US, with the latter preferred in the pediatric population. Technetium 99m-pertechnetate scintigraphy (Meckel scan) can be additionally performed to evaluate rectal bleeding in younger patients. MRI is reserved as a problem-solving tool. Meckel diverticulum should be differentiated from its common imaging mimics (eg, the appendix, ileal duplication cyst, and mesenteric small-bowel diverticulum). When Meckel diverticulum is not visualized at imaging, the radiologist still plays a key role by raising suspicion for an underlying Meckel diverticulum and identifying other critical imaging findings that can inform clinical management. An understanding of the common clinical manifestations associated with Meckel diverticulum and a systematic imaging approach can improve preoperative diagnosis and patient management.
42955837: Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) is a chronic fibroinflammatory cholangiopathy characterized by multifocal biliary strictures, cholestasis, and an increased risk of hepatobiliary malignancy and liver failure. MRI and MR cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) are central to diagnosis, surveillance, and risk stratification. Recent consensus guidelines from the International PSC Study Group emphasize standardized reporting for PSC with MRI and MRCP. Beyond anatomic assessment, established and emerging quantitative and functional imaging biomarkers include liver stiffness measurements, T1 mapping, extracellular volume fraction, and relative hepatobiliary phase enhancement. Imaging-based scoring systems such as Assessment of Noncontrast MRI for Advanced Liver Imaging (ANALI) scores provide additional prognostic information and correlate with clinical outcomes and established risk models. Hepatocyte-specific contrast-enhanced MRI allows evaluation of biliary excretion and regional liver function, facilitating identification of functional strictures and parenchymal dysfunction. The authors review current MRI and MRCP reporting standards, prognostic scoring systems, and evolving functional MRI techniques, with an emphasis on practical implementation in clinical radiology practice. ©RSNA, 2026 See the invited commentary by Ba-Ssalamah in this issue.
42955840: Vascular abnormalities are less common in the hand and wrist than in the lower extremities but can result in significant morbidity if unrecognized or untreated. The unique vascular architecture of the hand and wrist, with a dense network of arterial anastomoses, confers resilience to ischemia, but the superficial location makes them vulnerable to trauma and occupational injury. The authors describe and illustrate a comprehensive multimodality imaging approach to the diagnosis and evaluation of vascular abnormalities of the hand and wrist. They begin with an overview of vascular anatomy and normal variants, including a persistent median artery. Multimodality imaging, including US, CT angiography, MR angiography, and digital subtraction angiography, is reviewed with a focus on strengths, limitations, and clinical utility. Dynamic imaging techniques and photon-counting CT are highlighted for their evolving roles. A wide spectrum of vascular diseases, including atherosclerosis, trauma, iatrogenic injury, embolism, hypothenar hammer syndrome, hand-arm vibration syndrome, vasculitis, and frostbite, as well as their imaging appearances, are discussed. Vascular anomalies, including vascular malformations and vascular neoplasms, are also reviewed. The role of imaging in hand transplantation is addressed. The authors provide a framework for recognizing vascular diseases in the hand and wrist and selecting the appropriate imaging modality. Familiarity with vascular anatomy, imaging findings, and clinical context is essential for timely diagnosis, guiding management, and preserving limb function.
42955959: Anatomical changes during head and neck radiotherapy can impact dose distribution. Adaptive radiotherapy (ART) aims to address these changes, but the optimal strategy remains uncertain. To systematically evaluate whether the current evidence supports routine full re-optimization in ART for head and neck cancer by synthesizing dosimetric and clinical outcomes reported across different ART strategies. A systematic review was conducted according to PRISMA guidelines. Nine eligible studies evaluating ART strategies in head and neck cancer were included for qualitative synthesis. ART consistently improved target coverage and organ-at-risk sparing across diverse adaptive workflows. However, improvements in locoregional control, survival, toxicity, and quality of life were inconsistent across studies, and substantial heterogeneity existed in adaptation timing, imaging guidance, and planning target volume (PTV) margins. Current evidence demonstrates consistent dosimetric advantages of ART, but does not directly establish whether routine full re-optimization is necessary for all patients. Owing to the heterogeneity of ART strategies and limited direct comparative evidence, the optimal extent and timing of adaptive replanning remain uncertain and require further prospective investigation.
42956386:
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Accurate assessment and prognostication of patients with acute disorders of consciousness (DoC) after severe brain injury remain a substantial clinical challenge. Resting-state fMRI (rs-fMRI) measures spontaneous, temporally correlated brain activity in the absence of external stimulation and provides objective insight into the integrity of large-scale neural networks that support brain function. Emerging evidence suggests that assessing neural integrity using rs-fMRI may improve outcome prediction in patients with acute DoC. This review summarizes the current evidence of rs-fMRI as an assessment tool during the acute phase of severe brain injury.
METHODS: Following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines, we conducted a systematic literature search using MEDLINE and Embase databases from January 2006 to March 2026. Eligible studies included peer-reviewed empirical investigations of adult patients with acute DoC (<28 days postinjury) that examined associations between rs-fMRI measures and clinical outcomes. The systematic review protocol was registered in the PROSPERO International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (CRD420251085923).
RESULTS: Of 396 studies screened, 30 met eligibility criteria. Across these studies, a total of 800 patients (mean age = 48, 69% male) were scanned at a weighted average of 9.31 days after intensive care unit admission. Ten studies included patients exclusively with traumatic brain injury, 8 with cardiac arrest, 2 with encephalopathy, and 10 included mixed etiologies. The most frequently assessed resting-state networks were the default mode (n = 20) and executive control networks (n = 11), followed by visual (n = 6), salience (n = 6), sensorimotor (n = 6), and auditory (n = 5) networks. Across studies, significant associations between rs-fMRI measures and outcome were consistently reported, despite heterogeneity in methodology. The most commonly reported patient outcomes were functional or neurologic status, assessed at hospital discharge or between 3 and 12 months postinjury.
DISCUSSION: Current evidence consistently demonstrates that rs-fMRI acquired during the acute phase of brain injury is associated with neurologic and functional outcomes in patients with DoC. In addition, rs-fMRI may help identify patients more likely to recover consciousness and achieve favorable functional outcomes by characterizing the integrity of large-scale brain networks. However, substantial heterogeneity and small sample sizes limit comparability across studies. Standardized acquisition and analysis frameworks, along with larger prospective studies, are needed to validate the clinical utility of rs-fMRI and support translation into an assessment tool after brain injury.
42957053: The right ventricle (RV) is recognized as a critical contributor to cardiovascular outcomes. Cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) has emerged as the reference standard for comprehensive RV assessment, enabling precise evaluation of ventricular volumes, function, flow, and tissue characterization. In this review, we provide a state-of-the-art overview of RV imaging using CMR. We first outline the anatomical and physiological features that distinguish the RV from the left ventricle. Next, we highlight the key technical challenges in imaging the RV, notably its complex geometry, prominent trabeculation, and thin myocardial wall. We then summarize current clinical CMR approaches, including cine imaging for volumetric assessment, phase-contrast techniques for flow quantification, and methods for tissue characterization such as late gadolinium enhancement. Additionally, we discuss advanced and emerging CMR techniques aimed at overcoming current RV imaging limitations, including high-resolution three-dimensional cine imaging, four-dimensional flow imaging, parametric mapping, and novel reconstruction strategies. These innovations hold promise for improving accuracy, reproducibility, and mechanistic insight into RV structure and function. Finally, we review the clinical role of CMR in major RV pathologies, including congenital heart disease, pulmonary hypertension, arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy, and tricuspid regurgitation. Across these conditions, CMR provides vital diagnostic and prognostic information, with growing evidence supporting its role in guiding clinical management. As technical advancements continue and standardization improves, CMR is poised to transform RV evaluation from a historically challenging endeavor into a precise and impactful component of cardiovascular care.
42957079:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate longitudinal adoption of ACR Thyroid Imaging Reporting and Data System (TI-RADS) terminology, report-level documentation of fine needle aspiration (FNA) criteria, and associated ultrasound-guided FNA practice in a large multisite radiology network.
METHODS: In this retrospective, multicenter study across 89 imaging sites, 304,455 diagnostic thyroid ultrasound reports (Current Procedural Terminology [CPT] 76536) and 11,246 ultrasound-guided FNA reports (CPT 10005/10006) from 2017 through 2023 were analyzed. A linked prebiopsy cohort of 994 diagnostic reports immediately preceding FNA was examined. Automated text mining identified TI-RADS language and documentation of nodules meeting ACR size-based FNA thresholds. Trends were assessed using Cochran-Armitage, Spearman correlation, and χ2 tests.
RESULTS: TI-RADS language increased from 1.6% of thyroid ultrasound reports in 2017 to 54.1% in 2023. Among 112,036 TI-RADS-containing reports, 11,845 (10.6%) documented nodules meeting FNA criteria. This proportion declined from 23.3% in 2017 to 8.0% in 2023, an absolute decline of 15.3 percentage points (Z = -47.94; P < .001) and was inversely correlated with annual TI-RADS adoption across the seven annual observations (ρ = -1.000; P < .001). Among FNA-indicated reports, TR4 predominated (56.9%), followed by TR3 (21.0%) and TR5 (19.4%); category distribution shifted significantly over time, although the effect size was small (χ2 = 169.91; P < .001; Cramér's V = 0.086). In the prebiopsy cohort (n = 994), 498 (50.1%) contained TI-RADS language. The FNA rate per 1,000 thyroid ultrasound examinations remained stable (29.1 in 2017; 27.7 in 2023).
CONCLUSIONS: ACR TI-RADS terminology use increased substantially but remained incomplete. Increasing terminology use was associated with declining report-level FNA eligibility. Biopsy appropriateness could not be assessed from report-level documentation alone.
42957864:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the impact of a prostate imaging quality (PI-QUAL) v2 lecture on the accuracy and inter-reader agreement of prostate MRI image-quality assessment among radiologists and technologists from diverse professional backgrounds and institutions, and to evaluate its role in institutional-level quality improvement through a quality control (QC) process.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: Ten participants (five radiologists and five technologists) from five different hospitals independently evaluated 15 prostate MRIs before and after a standardized PI-QUAL v2 lecture. Reference scores were established by two experienced radiologists. Concordance with reference was assessed using accuracy and balanced accuracy. Inter-reader agreement was measured using percent agreement (PA) and Gwet's AC1. Subgroup analyses were conducted based on participant characteristics. For the quality assurance and QC (QA/QC), each center submitted 15 prostate MRIs before and after the lecture. Image quality was evaluated centrally to assess institutional improvement.
RESULTS: Overall accuracy increased from 66.7% to 76.7%, and balanced accuracy increased from 62.9% to 84.2%; the mixed-effects model indicated significantly higher post-lecture accuracy (p = 0.038). Accuracy was also higher across all subgroups. Inter-reader agreement improved from PA 57.6% to 72.6% and Gwet's AC1 from 0.214 to 0.466. Through the QA/QC process, three centers initially failed to meet PI-QUAL v2 technical criteria. After feedback, all post-intervention scans achieved PI-QUAL v2 scores > 1.
CONCLUSION: A structured PI-QUAL v2 lecture improved both the accuracy and inter-reader agreement of prostate MRI image-quality assessments among diverse evaluators. Incorporating QA/QC further enhanced institutional image quality. PI-QUAL v2 training is a feasible strategy for standardizing prostate MRI quality.
KEY POINTS: Question Does a structured PI-QUAL v2 lecture for radiologists and technologists improve prostate MRI quality assessment performance and institutional imaging practice across institutions? Findings PI-QUAL v2 training improved accuracy (66.7% to 76.7%) and inter-reader agreement in prostate MRI quality assessment, while QA/QC feedback enhanced institutional imaging quality. Clinical relevance statement Structured PI-QUAL v2 education combined with quality assurance and quality control feedback improves evaluator consistency and institutional prostate MRI quality, facilitating standardized image-quality assessment and broader implementation of high-quality prostate MRI in clinical radiology.
42958856: Thermal ablation (TA) is established for benign thyroid nodules, recurrent thyroid carcinoma, and low-risk papillary thyroid microcarcinoma. Its role in papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) remains unsettled. This review examines evidence and guideline recommendations for TA in T1b and selected T2 PTC. T1b studies suggest encouraging local control and low permanent morbidity, but retrospective, geographically concentrated, heterogeneous evidence leaves surgery as the reference treatment. Four retrospective T2 reports indicate a narrower procedural safety margin. The same anatomical selection criteria apply across T1a, T1b, and T2 disease; however, as tumors enlarge, fewer patients meet oncological and technical requirements, and incomplete staging or margins have greater consequences.
42959106:
BACKGROUND: Imaging-guided interventional radiotherapy (IG-IRT) is the standard of care for locally advanced cervical cancer but remains time-consuming and operator-dependent. Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a promising tool to improve efficiency and reproducibility.
METHODS: A systematic review was conducted according to PRISMA 2020 guidelines, searching PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science for studies published between 2010 and 2026 investigating AI-based imaging applications in cervical IRT. Eligible studies included original research evaluating segmentation (targets and organ at risk), planning, reconstruction, image registration and applicator selection.
RESULTS: Fifty-two studies were included. Deep learning-based segmentation showed variable performance across anatomical structures and studies, with Dice coefficients approaching or exceeding 0.90 for some organs at risk and target volumes in the best-performing models. Individual studies reported shorter processing times, reduced contouring variability, accurate applicator reconstruction, and potential support for applicator selection. However, the substantial methodological and clinical heterogeneity precluded direct comparisons among AI approaches.
CONCLUSIONS: The available studies suggest that AI may support the automation of selected workflow steps and assist treatment-related decision-making in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy. While several applications have achieved high technical performance, most remain at the proof-of-concept stage, and robust external validation and prospective clinical evaluation are needed before routine clinical adoption.
42961651: Major trauma is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, particularly among children and young adults, and rapid identification of life- or limb-threatening injuries through imaging is crucial. Whole-body CT (WBCT) is central in modern major trauma pathways, enabling early detection of critical findings to guide multidisciplinary decision-making. Our study suggests three evidence-based recommendations for WBCT in major trauma care. First, WBCT protocol selection should be tailored to haemodynamic status and injury mechanism rather than applied as a single universal protocol; incorporating split-bolus, dual-phase and triple-phase techniques, each offering different diagnostic strengths and trade-offs. Special considerations can apply in pregnancy, paediatric patients, and those with contrast allergy, who may require modified imaging strategies. Second, radiologists should play an active role in trauma multidisciplinary team (MDT) care, assisting in protocol adaptation and directly directing the trauma team to life-threatening injuries. Third, systematic, checklist-driven radiological reporting with defined communication pathways improves trauma diagnostics, increases reporting reproducibility and strengthens trauma decision-making. These recommendations are best implemented through locally agreed, mechanism and physiology-based WBCT protocols, supported by trauma-trained radiologists embedded in scanning processes and multidisciplinary trauma care. KEY POINTS: Whole-body CT enables rapid and comprehensive assessment of patients with major trauma and suspected multisystem injury. Radiologists play an active role in trauma team care through real-time CT assessment and early identification of life-threatening injuries. Modern trauma imaging should incorporate standardised, protocol-driven acquisition and structured image interpretation.
42961727: Accurate bronchopulmonary segment delineation on computed tomography (CT) is essential for segmentectomy planning, computer-assisted thoracic interventions, and fine-grained quantitative lung analysis. However, segment-level parenchymal partitioning remains technically challenging because intersegmental boundaries are often subtle or indistinct on routine CT, requiring bronchovascular priors-particularly airway and vascular trees-to guide anatomically plausible delineation. This review presents an imaging informatics-based synthesis of CT-based pulmonary segment delineation, covering conventional multi-stage pipelines and recent deep learning frameworks, including convolutional neural networks (CNNs), graph neural networks (GNNs), implicit neural representations, and continuous spatial modeling parameterized by Gaussian mixture models (GMMs). We organize evaluation practices into three complementary categories: direct ground-truth-based metrics, indirect anatomy-referenced criteria, and reference-free plausibility or quality-control measures. We further review publicly available datasets, annotation protocols, and benchmark limitations that currently hinder reproducible and fair segment-level comparison. From a deployment perspective, we discuss clinical workflow requirements, robustness challenges, and the need for anatomy-aware and data-efficient methods. Illustrative analyses of a single cystic fibrosis (CF) case using a distance-based method show how removal of a segmental airway branch or omission of lobar constraints can substantially alter the resulting segment territories. These case-specific observations motivate broader robustness evaluation, uncertainty-aware quality control, boundary-level plausibility checks, and deployment-oriented validation beyond conventional overlap-based metrics.
42963303:
BACKGROUND: In patients with coronary artery disease (CAD), both functional and anatomical assessment are required to guide revascularization. Computed tomography-derived fractional flow reserve (FFR-CT) has emerged as a tool to implement both anatomical and non-invasive functional assessment of coronary stenoses in a single setting, but the association with long-term outcomes is still controversial. We aimed to assess the correlation between FFR-CT with long-term outcomes in patients with CAD.
METHODS: Reconstructed individual patient data were provided by the authors of a previous report published in a previous issue of the Journal. The primary outcome was study-defined major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), while secondary outcomes included the single components of the primary outcome. One-stage and two-stage meta-analyses with mixed-effect and random-effect models were conducted, stratifying patients according to FFR-CT thresholds of 0.8. Heterogeneity sources were explored through sensitivity analyses.
RESULTS: Fifteen studies were pooled from the reconstructed data, encompassing a total of 14,437 patients, with 6335 (43.9%) having a FFR-CT<0.8. After a median follow-up of 16.8 (7.2-35.8) months, FFR-CT<0.8 was associated with higher rates of MACE (hazard ratio: 4.93; 95% CI 4.16-5.84; p < 0.001), myocardial infarction (incidence rate ratio [IRR] 4.38; 95% CI 1.16-16.54; p = 0.029), ischemia driven revascularization (IRR 2.90; 95% CI 1.31-6.44; p = 0.009), and any revascularization (IRR 9.62; 95% CI 3.02-30.61; p < 0.001). Results were consistent across sensitivity analyses.
CONCLUSIONS: In patients with CAD, an FFR-CT <0.80 is associated with a three-to four-fold increase in MACE, being primarily driven by significant increase in myocardial infarction, ischemia-driven revascularization and any revascularization.
42963548:
BACKGROUND: Age-based mammography screening fails to account for individual breast cancer risk variation, particularly in Asian populations where prospective evidence is absent.
METHODS: The BREAst Screening Tailored for HEr (BREATHE) study is a multicentre prospective cohort of 4,513 women aged 35-59 years recruited across six Singapore clinical sites (2021-2023). Risk-stratified screening recommendations were assigned using a five-year absolute risk threshold of 0.9% (equivalent to the population-average risk of an average 50-year-old Singaporean woman) to initiate screening based on polygenic risk score (PRS) and Gail model, as well as mammographic density, family history, abnormal prior screening. Two independent breast cancer case cohorts provided comparative analyses: Singapore Breast Cancer Cohort (SGBCC, n = 2,782) and Malaysian Breast Cancer Genetic Study (MyBrCa, n = 2,466); combined n = 9,761.
RESULTS: Among 2,003 healthy women aged 40-49 years currently recommended annual mammography, risk stratification downgraded 776 (38.7%) to no screening and 960 (47.9%) to biennial as they were not in the top 2.5th percentile of PRS and Gail risk and did not have any additional risk indicators. Of 41 breast cancers diagnosed after BREATHE enrolment, 35 (85.4%) occurred in women assigned to screening-eligible categories at baseline. Risk stratification combining PRS and Gail model captured 68-69% of cases aged 40-49 in SGBCC (n = 1,184) and MyBrCa (n = 1,122), versus ~ 54% by PRS alone. Relative to cases meeting screening criteria for both PRS and Gail model, PRS-missed cases were enriched for progesterone receptor negativity (OR 1.24; 95% CI 1.01-1.52), tumour size ≥ 50 mm (OR 1.43; 95% CI 1.02-2.00), and germline protein-truncating variants (PTVs) in breast cancer predisposition genes (OR 1.53; 95% CI 1.03-2.29).
CONCLUSIONS: Risk stratification combining PRS with classical risk factors reshapes mammography recommendations in Asian women. However, due to the limited number of events in BREATHE, this finding requires evaluation in larger prospective studies. PRS-missed cancers exhibit a biologically aggressive profile, defining the current limits of common-variant prediction and identifying the biology that future precision screening tools must address.
42965591: Despite advances in cross-sectional imaging, adrenal biopsy plays a role in a small subset of lesions that remain indeterminate after complete imaging work-up or in which tissue diagnosis would alter management. Anatomic constraints around the adrenal glands can make safe percutaneous access technically challenging. This technical report describes a transfemoral transcaval approach to biopsy of a right adrenal mass directly abutting the inferior vena cava (IVC) that was not safely accessible by conventional percutaneous routes. Additionally, a concise review of contemporary adrenal biopsy indications and access routes is performed. Adapted from transfemoral transcaval liver biopsy, the technique uses right common femoral venous access, positioning of a reshaped metal guide cannula within the IVC at the level of the lesion adjacent to the right renal vein, and deployment of a core biopsy needle across the caval wall under combined fluoroscopic and ultrasound guidance, with cone-beam CT confirmation of needle position and completion venography to exclude caval injury. Diagnostic tissue was obtained without periprocedural complication; histopathology demonstrated an unexpected pheochromocytoma, a finding discussed here in detail due to its implications for pre-procedure biochemical evaluation. This limited experience demonstrates technical feasibility in carefully selected patients. The safety and comparative effectiveness of the technique require evaluation in larger series.
42965614: Advances in laser lithotripsy have driven major progress in endourology over the past three decades. Although Holmium:YAG and, more recently, thulium-based lasers are widely used, the fundamental mechanisms governing laser-to-stone interaction remain incompletely understood and controversial. A systematic literature search was performed in MEDLINE/PubMed and Embase from database inception to December 2025. Experimental and translational studies investigating physical, thermal, chemical, or mechanical mechanisms of laser-to-stone interaction were included. Data on experimental models, laser parameters, environmental conditions, measurement techniques, and mechanistic outcomes were extracted. Methodological quality was assessed using the QUINN scale. Because of the marked heterogeneity in study designs, populations, and outcome measures, a meta-analysis could not be performed. Consequently, the findings were synthesized through a structured narrative systematic review. Twenty experimental studies published until 2025 were included. Early investigations primarily supported photothermal and thermochemical ablation under contact conditions. Contemporary studies employing high-speed imaging, hydrophone measurements, and controlled environmental manipulation consistently demonstrated that non-contact dusting is dominated by cavitation-driven erosion mediated by asymmetric bubble collapse. Recent evidence further identified confined intra-crater bubble expansion as the important mechanism underlying fracture of impacted stones. Mixed thermal and mechanical effects were observed under transitional conditions, particularly in the presence of pulse modulation and optimized energy transmission. Methodological quality improved over time, with the highest rigor observed in recent mechanistic studies. Laser lithotripsy is governed by distinct, strategy-dependent physical mechanisms rather than by a single dominant process. Contact ablation is primarily photothermal, non-contact dusting is cavitation-driven, and impacted stone fracture relies on confined bubble expansion. These findings support an integrated mechanistic framework linking laser settings, fiber positioning, environmental conditions, and stone geometry. This framework provides a rational basis for optimizing clinical strategies and guiding future technological development in laser lithotripsy.
42965692: Susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI) is a high-resolution 3D gradient-echo (GRE) magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) technique that combines magnitude and phase information to increase sensitivity to blood products, iron, calcification, thrombus, and venous structures. In routine practice, SWI should be interpreted together with source magnitude images, filtered phase images, processed SWI images, and minimum-intensity projection (minIP) images, keeping in mind blooming and other artefacts, as well as vendor-dependent phase conventions. Its most established role is in brain MRI, particularly in: suspected cerebral amyloid angiopathy; baseline and follow-up assessment of amyloid-related imaging abnormalities with haemosiderin deposition (ARIA-H) during anti-amyloid therapy; traumatic brain injury; multiple sclerosis work-up, when assessment of the central vein sign or paramagnetic rim lesions is clinically relevant; neuro-oncology; and vascular malformations. Overall, these constitute the core recommended brain scenarios for SWI supported by moderate to high levels of evidence. Outside neuroradiology (e.g., musculoskeletal, abdominal, breast, pelvic, and cardiac imaging), SWI remains promising but less standardised and should currently be reserved for selected problem-solving indications. KEY POINTS: SWI should be acquired as a high-resolution 3D GRE sequence and interpreted together with source magnitude images, filtered phase images, and post-processed minIP images, keeping in mind blooming and other artefacts, as well as vendor-specific phase conventions. SWI should be included in brain MRI protocols when haemorrhagic or microvascular susceptibility findings are expected to affect diagnosis or management, especially in cerebral amyloid angiopathy, anti-amyloid therapy monitoring, traumatic brain injury, and neuro-oncology or multiple sclerosis work-up. Outside neuroradiology, SWI can be used as a targeted problem-solving adjunct rather than as a routine sequence.
42966408:
BACKGROUND: Anhedonia is a core symptom of major depressive disorder (MDD) and may persist despite otherwise effective treatment. Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) is a widely used and effective intervention for severe and treatment-resistant depression, however, its specific effects on anhedonia remain poorly characterized.
OBJECTIVE: To conduct a systematic review and meta-analysis examining ECT-associated changes in anhedonia in adults with MDD.
METHODS: A systematic search was conducted across Embase, MEDLINE, PsycINFO, and Scopus. Studies were eligible if they included adults with MDD, administered ECT as a treatment, and assessed anhedonia using a validated scale. Standardized mean change ratios (SMCs) were calculated and pooled using a random-effects model.
RESULTS: Eleven studies were included in the systematic review, of which five provided quantitative data for meta-analysis. Across 132 participants, ECT was associated with a significant improvement in anhedonia severity (SMC = 1.02; 95% CI, 0.63-1.42).
CONCLUSIONS: ECT was associated with a statistically significant improvement in anhedonia among adults with MDD. However, given the small number of included studies and non-randomized pre-post designs, these findings should be interpreted cautiously. Future ECT studies should assess anhedonia as an outcome, while using a validated anhedonia measure.
42966440:
PURPOSE: To compare, using Bayesian network meta-analysis, the effectiveness and safety of treatments and embolic agents for symptomatic uterine fibroids.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: A PRISMA-compliant systematic review of randomized controlled trials (PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library; inception through July 2026) compared, via two prespecified Bayesian network meta-analyses, (1) uterine artery embolization (UAE) with hysterectomy, myomectomy, magnetic resonance-guided focused ultrasound, microwave ablation, and laparoscopic uterine artery occlusion, and (2) embolic agents used during UAE. Primary outcomes were technical success and major complications for treatment strategies, and complete/near-complete fibroid infarction for embolic agents; reintervention was secondary in both networks.
RESULTS: Twenty-three RCTs (N=2,055 women) were included. Technical success and major complication rates did not differ significantly across treatment strategies or embolic agents in the Bayesian analysis, though frequentist analysis showed slightly higher technical success with hysterectomy than UAE (RR, 1.09; 95% CI, 1.02-1.17). Myomectomy had significantly lower reintervention than UAE (OR, 0.21; 95% CrI, 0.10-0.40). Several Bayesian associations emerged for polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) particles versus tris-acryl gelatin microspheres (TAGM), including higher complete infarction (OR, 4.8; 95% CrI, 1.0-40), higher reintervention (OR, 5.3; 95% CrI, 1.4-28), and divergent findings with PVA700-900; none was reproduced in the frequentist analysis.
CONCLUSION: UAE did not differ significantly from alternative strategies in procedural success or safety, but myomectomy showed greater durability. Evidence is insufficient to establish definitive embolic-agent differences. Treatment strategy appears to influence outcomes more than embolic material, supporting individualized selection and larger trials.
42966551:
BACKGROUND: Antipsychotics (APs) induce functional, anatomical, and metabolic brain changes in schizophrenia, but the nature and clinical significance of these effects remain debated. Focusing on first-episode psychosis (FEP) allows distinction between medication-induced and illness-related brain changes and facilitates identification of early predictors of treatment response.
DESIGN: Following PRISMA guidelines (PROSPERO: CRD42021240369), we systematically reviewed longitudinal neuroimaging studies in FEP with the objective of 1) identifying APs-induced brain changes, 2) identifying brain changes associated with clinical improvement, and 3) exploring the potential of neuroimaging biomarkers to predict treatment response.
RESULTS: Eighty-six studies were included: 26 structural, 27 functional, and 16 metabolic, including 33 studies specifically addressing predictive biomarkers of treatment response. Across modalities, APs induced measurable brain changes within days to weeks of treatment Ainitiation, particularly in the striatum, thalamus, and prefrontal cortex (PFC), key regions of the striato-thalamo-cortical network. Increased basal ganglia gray matter volume was the most consistent anatomical finding; cortical findings, particularly in the PFC, were more heterogeneous, with both increases and decreases in thickness reported across studies. Functionally, APs normalized abnormal striatal activity and connectivity, correlating with improvement in positive symptoms. In contrast, no reliable imaging correlate has been identified for changes in negative or cognitive symptoms. Metabolic studies showed increased N-acetylaspartate in the thalamus and PFC and normalization of glutamate levels in associative and limbic regions. Baseline brain characteristics, particularly less severe structural or functional abnormalities in the striatum and anterior cingulate cortex, predicted better outcomes.
CONCLUSION: Together, these findings suggest that APs primarily act through modulation and normalization of striato-cortical circuits, with preserved neuroplasticity favoring recovery. Integrating multimodal neuroimaging and computational approaches may advance biomarker-based, individualized treatment strategies in early psychosis.
42966553: The ability to remember where objects are located is a fundamental cognitive function particularly vulnerable to aging and neurodegenerative disease. Previous functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) research has combined object-location memory (OLM) with broader spatial memory and navigation tasks, resulting in inconsistent findings. This systematic review and coordinate-based activation likelihood estimation (ALE) meta-analysis isolated OLM to characterize brain regions engaged during encoding and retrieval in healthy adults, with additional exploratory analyses of age effects. Searches of PubMed, PsycInfo, and the Cochrane Library identified 21 eligible task-based fMRI studies comprising 622 participants. Twelve studies contributed to an encoding ALE, which identified significant spatial convergence in left and right ventral occipitotemporal regions encompassing the fusiform and parahippocampal gyri. The left cluster was supported by 8 of 12 experiments, survived all leave-one-experiment-out iterations, and was recovered by an independent coordinate-based framework, supporting a robust ventral occipitotemporal substrate for OLM encoding. An OLM retrieval ALE including four studies yielded no significant convergence, most likely reflecting the limited number of eligible studies. Retrieval findings were therefore synthesized narratively. These studies most frequently implicated the hippocampus and precuneus, suggesting a different regional pattern from encoding, although the phases were not statistically compared. Only three studies directly compared age groups, suggesting altered hippocampal engagement during retrieval in older adults. By isolating OLM from broader spatial-memory constructs, this review identifies a robust encoding substrate while highlighting current research gaps that need to be addressed. This review was preregistered on PROSPERO (CRD420251023695).
42966675:
BACKGROUND: The blinded placebo-controlled PROTEUS (Perioperative Treatment with Erleada United with Surgery) study demonstrated that adding 1-yr perioperative apalutamide plus androgen-deprivation therapy (ADT) benefited patients with high-risk localized prostate cancer or locally advanced prostate cancer (HR-LPC/LAPC) who were undergoing radical prostatectomy with pelvic lymph node dissection (RP).
OBJECTIVE: This substudy evaluated 1-yr perioperative apalutamide plus ADT versus standard-of-care (SOC) RP.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: Patients with newly diagnosed HR-LPC/LAPC were randomized 1:3 to open-label perioperative apalutamide (240 mg/d) plus ADT (six 28-d cycles before and after RP) or RP.
OUTCOMES MEASUREMENTS AND STATISTICAL ANALYSIS: The primary end point was event-free survival (EFS), defined as time to biochemical failure, local/regional recurrence, distant metastasis, or death. Secondary/other end points included metastasis-free survival (MFS) by conventional or prostate-specific membrane antigen positron emission tomography (PSMA PET) imaging, MFS by conventional imaging, and time to first subsequent therapy; p values were nominal. Time-to-event end points were analyzed with the Kaplan-Meier method and stratified Cox proportional hazards models adjusted for the randomization stratification factors to estimate hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs).
RESULTS AND LIMITATIONS: In total, 408 patients (median age 66 yr [interquartile range 62-71]) were randomized: perioperative apalutamide plus ADT, n = 102; RP, n = 306. Median follow-up was 37.4 mo in patients without EFS events. Perioperative apalutamide plus ADT significantly improved EFS compared with RP alone (median not reached vs 19.1 mo; estimated 3-yr event-free rates 63% vs 41%; HR 0.38; 95% CI 0.26-0.55; p < 0.001). Because of the nonconstant HR over time, indicating that the proportional hazards assumption was not met, a post hoc restricted mean survival time analysis was performed. This analysis estimated that the average event-free time during the first 36 mo was 31.7 mo (95% CI 30.3-33.1) with perioperative apalutamide plus ADT versus 20.7 mo (95% CI 19.1-22.4) with RP alone, a difference of 11.0 mo (95% CI 8.8-13.1; p < 0.001). MFS by conventional or PSMA PET imaging favored perioperative apalutamide plus ADT over RP alone (estimated 3-yr event-free rates 87% vs 78%; HR 0.49; 95% CI 0.26-0.90; p = 0.019), and the hazard of subsequent therapy was reduced by 71% (HR 0.29; 95% CI 0.20-0.43; p < 0.001). MFS by conventional imaging showed no difference between study groups (estimated 3-yr event-free rates 94% vs 92%; HR 0.74; 95% CI 0.30-1.82; p = 0.5). Grade 3-4 treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 31 patients (31%) receiving perioperative apalutamide plus ADT versus 62 patients (22%) receiving RP.
CONCLUSIONS: Perioperative apalutamide plus ADT improved EFS and delayed subsequent therapy compared with SOC. Together with the blinded PROTEUS main study, these results support perioperative apalutamide plus ADT as a new therapeutic option for selected patients with HR-LPC/LAPC who are fit for surgery and 1-yr systemic therapy.
42966716: The year 2025 brought long-term outcome data supporting coronary CT angiography (CCTA)-guided management of stable chest pain, a proposed reframing of coronary artery disease around atherosclerosis rather than ischemia, and the first large-scale real-world evaluation of a national artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled CT-derived fractional flow reserve (FFR-CT) program. This review summarizes selected advances in cardiovascular computed tomography (CCT) published in print or online during 2025. The studies span coronary artery disease outcomes and prevention, quantitative plaque analysis, photon-counting detector CT, coronary artery calcium scoring, pericoronary inflammation imaging, AI and machine learning, structural and congenital heart disease, and consensus and training documents. For each study we summarize the design, principal findings, limitations, and likely clinical implications, and we close with the barriers, including technical standardization, vendor-specific thresholds, equitable access, and the need for randomized outcome trials, that must be addressed before many of these advances can be implemented broadly.
42969098:
BACKGROUND: Levothyroxine (LT4) is widely prescribed, often for subclinical hypothyroidism (SCH), despite limited evidence of clinical benefit in patients without overt hypothyroidism. This updated systematic review synthesizes current evidence on biochemical, symptom, and safety outcomes following thyroid hormone (TH) discontinuation.
METHODS: In this systematic review, electronic databases were searched from inception to September 25, 2026, for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and observational studies evaluating supervised TH discontinuation. Primary outcomes included postdiscontinuation thyroid function, symptom changes, adverse events, and need for therapy reinitiation. Random-effects meta-analyses estimated pooled proportions and mean differences.
RESULTS: Twenty-three studies met inclusion criteria (22 observational studies, 1 RCT), most evaluating LT4 monotherapy discontinuation (n = 20). Twenty-one studies including 2020 participants reported categorical TH status outcomes; 37% of participants (CI, 26%-48%; I2 = 94.5%) remained euthyroid after discontinuation. Euthyroidism was less frequent among patients with initial overt hypothyroidism (11%, CI, 2%-38%) than among those with SCH (41%, CI, 21%-65%). Eleven studies (1104 participants) reported TH reinitiation, with 60% of patients restarting therapy (CI, 39%-78%; I2 = 97.1%) in the overall population, increasing to 87% (CI, 66%-96%) among those with overt hypothyroidism. Thyroid autoantibody positivity, heterogeneous thyroid ultrasound findings, and higher baseline TSH levels were associated with therapy reinitiation. Thyroid-related symptoms after discontinuation were generally unchanged, and adverse events were uncommon.
CONCLUSIONS: Approximately 37% of patients remained euthyroid after TH discontinuation, with higher success rates among those initially treated for SCH. These findings support consideration of deprescribing in selected patients, particularly those without clear indications for treatment initiation, using a structured approach with close biochemical monitoring and predefined criteria for therapy reinitiation.
42970749:
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Genetic testing is increasingly used in presurgical evaluation, but the yield of resection and ablation across germline genetic epilepsies remains uncertain.
METHODS: We conducted a systematic review of MEDLINE (PubMed) and Scopus and added cases from 3 institutional cohorts and the Pediatric Epilepsy Research Consortium (PERC) databases, including individuals with pathogenic/likely pathogenic germline variants besides tuberous sclerosis who underwent resection or laser ablation. Etiologies were grouped into biologically informed categories (GATORopathies, vascular, overgrowth, copy number variants (CNVs), channelopathies, synaptopathies, and other). Primary outcome was seizure freedom (Engel I) at the last follow-up. Group comparisons used Fisher exact and Kruskal-Wallis tests (α = 0.05; Bonferroni when applicable). Prespecified sensitivity analyses stratified by lesional status, excluded GATORopathies, and restricted to literature-only cases.
RESULTS: We included 224 literature cases (65 studies), 36 institutional cases, and 12 PERC cases (n = 272). The median follow-up was 24 months (interquartile range 12-48.0). Seizure freedom was achieved in vascular disorders 14/19 (73.6%), GATORopathies 79/120 (65.8%), CNVs 18/31 (58.0%), overgrowth 9/16 (56.6%), channelopathies 13/43 (30.0%), synaptopathies 4/18 (22.2%), and other 11/25 (44.0%) (overall p < 0.001). Among cases with available imaging results, 208/253 (82.2%) had epileptogenic MRI lesions, including 64% of channelopathies and 80% of the synaptopathies. In univariate contrasts (each category vs all others), odds of seizure freedom were higher for vascular disorders (2.64-fold, 95% CI 0.87-9.65) and GATORopathies (2.41-fold, 95% CI 1.44-4.09), and lower for synaptopathies (∼4.2-fold lower, OR 0.23, 95% CI 0.05-0.77) and channelopathies (∼4.5-fold lower, OR 0.22, 95% CI 0.09-0.48). Direction and magnitude were consistent across prespecified sensitivity analyses (lesional only, literature only, exclusion of GATORopathies).
DISCUSSION: Resective surgeries can be effective in germline genetic epilepsies, but outcomes vary by pathway. Disorders with discrete, lesional substrates (GATORopathies, vascular) show the highest likelihood of seizure freedom, whereas channelopathies and synaptopathies, despite the presence of MRI lesions, have substantially lower yields even in lesional cases. Prospective, genotype-aware surgical registries with standardized reporting (EEG, imaging, and pathology) and time-to-event outcomes are needed to refine the selection of surgical candidates and quantify seizure and non-seizure-related outcomes.
42971525:
PURPOSE: To review ctDNA and cfDNA as biomarkers after locoregional therapy in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and colorectal liver metastases (CRLM).
MATERIALS AND METHODS: PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and Web of Science were searched (July 2026) for ctDNA/cfDNA studies in HCC or CRLM patients undergoing TACE, Y90, or ablation; Newcastle-Ottawa Scale assessed risk of bias.
RESULTS: Eleven studies were included (eight HCC, three CRLM; n≈820). Pre-treatment ctDNA mutations predicted survival after TACE (CTNNB1: HR 5.3, 95% CI 1.4-20.6; TP53: HR 5.3, 95% CI 1.4-10.1; KEAP1: HR 22.0, 95% CI 2.2-221.0). A cfDNA/ctDNA score stratified progression-free survival after TACE (1.3 vs 10.3 months; p=0.002). ctDNA predicted death after ablation in HCC (HR 2.6, 95% CI 1.5-4.7; p=0.001) and recurrence in CRLM (HR 2.97, 95% CI 1.47-6.03; P=0.003). Y90 evidence was limited.
CONCLUSION: CtDNA and cfDNA correlated with treatment outcomes after locoregional therapy; evidence is heterogeneous and biomarker-driven trials are required before clinical implementation.
42971782:
BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Ventral and lateral spinal dural tears are common causes of spontaneous intracranial hypotension, each requiring different myelographic approaches for leak localization. Spine MRI can infer the presence of a dural tear but has limited utility in localizing leaks. One recent case series described several patients with isolated facet effusions at the site of lateral dural tears. We investigated whether the presence of an isolated facet joint effusion on spine MRI could predict the type and location of a dural tear in patients with spontaneous intracranial hypotension.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: We identified consecutive patients with precisely localized ventral or lateral dural tears on advanced myelography at three centers. A single neuroradiologist at each center assessed for isolated facet effusions on pre-myelographic spine MRIs, defined as fluid accumulation in a single facet joint that was visually greater than any other joint in the spine. Myelographic studies were reviewed to confirm leak type/location. The frequency of isolated facet effusions was compared between patients with lateral and ventral dural tears using Fisher's exact test. The proximity of facet effusions to leak level/side was assessed.
RESULTS: Sixty-four patients (32 ventral and 32 lateral dural tears) were included. All patients had epidural CSF on MRI. Isolated facet effusions were more common in patients with lateral dural tears (21/32, 66%) compared with ventral dural tears (0/32, 0%) (p < .001). The effusion was at the same level and side as the leak in 11/21 (52%) patients and within one ipsilateral spinal level of the leak in 7/21 (33%) patients. Contrast filling of a facet joint was seen in 9/21 (43%) cases and corresponded to the site of MRI effusion in 8/9 (89%).
CONCLUSIONS: Isolated facet joint effusions on spine MRI were seen exclusively in patients with lateral dural tears and were usually located at or within one ipsilateral spinal level of the leak. This finding may provide a useful imaging clue that there is an underlying lateral dural tear, which is helpful to plan optimal myelographic positioning and technique.
42972039: Quantitative MRI can characterize cartilage and other joint tissues beyond visible structural damage, but its contribution to individual management of knee osteoarthritis remains uncertain. This narrative review examines the evidence needed to interpret quantitative measurements, combine parameters, and report their uncertainty. An initial PubMed search in June 2026 was supplemented on 14 September 2026 by an updated PubMed search and broader Embase and Web of Science searches. Targeted full-text assessment addressed incremental value, outcome timing, validation, and measurement error. Selected development studies found better discrimination with integrated diffusion and relaxation measurements than with individual parameters, whereas other combined imaging models did not improve on simpler comparators. Longitudinal associations were outcome-specific, and independent external validation was limited. Treatment studies showed inconsistent agreement between imaging changes and symptomatic benefit. We propose a five-step interpretation framework that establishes the clinical question, verifies technical adequacy, assesses morphology and comparable reference data, evaluates measurement uncertainty, and separates observations from clinical inferences. Two hypothetical scenarios illustrate its application. Quantitative MRI currently provides its strongest support as a controlled research measurement. Demonstrated reproducibility, an appropriate comparator, and evidence of added decision value are required before a quantitative finding can justify patient-level diagnostic, prognostic, or treatment-response claims.
42972079: Adrenal masses are found on roughly 4-5% of abdominal imaging studies, and the proportion rises with age. Most are benign, non-functioning adenomas that need imaging characterization and hormonal screening but no intervention. The remainder, comprising metastases, adrenocortical carcinoma, pheochromocytoma and hormonally active adenomas, raise questions that computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging cannot always settle; in these cases image-guided procedures can help. Percutaneous biopsy is reserved for hormonally inactive lesions whose benignity imaging has not established and whose histology would change management. Adrenal venous sampling remains the reference method for lateralizing aldosterone excess in primary aldosteronism and therefore decides who is offered adrenalectomy, although success depends heavily on operator experience and local protocol. Thermal ablation has produced biochemical and blood-pressure responses in selected aldosterone-producing adenomas and local control of limited metastases, but the evidence is largely nonrandomized and does not establish equivalence with surgery. Transarterial embolization serves three purposes: hemostasis in adrenal hemorrhage, devascularization before resection of hypervascular tumors, and functional treatment of aldosteronism, now supported by one small randomized trial. Each procedure carries hazards peculiar to the gland (catecholamine crisis, adrenal insufficiency after bilateral treatment, non-target embolization) that shape patient selection and periprocedural monitoring. This review covers indications, technique, outcomes and complications for each. Surgery remains the treatment of choice for most operable patients. Interventional radiology is most useful when the indications for sampling, ablation or embolization are recognized early and discussed at the multidisciplinary meeting, not only after surgery has been declined.
42972263:
BACKGROUND: The use of erector spinae plane (ESP) block has been reported to decrease opioid requirements for patients undergoing bariatric and metabolic surgeries (BMS). We aim to systematically review and examine the evidence for the use of ESP block in BMS.
METHODS: MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, and CENTRAL electronic databases were searched for all studies on ESP block in BMS from database inception through 21st July 2025. Two reviewers independently assessed and selected studies, collected data, assessed the risk of bias and quality of evidence. The primary outcome for this review is opioid consumption in 24 h post-operation. Secondary outcomes include intraoperative opioid consumption, time to first request for analgesia, and postoperative pain scores.
RESULTS: Nine randomised control trials involving 613 patients were found to be eligible. ESP block significantly reduced opioid consumption in the first 24 h after surgery, with a mean oral morphine equivalent daily dose (oMMED) reduction of 36.94 mg (95% CI -60.85 to -13.03, p = 0.009, I2 = 94%). Trial sequential analysis (TSA) suggests a potential benefit of ESP block though this interpretation is limited by marked statistical heterogeneity. Time to first request for analgesia was significantly prolonged with ESP block. Intraoperative opioid requirements, time to first request for analgesia, and postoperative reported pain scores were reduced in the ESP block group.
CONCLUSIONS: Current evidence suggests that the bilateral ultrasound-guided ESP block may be a practical technique to improve perioperative pain control and reduce opioid usage in patients undergoing BMS. However, these findings must be interpreted with caution due to the very low to moderate certainty of evidence and high clinical heterogeneity.
42972273:
BACKGROUND: Intracranial aneurysms (IAs) affect up to 5% of the general population and pose a significant risk of subarachnoid hemorrhage if undetected or misclassified. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), particularly deep learning, have shown promise in enhancing aneurysm detection and outcome prediction. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to evaluate the diagnostic performance of AI in IA detection and reviewed its applications in rupture risk and outcome prediction.
METHODS: Following PRISMA guidelines, we screened major databases for studies reporting AI-based IA detection and/or outcome prediction. Eligible studies included comparisons of AI versus clinicians or AI-augmented interpretations. Pooled sensitivity, specificity, and interrater agreement (Fleiss' κ) were calculated. Outcome prediction studies were reviewed narratively.
RESULTS: Twenty studies (n = 20) met the inclusion criteria for meta-analysis. Pooled AI sensitivity and specificity were 0.96 and 0.95 respectively. However, substantial heterogeneity across studies was observed. These estimates should therefore be interpreted as exploratory summaries of reported study performance rather than definitive measures of real-world diagnostic accuracy. Subgroup analysis revealed robust AI performance for aneurysms > 3 mm (sensitivity: 0.98), while performance declined for < 3 mm lesions (sensitivity: 0.75). AI assistance improved clinician sensitivity to 0.92 and increased interrater agreement from κ = 0.67 to 0.86. Review of outcome prediction models showed promising AUCs (up to 0.96) for predicting rupture risk, aneurysm growth, and complications like vasospasm.
CONCLUSIONS: AI shows promising performance in intracranial aneurysm detection and outcome prediction, particularly when used as a decision-support tool alongside clinicians. While limitations remain-especially in detecting very small aneurysms and generalizability across centers-AI represents a valuable adjunct in neurovascular diagnostics. Future directions include improved training datasets, multicenter validation, and seamless clinical integration to realize the full potential of AI-assisted neuroimaging and risk stratification.
CLINICAL TRIAL NUMBER: Not applicable.
42972295:
BACKGROUND AND AIMS: Limited data exist on the prognostic value of parametric mapping and late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) in patients with acute myocarditis (AM). This meta-analysis aimed to investigate the prognostic value of LGE as assessed by using cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) in patients with AM, including more recent evidence. Additionally, the prognostic value of CMR parametric mapping was narratively reviewed.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: The systematic search was conducted in the PubMed and Scopus databases from inception to January 17, 2026 (PubMed) and January 20th 2026 (Scopus). 1296 records were found through the search. Finally, sixteen studies were included in this systematic review. Thirteen studies were included in the meta-analysis on association between LGE and clinical outcomes in AM. The composite endpoint was defined as MACE and/or one of the following endpoints: all-cause death, heart failure decompensation requiring hospitalization, heart transplantation, and recurrent AM. MACE was defined as a composite of cardiovascular death (including sudden death), sustained ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation, complete atrioventricular heart block requiring a pacemaker, and cardiogenic shock. Five studies were reviewed for the prognostic value of parametric mapping parameters. After initial calculations, it appeared that studies using broader composite endpoints than only MACE introduced substantial heterogeneity. Therefore, we have additionally conducted analysis incorporating only eight studies with MACE as the endpoint.
RESULTS: The presence of LGE was associated with higher odds of the composite endpoint. The unadjusted pooled OR demonstrated a significant relationship between the presence of LGE and higher chances of the composite endpoint (ORLGE(+) vs. LGE(-)[95% CI] = 3.02 [1.40, 6.51], p < 0.001) with high heterogeneity (I2 = 81.98%, p < 0.0001) On the qualitative level, results obtained in the MACE studies subgroup remained the same (ORLGE(+) vs. LGE(-)[95% CI] = 2.88 [2.01, 4.13], p < 0.0001).
