Heel hooks are associated with rotational knee trauma involving the anterior cruciate ligament and collateral ligaments, with injury patterns varying according to whether valgus-external rotation or varus-internal rotation forces are applied. Less common but highly characteristic injuries include combined lateral collateral ligament and anterolateral ligament injury with intact cruciate ligaments as a result of grappling guard positions and choke manoeuvres. This review summarises the major MMA techniques, associated mechanisms of injury, and key imaging findings relevant to musculoskeletal radiologists.
42993301: Transcatheter mitral valve replacement (TMVR) is a minimally invasive treatment option for symptomatic patients with severe mitral valve disease who are at high surgical risk or ineligible for open-heart surgery. The procedure has been associated with improved quality of life and functional status in selected patients and is increasingly recognized as a valuable therapeutic option in the management of complex mitral valve disorders. A multidisciplinary Heart Team is essential to ensure the clinical success of TMVR, and imaging specialists play a central role in the preprocedural assessment for patient and device selection, during the procedure, to guide and monitor the implantation, and after the procedure, for follow-up and for the correct diagnosis of short- or long-term complications. Echocardiography is required for initial diagnosis, for assessment of valve hemodynamics, intraprocedural guidance and monitoring. However, a multimodality approach including CT and/or MRI is frequently needed to correctly manage the phase of preprocedural planning and the diagnosis of complications. This consensus document, developed by a working group of experts from the European Society of Cardiovascular Radiology (ESCR) and the North American Society for Cardiovascular Imaging (NASCI), provides evidence-based recommendations for CT and cardiac MRI acquisition and post-processing in procedural planning and postprocedural evaluation in patients undergoing TMVR. Emphasis is placed on the technical requirements and standardization of imaging protocols, which must account for the heterogeneity of imaging equipment used in clinical settings. The document also outlines recommendations for all necessary preprocedural measures to ensure consistency, accuracy, and effective communication among specialists. KEY POINTS: Question How can CT and MRI acquisition, measurement, and reporting for TMVR be standardized to support accurate procedural planning, device selection, and follow-up? Findings This expert consensus provides recommendations for standardized CT and MRI protocols, key measurements, and structured reporting throughout TMVR planning and follow-up. Clinical relevance CT and MRI assessment may improve patient selection, procedural planning, multidisciplinary communication, and detection of postprocedural complications, supporting safer and more consistent TMVR practice across centers.
42993412: The 2025 update of the International Society for the Study of Vascular Anomalies (ISSVA) classification introduced several imaging-relevant changes, including the recognition of potentially unique vascular anomalies. Although the main framework for vascular tumors remains unchanged, with continued subdivision into benign, borderline, and malignant tumors, the most radiologically relevant structural changes concern vascular malformations, which were reorganized into fast-flow lesions, slow-flow lesions, and developmental anomalies of named vessels. These updates are important for radiologists because imaging plays a central role in assessing hemodynamic characteristics, defining lesion extent, and identifying findings relevant to procedural planning and multidisciplinary management. This educational review presents an author-derived four-step framework that organizes established MRI observations for peripheral and soft-tissue vascular malformations according to the structure and terminology of the 2025 ISSVA classification, including hemodynamic assessment, vascular components, tissue composition, lesion extent, and treatment-relevant anatomy. KEY POINTS: Question Imaging-relevant organizational and terminology changes in the 2025 ISSVA classification require practical guidance for consistent MRI assessment and reporting of peripheral and soft-tissue vascular malformations. Findings An author-derived four-step, flow-based framework organizes hemodynamics, dominant vascular components, tissue composition, lesion extent, and treatment-relevant anatomy into structured MRI assessment. Critical relevance statement The MRI-focused framework provides a practical way to apply the 2025 ISSVA classification consistently in image interpretation, terminology, and reporting of peripheral and soft-tissue vascular malformations.
42993545:
IMPORTANCE: As the population of older women with breast cancer grows, an increasing number are considered for primary endocrine therapy (pET), yet clinicians lack a framework for identifying which patients are appropriate candidates, resulting in reliance on chronologic age and life expectancy rather than tumor biology.
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate survival and variables associated with response duration for patients treated with pET.
DATA SOURCES: PubMed, MEDLINE, Web of Science, and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials were searched from inception through March 26, 2026.
STUDY SELECTION: Randomized clinical trials (RCTs) and non-RCT (observational) cohorts comparing pET with surgery in operable, nonmetastatic, estrogen receptor (ER)-positive breast cancer.
DATA EXTRACTION AND SYNTHESIS: Data were extracted independently by 2 reviewers per Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines. Hazard ratios (HRs) not directly reported were reconstructed from Kaplan-Meier curves. Randomized clinical trial-derived HRs for overall survival (OS) and breast cancer-specific survival (BCSS) were pooled using a random-effects model, given anticipated heterogeneity across trials spanning 5 decades and differing tumor biology criteria. Observational cohorts were analyzed descriptively, not pooled for comparative survival, given susceptibility to confounding by indication.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The main outcomes were OS and BCSS (RCTs) assessed using meta-analysis. Time to progression, salvage intervention rates, and variables associated with progression and mortality (observational cohorts) were assessed using descriptive analyses.
RESULTS: Twenty-nine studies (6 RCTs and 23 observational cohorts; 22 821 patients; overall median [IQR] age, 83.1 [77.0-85.0] years) met the inclusion criteria. Patients from RCTs were generally younger (median [IQR] age, 77.0 [75.8-78.0] years) than those from the observational studies (median [IQR] age, 84.0 [81.5-86.0] years). Treatment with pET was not associated with a statistically significant OS difference vs surgery (HR, 1.14; 95% CI, 0.98-1.33), though the point estimate favored surgery. Median time to progression ranged from 19.7 months (range, 13.5-26.0 months) in tumor biology-unselected, tamoxifen-era cohorts to more than 50 months in ER-selected and aromatase inhibitor-treated cohorts. Tumor biology was consistently associated with progression risk.
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: This systematic review and meta-analysis of more than 22 000 patients with ER-positive breast cancer found no statistically significant survival difference between pET and upfront surgery. Durable disease control under pET seemed to be concentrated in patients with favorable biology. These findings support a framework incorporating tumor biology and frailty, rather than age alone, to identify candidates for pET.
42993906:
INTRODUCTION: The goal of this project was to develop a joint European clinical practice guideline for the diagnosis and treatment of obstructed defecation syndrome (ODS), based on the best available evidence. These guidelines are intended to support all healthcare professionals involved in the care of patients with ODS, such as general practitioners, colorectal surgeons, gastroenterologists, gynecologists, radiologists, physiotherapists, and psychologists, as well as to provide accessible information for patients themselves.
METHODS: A multidisciplinary Guideline Development Group representing seven European scientific societies and including patient representatives formulated PICO-based clinical questions. Evidence was identified through a systematic literature review and assessed using the GRADE approach. Recommendations were formulated according to the available evidence and, where evidence was insufficient, as expert opinions.
RESULTS: The final guideline includes 28 statements (1 moderate grade evidence, 2 low grade evidence, 3 very low grade evidence, 22 expert opinion) covering the diagnosis, conservative and surgical management of ODS, including indications for various imaging modalities, functional tests, and both transanal and transabdominal surgical approaches. Multidisciplinary assessment is recommended throughout the diagnostic and therapeutic pathway. Conservative treatment represents the initial management strategy, with biofeedback recommended before surgery in patients with ODS and dyssynergic defecation who fail dietary and laxative treatment. Surgery should be reserved for selected patients with persistent symptoms after conservative treatment and considered following multidisciplinary pelvic floor evaluation.
CONCLUSION: These multidisciplinary European guidelines offer a comprehensive and evidence-based framework for the diagnosis and management of ODS. They are intended to promote standardized, high-quality care across Europe and to improve outcomes and quality of life for individuals affected by this complex condition. Given the limited quality of evidence supporting many interventions, individualized decision-making within a multidisciplinary setting remains central to ODS management.
42994434: Artificial intelligence in medical imaging is shifting from task-specific algorithms toward adaptable foundation models (FMs) and vision-language models (VLMs). However, applying these models to MRI remains challenging because clinical interpretation requires integrating multi-parametric, volumetric imaging across multiple sequences with clinical context. This systematic review evaluates 35 studies on unimodal FMs and multimodal VLMs in MRI, summarizing emerging architectures, downstream applications, and challenges to clinical translation. Current research is concentrated in neuroimaging, with diagnostic classification representing the most mature application. Segmentation and outcome prediction also show promise, whereas automated report generation remains limited by poor clinical fidelity despite strong linguistic fluency. Broader adoption is hindered by heterogeneous MRI acquisition, limited large-scale paired image-text datasets, and inadequate safety-focused evaluation metrics. Advancing clinical translation will require standardized multicenter datasets, stronger integration with electronic health records and pathology, robust evaluation frameworks, and improved model explainability.
42994658:
BACKGROUND AND AIM: Pericardial diseases encompass a broad spectrum of infectious, inflammatory, metabolic, traumatic, iatrogenic, and neoplastic disorders occurring in the setting of both localized and systemic conditions. Advances in understanding of the pathogenesis and diagnosis of pericardial disease have been substantial. Despite extensive literature on the clinical aspects of pericardial disease, relatively few studies have focused on its pathologic features.
METHODS AND RESULTS: An international panel from volunteer members of the Society for Cardiovascular Pathology and the Association for European Cardiovascular Pathology conducted a comprehensive review of the literature to develop a consensus document on the recommendations for pathologic evaluation of the parietal pericardium. This first document summarizes our state-of-the-art understanding of the etiological and morphological aspects of pericardial diseases, including pericardial effusions, cardiac tamponade, infectious and non-infectious pericarditis, and constrictive pericarditis, and incorporates updated clinical definitions and diagnostic criteria.
CONCLUSION: This consensus review highlights the role of pathology in the diagnosis of pericardial disease. Future efforts should explore establishing contemporary reference ranges for normal pericardial fluid volume, refining the pathologic characterization of pericarditis, correlating histopathologic findings with advanced cardiac imaging, and elucidating the molecular mechanisms driving the progression of pericardial fibrosis to constrictive disease.
42995280: Despite advances in pain management, pain remains a major global health challenge in both oncological and non-oncological patients. Long-term pharmacological treatment is often restricted by insufficient therapeutic benefit and adverse events, highlighting the need for alternative approaches such as image-guided pain therapies. The idea of treating pain with cold has been recognized for centuries, and today cryotherapy has emerged as a valuable minimally invasive option for pain management. Cryoablation refers to the destruction of tissue with extreme cold and has an increasing role, especially in the treatment of benign (e.g., osteoid osteoma), malignant bone (i.e., metastases), and soft tissue tumors, either with a curative or palliative intent. Cryoneurolysis is a related but distinct application, focusing either on peripheral nerve modulation or nerve destruction. Cryoneurolysis may be highly effective for the treatment of acute or chronic pain, including sympathetic neurolysis in cancer and non-cancer-related pain syndromes. The general approach in patients with tumor-related pain depends on whether the lesion itself can be ablated or not. In non-oncologic patients, cryoneurolysis of the responsible nerve is typically performed following a positive response to a diagnostic nerve block. Potential indications for cryotherapy are constantly evolving; however, evidence, especially for cryoneurolysis, is still limited and based mostly on single-center case series and retrospective studies. Standardized ablation protocols are lacking, and for the duration of cycles, most experts rely on imaging visualization and validated protocols. Equally important, successful integration of cryoablation and cryoneurolysis into daily practice requires structured workflows across different patient pathways and interdisciplinary management. KEY POINTS: Question Pain management remains a major global health challenge and an unmet need in oncological and non-oncological patients. Findings Cryotherapy, in terms of cryoablation and cryoneurolysis, is increasingly incorporated in multimodal curative and palliative pain care concepts, for treatment of acute and chronic pain syndromes. Clinical relevance Advancement and validation of standardized treatment protocols are needed to strengthen evidence and further enhance clinical implementation in interventional radiology practice and interdisciplinary patient care.
42996395:
BACKGROUND: Deep-learning (DL) models may extract nodal-risk information from breast or axillary ultrasound, but the relevant studies differ in anatomical input, preprocessing, reference standard, and validation design.
METHODS: We updated PubMed, Web of Science Core Collection, and Cochrane CENTRAL, with supplementary OpenAlex and Crossref searches and repeated backward and forward citation searching through 24 August 2026. Eligible studies evaluated a deep-learning model using ultrasound as the sole imaging modality for pretreatment binary axillary or sentinel nodal status in breast cancer, used surgical pathology as the reference standard, and reported an independent patient-level validation cohort with an exact or uniquely reconstructable 2 × 2 table. One cohort per study was selected using a prespecified hierarchy. Sensitivity and specificity were synthesized with a bivariate random-effects model and an HSROC curve.
RESULTS: Eleven studies comprising 1,027 validation patients were included. Pooled sensitivity was 0.75 (95% CI 0.66-0.81; 95% prediction interval 0.50-0.90) and pooled specificity was 0.89 (95% CI 0.83-0.93; prediction interval 0.66-0.97). The summary HSROC area was 0.81. The positive likelihood ratio was 6.60 (95% CI 4.29-10.42), the negative likelihood ratio was 0.29 (0.21-0.38), and the diagnostic odds ratio was 23.12 (12.89-41.50). Descriptive univariate I² values were 64.2% for sensitivity and 73.8% for specificity. Deeks' test did not indicate funnel-plot asymmetry (P = 0.677).
CONCLUSIONS: Ultrasound-based DL models showed moderate sensitivity and high specificity in selected validation cohorts. Wide prediction intervals, heterogeneous anatomical inputs and preprocessing, incompletely reported definitions of nodal positivity, and the geographic concentration of studies limit immediate clinical transportability. These models should be evaluated as adjuncts to, rather than replacements for, pathological axillary staging.

42996467:
BACKGROUND: The DWI-ASPECT score (DWI-ASPECTS) can aid patients' selection for thrombectomy. This systematic review aimed to evaluate clinicians' interrater and intrarater agreement on DWI-ASPECTS for anterior circulation stroke patients.
METHODS: We conducted a broad search of electronic databases (CINAHL, EBM Reviews, MEDLINE, EMBASE & EMBASE Classic) between January 1st, 2000, and September 9th, 2026. Our primary outcome was to collect data on any available measures of agreement for DWI-ASPECTS. Measures of agreement collected included ICC (intraclass correlation coefficient), weighted or unweighted kappa.
RESULTS: Out of 3,658 articles screened, nineteen studies reporting 37 measures of agreement were included in the review. Populations, methods, analyses, and results were heterogeneous (poor to excellent agreement), precluding a meta-analysis. For interrater agreement, measures of agreement using full scale ICC ranged from strong to excellent, ranged from poor to strong using unweighted kappa, and ranged from moderate to excellent using weighted kappa. Only four studies offered interrater agreement values on DWI-ASPECTS<6. Only two studies offered information on intrarater agreement values.
CONCLUSION: Data on the reliability of DWI-ASPECTS in acute ischemic stroke is scant, while the methodologies and results in the studies assessed are heterogeneous. More robust studies are required, particularly for strokes with DWI-ASPECTS <6.
42997494: Evidence-based medicine represents the systematic approach through which physicians today use the best available scientific evidence from clinical research to guide their clinical decision-making process. However, the emergence of artificial intelligence (AI), with its diverse models and potential applications in medicine, is leading to a new form of research driven by 'big data' and heterogeneous datasets, extending beyond conventional statistical analysis and thereby making AI literacy an increasingly essential competence for clinicians. Artificial intelligence applications in cardiology have shown potential to support disease diagnosis, risk prediction, workflow efficiency, and therapeutic decision-making. However, despite these opportunities, AI may also represent a technological barrier for many physicians, due to its mathematical foundations and the speed at which models evolve. A solid understanding of AI concepts is therefore necessary for cardiologists to critically interpret results and engage with this new research landscape. This scientific statement explores AI in cardiology from an educational perspective, outlining the key knowledge required to build adequate AI literacy. The goal is to enable cardiologists not only to avoid reliance on external experts for methodological decisions, but also to collaborate with greater insight and informed judgment.
42998128: Endolymphatic hydrops MRI is used for the diagnostic evaluation of patients with primary or secondary endolymphatic hydrops. Delayed intravenous post-Gd 3-dimensional fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (3D-FLAIR) and 3-dimensional real inversion recovery (3D-real IR) sequences are the most widely applied techniques, because they exploit subtle Gd-related signal differences between perilymph and endolymph. Yet image quality and diagnostic confidence depend on protocol design, and variation persists between institutions, scanners, and vendors. This educational review provides a visually oriented, practical framework for optimising endolymphatic hydrops MRI, focusing on three core determinants: acquisition parameters, post-processing strategies, and contrast-agent selection. The physical principles underlying key sequence-parameter choices are explained, including the use of long echo trains to maximise acquisition efficiency, prolonged repetition times to enhance the perilymphatic signal, and inversion times tailored to the selected repetition time to achieve effective suppression of the endolymphatic signal. Representative graphs and imaging examples illustrate how protocol modifications influence contrast and diagnostic performance. The review further discusses post-processing approaches and emerging artificial intelligence-based techniques, including deep learning reconstruction, as tools to improve image quality, shorten scan time, or support higher spatial resolution. Finally, the role of gadolinium-based contrast agents, scan delay, and clinical protocol design is also addressed. Four-hour delayed intravenous imaging remains the current standard, although sequence-specific timing, single- or two-step protocols, and half-dose high-relaxivity agents may offer opportunities for tailored imaging, reduced Gd exposure, and improved sustainability. By linking sequence principles to practical protocol choices, this review aims to support reproducible, high-quality hydrops MRI across clinical settings. KEY POINTS: Question Optimisation and standardisation of 3D-FLAIR and 3D-real IR protocols are essential for accurate, reproducible assessment of endolymphatic hydrops across institutions, scanner platforms, and vendors. Findings Use TE 500-700 ms and a long echo train for efficiency/background suppression, TR ~ 16,000 ms to enhance perilymph, and TI 2400-3000 ms to suppress endolymph. Critical relevance statement Emerging deep-learning reconstruction techniques may shorten acquisition times or improve spatial resolution, while half-dose, high-relaxivity GBCAs may provide hydrops visualisation comparable to higher-dose conventional contrast protocols.
42998158:
OBJECTIVE: The relationship between myocardial bridging (MB) morphology and function and the pathways to clinical symptoms remained unclear. This study investigated the association between delta coronary computed tomographic angiography-derived fractional flow reserve (ΔCT-FFR) and angina-equivalent symptoms in left anterior descending MB without coronary atherosclerosis using photon-counting detector CT (PCD-CT).
MATERIALS AND METHODS: This retrospective cohort included 180 patients with deep MB (depth > 2 mm) and no plaques. All underwent PCD-CT angiography. CT-FFR was computed by machine learning; systolic (ΔCT-FFRsys) and diastolic (ΔCT-FFRdia) trans-bridge pressure gradients were derived. MB depth and length were measured. Associations with symptoms were assessed by logistic regression and mediation analysis.
RESULTS: Symptomatic patients (n = 81) had greater depth (median 3.30 mm vs. 2.45 mm), longer length (mean 36.06 mm vs. 26.10 mm), higher ΔCT-FFRsys (3.81% vs. 1.62%) and ΔCT-FFRdia (3.45% vs. 2.15%) than asymptomatic patients (n = 99) (all p < 0.001). Multivariable analysis identified depth (OR = 1.77, 95% CI: 1.27-2.46, p = 0.001) and ΔCT-FFRsys (OR = 1.16, 95% CI: 1.05-1.27, p = 0.002) as independent predictors. Mediation analysis indicated that ΔCT-FFRsys significantly mediated the effect of depth on symptoms (indirect effect = 0.1881, 95% CI: 0.1023-0.2897).
CONCLUSIONS: MB depth and ΔCT-FFRsys were independent risk factors for symptoms, and ΔCT-FFRsys appeared to mediate the morphological-clinical symptoms link. These findings suggested that integrated assessment, particularly ΔCT-FFRsys, might be a new non-invasive imaging biomarker for clinically identify symptomatic MB and understand its potential pathogenic mechanisms.
KEY POINTS: Question The precise relationship between myocardial bridging morphological and functional features and clinical symptoms, and whether underlying key mediating factors exist, remains currently incompletely determined. Findings Depth, length, and systolic trans-bridge pressure gradient of myocardial bridging independently predicted symptoms, with the gradient significantly mediating the relationship between morphology and clinical presentation. Clinical relevance Noninvasive assessment of depth and systolic trans-bridge pressure gradient can assist in identifying patients with symptomatic myocardial bridging, serving as potential imaging biomarkers and providing insights into the underlying pathophysiology of symptom presentation.
42998159:
OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic performance of photon-counting detector computed tomography (PCD-CT) for gastric cancer T staging compared with conventional energy-integrating detector CT (EID-CT).
MATERIALS AND METHODS: Fifty-three patients with preoperative PCD-CT and 54 patients with preoperative EID-CT were retrospectively enrolled. Two radiologists independently assessed the visibility and T stages using all available sequences, including virtual monoenergetic images (VMIs) from PCD-CT at 40, 50, 60, and 70 kiloelectron volt (keV) levels. The lesion detectability and diagnostic accuracy of the two CT systems were analyzed and compared. Signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR) of gastric cancer lesions were also measured.
RESULTS: Five lesions in the PCD-CT group and 12 lesions in the EID-CT group could not be confidently identified. For visible lesions, the overall T staging accuracies were 85.4% (95% CI: 72.8-92.8%) for Reader 1 and 83.3% (95% CI: 70.4-91.3%) for Reader 2 on PCD-CT, compared with 73.8% (95% CI: 58.9-84.7%) for Reader 1 and 78.6% (95% CI: 64.1-88.3%) for Reader 2 on EID-CT. The interobserver agreement for both CT systems was excellent, with weighted kappa values of 0.807 (95% CI: 0.693-0.921) for PCD-CT and 0.832 (95% CI: 0.720-0.943) for EID-CT. Quantitative analysis showed significantly higher SNR and CNR on PCD-CT than EID-CT (both p < 0.05).
CONCLUSION: PCD-CT demonstrated significantly higher quantitative image quality metrics (SNR and CNR) and numerically higher diagnostic performance than EID-CT in this exploratory retrospective comparison. The potential value of PCD-CT in gastric cancer T staging warrants further validation.
KEY POINTS: Question The diagnostic performance and potential value of PCD-CT in gastric cancer T staging are still unclear. Findings PCD-CT showed significantly higher quantitative image quality metrics (SNR and CNR) and numerically higher diagnostic performance than EID-CT in this exploratory comparison. Clinical relevance PCD-CT may offer potential value in gastric cancer T staging.
42998190:
PURPOSE: To summarize optical coherence tomography (OCT)-detected retinal and choroidal changes in pre-eclampsia (PE), to support clinicians in interpreting these changes within the clinical context.
METHODS: We systematically searched four databases (PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Scopus) through February 2025 to identify observational studies comparing OCT metrics in PE versus control groups. Pooled mean differences (MD) and standardized mean differences (SMD) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated using random-effects models. Between-study heterogeneity was quantified with the I2 statistic and its sources explored by meta-regression and by subgroup analysis (PE severity, presence of retinal changes, risk of bias, OCT device, eye-selection method, and country); for each subgroup analysis the residual I2 was compared with the I2 of the corresponding overall analysis. Risk of bias was assessed using the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) checklist.
RESULTS: Fifteen studies with 854 eyes from women with PE, 631 eyes from women with normal pregnancy (NP), and 245 eyes from non-pregnant controls (NC) were included. Compared with NP, PE was significantly associated with reduced peripapillary retinal nerve fiber layer (p-RNFL) thickness (SMD: - 0.13, 95% CI: - 0.20 to - 0.06, P = 0.01, I2 = 0%). No statistically significant differences were observed for subfoveal choroidal thickness (SFCT; pre- and post-partum), nasal and temporal choroidal thickness, or central subfield macular thickness (CSMT) in the primary pooled analyses, most of which demonstrated substantial to considerable heterogeneity (I2 up to 94%). Exploratory subgroup analysis suggested that pathological retinal changes and PE severity partially (I2 reduction = 40%) or fully (I2 reduction = 92%) accounted for heterogeneity in pre-partum SFCT estimates.
CONCLUSION: The p-RNFL thickness is subtly reduced in PE compared to NP, representing subclinical structural change. While primary analyses found no significant choroidal or macular differences, subgroup analyses suggest a potential increase in SFCT in severe PE or in the presence of retinal pathology, warranting further investigation.
42998304:
PURPOSE: Lumbar interbody fusion (LIF) procedures are associated with postoperative paraspinal muscle atrophy and fatty infiltration (FI), which may influence long-term pain and functional recovery. However, the relationship between muscle quality, both pre- and postoperatively, and patient-reported outcomes remains unclear for patients undergoing lumbar fusion. This correlation was compared between minimally invasive surgery (MIS) and conventional open surgery (COS) approaches to assess differences in postoperative muscle preservation and functional outcomes.
METHODS: A systematic review, conducted following PRISMA guidelines and registered in PROSPERO (CRD420250650064), examined studies found in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science through February 2025. Studies were included if they assessed adult patients undergoing LIF with preoperative CT or MRI evaluation of the multifidus (MF) or erector spinae (ES) and reported postoperative cross-sectional area (CSA), FI, or patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs).
RESULTS: Twenty studies met inclusion criteria; risk of bias was assessed with ROBINS-I for 19 non-randomized studies and RoB 2 for one randomized trial. Seven of nine COS intervention studies found significant pre- to postoperative muscle damage, including all three COS-only studies, measured by CSA and FI. Two of twelve MIS intervention studies found significant pre- to postoperative muscle damage, with four of six direct comparisons found smaller declines in CSA, increases in FI, or both after MIS compared to COS in at least one muscle or setting. Higher preoperative muscle quality, particularly lower FI, and smaller pre- to postoperative muscle changes were associated with greater PROM improvements. Across the PROM-focused studies, four of the five reported that higher preoperative CSA or lower FI predicted better postoperative improvements in functional outcomes, with one identifying that MF FI of 61% or greater as a threshold for failing to achieve clinically meaningful ODI improvements.
CONCLUSION: MIS techniques were associated with a decrease in pre- to postoperative FI compared with COS, although PROM improvement occurred across both approaches. While preoperative paraspinal muscle quality and size decreases are generally smaller with better functional outcomes following postoperative LIF, this relationship is not consistently observed across all studies or surgical techniques. These findings suggest that the current imaging-based biomarkers may not fully capture the multifactorial nature of functional recovery and underscore the need for further research into additional predictors of muscle recovery.
42998673:
OBJECTIVE: To characterise the frequency and nature of radiologists' recommendations in magnetic resonance imaging and computed tomography reports for patients with papilledema attributable to idiopathic intracranial hypertension.
DESIGN: Retrospective chart review.
PARTICIPANTS: In total, 146 consecutive patients with papilledema secondary to idiopathic intracranial hypertension were included. They were all ≥18 years of age with optic disc edema and preserved visual function or a visual field defect consistent with papilledema and underwent structural neuroimaging.
METHODS: Electronic medical records were assessed for clinical and imaging characteristics.
RESULTS: In total, 146 patients (131 female and 15 male) were analysed. The mean age was 32.9 ± 10.8 years. Recommendations were provided in 33 reports (22.6%). Lumbar puncture (LP) was the most common recommendation (72.7%), followed by additional imaging (15.2%), and referral to other providers (9.1%). Of the 67 radiologists who contributed to the 146 reports, 11 (16.4%) recommended LP in at least 1 of their reports. Incidental findings were characterised in 15 (10.3%) reports.
CONCLUSIONS: In this study, radiologists provided recommendations in 22.6% of radiology reports, with LP being the most frequent recommendation. Future studies evaluating the appropriateness and impact of such recommendations are warranted.
43000287:
BACKGROUND: Adult diffuse lower-grade gliomas (LGGs, WHO grades 2-3) are heterogeneous CNS tumors. The 1p/19q codeletion defines oligodendrogliomas (IDHmut-Codel) and predicts better prognosis. Noninvasive imaging biomarkers could aid preoperative tumor characterization, particularly when molecular testing is limited.
PURPOSE: To systematically evaluate the diagnostic performance of calcifications on CT and MRI as a predictor of 1p/19q codeletion status in gliomas.
DATA SOURCES: Seven electronic databases were systematically searched up to August 2025.
STUDY SELECTION: Studies evaluating calcifications on CT or MRI for predicting 1p/19q codeletion status were included, with FISH, PCR, or NGS as reference standards. Ten studies comprising 1,256 patients met inclusion criteria.
DATA ANALYSIS: Pooled sensitivity, specificity, diagnostic odds ratios (DOR), and hierarchical summary receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (HSROC-AUC) were calculated using bivariate random-effects meta-analysis.
DATA SYNTHESIS: Calcifications showed pooled sensitivity of 0.45 (95% CI: 0.38-0.53) and specificity of 0.93 (95% CI: 0.88-0.95), with a DOR of 12.0 (95% CI: 6.41-22.46) and HSROC-AUC of 0.76 (95% CI: 0.46-0.94). The high specificity indicates that the presence of calcification strongly supports 1p/19q codeletion, whereas the lower sensitivity indicates that its absence should not be used to exclude codeletion.
LIMITATIONS: Heterogeneity was related to variations in imaging protocols and difficulties differentiating calcifications from hemorrhage or microbleeds across studies.
CONCLUSIONS: Calcifications on CT and MRI are a reliable noninvasive marker for identifying IDHmut-Codel gliomas and excluding IDHmut-Noncodel tumors. Their detection provides clinically relevant information for preoperative decision-making, particularly in resource-limited settings. Combining calcification assessment with other imaging features may further improve diagnostic accuracy.
43000449:
OBJECTIVES: Patient-specific computed tomography (CT) phantoms can be produced using a novel 3D-printing technique that aims at replicating measured CT image volumes with high anatomic fidelity and accurate CT values. The purpose of this study is a comprehensive physics-based evaluation of both technical phantoms and a full-size adult abdominal phantom with regard to image-quality metrics and the reproducibility of CT values. In addition, the visualization of abdominal pathologies will be assessed.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: The study was conducted in 3 steps. First, a geometric reference disc phantom (40 mm thickness, 150 mm diameter) was 3D-printed using multimaterial jetting and scanned on a commercial photon-counting detector CT (PCD-CT) to assess the CT values of the base materials used for printing and to evaluate the influence of the printing process on spatial resolution and noise properties. Second, CT images of the reference phantom reconstructed with a medium-sharp and a sharp kernel were used as templates to print 2 CT-derived disc phantoms using multimaterial jetting with voxel-based material mapping. These phantoms were then scanned to assess how template image sharpness propagates into the image-quality properties of the final printed phantoms. Spatial resolution was evaluated using edge spread function (ESF) analysis and edge rise distance (ERD), whereas noise characteristics were assessed using noise power spectrum (NPS) analysis. Third, as a proof of concept, a full-size adult abdominal phantom was 3D-printed with a patient CT data set as template. Phantom images were compared with patient images regarding CT values, spatial resolution, noise properties, and the depiction of pathologic structures.
RESULTS: Evaluation of the CT attenuation of the base materials showed that CT values ranging from -37 HU to 995 HU in virtual monoenergetic images at 60 keV can be printed.For the reference disc, measured ESF curves showed close agreement with theoretical expectations across all reconstruction kernels, indicating preservation of spatial resolution by the printing process. CT-derived discs showed minor edge smoothing compared with the reference for smooth and medium-sharp reconstructions. For sharp reconstructions, edge smoothing was severe, with an ERD increase of up to 32% compared with the reference. Edge smoothing was more pronounced for the disc based on a sharp template. NPS were highly consistent across all discs, with only minor differences in peak amplitude. In the abdominal phantom images ESF and NPS closely matched those of the patient CT images. Measured attenuation agreed well for tissues with positive CT values up to 1000 HU. Fat was represented with increased CT values because of print material limitations. Clinically relevant pathologic structures, including a large hepatocellular carcinoma and a smaller focal liver lesion, were displayed comparably in the phantom images.
CONCLUSIONS: CT phantoms generated from CT image volumes using 3D printing with multimaterial mapping on a voxel level accurately reproduce the template images in terms of image sharpness, noise characteristics, and attenuation properties of tissues with positive CT values not exceeding 1000 HU. The achievable spatial resolution is limited to medium-sharp levels and does not improve by using sharper template images. These findings support the use of image-based multimaterial 3D printing to produce realistic anthropomorphic phantoms for advanced CT image-quality assessment and optimization, and for validation of reconstruction algorithms and quantitative CT imaging methods.
43000706:
PURPOSE: To compare LNG-IUS stability, clinical outcomes, and safety after direct versus hysteroscopy-assisted placement following high-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU) ablation for adenomyosis.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: This single-center retrospective cohort study included 229 premenopausal patients with adenomyosis who underwent HIFU ablation and attempted LNG-IUS placement (direct, n = 135; hysteroscopy-assisted, n = 94). Post-placement outcomes were evaluated among patients with successful first-attempt placement and included LNG-IUS-related events, treatment continuation, symptom scores, lesion volume, and adverse events. Event-free survival was analyzed using Kaplan-Meier and Cox regression, with propensity score matching as a sensitivity analysis.
RESULTS: First-attempt placement succeeded in 135 of 135 direct and 91 of 94 hysteroscopy-assisted patients. LNG-IUS-related events were less frequent with hysteroscopy-assisted placement (7.69% vs. 25.93%; p < 0.001), and treatment continuation at last follow-up was higher (92.31% vs. 74.07%; p < 0.001). Event risk remained lower with hysteroscopy-assisted placement before and after adjustment (HR = 0.393, 95% CI 0.173-0.891, p = 0.025; adjusted HR = 0.396, 95% CI 0.158-0.996, p = 0.049). Propensity score matching showed a similar but less precise association (HR = 0.265, 95% CI 0.070-1.002; p = 0.050). Symptom scores and lesion volume decreased in both groups, with no significant between-group difference in adverse events.
CONCLUSIONS: Hysteroscopy-assisted LNG-IUS placement after HIFU may be associated with fewer displacement or expulsion events and a higher rate of treatment continuation than direct placement. Symptom improvement and recorded adverse events were similar between groups. It may be considered for selected patients with suspected residual intrauterine necrotic tissue or unfavorable uterine cavity conditions.
43001267: There has been a recent surge in interest in portal vein thrombosis (PVT), as evidenced by the increase in publications on this topic, along with heterogeneity in the terminology, classification, and management of this disorder. The Indian National Association for Study of the Liver vascular liver disease task force, with extensive expertise in portal hypertension, along with other invited experts actively working in this field, has formulated a consensus guideline on the definition, nomenclature, epidemiology, clinical features, natural history, diagnosis, and management of PVT using evidence from published literature. Whenever there was a paucity of evidence, expert opinion was included after detailed deliberations.
43001744: Timely hemorrhage control is a critical determinant of survival after traumatic injury, and advances in transarterial embolization have made rapid access to endovascular intervention an increasingly important component of contemporary trauma care. This joint position statement from the American College of Surgeons Committee on Trauma and the Society of Interventional Radiology clarifies expectations for interventional radiology under ACS Verification, Review, and Consultation Program Standard 4.15 and provides practical guidance for integrating endovascular hemorrhage control into trauma centers. Standard 4.15 reflects a requirement for system readiness rather than a universal mandate that every vascular intervention begin within 60 minutes. Rapid intervention is expected when clinically indicated, particularly for patients with an endovascular target who are hemodynamically labile, and the relevant performance interval is the time from a shared decision by trauma surgery and interventional radiology to proceed with intervention to arterial puncture. Trauma centers should establish multidisciplinary activation pathways that enable rapid mobilization of personnel and resources while preserving clinical judgment regarding patient selection and competing priorities. Recommended strategies include standardized activation protocols, process mapping, parallel rather than sequential workflows, early patient transport when appropriate, documentation of key time points, structured debriefing, and continuous performance monitoring. Interventional radiologists should be integrated as essential members of multidisciplinary trauma teams rather than engaged late as procedural consultants. Applying the 60-minute expectation according to clinical urgency and monitoring decision-to-puncture time focuses Standard 4.15 on its intended objectives: institutional readiness, timely definitive hemorrhage control in appropriately selected high-risk patients, and continuous performance improvement.
43002583:
INTRODUCTION OR BACKGROUND: Musculoskeletal disorders such as osteoarthritis, chronic low back pain, radicular syndromes, and osteoporosis require noninvasive treatments reaching deep anatomical structures. Nuclear magnetic resonance therapy (NMRT/MBST) delivers depth-independent resonance-based stimulation. This systematic review consolidates clinical and mechanistic evidence to evaluate NMRT/MBST among deep-tissue biophysical therapeutics.
SOURCES OF DATA: A systematic search of PubMed, Ovid/Embase, and peer-reviewed literature identified 26 original studies spanning randomized and observational clinical evidence, imaging evaluations, veterinary trials, and in vitro research. Experimental findings on inflammatory, metabolic, mitochondrial, redox, and circadian pathways were integrated with clinical observations.
AREAS OF AGREEMENT: NMRT/MBST shows a strong safety profile with no reported treatment-emergent adverse events. Across indications, studies demonstrate improvements in pain, function, and, selectively, structural or densitometric changes. Mechanistic evidence indicates modulation of mitochondrial bioenergetics, redox balance, inflammatory cascades, chondrogenic and osteogenic pathways, neurotrophic activity, and circadian regulation. These convergent processes mirror photobiomodulation, supporting NMRT/MBST as a deep-acting analog influencing regenerative biology in inaccessible tissues. Conventional pulsed electromagnetic field therapy is physically the closest comparator but shows narrower mechanistic overlap.
AREAS OF CONTROVERSY: Evidence remains heterogeneous in methodology, outcome measures, and structural responses. The only placebo-controlled knee osteoarthritis trial found no superiority over sham, although baseline imbalance limits interpretation.
GROWING POINTS: The depth-independent profile and mechanistic parallels suggest applications in deep cartilage, subchondral bone, intervertebral discs, and nerve-root environments, supporting multimodal biophysical strategies.
AREAS TIMELY FOR DEVELOPING RESEARCH: Priorities include larger randomized trials, longitudinal structural evaluation, comparisons with optical modalities, and biomarker-guided personalization.
43003323:
PURPOSE: Health-related social needs (HRSNs), such as food insecurity or transportation difficulties, may affect breast cancer screening and follow-up. We assessed the use of screening mammography (SM) encounters to identify HRSNs and the association between the presence of any HRSN and adherence to recommended breast imaging.
METHODS: Women presenting for SM received an optional questionnaire assessing desire for assistance with 8 HRSNs. Demographic and imaging data were extracted for each respondent. Multivariable logistic regression identified factors independently associated with adherence.
RESULTS: 86% (1463/1704) of women completed the questionnaire, of whom 244 (17%) reported ≥1 HRSN. HRSNs were more common with younger age (p=0.0009), as well as non-White race, Hispanic/Latino ethnicity, non-English primary language, and Medicaid/MassHealth (all p<0.0001). Among women with BI-RADS 1 or 2 index SMs, subsequent SM adherence was lower with ≥1 HRSN (73% vs 87%; p<0.0001). Among women with BI-RADS 0 index SMs, diagnostic imaging adherence was 76% with ≥1 HRSN compared with 95% without HRSNs (p=0.05). On multivariable analysis, ≥1 HRSN was independently associated with lower odds of breast imaging adherence (aOR, 0.57; 95% CI, 0.40-0.83). Among women who completed recommended imaging, median (IQR) time to follow-up did not differ by HRSN status for BI-RADS 1 or 2 (366 [363,370] vs 366 [364,378] days; p=0.16) or BI-RADS 0 (30 [15,37] vs 30 [13,130] days; p=0.61).
CONCLUSIONS: SM encounters can be used to identify HRSNs. Women reporting ≥1 HRSN were less likely to adhere to breast imaging recommendations, suggesting that HRSN screening during mammography may identify women at increased risk of non-adherence.
43003702: Mitral annular calcification (MAC) is a chronic, progressive, and degenerative process characterized by calcium deposition along the mitral annulus. This leads to stiffening and distortion of normal mitral annular architecture and ultimately MAC-related valvular dysfunction, which can manifest as mitral stenosis, mitral regurgitation, or mixed valvular disease. Due to its anatomic complexity, transcatheter and surgical interventions for MAC carry significant procedural challenges. As such, multi-modality imaging and multi-disciplinary heart team discussions are critical in MAC evaluation and procedural planning. This review summarizes the epidemiology and pathophysiology of MAC, highlights the critical role of multimodality imaging in the evaluation and procedural planning of MAC, and reviews established transcatheter mitral valve procedures and surgical options for managing MAC, MAC-related valvular dysfunction, and potential complications.
43004027: Predatory journals typically use practices based on deceit, misleading information, lack of transparency, and the absence of rigorous peer review. Within radiology, such journals frequently publish articles with minimal editorial oversight and limited scientific credibility. The relevance of this issue in radiology has grown as imaging research has expanded rapidly, particularly in artificial intelligence (AI), quantitative imaging, and subspecialty-driven innovation. Given the academic pressure created by the "publish or perish" culture, this environment makes early-career radiologists especially vulnerable to predatory journals that promise rapid publication and high acceptance rates. Predatory journals exploit this environment by sending unsolicited invitations to publish or join editorial boards, frequently using flattering language and promising unrealistic publication timelines. These journals generally lack robust peer review, methodological scrutiny, and transparency and are typically not indexed in established databases such as PubMed, Scopus, or Web of Science. Consequently, articles published in these outlets have reduced visibility, limited citation potential, and minimal impact on radiological science or clinical practice. Furthermore, publication in predatory journals may adversely affect academic reputation and career advancement, as hiring and funding committees increasingly prioritise journal quality and publication integrity. The rapid expansion of radiology research, particularly in diagnostic imaging, interventional radiology, and AI-powered applications, may increase opportunities for the dissemination of low-quality or insufficiently validated evidence through predatory journals. Raising awareness of predatory publishing practices and consistently applying evaluation tools such as the "Think. Check. Submit." framework, are fundamental to safeguarding scientific integrity and ensuring the dissemination of high-quality radiological research. KEY POINTS: Question Predatory publishing is a growing concern in radiology, driven by rising publication pressure and the "publish or perish" culture. Early-career researchers are particularly susceptible to unethical journals that offer rapid publication. Findings Predatory journals frequently bypass rigorous peer review, lack transparency, and are often not indexed in major databases. These journals exploit authors through unsolicited invitations and prioritise profit over scientific quality. Critical relevance statement Avoiding predatory journals is important for protecting research credibility, career progression, and scientific integrity. Publications in these outlets may disseminate unreliable evidence and are often disregarded in academic and clinical evaluations.
43005086:
BACKGROUND: Machine learning-based assessment of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) has been proposed to improve the reproducibility and clinical utility of immune-contexture evaluation in breast cancer histopathology. However, existing studies differ substantially in task definition, annotation strategy, model architecture, validation design, and clinical endpoint. This systematic review and evidence-gap analysis aimed to map the translational readiness of TIL-related machine learning studies in breast cancer histopathology and to identify cluster-specific methodological gaps.
METHODS: A systematic search of PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, ScienceDirect, and Google Scholar was conducted up to 20 April 2026, supplemented by backward citation tracing and a targeted Google search of the 30 most relevant additional results. Eligible studies included breast cancer histopathology-based machine learning, deep learning, artificial intelligence, or computational image-analysis studies evaluating TILs or TIL-related immune-cell features. Studies were grouped by principal application into detection/classification, outcome prognostication, and treatment-response prediction. Extracted variables included data source, specimen type, model family, annotation strategy, validation design, clinical comparator use, calibration, decision-curve analysis, incremental value, reproducibility, and methodological challenges. Because of heterogeneity in endpoints and performance metrics, synthesis was descriptive and evidence-map based.
RESULTS: The primary evidence map included 51 histopathology-image studies: 19 detection/classification, 18 outcome prognostication, and 14 treatment-response prediction studies. External validation was reported in 31.6% of detection/classification studies, 61.1% of prognostication studies, and 57.1% of treatment-response prediction studies. Clinical comparator reporting increased across the same continuum, from 63.2% to 94.4% and 92.9%, respectively. However, calibration was reported in only one prognostication study (5.6%) and in no detection/classification or treatment-response prediction studies. Decision-curve analysis was similarly limited to one prognostication study. Class imbalance was near-universal (94.7-100% across clusters). Scanner/stain robustness was addressed in a majority of studies (63.2-83.3%), but fairness or subgroup analyses remained inconsistently reported (27.8-57.1%).
CONCLUSIONS: TIL machine learning in breast cancer is technically active but clinically under-validated. Future studies should move beyond model development toward externally validated, calibrated, clinically benchmarked, reproducible, and decision-relevant evidence, using cluster-specific planning standards for detection, prognostication, and treatment-response prediction.
SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD42024574566, identifier CRD42024574566.
43007046:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate evidence on non-invasive vascular assessment techniques used during pregnancy and/or the postpartum period to identify vascular abnormalities associated with gestational hypertension and explore potential implications for long-term cardiovascular health.
METHODS: A systematic search of MEDLINE, PubMed, Scopus, the Cochrane Library, and gray literature (to May-2024) identified studies assessing vascular structure or function using pulse-wave velocity, carotid intima-media thickness, flow-mediated dilation, ophthalmic artery Doppler, and retinal imaging. Forty-nine studies involving 32,683 participants. Due to the heterogeneity in study design and methodology, findings were synthesized narratively.
RESULTS: Women with gestational hypertension generally demonstrated increased arterial stiffness (elevated pulse wave velocity and augmentation index), impaired endothelial function (reduced flow-mediated dilation), and increased intima-media thickness during pregnancy and the postpartum period. Several studies reported persistence of these abnormalities from weeks to years after delivery, although findings were inconsistent. Ophthalmic artery Doppler studies showed variable alterations in peak systolic velocity ratios and pulsatility index reported in hypertensive pregnancies. Retinal imaging identified alterations in retinal vessel caliber during pregnancy and the postpartum period, with some abnormalities reported up to six years postpartum.
CONCLUSION: Non-invasive vascular assessments can help identify macrovascular, microvascular, and endothelial abnormalities in women with gestational hypertension and preeclampsia during pregnancy and the postpartum period. Although some abnormalities persist beyond delivery and may contribute to long-term cardiovascular risk, evidence remains insufficient to support their use as independent predictors of future cardiovascular events. Further standardized, prospective longitudinal studies are needed to determine their prognostic and clinical value.
43007078:
BACKGROUND: Pazopanib showed clinical activity in progressive radioiodine-refractory differentiated thyroid carcinoma (RAIR-DTC), although its use is limited by substantial toxicity not reduced by intermittent treatment. We aimed to identify biomarkers associated with outcome and treatment-related toxicity in these patients.
METHODS: This study reported exploratory results related to the Pazothyr trial (NCT01813136) investigating pazopanib efficacy in RAIR-DTC patients. We evaluated lymphopenia and neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) from the Pazothyr clinical database (n = 168). Dedicated informed consent for additional plasma and tumor sample collection allowed quantification of plasma angiogenic factors and cytokines at baseline and after one month of pazopanib (n = 111). Immune markers (CD8, FOXP3, CD163, and PDL1) analyzed by immunohistochemistry in archived primary tumors from patients (n = 68) with response or stable disease after 6 months of pazopanib were scored semiquantitatively. Associations with response, progression-free survival (PFS), overall survival (OS), and substantial treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs) were evaluated. Given the exploratory nature of this study, no adjustment for multiple comparisons was performed.
RESULTS: At baseline, moderate and severe lymphopenia were associated with shorter PFS, unlike high NLR. Elevated Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor A (VEGF-A), Interleukin 6 (IL-6), and CXCL8 correlated with poorer PFS. High VEGF-A, hepatocyte growth factor (HGF), IL-6, CXCL8, and CXCL9 were associated with shorter OS. X Early changes in placental growth factor (PlGF), HGF, interleukin 12 subunit p40, and CXCL10 were associated with substantial TRAEs. Multivariable analyses identified baseline severe lymphopenia (hazard ratio [HR] = 2.39 [confidence interval or CI 1.27-4.48], p = 0.007) and high CXCL8 (HR = 2.01 [CI 1.26-3.21], p = 0.004) as independent factors associated with progression. High baseline NLR (HR = 2.26 [CI 1.21-4.22], p = 0.01), HGF (HR = 2.37 [CI 1.33-4.20], p = 0.003), and CXCL8 (HR = 2.20 [CI 1.25-3.87], p = 0.006) were similarly associated with death. One-month increases in PlGF (odds ratio [OR] = 2.49 [CI 1.13-5.50], p = 0.024) and HGF (OR = 2.91 [CI 1.32-6.43], p = 0.008) were independently associated with substantial TRAEs. In patients with tumor samples, Programmed cell Death-Ligand 1 (PDL1)-immune cell score (ICS) >1% (HR = 2.05 [CI 1.15-3.66], p = 0.015) was also associated with progression.
CONCLUSIONS: Baseline lymphopenia and inflammatory plasma biomarkers were associated with clinical outcome, whereas early changes in circulating factors were associated with substantial TRAEs. These exploratory results require prospective validation in RAIR-DTC patients treated with pazopanib or other VEGF receptor-targeting multikinase inhibitors. The relevance of PDL1-ICS expression for anti-PD1/PDL1-based therapies requires dedicated prospective trials.
43007412:
OBJECTIVES: Accurate assessment of treatment response to neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAC) in breast cancer (BC) is crucial for guiding surgical planning. While size-based criteria remain standard, they may underestimate therapy-induced biological changes. To develop and validate the neoadjuvant breast imaging reporting and data system (NacBI-RADS), a structured multiparametric MRI (mp-MRI) lexicon was designed to evaluate NAC response and support surgical decision-making.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: This retrospective study included 68 BC patients who underwent staging and post-NAC MRI, followed by surgery. mp-MRI examinations included contrast-enhanced T1, T2-weighted, and diffusion-weighted imaging. NacBI-RADS integrates four parameters: peritumoral edema, ΔADC (apparent diffusion coefficient change), post-contrast tumor size, and lymph node status (Node-RADS). Three independent breast radiologists evaluated all cases. Inter-reader agreement was assessed with Cohen's and Fleiss' kappa.
RESULTS: Of 88 patients assessed, 68 were included. Residual disease was found in 43 patients (63%) and pathological complete response in 25 (37%). Most lesions were categorized as NacBI-RADS 1-2, while categories 4-5 were less frequent (12-15%). NacBI-RADS showed high diagnostic performance (AUC 0.942-0.960) with excellent reproducibility (κ 0.931-0.953). Lower categories were associated with complete or near-complete response, and higher categories with residual disease (p < 0.001).
CONCLUSION: This exploratory study suggests that NacBI-RADS may offer a standardized and reproducible mp-MRI framework for assessing NAC response. Further studies are needed to confirm its role in imaging-guided surgical planning.
KEY POINTS: Question Can a structured mp-MRI framework improve the accuracy and reproducibility of assessing BC response to NAC compared with conventional size-based criteria? Findings NacBI-RADS showed high diagnostic accuracy (AUC up to 0.960) and excellent inter-reader agreement, reliably distinguishing complete/partial-complete responders from patients with residual disease. Clinical relevance NacBI-RADS may support more accurate and reproducible response assessment after NAC, helping identify true complete responders and aiding safe, personalized surgical de-escalation strategies in BC management.
43007457:
PURPOSE: To evaluate the pathological, oncological, and functional outcomes of radical prostatectomy (RP) performed without prior histopathologic confirmation of prostate cancer in patients with a high clinical suspicion of clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa).
METHODS: We systematically searched PubMed, Embase, Google Scholar, and Cochrane databases for studies evaluating biopsy-free RP. Adult men with a high clinical suspicion of csPCa based on multiparametric MRI and/or PSMA-PET with elevated PSA or PSA density were included. A single-arm random-effects meta-analysis was performed to estimate the pooled proportions of csPCa, benign pathology, overtreatment, and positive surgical margins (PSM).
RESULTS: Eleven studies comprising 648 patients were included, csPCa was identified in 94.2% of patients (95% CI, 88.4-97.2), whereas benign pathology occurred in only 0.3%. The pooled overtreatment rate was 5.7%, and PSM was observed in 25.4% of cases. Study-level subgroup analysis suggested a higher diagnostic yield in biopsy-naïve cohorts than in cohorts including patients with a previous negative biopsy (95% vs. 80%; p = 0.005), with no significant differences according to imaging modality or surgical approach. Functional outcomes suggested favorable early urinary continence and erectile function recovery; however, heterogeneous and incomplete reporting precluded quantitative synthesis, and these findings were based on descriptive data only. Overall risk of bias was serious, primarily because of verification bias arising from participant selection.
CONCLUSIONS: Biopsy-free RP is a promising imaging-driven strategy for highly selected patients with a high probability of csPCa, demonstrating a high pathological yield of clinically significant disease and a very low observed rate of benign surgery. However, the PSM rate of 25.4% remains a concern, particularly given the absence of a comparator arm. Until further prospective studies confirm these findings, this approach should be reserved for carefully selected patients at high-volume centers following multidisciplinary evaluation and counseling.
43008235:
PURPOSE: To describe the safety and efficacy of planned transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) prior to external beam radiotherapy (EBRT) in patients with prostate cancer and lower urinary tract symptoms.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: Patients who underwent TURP ≤9 months before EBRT between March 2015 and March 2025 were included in this multicentre retrospective cohort. Urinary adverse events (UAE) were graded using Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events version 6. Cumulative incidence of grade ≥2 and ≥3 UAE was estimated with the Aalen-Johansen method with dead as a competing event, and associations with UAE after EBRT were explored with multivariable Cox regression. International Prostate Symptom Scores (IPSS) were analysed with linear mixed effects models.
RESULTS: A total of 200 patients were included. Median follow-up after EBRT was 30 months among patients without a grade ≥3 UAE. The cumulative incidence at 36 months after EBRT was 53% (95% CI 46 - 61) for grade ≥2 and 14% (95% CI 9.1 - 20) for grade ≥3 UAE. A longer TURP-EBRT interval was associated with grade ≥2 UAE (hazard ratio 1.18 per month, 95% CI 1.03 - 1.36), likely reflecting confounding by indication. A larger clinical target prostate volume was associated with a lower risk of grade ≥3 UAE (HR 0.95 per mL, 95% CI 0.92 - 0.99). The estimated mean IPSS decreased from 19.8 before to 11.1 after TURP and remained close to or below this level after EBRT.
CONCLUSIONS: Pre-EBRT TURP is feasible, with manageable but clinically relevant urinary toxicity. Symptom improvement is maintained after EBRT. These findings support its use as a de-obstructive strategy in patients with prostate cancer and lower urinary tract symptoms requiring EBRT.
43008744:
ABSTRACT: This article provides an update of the 2021 recommendations of the German Radiological Society (DRG) and the German Professional Association of Radiologists (BDR) on prostate MRI in accordance with the German S3 guideline on prostate cancer (version 8.1, published August 2025). The recommendations define the "current quality standards" for prostate MRI referenced in the S3 guideline and provide detailed guidance on patient history requirements, scheduling and preparation, and current indications for prostate MRI. Newly added sections cover the recommended imaging protocol, applications of artificial intelligence, and requirements for quality and structured reporting. MRI-guided (in-bore) prostate biopsy, including laboratory workup, management of anticoagulation, and antibiotic prophylaxis, is also discussed in detail.
KEY POINTS: · Update of the DRG/BDR recommendations regarding prostate MRI in accordance with the new S3 guideline on prostate cancer (version 8.1, 2025).. · Definition of the "current quality standards" for prostate MRI referenced in the S3 guideline.. · New guidelines regarding indications, applications of artificial intelligence, quality/structured reporting requirements.. · Detailed discussion of MRI-guided (in-bore) prostate biopsy..
CITATION FORMAT: · Franiel T, Asbach P, Beyersdorff D et al. Updated Recommendations of the German Radiological Society and the German Professional Association of Radiologists on Prostate MRI in the Context of the New S3 Guideline on Prostate Cancer. Rofo 2026; DOI 10.1055/a-2979-8879.
43008843:
OBJECTIVE: This study compared outcomes between patients undergoing elective open surgical repair (OSR) and fenestrated branched endovascular aortic repair (FBEVAR) for thoraco-abdominal aortic aneurysms (TAAAs) through a systematic review and meta-analysis.
DATA SOURCES: PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane.
REVIEW METHODS: A total of 5 980 articles were screened following the PRISMA protocol. Primary endpoints were thirty day or in hospital major adverse events (MAEs) and mortality, and late all cause mortality. Secondary endpoints were thirty day or in hospital permanent paraplegia, stroke, bowel ischaemia, and new onset dialysis, as well as late re-interventions. A DerSimonian-Laird random effects model was employed to calculate risk ratios (RRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for binary endpoints. Significance was defined as a p value of . Risk of bias was assessed with ROBINS-I and evidence certainty with GRADE.
RESULTS: A total of 1 567 patients from five retrospective observational comparative studies were included. FBEVAR was used to treat TAAA in 824 patients (52.6%). Thirty day MAEs (RR 0.51, 95% CI 0.34 - 0.78; p = .002; I2 = 77.0%), mortality (RR 0.60, 95% CI 0.37 - 0.97; p = .040; I2 = 29.0%), and dialysis (RR 0.18, 95% CI 0.06 - 0.54; p = .002; I2 = 80.0%) were significantly less frequent among patients undergoing FBEVAR. Conversely, late aortic related re-interventions were significantly more common in the elective FBEVAR cohort (RR 1.80, 95% CI 1.04 - 3.13; p = .040; I2 = 18.0%). No statistically significant differences were observed between groups in thirty day or in hospital permanent paraplegia (RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.51 - 1.91; p = .96; I2 = 39.0%), bowel ischaemia (RR 0.46, 95% CI 0.09 - 2.33; p = .35; I2 = 81.0%), and stroke (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.37 - 2.06; p = .76; I2 = 0.0%), or late mortality (RR 1.29, 95% CI 0.87 - 1.92; p = .20; I2 = 57.0%). According to GRADE, certainty of evidence was low to very low across outcomes.
CONCLUSION: Elective FBEVAR was associated with a significantly lower incidence of thirty day MAEs, mortality, and acute kidney injury requiring dialysis compared with OSR. In contrast, elective OSR was associated with a significantly lower incidence of late aortic related re-interventions, whereas overall re-intervention rates were similar between groups.
43008994:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate racial and ethnic differences in longitudinal, age-appropriate breast imaging surveillance among carriers of BRCA1/2 variants.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: This retrospective cohort study included females with pathogenic or likely pathogenic BRCA1/2 variants in the All of Us Research Program. Surveillance was evaluated at semiannual timepoints from 2016-2024 using rolling 12-month windows. Guideline-concordant surveillance was defined as breast MRI at ages 25-29 years and MRI and screening mammography at age 30 years or older. Generalized estimating equation models evaluated racial and ethnic associations in surveillance, adjusting for age, body mass index, Area Deprivation Index, calendar time, and electronic health record (EHR) activity.
RESULTS: Among 6,125 participants, 3,221 (52.6%) were Hispanic, 2,321 (37.9%) non-Hispanic White, 300 (4.9%) non-Hispanic Black, and 283 (4.6%) Other/Multiracial. Compared with non-Hispanic White participants, Hispanic (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 0.14; 95% CI: 0.08-0.28) and Other/Multiracial participants (aOR, 0.37; 95% CI: 0.15-0.95) had lower odds of guideline-concordant surveillance. Hispanic participants had lower odds of MRI (aOR, 0.22; 95% CI: 0.13-0.37) and mammography (aOR, 0.67; 95% CI: 0.56-0.79); non-Hispanic Black participants had lower odds of mammography (aOR, 0.57; 95% CI: 0.36-0.91). Over time, the difference in the odds of screening mammography between Hispanic and non-Hispanic White participants widened (OR per year, 0.95; 95% CI, 0.91-0.99).
CONCLUSION: Racial and ethnic differences in guideline-concordant breast imaging surveillance were observed among BRCA1/2 variant carriers, particularly among Hispanic participants, indicating persistent disparities in recommended surveillance within this high-risk population.
43009612: Delirium and cognitive decline may complicate recovery after robot-assisted pelvic surgery, but their frequency and relationship to positioning remain uncertain. We assessed reported proportions, comparative surgical risk and prognostic factors. PubMed, CENTRAL, Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar, ClinicalTrials.gov and WHO ICTRP were searched through 4 August 2026. Eligible adult robotic pelvic studies reported objective cognitive testing or delirium. Two reviewers performed original screening, extraction and question-specific bias appraisal. Post hoc logit random-effects meta-analyses summarized prospective cohorts using restricted maximum likelihood and modified Hartung-Knapp intervals in R. Twenty-six reports represented 25 studies. Five cognitive cohorts (356 participants) yielded 29.0% (95% confidence interval [CI] 20.2-39.8%); excluding Beck yielded 31.8% (20.7-45.4%). Three delirium cohorts (245 participants) yielded a descriptive model summary of 10.3% (2.2-37.0%). Individual delirium proportions were 8/82 (9.8%; exact 95% CI 4.3-18.3%), 4/80 (5.0%; 1.4-12.3%) and 14/83 (16.9%; 9.5-26.7%). The approximate 95% prediction interval from the delirium meta-analysis was very wide (<0.1-99.8%). The same-procedure prostatectomy comparison yielded an unadjusted risk ratio of 1.06 (0.73-1.55) for early cognitive decline. Comparative evidence was of low or very low certainty. Definitions, surveillance and selection limited interpretation; Trendelenburg-duration findings were inconsistent. These proportions describe selected study-defined outcomes. They do not establish attributable robotic or positioning risk, a safe exposure threshold, or benefit from horizontal breaks. Standardized prospective measurement is needed.
43012109: US veterans represent a large and diverse population with distinctive demographic characteristics, comorbidity profiles, and social determinants of health shaped by military service. These factors contribute to a high burden of cardiovascular risk and low attainment of ideal cardiovascular health. At the same time, the Department of Veterans Affairs, which operates the nation's largest integrated healthcare system, provides a unique infrastructure for delivering population-level cardiovascular disease prevention for veterans. Understanding its successes and ongoing challenges can inform broader strategies across all health systems for promoting health among veterans. This scientific statement applies the American Heart Association's Life's Essential 8 framework, expanded to include mental health and substance use, to evaluate veteran cardiovascular health. For each domain, we review guideline recommendations, barriers to achieving optimal health, and major Veterans Affairs programs such as Patient Aligned Care Teams, the MOVE! Weight Management Program for Veterans, Whole Health, telehealth-based interventions, and integrated mental health and substance use disorder services. Across domains, veterans receiving Veterans Affairs care often achieve outcomes that are equal to or better than those of their non-Veterans Affairs counterparts, reflecting the strengths of the system in coordinated, team-based care and research-driven implementation. Despite substantial progress, opportunities remain to improve veteran lifestyle behaviors, metabolic health, lipid and blood pressure control, engagement in mental health and substance use care, and detection and management of sleep disorders. Addressing these challenges at the Veterans Affairs will require continuing to expand care access, enhancing digital data integration, tailoring interventions to high-risk subgroups, and strengthening implementation strategies to improve uptake and engagement across Veterans Affairs services.
43012121:
BACKGROUND: Morphometric measurements from structural brain MRI are sensitive to analysis pipelines and software versions.
PURPOSE: To evaluate inter-pipeline agreement, reliability, and systematic measurement differences across automated morphometric software packages on identical structural MRI datasets.
STUDY TYPE: Systematic review (PROSPERO CRD420261456493).
POPULATION: One hundred eleven studies comprising healthy and clinical cohorts across the lifespan.
FIELD STRENGTH/SEQUENCE: Predominantly 1.5 T and 3 T, with 7 T data also included.
ASSESSMENT: Automated and semi-automated processing pipelines (predominantly FreeSurfer, FSL, and SPM/CAT) evaluated for brain volumes and cortical thickness.
STATISTICAL TESTS: Intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC), Pearson/Spearman correlation (r), Lin's concordance correlation coefficient (CCC), and Bland-Altman bias (p < 0.05).
RESULTS: Agreement varied across anatomical regions, software pairs, versions, and processing conditions. Strong associations coexisted with systematic measurement differences in several comparisons, but neither high association nor high agreement was consistent across global and regional outputs. Manual-reference comparisons showed structure- and population-dependent volume overestimation, with rankings differing by outcome metric. Cortical thickness, intracranial-volume normalization, and normative percentiles showed additional method-dependent differences. Software updates and preprocessing choices altered measurements and, in some studies, downstream findings. Computational repeatability, anatomical accuracy, and longitudinal-change agreement represented distinct properties and did not consistently favor the same method.
DATA CONCLUSION: High correlation or consistency does not ensure absolute agreement or interchangeability in MRI morphometry. Regional discrepancies vary across software pairs, versions, and processing conditions, limiting generalization of individual comparisons to other methods or populations.
EVIDENCE LEVEL: 1.
TECHNICAL EFFICACY STAGE: Stage 2.
43012262: Objective The aim of this study is to investigate the clinical characteristics, diagnostic challenges and treatment strategies for prostatic acinar adenocarcinoma combined with squamous cell carcinoma (SASC), which provides the reference for clinical decision-making. MethodsThe clinical history, imaging findings and pathological features of an 82-year-old male with prostatic adenosquamous carcinoma (ASC) were introduced in this article. A systematic literature review was conducted using the CNKI and PubMed databases to summarize pathological mechanisms, diagnostic criteria, and therapeutic approaches for ASC. ResultsThe patient initially presented with an elevated prostate-specific antigen (PSA) level and declined a diagnostic prostate biopsy at the first visit. Following endocrine therapy, PSA decreased to castration levels. Due to persistent lower urinary tract symptoms, the patient re-presented and was subsequently diagnosed with prostatic adenosquamous carcinoma via biopsy. Immunohistochemistry showed the coexistence of squamous cell carcinoma markers (CK5/6, p63, p40 positive) and adenocarcinoma markers (NKX3.1). As the family declined radical prostatectomy, ongoing endocrine therapy was combined with local radiotherapy for disease control. Ultimately, due to disease progression accompanied by hematuria and severe urinary obstruction, the patient underwent palliative transurethral resection of the prostate and cystoscopy, during which a bladder perforation was identified. Literature analysis indicates that prostatic ASC is rare, with aggressive squamous components resistant to endocrine therapy and a median survival of 11 months. Early radical surgery combined with chemoradiotherapy may improve prognosis, but most patients with advanced-stages disease require palliative interventions (transurethral resection, prostatic artery embolization). ConclusionProstatic ASC exhibits dual adenocarcinoma-squamous differentiation, necessitating extensive pathological sampling and immunohistochemical differentiation to avoid misdiagnosis.
