Personalized comprehensive strategies were required for its poor prognosis, which includes radical surgery with adjuvant therapy for early-stage disease and symptom-focused palliation (e.g., platinum-based chemotherapy, targeted therapies) for advanced cases, though evidence remains limited. Multicenter studies are urgently needed to optimize diagnostic and therapeutic protocols.
43012473: Aeromedical certification is based on a safety-first principle: a pilot or other aircrew member must not have a medical disorder that creates an unacceptable risk of sudden or subtle incapacitation during flight. Cardiovascular disease remains one of the most important determinants of flight fitness, as it may impair consciousness, judgment, rhythm stability, exercise capacity, and hemodynamic reserve. Modern aeromedical decision-making therefore requires the integration of aviation law, operational risk, contemporary cardiology guidelines, advanced imaging, biomarkers, and long-term surveillance. The International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) Annex 1 provides the global licensing framework; the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) Part-MED, together with its Acceptable Means of Compliance and Guidance Material, defines detailed operational standards in Europe; and the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) employs a protocol- and special issuance-based system for many cardiovascular and metabolic disorders. This review summarizes the aeromedical assessment of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, chronic and acute coronary syndromes, heart failure, cardiomy-opathies, arrhythmias and conduction disorders, pacemakers and implantable cardiac devices, valvular heart disease, aortic disease, congenital heart disease, venous throm-boembolism, cardiovascular pharmacotherapy, and major respiratory conditions rel-evant to flight certification. The manuscript is aligned with current European Society of Cardiology cardiovascular guidance and with the operational aeromedical principles applied by ICAO, EASA, FAA, and the Turkish Directorate General of Civil Aviation. In general, preserved ventricular function, absence of significant symptoms, low thrombo-embolic and arrhythmic risk, stable treatment, and adequate exercise capacity support certification or restricted certification. In contrast, uncontrolled hypertension, unstable diabetes, significant residual myocardial ischemia, reduced ejection fraction, malignant ventricular arrhythmias, implantable defibrillator therapy, severe valvular disease, significant aortic pathology, major congenital hemodynamic lesions, or poorly controlled sleep apnea usually preclude certification. Final decisions remain individualized and depend on license class, operational role, treatment burden, surveillance data, and the judgment of the aeromedical authority.
43013093:
OBJECTIVE: Artificial intelligence (AI) may improve prostate MRI interpretation and reduce radiologist workload, but evidence supporting clinical implementation remains limited. This scoping review summarises evidence on commercially available AI medical devices for prostate MRI.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: PubMed was searched for studies published through October 1, 2026. Eligible devices were cleared by the United States Food and Drug Administration and/or CE marked, with commercial availability corroborated through manufacturer websites. Data extraction addressed standalone AI performance, AI-assisted radiologist performance, workflow efficiency, and downstream clinical impact.
RESULTS: Twenty-one studies evaluating 7 commercial AI systems were included; 17/21 (81%) were retrospective and 14/21 (67%) were single-centre. AI assistance suggested greater benefit for less-experienced readers, but improvements were inconsistent and increased specificity sometimes accompanied reduced sensitivity. Standalone evaluations, outside the devices' approved intended use, showed discrimination comparable to that of radiologists in selected cohorts. Inter-reader agreement and workflow benefits were mixed. We identify three key limitations of the current body of evidence that require thoughtful consideration before routine implementation: (1) incomplete verification strategies, (2) limited determination of workflow benefit, and (3) lack of analyses of cost-effectiveness and patient outcomes, e.g., time to treat or cancer-free survival.
CONCLUSION: Evidence supporting the use of commercial AI for prostate MRI remains limited and heterogeneous, with inconsistent diagnostic benefits. Prospective comparative studies in real clinical workflows are needed to determine its potential role within the prostate cancer diagnostic pathway.
KEY POINTS: Question Evidence for clinical implementation of prostate AI remains limited-most studies are retrospective and single-centre, with heterogeneous populations and reference standards. Findings AI may improve diagnostic performance for less-experienced readers, but gains for expert readers and assessment of workflow efficiency are limited. Clinical relevance Prospective multicentre studies embedded in real-world pathways are needed, together with analyses of cost-effectiveness and patient outcomes.
43013133: Chronic subdural haematoma (cSDH) frequently recurs following standard treatment. Middle meningeal artery embolisation (MMAE) may reduce recurrence by decreasing perfusion of the vascularised subdural membranes. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the efficacy and safety of MMAE versus standard management. This PRISMA-compliant systematic review and meta-analysis (PROSPERO: CRD420261325584) searched PubMed, Ovid (MEDLINE and Embase), Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library from inception to 28 September 2026. Randomised controlled trials comparing MMAE-based treatment with standard management in adults with radiologically confirmed cSDH were included. Risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were pooled using random-effects models. The primary outcome was study-defined treatment failure. Twelve randomised controlled trials (n = 2,429; 1,202 MMAE; 1,227 control) were included in the primary analysis. Treatment failure occurred in 9.1% versus 18.3%, respectively. MMAE reduced treatment failure (RR 0.52, 95% CI 0.39-0.69), corresponding to an absolute risk reduction of approximately 8.8% and an NNT of approximately 12. In subgroup analyses, benefit was observed in both surgery-only comparator trials (RR 0.41, 95% CI 0.23-0.76) and mixed surgical/conservative comparator trials (RR 0.55, 95% CI 0.37-0.81), with no significant subgroup difference (p = 0.317). MMAE also reduced reoperation/surgical rescue (RR 0.40, 95% CI 0.31-0.52). All-cause mortality (RR 0.72, 95% CI 0.37-1.43) and severe adverse events (RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.60-1.16) did not differ significantly between groups. Certainty was moderate for treatment failure and reoperation/surgical rescue and low for mortality and severe adverse events. MMAE-based treatment reduces treatment failure in cSDH, with no statistically significant difference in mortality or severe adverse events. Further well-powered randomised trials using standardised efficacy and safety outcomes are needed to define the optimal role of MMAE in cSDH management.
43013146:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: To review the current evidence on local treatment strategies for oligometastatic soft tissue sarcoma at pulmonary and extrapulmonary sites, and evaluate their impact on oncological outcomes.
RECENT FINDINGS: Pulmonary metastasectomy remains the most established local treatment, with 5-year survival rates of 20-58%. Complete (R0) resection, a longer disease-free interval, and fewer metastases are associated with improved outcomes. Stereotactic radiotherapy achieves high local control rates with low toxicity, and a recent systematic review reported survival outcomes comparable to surgery. Image-guided thermal ablation also achieves high local control rates for lung metastases of 1 cm or smaller and offers a minimally invasive option for extrapulmonary metastases. For all modalities, current data are derived predominantly from retrospective studies, and direct comparisons are lacking. Local treatment offers promising outcomes for carefully selected patients with oligometastatic soft tissue sarcoma. Surgery, stereotactic radiotherapy, and thermal ablation should be considered complementary options, selected within a multidisciplinary tumor board according to lesion size, number, and location. Prospective studies are needed to define optimal patient selection and determine the comparative effectiveness of these modalities.
43013192:
BACKGROUND: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) frequently recurs after curative-intent resection, and conventional imaging and CA19-9 have limited sensitivity for detecting molecular residual disease (MRD). Tumor-informed circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) may identify postoperative MRD, although the evidence is limited and heterogeneous.
METHODS: PubMed, Scopus, and Embase were searched from inception to July 9, 2026, following PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Eligible studies compared postoperative tumor-informed ctDNA-positive and ctDNA-negative patients after curative-intent treatment of pancreatic cancer for recurrence, survival, or lead time outcomes. Random-effects models were used to pool risk ratios (RRs) and hazard ratios (HRs). Heterogeneity, leave-one-out sensitivity, prespecified subgroups, ROBINS-I risk of bias, and GRADE certainty were assessed.
RESULTS: Five observational cohorts contributed 237 patients to the radiological recurrence comparison (84 ctDNA-positive and 153 ctDNA-negative). Postoperative ctDNA positivity was associated with increased radiological recurrence (RR 2.50; 95% CI 1.90-3.28; I²=20%), poorer disease-free survival (HR 8.11; 95% CI 3.51-18.73; I²=45%), and poorer overall survival (HR 5.15; 95% CI 2.67-9.94; I²=0%). The direction of the associations persisted in the reported leave-one-out assessments. Recurrence risk was higher in both the early-MRD/landmark and surveillance subgroups, with no statistically significant subgroup difference (P = 0.17).
CONCLUSION: Postoperative tumor-informed ctDNA positivity was associated with an increased recurrence risk and inferior survival after curative-intent PDAC treatment, although a negative result did not reliably exclude residual disease. Prospective interventional studies are needed before ctDNA-guided surveillance or treatment modifications can be recommended for routine practice.
43013735:
BACKGROUND: Portal vein thrombosis (PVT) in cirrhosis has a quite unpredictable natural history. Spontaneous recanalization may occur, but predictors and prognostic impact remain uncertain. We performed an individual patient data (IPD) meta-analysis to evaluate survival according to spontaneous recanalization and to identify predictors of recanalization.
METHODS: We included cohort studies of patients with cirrhosis and PVT not receiving anticoagulation and obtained de-identified IPD. All-cause mortality was analyzed using a competing-risk model (competing event: liver transplantation) adjusted for prespecified baseline covariates. Predictors of recanalization were assessed with mixed-effects ordinal logistic regression including a random study intercept.
RESULTS: Eight studies contributed 586 patients. Spontaneous recanalization occurred in 264 (47.7%). Overall recanalization was independently associated with lower mortality (aSHR 0.51; 95% CI 0.28-0.90), with the benefit driven by complete recanalization (aSHR 0.45; 95% CI 0.21-0.94). Recanalization of PVT localized in the main portal vein trunk was linked to a strong survival benefit (interaction SHR 0.39; 95% CI 0.16-0.91; p=0.02), whereas no benefit was observed after recanalization of isolated intrahepatic branch thrombosis. PVT recanalization was more likely to occur in Child-Pugh A (aOR 2.63; 95% CI 1.18-5.88), partial thrombosis (aOR 1.69; 95% CI 1.09-2.56), and isolated intrahepatic location (aOR 2.04; 95% CI 1.23-3.33).
CONCLUSIONS: Spontaneous recanalization occurs in approximately half of patients with cirrhosis and PVT and is associated with improved survival, particularly when complete and involving the main portal vein trunk. These findings underscore its prognostic relevance and indirectly support anticoagulation to promote recanalization.
43013751:
PURPOSE: Since 1986, the Mayo Clinic Prostate Cancer Registry has followed over 30,000 patients who underwent radical prostatectomy. Advances in LLMs may modernize data collection, reduce human abstraction burden, and improve registry efficiency. Herein, we report the results of LLM data abstraction for surgical pathology and prostate MRI data in the Mayo Clinic Prostate Cancer Registry.
MATERIAL AND METHODS: Surgical pathology and MRI reports were obtained for 3,210 and 4,739 patients, respectively, who underwent radical prostatectomy from 2010-2022. LLM prompts for 13 pathology and 20 MRI variables were developed and ran through two independent LLMs (Google Gemini Flash 1.5, 2.0, or 2.5). LLM outputs were compared to human-abstracted data.
RESULTS: Median consensus LLM error rate for pathology report data was 0.09%(IQR 0.03-0.16%), compared with median human error rate of 2.81%(IQR 1.83-3.17%). Individual LLMs had threefold higher error rates compared to consensus LLM (LLM 1: 0.27%(IQR 0.09-0.34%), LLM 2: 0.30%(IQR 0.17%-0.48%)). For MRI reports, median consensus LLM error rate was 0.17%(IQR 0.00-0.68%), compared with human error rate of 1.01%(IQR 0.59-3.20%). Individual LLMs had error rates of 0.84%(IQR 0.34-2.79%) and 1.02%(IQR 0.34-1.67%). Estimated time for human data abstraction across all 136,510 data elements was 952 hours, compared with 32 hours for our LLM pipeline.
CONCLUSION: LLM data abstraction employing a consensus vote across two independent LLMs consistently yielded higher accuracy than human or single-LLM abstraction. A dual-LLM consensus architecture may improve data abstraction efficiency, reduce errors, and should be considered for integration into all prospectively maintained longitudinal clinical registries.
43013774:
BACKGROUND: Imaging-based AI may help predict pathological complete response (pCR) after neoadjuvant therapy for esophageal cancer. However, an encouraging average diagnostic performance does not establish reliable performance across clinical settings or justify treatment decisions without further validation.
OBJECTIVE: We aimed to assess the predictive performance of imaging-based AI across neoadjuvant strategies, distinguish internal from external validation, and examine limitations affecting interpretation.
METHODS: PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library were searched through August 7, 2026. Eligible English-language studies evaluated imaging-based AI against pathological assessment of pCR. PROBAST+AI (Prediction Model Risk of Bias Assessment Tool plus Artificial Intelligence) assessed study quality and risk of bias; GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) assessed certainty for sensitivity, specificity, and diagnostic odds ratio (DOR). Bivariate random-effects models synthesized validation groups separately. CIs described uncertainty in average performance, whereas 95% prediction intervals (PIs) described true performance in a similar new study.
RESULTS: Thirty-three studies contributed 27 internal-validation datasets with 1891 patients and 16 external-validation datasets with 777 patients. Ten publications contributed to both groups. The sum was 2668 validation observations; the unique patient count across datasets and publications could not be verified. Internal sensitivity was 0.77 (95% CI 0.72-0.81; PI 0.57-0.89), specificity 0.82 (95% CI 0.78-0.86; PI 0.60-0.93); DOR, 15.49 (95% CI 11.16-21.50); and area under the curve (AUC), 0.86 (95% CI 0.83-0.89). External sensitivity was 0.73 (95% CI 0.61-0.81; PI 0.34-0.93), specificity 0.83 (95% CI 0.73-0.90; PI 0.36-0.98), DOR 12.93 (95% CI 7.25-23.07), and AUC 0.84 (95% CI 0.79-0.89). DOR PIs were 5.40-44.44 and 2.40-69.62, respectively. Thirty-two studies were conducted in China, and 12 had high validation risk of bias. All GRADE-assessed outcomes had very low certainty. Selecting the first eligible imaging model reported in each article instead of the highest-AUC model showed modest decreases in average performance across 16 internal and 10 external datasets; incomplete alternative-model reporting limited interpretation. Single study algorithm estimates were reported descriptively, without ranking algorithms or interpreting their CIs as evidence of between study consistency or generalizability.
CONCLUSIONS: By combining multiple neoadjuvant strategies and separating validation stages, this review extends earlier neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy (NCRT)-focused syntheses and identifies priorities for further model evaluation. Imaging-based AI may support response assessment, but wide PIs, risk of bias, and very low evidence certainty preclude routine clinical adoption without prospective, geographically diverse validation. Future studies should evaluate prespecified models in independent populations, report clinically relevant decision thresholds, and assess calibration and patient outcomes. Until such evidence is available, these models should be considered investigational adjuncts to response assessment and should not independently guide organ preservation or omission of surgery after neoadjuvant treatment.
43014493: Addiction-related cues trigger craving and precipitate relapse, yet whether substance use disorders (SUDs) and behavioral addictions (BAs) share a universal neurobiological cue-reactivity core remains unresolved. We conducted a coordinate-based meta-analysis using Seed-based d Mapping with Permutation of Subject Images (SDM-PSI) to synthesize whole-brain fMRI studies comparing visually evoked cue-reactivity in strictly diagnosed SUDs and BAs versus healthy controls. An updated systematic search through September 12, 2026, yielded 50 eligible articles comprising 53 independent contrasts and 2578 participants. Pooled analyses across all addictions revealed convergent cue-elicited activations in the mid-cingulate cortex, precentral gyrus, and a midline midbrain region. However, a formal SUD ∩ BA conjunction analysis yielded no family-wise error (FWE)-corrected shared clusters. Direct comparisons demonstrated greater activation in the left hippocampus, pregenual anterior cingulate cortex, and precuneus for SUDs relative to BAs. Importantly, the left hippocampal and precuneus differences survived age adjustment; furthermore, the hippocampal finding remained robust when restricting analyses to highly controlled cue-versus-neutral paradigms, while the precuneus finding was retained within picture-cue modalities. Furthermore, exploratory analyses of clinical characteristics indicated that cue-elicited neural responses were associated with specific clinical states and treatment variables (e.g., methadone maintenance in heroin use disorder), highlighting the modulatory effect of clinical symptom profiles on these regional functional signatures. Overall, the results motivate further investigation of memory- and self-related processes, as well as control- or action-related processes. These findings offer a critical foundation for developing targeted clinical interventions, distinguishing between generalized transdiagnostic neuromodulation targets and disorder-specific therapies tailored to distinct clinical and demographic profile.
43014553:
BACKGROUND: Despite the ubiquity of Theraphosidae (tarantulas) in the pet trade, the clinical literature on theraphosid envenomation is heterogeneous, geographically uneven, dominated by selective self-report, and frequently obscured by taxonomic misidentification.
METHODS: PubMed/MEDLINE and supplementary sources were screened against pre-specified criteria for published reports of human theraphosid bites (PRISMA).
RESULTS: Forty-two reports (1889-2026) entered the primary synthesis: 39 were localizable to 17 countries, one did not state the bite country, and two were international hobbyist compilations. Reporting concentrated in South Asia, in captive-keeper bites in Europe and North America, and in Australia. Among Old World species (native to Africa, Asia, and Australasia), African, South Asian, and Southeast Asian lineages were repeatedly associated with intense local pain, delayed generalized muscle cramping, creatine kinase elevation, and, rarely, transient atrial fibrillation, whereas Australian bites caused severe local pain without cramping. New World bites (species native to the Americas) predominantly produced minor local effects, with rare systemic exceptions (suspected anaphylaxis, prolonged cramping, thrombocytopenia). Only 8 of 42 reports had identification by a named arachnologist, zoologist, or institutional laboratory. No validated antivenom and no death attributable to a verified Theraphosidae bite were identified; two deaths attributed to the genus Chilobrachys in a 1997 Indian report lack documented taxonomic and causal confirmation.
CONCLUSIONS: Most reported theraphosid bites were minor, but the literature cannot estimate population-level risk without defined denominators. Some Old World bites were high-acuity events, and the literature has emphasized less heterogeneity in Old World envenomations than exists. Priorities include standardized species identification, prospective registries, and consistent severity reporting.
43014990:
OBJECTIVES: Aortic stenosis (AS) assessment requires integration of discordant echocardiographic and clinical information. The reliability of large language models (LLMs) across prompts and AS phenotypes remains uncertain. This study aimed to compare five LLMs across four prompting strategies for AS severity classification, real-world intervention concordance and exploratory prognostic associations.
METHODS: This retrospective study evaluated five LLMs across four prompting strategies in 1455 patients with AS. Task 1 assessed AS severity classification and Task 2 assessed real-world intervention concordance. Performance was summarised by accuracy, balanced accuracy and macro-F1. Exploratory associations of the best performing Task 2 configuration with all-cause mortality and heart failure progression were examined using Kaplan-Meier analysis and multivariable Cox regression.
RESULTS: GPT-o1/chain-of-thought (CoT) achieved the highest Task 1 accuracy (97.53%), balanced accuracy (90.93%) and macro-F1 (83.19%). Grok-2/CoT achieved the highest Task 2 concordance (88.32%). Grok-2/CoT recommendations separated heart failure progression-free survival in unadjusted analysis (p=0.006) but not overall survival (p=0.105). After adjustment, recommendation group was not independently associated with mortality (HR 1.41, 95% CI 0.58 to 3.45, p=0.453) or heart failure progression (HR 1.10, 95% CI 0.44 to 2.74, p=0.832).
DISCUSSION: LLM performance varied by model, task and prompt. Apparent prognostic separation observed in unadjusted analysis was not retained after adjustment for clinical characteristics, AS severity and actual intervention.
CONCLUSION: LLMs require prompt standardisation, class-specific evaluation and prospective validation before clinical use.
43015151:
PURPOSE: To assess the prognostic value of plaque burden based on CACS and SIS categories over CAD-RADS.
METHODS: In this retrospective, single-center study, 2850 adults who underwent elective CCTA between 2016 and 2020 were screened. A total of 1818 patients were enrolled based on very low-to-intermediate pre-test risk, good image quality (Likert score ≥4), and ≥3 years of follow-up. Clinical data were collected, and CAD-RADS 2.0 with CACS-based plaque burden (CACS-P score) and SIS-based plaque burden (SIS-P score) was quantified. Prediction of 5-point MACE composite outcome (late unplanned coronary revascularization, non-fatal myocardial infarction, hospitalization for heart failure, hospitalization for angina, all-cause mortality) and 2-point MACE composite outcome (non-fatal myocardial infarction and all-cause mortality) was evaluated using survival analysis and multivariable models.
RESULTS: During a median available follow-up of 62 months, 178/1818 patients (9.8%) experienced a 5-point MACE and 96/1818 (5.3%) experienced myocardial infarction/death within the fixed 36-month analysis horizon. Both CAD-RADS severity and plaque burden scores were associated with adverse outcomes. Integration of the CACS-based P-score identified revealed heterogeneity in risk estimates within CAD-RADS categories. For the primary endpoint, CAD-RADS 3/P0 showed HR point estimates of similar magnitude to those observed in CAD-RADS 4-5/P0 and CAD-RADS 4-5/P3-P4 (HR 15.95 [95% CI:3.95-64.36], HR 16.21 [3.23-81.31], and HR 14.13 [5.70-35.01], respectively). For myocardial infarction/death, CAD-RADS 2-3/P0 showed HR point estimates of similar magnitude to those observed in CAD-RADS 4-5/P1-P2. Conversely, SIS-P provided limited additional within category risk stratification.
CONCLUSIONS: CACS-based P score may refine risk stratification in patients with mild-to-moderate stenosis.
43015530: Bone age assessment (BAA) and fracture detection are essential tasks in orthopedic radiography, since they aid diagnosis and clinical decision-making in trauma treatment. Recent technologies in artificial intelligence (AI), particularly deep learning (DL), have enhanced the ability to analyze radiological images with greater accuracy and consistency. However, current studies are incomplete, with inconsistent evaluation methodologies, limited external validation, and insufficient interpretability, limiting clinical implementation. This study provides a systematic PRISMA-based review of 116 studies (2017-2025) that analyze imaging modalities, datasets, model architectures, evaluation techniques, and clinical relevance. A uniform taxonomy is introduced to define techniques based on task, modality, and learning paradigm, along with a comparative methodology to address inconsistencies across studies. The findings indicate that CNN and transformer-based models achieve MAE as low as 0.4-0.7 years and accuracy exceeding 95% in controlled datasets but are limited by dataset bias, poor generalization, and a lack of standardized benchmarks. Although explainable AI (XAI) approaches increase interpretability, their clinical reliability is still limited. This review synthesizes current methodologies, identifies key problems, and proposes future directions for AI systems that are robust, interpretable, and clinically deployable, while unifying BAA and fracture detection under a single taxonomy that integrates modality, task, and learning paradigm.
43015648:
BACKGROUND: Ischemic cardiomyopathy remains a leading cause of cardiovascular mortality. Although autologous CD133⁺ progenitor cell therapy has been investigated as an adjunct to coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG), its clinical efficacy and safety remain uncertain. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of autologous CD133⁺ cell therapy administered during CABG in patients with ischemic cardiomyopathy.
METHODS: A comprehensive search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, Google Scholar, and the Cochrane Library was conducted from database inception to January 2026. Eligible studies included randomized controlled trials and observational studies involving adults with ischemic cardiomyopathy in whom intraoperative administration of autologous CD133⁺ cells during CABG was compared with CABG alone. Random-effects meta-analyses were performed using maximum likelihood estimation with Hartung-Knapp adjustment. The certainty of evidence for critical and important outcomes was assessed using GRADE.
RESULTS: Eleven studies encompassing 495 participants were included (7 RCTs, 4 cohort studies). No significant between-group difference was observed in MRI-assessed LVEF (MD - 1.34% [95% CI, - 9.09 to 6.41]; 4 studies), echocardiographic LVEF (MD 0.67% [95% CI, - 5.32 to 6.65]; 4 studies), or all-cause mortality (RR 0.88 [95% CI, 0.23 to 3.32]; 5 studies). MRI-derived LVESV showed no statistically significant reduction (MD - 21.57 mL [95% CI, - 67.07 to 23.92]; 2 studies). No significant between-group difference was observed in arrhythmia (RR 1.02 [95% CI, 0.68 to 1.54]; 2 studies; low certainty), and six-minute walk test results were highly imprecise, limiting clinical interpretability (MD 13.98 m [95% CI, - 530.79 to 558.76]; 2 studies; very low certainty). The certainty of evidence was very low or low across outcomes assessed with GRADE. Subgroup analysis by risk of bias demonstrated a statistically significant difference for MRI-assessed LVEF (p = 0.008), with no benefit observed in low-risk-of-bias studies.
CONCLUSION: Adjunctive autologous CD133⁺ cell therapy during CABG was not associated with consistent improvements in global left ventricular function or major clinical outcomes in ischemic cardiomyopathy. The certainty of evidence was very low across critical outcomes, and the LVESV finding should be considered exploratory and hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory evidence of structural remodeling. Larger adequately powered randomized trials with standardized protocols are needed before this therapy can be recommended for routine clinical use.
43015946: Accurate, rapid, and standardized interpretation of multiparametric flow cytometry findings is essential for clinical decision-making in patients evaluated for suspected acute leukemia. This study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic performance of ChatGPT, a general-purpose large language model, in interpreting de-identified, laboratory-generated flow cytometry graphical outputs from patients with suspected acute leukemia and to assess its agreement with the consensus interpretation of two hematologists in terms of diagnostic classification, blast percentage estimation, and hematogone detection. This retrospective observational validation study included 560 patients who underwent bone marrow aspiration and flow cytometric immunophenotyping during their initial diagnostic evaluation for suspected acute leukemia. All included patients were undergoing initial diagnostic evaluation and had neither a previous diagnosis of leukemia nor prior leukemia-directed treatment. The consensus diagnosis established by two hematologists was considered the reference standard. Between May 4 and 15, 2026, de-identified, laboratory-generated PDF images containing flow cytometry dot plots from a three-tube acute leukemia panel comprising 28 antibody-fluorochrome combinations were uploaded directly through the ChatGPT Plus web interface and interpreted using GPT-5.5 (OpenAI). Raw FCS files were not provided. Using the same standardized prompt for each case, the model was asked to estimate the blast percentage, select a single most likely diagnosis from five predefined categories (no pathology, MDS, AML, B-ALL, or T-ALL), and determine the presence or absence of hematogones. The initial response for each case was archived and directly encoded without adjudication. Diagnosis-specific performance was evaluated using one-versus-rest sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, negative predictive value, accuracy, and F1-score. Overall agreement between ChatGPT-generated classifications and hematologist consensus was assessed using Cohen's kappa. Pearson's correlation coefficient was used to evaluate the association between blast percentage estimates, whereas Bland-Altman analysis was used to quantify agreement, systematic bias, and 95% limits of agreement. Hematogone detection was evaluated as a binary classification task using sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy. ChatGPT achieved an overall diagnostic accuracy of 78.8% (95% CI, 75.2%-81.9%), with substantial agreement with hematologist consensus (Cohen's κ = 0.712; 95% CI, 0.664-0.757). Diagnosis-specific sensitivity ranged from 69.2% to 87.3%, and PPV ranged from 60.0% to 93.5%. The highest sensitivity was observed for MDS, whereas the highest PPV was observed for no pathology. McNemar's test identified significant systematic differences between ChatGPT and hematologist classifications for no pathology (p = 0.041), AML (p = 0.008), and T-ALL (p = 0.023). Blast percentage estimates were strongly correlated (Pearson's r = 0.818; 95% CI, 0.789-0.844; p< 0.001); however, Bland-Altman analysis demonstrated a mean positive bias of 3.92 percentage points, indicating systematic overestimation by ChatGPT. For hematogone detection, ChatGPT achieved an accuracy of 89.5%, sensitivity of 70.3%, and specificity of 92.4%. ChatGPT-based flow cytometry interpretation showed promise for preliminary diagnostic classification and quality assurance applications. However, expert hematologist validation remains essential, particularly in scenarios associated with high diagnostic consequences, including AML and T-ALL classification, blast percentage estimation, and accurate discrimination of hematogones.
43016123:
PURPOSE: Although professional societies provide standardized resources, the reliability of online health content remains inconsistent, particularly as large language models (LLMs) become a growing source of patient information. Therefore, the primary objective of this study was to determine whether patient-focused prompt optimization improves the readability of Generative Pre-trained Transformer-5 (GPT-5) Thinking responses compared with standard prompting while evaluating potential changes in expert-rated factual accuracy using educational materials published by the European Society of Breast Imaging (EUSOBI).
METHODS: All GPT-5 Thinking outputs were prospectively generated in January 2026. The dataset included frequently asked questions (FAQs) and special information notes (SINs) derived from EUSOBI articles, each submitted under two distinct prompts (standard-Prompt 1 vs. patient-focused-Prompt 2). Readability was quantified using four indices with an averaged composite "reading grade level." Accuracy was scored by two radiologists using a 5-point Likert scale.
RESULTS: A total of 48 questions (15 FAQs and 33 SIN-derived questions) were each answered under two prompt conditions, yielding 96 responses for analysis. Prompt 2 produced significantly lower readability levels than Prompt 1 across all indices (P < 0.001). These improvements occurred without significant differences in word count (P = 0.12) or sentence count (P = 0.63). The mean accuracy scores remained high and comparable between prompts for all questions (4.54 ± 0.63 vs. 4.52 ± 0.59, P = 0.75). The inter-rater agreement was almost perfect for both the FAQ and SIN-derived question sets (κ = 0.82 and 0.81, respectively).
CONCLUSION: Patient-focused prompting substantially reduced the linguistic complexity and reading grade level of GPT-5 Thinking responses without a statistically significant reduction in expert-rated accuracy, demonstrating its ability to produce more accessible breast imaging content, although the resulting grade level remained above widely recommended patient-education thresholds.
CLINICAL SIGNIFICANCE: A simple, low-cost prompt modification can substantially improve the readability of LLM-generated patient education content in breast imaging without a measurable reduction in expert-rated accuracy, although further work is needed to confirm this translates into improved patient comprehension.
43017794:
BACKGROUND: CT perfusion (CTP) hemodynamic thresholds may overestimate the ischemic core (ghost core) in early presenters. We hypothesized that a metabolic model, defining the core by decreased cerebral metabolic rate of oxygen and penumbra by increased oxygen extraction fraction, estimated from standard CTP, would better predict tissue fate and early neurological outcome.
METHODS: This retrospective single-center study (October 2015 to October 2025) included consecutive thrombectomy-treated patients with anterior-circulation large-vessel occlusion, admission CTP, and 48±12-hour diffusion-weighted imaging. Predefined relative cerebral metabolic rate of oxygen and oxygen extraction fraction thresholds (metabolic model) were compared with relative cerebral blood flow ≤30% and time-to-maximum (Tmax) ≥6 seconds (hemodynamic model) against diffusion-weighted imaging. Each imaging model (core and penumbra volumes) was added to clinical covariates predicting 48-hour lesion volume (linear regression) and 24-hour and discharge National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (ANCOVA), tested by nested F-tests; imaging models were compared by paired bootstrap of cross-validated R2.
RESULTS: Of 3011 thrombectomy patients, 227 were included (median age, 70 years; 46% male; median onset-to-CTP, 108 minutes; 162 recanalized). Relative cerebral metabolic rate of oxygen ≤30% reduced core overestimation versus relative cerebral blood flow ≤30% (bias, +2.6 versus +20.0 mL; dice, 0.20 versus 0.18; both P<0.001; reproduced in temporal validation), but >10-mL underestimation was more frequent (17% versus 6%). Relative cerebral blood flow error decreased with onset-to-recanalization delay (ρ=-0.30), unlike relative cerebral metabolic rate of oxygen (ρ=0.01). In 65 nonrecanalized patients, relative oxygen extraction fraction ≥125% outperformed time-to-maximum on bias (+14.3 versus +19.3 mL; P<0.001) and dice (P=0.002), but not absolute error (P=0.24). The metabolic model better explained 48-hour lesion volume (cross-validated R2, 0.32 versus 0.22; P=0.002). Only the metabolic model improved 24-hour (P=0.004) and discharge (P=0.009) National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale score prediction over clinical covariates, outperforming the hemodynamic model at discharge (P=0.04) but not at 24 hours (P=0.21).
CONCLUSIONS: A CTP-derived metabolic model reduced ghost-core misclassification, particularly in early presenters, and better explained 48-hour lesion volume than hemodynamic thresholds, with modest added value for early neurological outcome. Positron emission tomography and external validation are warranted.
43017920:
OBJECTIVES: Benign-appearing endometrial cells (BECs) are reported on Papanicolaou tests in women aged 45 years or older per the 2014 Bethesda System, and current American Society for Colposcopy and Cervical Pathology guidelines recommend endometrial evaluation for postmenopausal women with BECs. However, the clinical significance of BECs across age groups and menopausal status varies among published studies.
METHODS: We retrospectively identified Papanicolaou tests reporting BECs in women aged 45 years or older at our institution (2021-2023). Histologic follow-up diagnoses were analyzed by age and menopausal status. A random-effects meta-analysis combined our cohort with 6 comparable published series.
RESULTS: Among 133 280 Papanicolaou tests, BECs were reported in 2030 women aged at least 45 years (1.5%). Of 604 women with histologic follow-up, clinically significant pathology (atypical endometrial hyperplasia or endometrial carcinoma) was identified in 6.0% (36/604). Endometrial carcinoma risk increased with age, from 0.9% (45-49 years) to 6.9% (≥60 years; P < .001) and was higher in postmenopausal than in premenopausal women (5.2% vs 0.6%; P <0.001). Clinically significant pathology risk remained at or below 5% through age 59 years but rose to 12.8% at or beyond 60 years of age. Meta-analysis of 7 cohorts (4989 women) yielded a pooled estimate of 4.5% (95% CI, 3.3%-6.0%; I2 = 75%), with our cohort toward the upper end of the range.
CONCLUSIONS: The risk of atypical endometrial hyperplasia and endometrial carcinoma increases substantially after age 60 years and in postmenopausal women while remaining low in younger, premenopausal women. Meta-analysis confirmed a modest but clinically meaningful overall risk. Incorporating both age and menopausal status into clinical triage may improve risk stratification beyond age alone.
43018083: The goal of prostate cancer screening is to reduce morbidity and mortality through the early detection of clinically significant disease. Accumulating evidence shows that prostate-specific antigen (PSA)-based screening significantly reduces prostate cancer mortality and advanced-stage diagnosis, and approaches to reduce harms associated with screening are increasingly being used. The ACS conducted a systematic review and commissioned a modeling study to evaluate PSA-based screening strategies, and concluded that the benefits of screening outweigh the harms. Before initiating screening, clinicians should ensure that patients are informed about the benefits, limitations, and harms of screening; the potential follow-up evaluations of elevated PSA levels; and the expectation that low-risk cancers will initially be managed with active surveillance. The ACS recommends biennial screening from ages 50-69 years for average-risk men (i.e., non-Black men without a family history of prostate cancer). Annual screening from ages 45-69 years is recommended for Black men. Annual screening from ages 45-69 years is recommended for non-Black men with a strong family history (i.e., multiple first-degree relatives diagnosed with prostate cancer at any age or one diagnosed before age 65 years). Biennial screening from ages 45-69 years is recommended for non-Black men with a single first-degree relative diagnosed at age 65 years or older. For men ages 70-74 years, the balance of benefits and harms is uncertain, and individualized decision making is recommended. The ACS recommends further evaluating men ages 45-69 years with PSA levels ≥3.0 ng/mL and men ages 70-74 years with PSA levels ≥6.5 ng/mL. Most men who have elevated PSA levels confirmed on repeat testing should be offered magnetic resonance imaging and/or a validated biomarker test to guide biopsy decisions. Screening is not recommended for men with a life expectancy <10 years and should be discontinued at age 75 years.
43018111:
OBJECTIVE: Near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) is a point-of-care imaging modality that provides real-time measurement of tissue oxygenation and hemoglobin dynamics. Conventional vascular testing remains an essential component of wound care and limb preservation but evaluates vessel anatomy, blood flow, and other aspects of vascular status that differ from the tissue-level physiological information provided by NIRS. Although the 2 approaches may be complementary, NIRS can independently inform clinical decision-making by providing immediate physiological information at the point of care. This study employed a modified Delphi process to characterize expert perspectives regarding the clinical role, integration, workflow, and value of NIRS across wound care, tissue assessment, and related procedural settings.
METHODS: A modified Delphi process was conducted with a multidisciplinary panel representing diverse specialties, practice settings, and geographic regions. Survey items addressed clinical indications, workflow integration, decision-making impact, operational considerations, and the relationship between NIRS and conventional vascular assessment. Consensus was predefined as ≥80% agreement. A supplementary workflow and time analysis was performed using a subset of experienced users to characterize procedural steps and associated time requirements.
RESULTS: Survey responses generally supported confidence in vascular testing when appropriately selected, performed, and interpreted; however, the Round 1 panel discussion highlighted concerns regarding study selection, interpretation, repeat testing, and variability across testing pathways. Access and timeliness emerged as additional challenges that were consistently identified across both survey responses and the panel discussion. Delays in obtaining clinically meaningful physiological information were reported to contribute to clinically significant consequences, including hospitalization and amputation, particularly in lower-access environments. There was strong agreement that point-of-care NIRS enables earlier recognition of underlying pathophysiology and more timely initiation of appropriate interventions. NIRS was described as integrated across the continuum of care, including initial evaluation, procedural planning, treatment modification, referral support, and longitudinal monitoring. Of the 40 consensus items evaluated by the 18-member panel, 37 (92.5%) met the predefined ≥80% agreement threshold. Overall interrater agreement was very strong (median rWG: 0.92; interquartile range: 0.84 to 1.00). The supplementary workflow and time analysis demonstrated that image acquisition activities were generally efficient, whereas interpretation, documentation, reporting, and care coordination accounted for a substantial proportion of total clinician effort.
CONCLUSIONS: This study identifies a clinically meaningful gap between the availability of diagnostic testing and the timely delivery of actionable physiological information within wound care workflows. Although conventional vascular testing remains essential, clinicians described challenges related to testing pathways, study selection, interpretation, access, timeliness, and integration of physiological information into clinical decision-making. Within this context, NIRS provides point-of-care physiological information and supports longitudinal monitoring of tissue oxygenation throughout treatment. By providing real-time physiological insight, NIRS may facilitate earlier recognition of deteriorating tissue status, support more timely intervention, and help bridge episodic diagnostic assessment with continuous clinical management. More broadly, these findings suggest that the value of emerging diagnostic technologies should be evaluated not only by the information they generate, but also by their ability to deliver actionable data within clinical workflows, support longitudinal monitoring, and account for the clinician effort required to interpret, integrate, document, and act upon physiological findings.
43018449: Purpose To identify accurate imaging protocols for energy-integrating detector (EID) CT and photon-counting detector (PCD) CT, to establish comparable protocols across systems, and to evaluate the reproducibility of lung densitometry across body sizes, sites, and dose levels. Materials and Methods A chest phantom and a multidiameter phantom were scanned across four academic medical centers with PCD CT and EID CT systems across three doses. PCD CT included standard-resolution and ultrahigh-resolution (UHR) acquisitions with low-energy threshold (T3D) and virtual monoenergetic image (VMI) reconstructions, whereas EID CT used filtered back projection. Soft and sharp body and quantitative kernels were evaluated. Optimal protocols minimized mean absolute error (MAE) from reference CT attenuation values. Comparable protocols were identified using the histogram similarity index (HSI) within the lung sample (chest phantom), and reproducibility was assessed using air-insert density measurements. Statistical analyses included a Gaussian linear mixed-effects model and nonparametric tests for reproducibility. Results PCD CT outperformed both EID CT systems (P < .05) across 7392 measurements, achieving a lower MAE (3.7 HU ± 3.7 [SD]) than EID CT1 (6.4 HU ± 4.0; P < .05) and EID CT2 (12.4 HU ± 9.7; P < .05). The optimal PCD CT protocol used the UHR mode, high-dose, standard-resolution VMI, and soft quantitative reconstructions. Protocol matching across scanners was feasible, yielding an HSI of 95.6% ± 1.2 under optimal settings. Compared with EID CT, PCD CT exhibited greater reproducibility across body sizes (<2.2 HU), across sites (<2.5 HU), across dose levels (<3.9 HU), and within dose levels (<2.5 HU). Conclusion PCD CT provided more accurate and reproducible lung densitometry while maintaining comparability with EID CT protocols. Keywords: Phantom Studies, CT, CT-Photon Counting, CT-Quantitative, Thorax, Lung, Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease, Comparative Studies, Technology Assessment, Physics Supplemental material is available for this article. © RSNA, 2026.
43018656:
BACKGROUND: Subtalar joint (STJ) injections are used for chronic hindfoot pain but evidence comparing guidance methods remains limited.
METHODS: This systematic review followed PRISMA 2020. PubMed, Embase (via Ovid), Scopus and Web of Science were searched from inception to December 2025, and the searches were re-run in a broadened form in July 2026. Eligible studies included comparative studies, single-arm cohort or case-series studies with 10 or more procedures and technical/cadaveric accuracy studies reporting subtalar-specific outcomes. Two reviewers independently screened studies, extracted data and assessed risk of bias. Heterogeneity and scarce direct comparison precluded meta-analysis.
RESULTS: Seventeen studies were eligible: 12 reported clinical data and five reported cadaveric technical accuracy data only (one clinical study also contributed a cadaveric control arm). Denominators are reported in their own units and are not combined: the clinical studies contributed 129 patients (six studies), 100 injected joints (four studies) and 779 injections (two studies). Ultrasound, fluoroscopy and landmark-guided injection were each reported in five studies. No study of CT or SPECT-CT guidance provided a subtalar-specific outcome. Needle placement accuracy ranged from 68 to 100%, but difference in design, populations and confirmation methods prevented comparison between modalities.
CONCLUSION: STJ injections are associated with clinical improvement but evidence is predominantly observational and heterogeneous. Differences in reporting technical accuracy, injectate, clinical response and adverse events prevent comparison of guidance methods. No modality's superiority is established. Prospective comparative studies using standardised outcomes and consistent safety reporting are needed.
43018718: Extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) can be considered as a rescue strategy in highly selected patients with refractory cardiac arrest and a potentially reversible cause of cardiac arrest. Both ECPR itself and the subsequent treatment under extracorporeal life support (ECLS) are complex and resource intensive. There is currently no robust evidence for the superiority of ECPR over conventional cardiopulmonary resuscitation. The implementation and maintenance of an effective ECPR program requires clearly structured processes, defined communication channels and robust institutional infrastructure for quality assurance. Ensuring comprehensive and intersectoral quality of care requires the cooperative collaboration of many necessary disciplines. This consensus paper updates the document published in 2018 and defines a common framework of central structural, procedural and clinical requirements.

43018864:
OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to evaluate atrioventricular interaction in patients with chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) and to determine the effects of balloon pulmonary angioplasty (BPA) on reversible cardiac remodeling assessed by cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: In this prospective single-center study, 52 patients with CTEPH (mean age: 58 ± 11 years; 34 females) and 35 healthy controls underwent CMR imaging. Twenty-five patients (mean age: 60 ± 12 years; 19 females) who underwent BPA received follow-up CMR at a mean interval of 7 ± 5 months. Cardiac structure, function, myocardial deformation, and epicardial adipose tissue (EAT) were assessed based on cine images.
RESULTS: Compared with controls, patients with CTEPH demonstrated predominant right-sided cardiac involvement, characterized by reduced right ventricular ejection fraction (p < 0.001), marked enlargement of right atrial (RA) and ventricular (RV) volumes, and severely impaired right heart strain (all p < 0.001). Left ventricular systolic function was relatively preserved, with mildly impaired global circumferential strain (p = 0.011) and a trend toward attenuated longitudinal strain (p = 0.055), whereas all left atrial (LA) strain components were markedly impaired (all p < 0.05), indicating altered atrioventricular interaction. Following BPA, the right heart structure, RV function and deformation, and LA conduit strain improved. EAT was comparable between groups and remained unchanged after BPA.
CONCLUSION: CTEPH involves marked right heart systolic dysfunction and early biventricular diastolic abnormalities associated with impaired atrioventricular interaction. BPA could reverse cardiac remodeling by improving right heart structure, function, and partially recovering atrial deformation after pressure relief.
KEY POINTS: Questions Atrioventricular interaction abnormalities and reversible cardiac remodeling in chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) after balloon pulmonary angioplasty (BPA) remain insufficiently characterized. Findings CTEPH is associated with impaired right heart strain and altered atrioventricular interaction; BPA improves right heart structure and function and partially recovers atrial deformation. Critical relevance statement Cardiac MRI-derived myocardial deformation and atrial phasic function may reflect alterations in atrioventricular interaction in CTEPH and complement conventional metrics in assessing cardiac remodeling and recovery after BPA.
43018894:
OBJECTIVES: Lung cancer screening (LCS) with low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) significantly reduces mortality among high-risk individuals, yet implementation remains limited at national and European levels. The Strengthening the Screening of Lung Cancer (SOLACE) Project aims to facilitate the implementation of equitable LCS. While considering the overall impact of LCS, we identified a lack of systematic evaluation on the impact on the workload of radiology professionals, including radiologists and radiographers. This multicentric, European-wide study prospectively examines the effects of LCS on radiology healthcare workers.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: A survey-based cross-sectional study was conducted among European radiology professionals engaged in LCS to evaluate their experiences across seven domains: impacts on workload, workflow specifics, reporting practices, artificial intelligence (AI) use, participation in training programmes, potential professional development, and overall support for LCS.
RESULTS: We evaluated 56 responses (mean age 46 ± 10.8 years; 27 men) from 14 countries. About half of respondents (53.6%; n = 30) reported increased working hours, but only 21.6% (n = 11) felt overworked due to LCS. No significant factors were directly associated with feeling overworked. Most respondents (86.7%; n = 39) perceived increased expertise in assessing LCS LDCTs throughout screening, and 91.1% (n = 51) expressed support for the implementation of LCS.
CONCLUSION: Although LCS increased workload for many radiology professionals, few reported feeling overworked. Despite the added demands, there may be added benefits for radiology professionals. Taken together, these findings emphasise the importance of continuously evaluating and monitoring how LCS affects the workload of radiology healthcare professionals.
KEY POINTS: Question As wider implementation of lung cancer screening occurs in Europe, it is critical to consider its impact on radiology professionals' workload and associated workforce demands. Findings Although lung cancer screening increased workload for many radiology professionals, few felt overworked, and the majority perceived increased diagnostic confidence and support for screening implementation.
CRITICAL RELEVANCE STATEMENT: Lung cancer screening via LDCT plays a critical role in detecting cancer earlier and improving survival. With growing support for the broader implementation of LCS, it is essential to consider its potential impact on the workload of radiology professionals.
43018984:
BACKGROUND: Differentiated thyroid cancer (DTC) generally carries an excellent prognosis, yet recurrence occurs in up to 8-9% of patients. Artificial intelligence (AI) models are increasingly proposed to predict DTC recurrence; however, their methodological quality and clinical readiness are poorly defined. We conducted a systematic review to evaluate the methodological quality, risk of bias, and applicability of these models using the PROBAST + AI framework.
METHODS: We searched Ovid MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane databases, Scopus, and Web of Science from inception to July 13, 2026. Eligible studies included original research developing or validating AI models for recurrence in DTC. Model quality (for development), risk of bias (for evaluation), and applicability were assessed using the PROBAST + AI framework, with a focus on discrimination, calibration, and validation strategies (PROSPERO; registration number [CRD420251004644]).
RESULTS: Of 673 records screened, 34 studies were included (21 unique datasets and 13 UCI-derived publications), encompassing 21,267 patients with a recurrence rate of 7.8%. Most were developed in Asian cohorts (17 of 21 datasets) and were structured clinical/tabular variables (82.4%), including demographic, clinical, laboratory, and pathological data, whereas the remaining models incorporated multimodal inputs such as imaging-derived or radiomic features. Notably, nearly one quarter of included studies (13 of 34, 38%) represented reanalysis of a single dataset. Discrimination was reported in 22 of 34 studies (64.7%) (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUC] 0.67-1.00), though only 10 studies assessed calibration, none with standardized metrics. The PROBAST + AI assessment revealed high overall quality concerns in 26 of 34 (76.5%) development studies due to reliance on single-center cohorts, inadequate handling of missing data, and absence of external validation. Only 6 of 34 included studies (17.6%) were judged to have low overall quality concern, whereas 17 of 34 (50.0%) were rated as having low applicability concern.
CONCLUSIONS: AI models for predicting DTC recurrence show promising discriminatory performance but have substantial methodological shortcomings in development, and a lack of calibration and external validation necessary for clinical use. Given the guidelines' emphasis on risk-adapted de-escalation of therapy, the development of robust, validated, and clinically calibrated AI tools is a priority. Current evidence remains insufficient to support routine clinical use.
43019229: Primary amenorrhea is the absence of menarche in a 15-year-old adolescent girl who has developed secondary sex characteristics or a 13-year-old girl without development. Primary amenorrhea reflects disruption along the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian-uterine axis and may arise from a spectrum of anatomic, genetic, or functional abnormalities. Although primary amenorrhea is less common than secondary amenorrhea, recognition of the underlying level of dysfunction is essential for appropriate diagnosis and management as well as informed counseling regarding the patient's reproductive potential. A structured anatomic approach allows categorization of the causes into three levels based on the predominant site of dysfunction: level I, which involves the uterus and vaginal outflow tract; level II, which involves the ovaries and gonads; and level III, which involves the hypothalamus and pituitary gland. This classification system emphasizes a systematic and multidisciplinary approach to diagnosis and treatment, integrating clinical and biochemical testing and targeted imaging to localize the underlying dysfunction and guide treatment. Transabdominal US serves as the first-line imaging modality to help determine the presence and morphology of the pelvic organs. MRI provides detailed characterization of müllerian and urinary tract anomalies and allows evaluation of the hypothalamic-pituitary region when central causes are suspected.
43019230: Systemic sclerosis (SSc) or scleroderma is a multisystem autoimmune disorder characterized by a variable pattern of skin thickening and involvement of visceral organs. The pathophysiology is similar across all organs, which is chronic low-grade inflammation, with vasculopathy and eventual fibrosis. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, particularly in patients with established disease comprising characteristic skin and visceral manifestations, with a supportive role of laboratory and imaging findings. The presence of radiologic signs such as hidebound bowel or a combination of patulous lower esophageal sphincter, pulmonary fibrosis, skin thickening, and Raynaud phenomenon is relatively specific for SSc. Nevertheless, imaging in SSc is primarily used to determine the pattern, severity, and complications of visceral organ involvement, rather than for diagnosis of SSc. Radiologic evaluation in SSc employs a wide gamut of investigations, depending on the organ of interest. For example, US is used for the skin and superficial tissues; fluoroscopy, CT, or MR enterography for the gastrointestinal tract; endoanal US or MRI for the internal anal sphincter; high-resolution CT for the lungs; echocardiography and cardiac MRI for SSc-related pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) and cardiac disease; and radiography, CT, or MRI for musculoskeletal involvement. Early diagnosis of treatable features, such as PAH and gastroesophageal reflux, can help reduce the morbidity and mortality associated with SSc. Imaging is additionally useful to prognosticate and monitor the disease. The authors focus on the multisystem, multimodality imaging manifestations of SSc with relevant differential diagnoses to bridge the gaps in knowledge about SSc. ©RSNA, 2026.
43019231: Gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GISTs) have evolved from historically misclassified smooth muscle tumors to a distinct disease entity, defined by gain-of-function mutations in KIT or PDGFRA proto-oncogenes. The advent of targeted therapy for this entity in the form of a tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI), imatinib mesylate, has transformed the treatment for GISTs, reducing recurrence and improving survival in patients with advanced disease. Radiologists play a critical role in initial lesion identification, surgical planning, and posttherapy surveillance, with cross-sectional imaging (CT and MRI) being vital in characterizing tumor features such as endophytic or exophytic nature, pseudocapsule, ulceration, necrosis, and changes in enhancement. Incorporating the Choi criteria into routine practice further refines response assessment, guiding adjustments in therapeutic strategy. A multidisciplinary approach is essential for optimal GIST management, requiring close collaboration between surgeons, oncologists, pathologists, and radiologists to establish a diagnosis, determine resectability, consider neoadjuvant or adjuvant TKIs, and monitor for disease recurrence (with imaging intervals tailored to risk classification). Future directions involve greater incorporation of molecular profiling to personalize treatments and the integration of newer-generation TKIs for imatinib-resistant cases, highlighting the continued importance of interdisciplinary coordination.
43020361:
PURPOSE: To determine if the proportion of patients receiving thoracic imaging, invasive diagnostic, or surgical procedures following community lung cancer screening (LCS) differed from that in the National Lung Screening Trial (NLST).
METHODS: We compared the proportion of NLST participants and 2018 Medicare beneficiaries receiving imaging, invasive, or surgical procedures in the six months and one year following LCS, as well as lung cancer incidence and all-cause mortality. To create comparable cohorts, we used NLST chart abstraction data to impute information on procedures for participants with no abstraction.
RESULTS: Within six months and one-year of LCS, NLST participants were significantly more likely to have at least one imaging test than Medicare beneficiaries (21.4 versus 16.5%); (difference=4.97%; 95% confidence limits (CL) 1.85%, 8.09) and 26.6% versus 22.3% (difference=4.28; 95% CL: 0.55, 8.02) respectively. NLST participants were significantly less likely to have an invasive or surgical procedure within six months of LCS (0.60 versus 4.64%; difference: -4.04% ; 95% CL: -5.23%, -2.84%) and (0.28 versus 1.51%; difference: -1.22% ; 95% CL: -1.80%, -0.65%) respectively, but neither differed significantly at one year. NLST had more cases of lung cancer diagnosed (3.83% [95% CL: 3.33,4.33] versus Medicare 2.26% [95%CL:1.51,3.01]). Mortality was not significantly different.
CONCLUSIONS: Medicare beneficiaries were less likely to have follow-up imaging within six months and one year of LCS, and they were more likely to undergo invasive diagnostic or surgical procedures at six months, but were not statistically significant at one year following LCS.
43020703:
OBJECTIVES: Childhood central nervous system (CNS) vasculitis is a rare and serious disease for which no evidence-based consensus guidance, standardised terminology, or definitions of treatment response exist. We aimed to develop the first international recommendations for the diagnosis, classification, monitoring, and treatment of CNS vasculitis in children.
METHODS: Adapting the European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology standardised operating procedures, an international multidisciplinary panel of 42 experts from 15 countries was assembled through the European Reference Network on Rare Immunodeficiency, Autoinflammatory, Autoimmune and Paediatric Rheumatic Diseases, and the Paediatric Rheumatology European Society. A systematic literature review across 4 databases identified 182 eligible studies, graded per the Oxford Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine hierarchy. A modified Delphi survey (42 respondents) was followed by a 2-day face-to-face consensus conference (26 voting members; ≥70% agreement required).
RESULTS: The panel formulated 83 consensus statements (3 overarching principles, 14 principles, and 66 recommendations) across 7 clinical domains. Of 182 included articles, 152 (83.5%) reported paediatric data; no level 1 evidence was identified. Key advances include an 8-domain nomenclature system replacing the 'primary/secondary' dichotomy with 'idiopathic/disease-associated' terminology, a paediatric-specific vessel wall imaging interpretive principle, a prospective risk-stratification model for disease progression, genome-wide sequencing as the preferred genetic testing approach, and formal definitions of remission, relapse, and refractory disease. None of these elements had been previously codified for childhood CNS vasculitis.
CONCLUSIONS: These recommendations establish a comprehensive, evidence-graded framework for childhood CNS vasculitis. The absence of level 1 evidence across all domains points to the need for an international prospective registry and collaborative clinical trials.
43020914:
PURPOSE: To synthesize the technical success, safety, durability, and clinical efficacy of percutaneous portal vein recanalization in children with non-cirrhotic extrahepatic portal vein obstruction without underlying liver disease.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, the Cochrane Library, and Web of Science were searched from inception to May 2026 for pediatric patients with non-cirrhotic extrahepatic portal vein obstruction who underwent percutaneous portal vein recanalization. Random-effects meta-analyses estimated pooled proportions with 95% confidence intervals and prediction intervals.
RESULTS: Five retrospective single-center cohorts (73 children; variceal bleeding, hypersplenism, or both) were included. Pooled denominators were 67 for technical success, 54 for safety and mortality (Pimpalwar contributed to technical success only), and 16 for post-recanalization durability. Technical success was 55.0% (95% confidence interval 41.0-68.0; prediction interval 28.6-79.4). Procedure-related and all-cause mortality were both 0% (0/54); procedure-related hemorrhage 7% (95% confidence interval 2-23); and portal-biliary fistula 3% (95% confidence interval 0-27). Among the 16 children with successful recanalization and imaging follow-up, assisted portal vein patency was 87% (95% confidence interval 61-97); 50.8% required at least one endovascular re-intervention during surveillance, without surgical conversion; freedom from recurrent variceal or gastrointestinal bleeding among those with variceal bleeding as indication was 100% (prediction interval 73.8-100).
CONCLUSION: In children with chronic native-vessel extrahepatic portal vein obstruction, percutaneous portal vein recanalization may be feasible. No procedure-related mortality was observed, bleeding events were infrequent, and no recurrent variceal bleeding occurred after successful recanalization in patients for whom this outcome was reported.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 4, meta-analysis of case series and retrospective cohort studies.
TRIAL / PROTOCOL REGISTRATION: Prospectively registered with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO): CRD420261395918.
43021014:
OBJECTIVES: To compare a highly accelerated ECG-triggered and navigator-gated, non-contrast respiratory-compensated 3D magnetic resonance angiography with Dixon water-fat separation (NC-MRA) to respiratory-suspended non-ECG-triggered multiphase contrast-enhanced MRA (CE-MRA) in pediatric patients with partial or total cavopulmonary connection (PCPC/TCPC).
MATERIALS AND METHODS: In this prospective single-center study, between 02/2021 and 09/2023, 30 consecutive pediatric patients (mean age 3.6 ± 0.8 years) with PCPC or TCPC underwent 1.5 T cardiovascular MRI under deep sedation and mechanical ventilation. NC-MRA was acquired before contrast administration alongside standard CE-MRA. Two blinded readers independently evaluated image quality using a 5-point Likert scale and measured vascular diameters of predefined aortic segments, the Glenn anastomosis, Fontan conduit, and pulmonary arteries in consensus. Datasets were presented in randomized order. We used paired statistical testing for method comparison and Cohen's kappa to assess inter-rater agreement.
RESULTS: Mean NC-MRA acquisition time (5:55 ± 2:19 min) was comparable to that of multiphase CE-MRA (5:48 ± 3:03 min), including pre-contrast acquisition p = 0.54). Overall image quality was generally comparable between techniques for most vascular segments (NC-MRA median 5, IQR 5-5, CE-MRA median 5, IQR 4-5, p = 0.06-0.52). No significant differences were found in vascular diameter measurements across all segments (p = 0.06-0.59). Inter-reader agreement was at least substantial (κ > 0.65).
CONCLUSION: Respiratory-compensated NC-MRA at 1.5 T provides image quality and vascular diameter measurements comparable to CE-MRA in pediatric PCPC/TCPC patients. Eliminating breath-holds and contrast administration, the technique simplifies workflow, avoids mechanical ventilation, and improves patient safety in this vulnerable population.
KEY POINTS: Question Is a non-contrast, ECG-triggered, and navigator-gated 3D MRA sequence diagnostically equivalent to conventional breath-hold CE-MRA for vascular assessment in pediatric Fontan patients? Findings There were no significant differences in vascular diameters, and image quality was comparable between both sequences in most segments, showing substantial inter-rater agreement and diagnostic reliability. Clinical relevance Non-contrast, ECG-triggered, and navigator-gated MRA enables reliable vascular assessment in pediatric Fontan patients without gadolinium or breath-holds, reducing anesthesia requirements, improving safety, and simplifying workflow in this vulnerable population.
43021107:
BACKGROUND: Computed tomography urography (CTU) is widely used for evaluating urinary tract disorders, but the optimal number of acquisition phases remains uncertain because additional phases increase radiation exposure. This study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of single-, tri-, and four-phase CT urography and to synthesize available evidence on radiation dose characteristics and dose-reduction strategies.
METHODS: A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines and registered in PROSPERO. PubMed, Scopus, Embase, Web of Science, and CINAHL were searched for studies published between January 2000 and July 2026. From 2,247 identified records, 38 studies (26 diagnostic accuracy and 12 radiation dose studies) met the inclusion criteria. Diagnostic accuracy was pooled using a bivariate random-effects model, with phase-wise subgroup analyses where feasible. Radiation dose metrics (CTDIvol and dose-length product) were synthesized using random-effects models. Study quality was assessed using QUADAS-2 for diagnostic accuracy studies and the Joanna Briggs Institute checklist for radiation dose studies.
RESULTS: For urothelial carcinoma, pooled sensitivity and specificity were 0.88 and 0.93, respectively. Compared with single-phase CTU (specificity 0.87), specificity increased to 0.95 for both tri-phase and four-phase CTU, while sensitivity remained high across protocols. For renal cell carcinoma, pooled sensitivity and specificity were 0.90 and 0.97, respectively; however, phase-wise comparisons were not feasible because of the limited number of eligible studies. Tri-phase CTU demonstrated a pooled CTDIvol of approximately 9 mGy, with reported values ranging from 5 to 16 mGy across studies. Low-dose strategies, including phase reduction, low tube voltage, and advanced reconstruction techniques, achieved radiation dose reductions of 20-72% while maintaining diagnostic performance.
CONCLUSIONS: CT urography provides high diagnostic accuracy across urinary tract pathologies. For urothelial carcinoma, tri-phase CTU provides the most favorable balance between diagnostic performance and radiation exposure. In contrast, single-phase CTU may be appropriate for patients with microscopic haematuria and a low pre-test probability of urothelial malignancy, whereas four-phase CTU may be reserved for patients with a high pre-test probability of urothelial carcinoma or equivocal findings requiring further characterization. Indication-based protocol selection and dose-optimization strategies should be adopted to minimize radiation exposure while maintaining diagnostic quality.
STUDY REGISTRATION: The review was developed and recorded in accordance with the PRISMA guidelines and has been registered with PROSPERO (CRD420251163062).
43021502:
AIMS: Heart failure (HF) prevention remains limited because early multisystem cardiometabolic dysfunction is not captured by conventional risk tools. We evaluated whether liver radiomic phenotypes derived opportunistically from coronary artery calcium computed tomography (CAC-CT) identify imaging-defined hepatic stress states associated with incident HF.
METHODS AND RESULTS: We analysed 59 237 individuals undergoing CAC-CT (CLARIFY: 46 028; Houston Methodist: 13 209). Liver regions were segmented and radiomic features extracted to derive a Liver Radiomics Score (LRS). The model was trained in a CLARIFY derivation cohort (Dtr, n = 9205), validated in a hold-out cohort (Dts, n = 36 823), and externally evaluated in Houston Methodist (Dext, n = 13 209). The mean follow-up was 1411 days (SD 760.1) in the pooled Dtr and Dts cohorts (1144 HF events) and 470 days (SD 596) in Dext (212 HF events). Continuous LRS was associated with incident HF [Dts: hazard ratio (HR) 1.63, 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.52-1.74; P < 0.001; Dext: HR 1.04, 95% CI 1.01-1.07; P = 0.004] and remained significant after multivariable adjustment in Dts. Increasing LRS quartiles showed progressively adverse hepatic, haemodynamic, and cardiometabolic profiles and higher HF risk. Among 17 806 Dts participants with PREVENT data, adding LRS modestly improved discrimination across CAC- and PREVENT-based models (P < 0.001) and improved reclassification metrics (7-year net reclassification improvement up to 0.25; including integrated discrimination improvement up to 0.015). High LRS identified elevated risk in low-risk groups: among participants with CAC=0, high LRS conferred ∼2.5-fold higher 5-year HF incidence, and ∼2.9-fold in PREVENT-low individuals.
CONCLUSION: In this large multicentre cohort, liver radiomics from CAC-CT captured hepatic stress states linked to HF risk and modestly improved risk stratification beyond CAC and PREVENT scores.
43021633: People with neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) are at risk for developing peripheral nerve sheath tumors (PNSTs) ranging from benign neurofibromas to high-grade sarcomas. PNSTs known as atypical neurofibromas are at increased risk for malignant transformation. In 2017 the term ANNUBP (atypical neurofibromatous neoplasm of uncertain biologic potential) was proposed for PNSTs at increased risk for malignant transformation based on histopathologic features. Subsequently it was recognized that PNSTs not meeting ANNUBP criteria could still have concerning clinical, imaging and molecular features. A State of the Science conference addressed how to define these pre-cancerous PNSTs and reached consensus regarding clinical management and priority areas of research. Key recommendations from this symposium include: (1) using a combination of histologic, molecular and imaging features to define pre-malignant "at-risk" PNST; (2) recognizing that people with NF1 may be divided into "higher-risk" and "average-risk" for MPNST based on features such as their germline NF1 variant, internal tumor burden and history of malignancy or radiotherapy and; (3) the need to validate consensus screening and surveillance strategies based on personal and tumor-related risk factors. These recommendations will advance the ability to standardize care, and potentially fuel research that enables early diagnosis, prevention of malignant transformation and improved outcomes.
43022089:
BACKGROUND: The American College of Radiology Thyroid Imaging Reporting and Data System (ACR TI-RADS) and European Thyroid Imaging Reporting and Data System (EU-TIRADS) estimate thyroid nodule malignancy risk but use different category definitions and fine-needle aspiration thresholds. This diagnostic test accuracy (DTA) systematic review compared their performance, focusing on ACR TR5 and EU-TIRADS 5.
METHODS: PubMed, Europe PMC, Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex, Google Scholar, and Crossref were searched through October 12, 2026. Adult studies reporting diagnostic findings for either system were assessed. All three authors participated in selection and extraction; disagreements were resolved by discussion. Risk of bias was assessed using the Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies 2 (QUADAS-2) tool and certainty with the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation approach for DTA studies (GRADE-DTA). Findings were synthesized narratively. The review was not prospectively registered; no public protocol was available.
RESULTS: Twenty-five reports representing 24 cohorts were included. Two studies provided verified 2×2 data for the highest-risk-category comparison (2,786 nodules; 2,742 patients). In Wang et al., ACR versus EU-TIRADS sensitivity was 86.1% versus 86.3%, and specificity was 90.3% versus 85.8%. In Shen et al., sensitivity was 88.2% versus 93.3%, and specificity was 87.5% versus 80.9%. QUADAS-2 identified important risk-of-bias concerns in two studies. GRADE-DTA certainty was moderate for ACR sensitivity and specificity and EU-TIRADS specificity, and low for EU-TIRADS sensitivity. Pooling and formal paired comparison were not possible.
