RESULTS: The panel produced updated consensus guidance for assessing treatment responses and defining study outcomes in clinical trials of IMD in both adults and children.
CONCLUSIONS: Along with guidance, potential pitfalls in assessing outcome, such as discordant clinical, radiologic, and/or mycologic data and areas for future research are discussed.
43043428: Progressive collapsing foot deformity (PCFD) is a three-dimensional deformity characterized, to varying degrees, by hindfoot valgus, midfoot or forefoot abduction, medial column collapse, peritalar subluxation, and valgus instability of the ankle. Conventional weightbearing radiographs remain the cornerstone of imaging assessment, whereas weightbearing computed tomography (WBCT) enables multiplanar and three-dimensional analysis of osseous alignment and articular relationships under load. This narrative review summarizes WBCT-based methods for the assessment of PCFD, including two-dimensional measurements, three-dimensional alignment parameters, articular distance and coverage mapping, diagnostic performance, and automated segmentation methods. WBCT enables quantification of the different components of the contemporary A-E classification and is valuable for assessing peritalar subluxation and lateral impingement. The Foot and Ankle Offset provides a reproducible measure of global alignment, whereas middle facet subluxation and regional mapping more directly characterize local abnormalities in peritalar relationships. Available evidence indicates that class D parameters contribute to distinguishing symptomatic PCFD from asymptomatic flatfoot morphology. However, published diagnostic thresholds remain dependent on the populations and methods used and should not be interpreted in isolation as diagnostic or therapeutic criteria. Automation substantially reduces the time required for three-dimensional analyses, and initial predictive models demonstrate the feasibility of quantitative preoperative planning. However, interchangeability between methods, external validation of thresholds, establishment of normative values, and longitudinal associations with symptoms and clinical outcomes remain insufficiently established. WBCT should therefore be considered complementary to conventional radiographs and MRI. Its principal contribution lies in the multiplanar and three-dimensional characterization, under weightbearing conditions, of the osseous and articular components of PCFD.
43043431:
OBJECTIVE: To examine the association between residential altitude and bone health index (BHI) in children.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: In this retrospective multicenter study, healthy children aged 0-17 years who underwent left hand-wrist radiographs were screened at four hospitals at three different altitudes (Beijing 43.5 m, Lhasa 3650 m, Nagqu 4500 m) between September 2013 to July 2022. BoneXpert automatically generated bone age (BA) and BHI. Regional differences were evaluated overall and by chronological age (CA), BA, sex, and ethnicity. Linear regression models were performed to assess the association between residential region and BHI.
RESULTS: In total, 1,132 children (CA: 10.60 [6.00, 15.00] years; male: n = 723, 63.9%; Tibetan: n = 666, 58.8%) were included: 376 from Beijing, 454 from Lhasa, and 302 from Nagqu. After adjusting for age, sex, and ethnicity, the increase in BHI with age was attenuated in Lhasa and Nagqu compared with Beijing in models based on CA (region-by-age interaction β = -0.038 and -0.078, respectively; both p < 0.001) and BA (interaction term β = -0.034 and -0.065, respectively; both p < 0.001).
CONCLUSION: Higher residential altitude was associated with lower BHI and an attenuated age-related increase in BHI.
43043467: Contrast-enhanced ultrasound Liver Imaging Reporting and Data System (CEUS LI-RADS) version 2017 provides a standardized framework for characterizing focal liver observations in patients at high risk for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Although the system has demonstrated clinical utility and is endorsed by the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases, accumulating validation evidence reveals an existing gap that limits the application of CEUS LI‑RADS to liver observations beyond those categorized as CEUS LR‑5 for HCC. This limitation arises mainly from the specificity‑prioritized design of CEUS LR‑5 for HCC, which comes at the cost of sensitivity. In this review, we summarize a group of studies on CEUS LI‑RADS for liver observations, addressing their merits, limitations, and proposals for revision. The proposed modifications are investigational, and have not been incorporated into current guidelines. Our objectives are to reduce misclassification, improve the sensitivity of CEUS LR-5 for HCC while maintaining reasonably high specificity, expand the utility of CEUS LI-RADS to a broader range of liver observations, and ultimately optimize patient management. The 60-s threshold for early washout onset lacks statistical derivation and leads to substantial misclassification of HCC as LR-M (probably or definitely malignant, not necessarily HCC); reported HCC proportions among LR-M lesions range from 41.8% to 86.7%. The definitions of washout degrees (mild vs. marked) are somewhat ambiguous, which cause inter-reader variability, and the absence of objective quantitative metrics. Current discussions regarding potential modification of CEUS LI-RADS v2017 include: (1) shortening the early washout threshold from 60 to < 45 s or other threshold, which markedly improves sensitivity of CEUS LR 5 for HCC with minimal loss of specificity; (2) redefining marked washout as occurring at 3 min or later as an adjunctive criterion; (3) incorporating Kupffer-phase findings when using perfluorobutane (Sonazoid); (4) integrating ancillary features; and (5) considering size-stratified thresholds.
43043606:
INTRODUCTION: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the leading cause of morbidity and mortality in patients with advanced chronic kidney disease (CKD), yet its impact on economic and humanistic burden remains insufficiently characterized. We aimed to systematically review the published literature reporting economic outcomes, healthcare resource utilization (HRU), and humanistic impact of the association between advanced CKD and CVD.
METHODS: A systematic literature review (SLR) was conducted using MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane databases, and conference abstracts to identify evidence published between 2020 and December 31, 2025. Studies reporting economic or humanistic burden outcomes among adults with CKD G4-G5 or kidney failure and coexisting cardiovascular conditions were included.
RESULTS: In total, 6350 records were screened, with 87 studies meeting inclusion criteria. Across studies, coexisting CVD markedly increased costs and HRU in advanced CKD. In the USA, the costs per event ranged from $12,410 USD for systolic heart failure to $92,898 for chronic heart failure. Compared to CKD G4, patients in G5 incurred higher annual per patient hospitalization costs (77%), outpatient costs (65%), and total healthcare costs (61% (US) to 64% (non-US)). Emergency visits, intensive care unit (ICU) admissions, and rehospitalizations were more frequent among patients with coexisting CVD and advanced CKD compared to those without CVD, with 30-day readmission rates of 41% for critical limb ischemia. Evidence on humanistic burden, though limited, showed significant declines in mental health and quality of life among patients with CVD.
CONCLUSIONS: Concomitant CVD and advanced CKD or kidney failure substantially elevates the economic and humanistic burden compared to CVD or CKD alone, driving higher costs, increased healthcare utilization, and impaired quality of life. Targeted strategies addressing cardiovascular risk in patients with advanced CKD are essential to mitigate downstream clinical and financial consequences.
43044705: Poor bone health and low-trauma fractures are common in Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), reflecting the combined effects of progressive muscle weakness, reduced mechanical loading, delayed puberty and/or hypogonadism, and long-term glucocorticoid exposure. Although paediatric bone health guidance in DMD is well established, adult-specific recommendations remain limited, particularly for individuals who enter adult services having received many years of bisphosphonate therapy during childhood or adolescence. We developed national expert consensus recommendations for the monitoring and management of bone health in adults with DMD, with particular emphasis on transition from paediatric to adult care. Recommendations were informed by review of the literature, a clinician survey, input from adults with DMD and carers, and discussion within a multidisciplinary expert group. A modified Delphi process was undertaken, with 16 clinicians voting on draft statements using a 9-point agreement scale; consensus was defined as at least 80% of participants scoring 7-9. Thirteen evidence-informed expert consensus clinical recommendations were agreed, covering fracture risk assessment, DXA and vertebral fracture monitoring, vitamin D and gonadal status, indications for specialist bone review, initiation and review of osteoporosis therapy, management of possible treatment failure, and structured review of long-term therapy during transition. The recommendations emphasise individualised decision-making, recognising the technical challenges of imaging, limited adult DMD-specific evidence, cumulative treatment burden, and the functional impact of fractures in this population. These consensus recommendations provide a practical framework to support adult neuromuscular and bone clinicians managing bone health in a rare, high-risk and increasingly adult DMD population.
43044777:
BACKGROUND AND AIMS: Endoscopic ultrasound-guided gastric variceal coil embolization (EUS-GVE) has emerged as a safe and efficacious treatment for gastric variceal bleeding. However, significant practice variability exists for this novel technique. Using the modified Delphi process, we aimed to establish consensus among international experts on best practices and future research directions for EUS-GVE.
METHODS: A steering committee drafted statements encompassing four principal domains: pre-procedural protocol, intra-procedural technique, post-procedural monitoring, and future research directions. Thirty-seven advanced endoscopists with clinical and research expertise in EUS-GVE and representing international practice settings were invited to participate in online surveys where statements were independently ranked using a Likert numerical scale. Consensus was defined as ≥70% agreement. Statements not reaching consensus were revised based on comments and brought for a re-vote.
RESULTS: Thirty of 37 (81%) experts responded to the first round with 24 of 30 (80%) participating in the second round. Half of the participants represented North America while the other half practiced internationally. Fifty of 52 (96%) statements met consensus after 2 voting rounds. Final statements emphasized general themes of the importance of proper variceal description and classification, preference for EUS-GVE with adjunctive therapies, and the safety and versatility of the procedure. Definitions for clinical outcomes and future research topics were identified.
CONCLUSIONS: The results of this modified Delphi process represent the first consensus document for EUS-GVE and capture best practices from an international expert base. These statements provide practical guidance to optimize procedural performance and could aid future research involving EUS-GVE.
43045569:
CONTEXT AND OBJECTIVE: Benign prostatic enlargement (BPE) and related lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS/BPE) represent highly prevalent health issues globally, and related modifiable risk factors are recognized as a sensitive topic for prevention strategies. We summarized evidence on associations between the epidemiology of these conditions and modifiable risk factors.
EVIDENCE ACQUISITION: We performed a systematic review with meta-analysis of studies in MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science according to Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Protocols.
EVIDENCE SYNTHESIS: Twenty-four studies (four cohort and 20 cross-sectional) were included. Pooled synthesis showed positive associations between waist circumference (WC) >90 cm (two studies) and body mass index >24 kg/m2 (three studies) and prevalent BPE in Asian males. WC >90 cm was positively associated with prevalent moderate-to-severe LUTS in the same ethnicity (two studies). Narrative synthesis showed associations between abnormal adiposity and prevalent BPE/moderate-to-severe LUTS also in non-Asian males as well as associations between the epidemiology of LUTS and physical activity, alcohol intake, metabolic syndrome, and smoking status in both ethnicities. Associations between dietary/sleep patterns and LUTS epidemiology were evident in Asian males. The certainty of evidence was very low.
CONCLUSIONS: BPE and related LUTS represent highly prevalent health issues with global incidence and prevalence rates projected to increase in the next decade. Positive associations between high adiposity indices and prevalent BPE have been observed in both Asian and non-Asian males. Modifiable risk factors associated with moderate-to-severe LUTS include: abnormal adiposity indices, levels of physical activity, smoking status, alcohol intake, metabolic syndrome (all in both ethnicities), and sleep/dietary patterns (in Asian males). However, definitive clinical recommendations could not be provided.
43045595:
STATEMENT OF PROBLEM: Restoring endodontically treated teeth requires careful evaluation of the supracrestal tissue attachment, ferrule integrity, and post-space dimensions to ensure long-term success. Manual radiographic analysis for crown lengthening indication and post selection is often time-consuming, subjective, and inconsistent, particularly in resource-limited settings where specialist access may be constrained.
PURPOSE: The purpose of this study was to design and validate an artificial intelligence (AI)-driven system that automated 2 essential restorative planning tasks, evaluating the clinical need for crown lengthening and recommending appropriate post dimensions in endodontically treated teeth, using dental radiographs as the input.
MATERIAL AND METHODS: Two deep learning pipelines were developed and trained on annotated panoramic and periapical datasets with annotations created under the supervision of dentistry professionals. The crown measurement pipeline employed a U-shaped network (U-Net) model for initial tooth segmentation (assigning unique instance masks to each tooth), then cropping individual teeth and feeding them into a Mask Region-based Convolutional Neural Network (Mask R-CNN) for precise detection and crown length calculation, facilitating the assessment of parameters such as supracrestal tissue attachment and ferrule height, for identification of potential violations or restoration limitations. The post measurement pipeline utilized Mask R-CNN directly on the original images to detect endodontic posts and measure their length and width, enabling comparison against established prosthodontic criteria. Both models were trained in a graphics processing unit (GPU)-enabled environment (Kaggle; Google LLC) and evaluated using standard metrics including Intersection over Union (IoU), Dice coefficient, and measurement accuracy, with validation involving visual overlays and quantitative comparisons to expert annotations.
RESULTS: The segmentation model achieved a mean IoU of 0.52 and a Dice coefficient of 0.66, with diagnostic accuracy exceeding 99% in identifying post locations and assessing ferrule presence. The system accurately detected supracrestal tissue attachment violations and provided clinically relevant post dimension recommendations, closely aligning with expert-guided decisions. GPU acceleration reduced model training time by over 70% compared to local central processing unit (CPU)-only workflows.
CONCLUSIONS: The AI-powered system demonstrated promising performance in automating radiographic evaluations critical to restoring endodontically treated teeth. By identifying crown lengthening requirements and suggesting post dimensions, the integrated pipelines supported objective and reproducible treatment planning. This approach may enhance prosthodontic workflows, especially in settings with limited specialist availability, and holds potential for integration into commercial dental imaging platforms.
43045745: The brainstem is a highly conserved integrative hub that is essential for arousal, emotion, and motor control, which are functions profoundly affected in Parkinson's disease (PD). However, low signal-to-noise ratios in neuroimaging of subcortical nuclei hinder the construction of brainstem parcellations that integrate complementary functional and structural information, limiting our understanding of circuit-specific pathology. Here, we developed the Multimodal Consensus Brainstem Parcellation (MCBP), a fine-grained atlas that integrates high-resolution naturalistic 7 T functional MRI and diffusion MRI acquired in the Human Connectome Project (N = 160). The MCBP exhibits high reproducibility, symmetry, and homogeneity. Using this parcellation, we find a pronounced structure-function dissociation within the brainstem. Furthermore, MCBP reveals a hierarchical brainstem organization aligned with the unimodal-to-transmodal axis, distinguishing motor execution from visually guided motor preparation that closely resembles the Somato-Cognitive Action Network (SCAN). Crucially, in an independent PD cohort, MCBP-derived connectivity improved disease classification and symptom-severity prediction compared with existing brainstem atlases, supporting its sensitivity to both categorical disease status and dimensional clinical variation. Feature decoding revealed a dual-system pattern of PD-related alterations across sensorimotor and cognitive-affective networks. Notably, it identified a specific brainstem-limbic circuit linked to emotional heterogeneity, providing circuit-level insights for distinguishing anxiety- and depression-related neuropsychiatric PD subtypes independent of motor severity. Beyond distinguishing and grading disease, the MCBP-derived connectivity measure also outperformed those derived from existing atlases in predicting multidimensional behavioral traits in a large healthy participant cohort (N = 976). Together, MCBP offers a fine-grained, biologically grounded brainstem parcellation and a framework for probing circuit-specific changes in neurodegenerative disorders.
43045752: Acute ischemic stroke (AIS) requires rapid integration of multimodal imaging, contraindication screening, and treatment selection within minutes, yet real-world decision-making is limited by fragmented workflows and uneven specialist availability. We developed an imaging-grounded multi-agent multimodal large language model (MLLM) framework that emulates a multidisciplinary stroke team for structured treatment recommendation. The framework decomposes the AIS workflow into coordinated agents for triage, time-window assessment, multimodal imaging interpretation, contraindication screening, and final treatment recommendation, with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) incorporating evidence-grounded knowledge. We retrospectively evaluated the framework in 1,658 consecutive suspected-AIS cases from two centers. Compared with a single-prompt baseline, treatment recommendation accuracy improved from 0.636 to 0.755 with multi-agent coordination and further to 0.785 after RAG augmentation, while Macro-F1 increased from 0.562 to 0.732 and 0.768, respectively. The framework showed improvements in reperfusion pathways, more effectively retaining candidates for intravenous thrombolysis and mechanical thrombectomy. Imaging agent yielded sensitivity/specificity of 0.490/0.999 for non-contrast CT intracranial hemorrhage detection, 0.883/0.851 for CT angiography large-vessel occlusion identification, and 0.939/0.739 for CT perfusion deficit assessment. These results suggest that structured imaging-grounded multi-agent coordination enhances reliability and clinical alignment of MLLM-based decision support in AIS, supporting potential deployment in time-critical stroke care settings with limited specialist availability.
43045815: This Consensus Statement (the primary aldosteronism imaging outcome (PAIO) consensus) from an international, multidisciplinary team of experts offers evidence-based graded consensus recommendations and key summary points for clinical practice on the use of conventional and molecular imaging in the diagnosis and therapeutic management of primary aldosteronism. We review the evolving role of these imaging techniques and offer practical recommendations for clinical management. The following predefined clinical questions relevant to the management of primary aldosteronism were addressed: (1) What radiological parameters define normal versus altered adrenal morphology in primary aldosteronism? (2) What imaging morphological abnormalities are observed in the different subtypes of primary aldosteronism (lateralized and non-lateralized primary aldosteronism)? (3) How reliable are features detectable by CT, MRI and molecular imaging for predicting biochemical remission following unilateral adrenalectomy? Among other key topics, these recommendations address CT-, MRI- and molecular imaging-based approaches to guide patient selection for unilateral adrenalectomy in primary aldosteronism.
43045903:
OBJECTIVE: To assess the diagnostic accuracy of point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) for detecting reduced left ventricular systolic function (LVSF) using visual qualitative assessment (VQA), E-point septal separation (EPSS), and artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted assessment, compared with transthoracic echocardiography (TTE).
METHODS: We searched PubMed, Ovid MEDLINE, Embase, and the Cochrane Library from January 1, 1985, through July 8, 2025. Eligible studies compared POCUS-assessed LVSF with left ventricular ejection fraction measured by TTE (or cardiac MRI in one study). Data were pooled using random-effects meta-analysis to determine the diagnostic odds ratio (DOR) and likelihood ratios (LR) for each of the three methods.
RESULTS: Twenty-eight studies, including 4,647 participants, met inclusion criteria. Nine studies evaluating VQA yielded a DOR of 40.53 (95% CI, 15.07 to 109.00; P < 0.001) and a positive LR (LR + ) of 6.90 (95% CI, 3.75 to 12.69). Seven studies evaluating EPSS resulted in a DOR of 21.77 (95% CI, 10.25 to 46.28; P < 0.001) and a LR + of 5.70 (95% CI, 2.89 to 11.22). Five studies evaluating AI-assisted POCUS resulted in a DOR of 47.35 (95% CI, 16.87 to 132.93; P < 0.001) and a LR + of 8.37 (95% CI, 4.40 to 15.93). Meta-regression analyses revealed no statistically significant differences in diagnostic performance among the three methods. Subgroup analysis by operator experience level also showed no statistically significant difference between novice and experienced operators for each method.
CONCLUSIONS: VQA, EPSS, and AI-assisted POCUS all demonstrate moderate-to-high diagnostic accuracy for identifying reduced LVSF, with no significant differences among methods on meta-regression or by operator experience level. Moderately strong LR + across all three methods supports the use of POCUS for ruling in reduced LVSF. EPSS cutoffs at the lower and upper ends of the reported range showed higher sensitivity and specificity, respectively, suggesting utility as a rule-in or rule-out tool where formal echocardiography is not readily available.
REGISTRATION: PROSPERO CRD42024626542.
43046010:
BACKGROUND: Hypertension drives premature cardiovascular disease among working-age adults in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA), yet evidence from occupational blood pressure (BP) screening remains fragmented. We synthesised available data on blood pressure levels and hypertension prevalence among workforce populations in the region.
METHODS: We conducted a systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis of observational studies reporting BP levels or hypertension prevalence among adult workforce cohorts in SSA. Medical and scientific bibliographic databases were searched for English-language studies published between 2010 and 2021. Eligible studies included adult workers from occupational or workplace settings. Data extraction and risk-of-bias assessment (Hoy tool) were performed independently. Pooled prevalence, mean systolic and diastolic BP (SBP/DBP), and sex-specific prevalence ratios were estimated using DerSimonian-Laird models, with between-study heterogeneity quantified byI².
RESULTS: Twelve cross-sectional studies with 7,652 participants (4,759 men [62%] and 1,837 women) from six countries were analysed. The pooled prevalence of hypertension was 26% (95% CI 22-31%; I² = 93.7%). Mean SBP and DBP were 125 mmHg (95% CI 122-128) and 80 mmHg (95% CI 78-82), respectively. There were more males than females (prevalence ratio 1.54; 95% CI 1.12-2.12) with hypertension. Sensitivity analyses showed stable estimates, and no publication bias was detected (Egger's test) whilst heterogeneity was medium-to-high across (I² ≈ 67.2% to 94%; all P < 0.005).
CONCLUSIONS: Hypertension remains prevalent among working adults in SSA. Accordingly, more systematic workforce screening for, and proactive management of, hypertension in this vitally important group (from multiple health and socio-economic perspectives) is needed.
43046093:
PURPOSE: We synthesized evidence for three questions on screening for lung cancer with computed tomography (CT): benefits (from randomized trials) and harms of screening versus no screening/minimal intervention or alternative screening approaches (e.g., selection criteria, screening intervals); relative importance that informed patients place on the potential benefits and harms of screening (patient preferences); and comparative effects from observational studies of different CT screening selection criteria (using risk prediction models) or nodule classification systems compared with those used in the screening trials.
METHODS: An expert working group provided input on eligibility criteria and potential effect moderators, rated outcomes, and developed decision thresholds for assessing certainty of the evidence and making conclusions. Critical outcomes of screening effects included all-cause mortality, lung-cancer mortality, and overdiagnosis; important outcomes included false positives (FPs), incidental findings, major complications, and psychosocial harms. For patient preferences, we sought data on (i) disutilities of relevant health states, (ii) direct preference-based data, such as outcome trade-offs, and (iii) relative importance of benefits versus harms inferred from attitudes, intentions, and behaviors towards screening among informed patients. For screening benefits and harms and for patient preferences, we searched three databases (MEDLINE, Embase, and Central and MEDLINE, Scopus, and EconLit, respectively) to July 2025. For screening studies published prior to 2015, we relied on other reviews, and for patient preferences our search was limited to 2012 onwards. For comparative effects, we searched MEDLINE and Embase from 2019 to September 2025, relying on other reviews for studies published 2012-2018. Reference lists were scanned and trial registries searched. Two independent reviewers screened titles and abstracts then full texts. Data extraction and analysis were undertaken by single reviewers, with verification; risk of bias and GRADE certainty assessments were undertaken independently by at least two reviewers. Data were pooled where suitable using random-effects methods appropriate to the outcome metric and prevalence. Subgroup analyses explored heterogeneity. When not pooled, data were analyzed by grouping studies based on PICO factors, with consideration of study size and risk of bias. Conclusions and certainty assessments for screening effects were based on estimates of absolute effects.
RESULTS: We included 85 studies (N = 640,537; 13 trials) on screening benefits and harms, 59 on patient preferences (33 [N = 42,219] on disutilities; 26 [N = 10,829] other studies), and 16 for comparing trial (National Lung Screening Trial [NLST]) and LungRADs nodule management, either directly (2 studies, N = 26,978) or indirectly (14 studies, N = 1,102,285). Screening benefits and harms: Nine trials (N = 94,530) examining low-dose CT (LDCT) screening on all-cause (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.93 to 1.01; 3.7 fewer [8.5 fewer to 1.2 more] per 1000) and lung-cancer mortality (RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.79 to 0.96; 4.0 fewer [1.2 to 6.4 fewer] per 1000) offered low and moderate certainty, respectively, that screening previous/current 20-30 pack-year smokers 50-74 years old 3-4 times will probably result in at least 1 (all-cause) and 2 (cause-specific) fewer deaths per 1000 screened after 10-12 years. The absolute effects may not apply to participants at the lowest baseline risk for lung-cancer incidence (e.g., < 1.5% over 6 years) or death. Certainty for overdiagnosis (7 trials, N = 35,161; RR 1.19, 95% CI 1.03 to 1.37; 8.4 [1.3 to 16.3] per 1000) was moderate that LDCT screening 3-4 times will probably result in at least 2.5 cases of overdiagnosis per 1000 screened over 10 years. High-certainty evidence was found for results for FPs and incidental findings (any and clinically significant) surpassing their decision thresholds, whereas little-to-no harm was found for major complications from invasive procedures among those having a FP. Requiring diagnostic follow-up after a positive scan probably causes at least some psychosocial harm. Patient preferences: Most results had low-certainty evidence, with the exception of moderate certainty for little-to-no (< 0.04 [range 0-1.0]) disutility from a positive screening test; a small, but important disutility (0.04-0.08) for stage IIIB-IV lung cancer during first-line treatment; and a small majority (51-75%) of people eligible for screening probably weighing the benefits as more important than the harms from screening in a relatively moderate net-benefit scenario. Comparative effects: Using LungRADs instead of NLST nodule management (among NLST-eligible people) probably reduces the FP rate substantially (about half), though the number of FPs still exceeded the decision threshold of 75 per 1000 and the effects for benefits or other harm outcomes are not known.
CONCLUSIONS: This review provides contemporary data on the benefits and harms of LDCT screening after at least a decade of follow-up. Findings indicate that screening previous/current 20-30 pack-year smokers aged 50-74 years with 3-4 rounds of LDCT will lead to benefits and harms for which a majority probably find acceptable and worthwhile. While current nodule management using LungRADs likely reduces FPs, whether it impacts the benefits of screening is less certain and worth further research. Further, comparative prospective studies are lacking to determine the effects from screening for those not meeting the minimum age (50 years) and smoking history criteria in the trials, despite having an equivalent risk for lung cancer.
43046499:
OBJECTIVE: To compare real‑time synchronous aspiration‑guided radiofrequency ablation (RFA) with conventional staged aspiration‑followed‑by‑RFA for patients with predominantly cystic thyroid nodules (PCTNs).
MATERIALS AND METHODS: Ninety‑eight patients with 102 PCTNs who underwent RFA were retrospectively enrolled, including 52 patients (54 nodules) in the real‑time aspiration group and 46 patients (48 nodules) in the conventional group. The volume reduction ratio (VRR), procedural parameters, treatment success rate, cyst‑fluid reaccumulation rate, and complication rate were compared between the two groups.
RESULTS: Baseline characteristics were comparable between groups (all p > 0.05). The technical success rate was 100% in both groups. The real‑time aspiration group obtained significantly higher VRR at postoperative day 1 (51.2% vs. 24.8%), 6‑month follow‑up (96.8% vs. 87.3%), and 12‑month follow‑up (98.1% vs. 91.4%; all p < 0.001). This group also demonstrated shorter procedure time (24.3 vs. 33.5 min, p < 0.001), fewer RFA electrode insertions (1.2 vs. 2.9, p < 0.001), lower overall complication rate (5.8% vs. 28.3%, p < 0.001), higher 12‑month treatment success rate (98.1% vs. 85.4%), and lower cyst‑fluid reaccumulation rate (1.9% vs. 12.5%, p = 0.038).
CONCLUSION: Real‑time aspiration‑integrated RFA provides superior nodule volume reduction, procedural efficiency, and safety for PCTNs. Prospective multicenter studies are warranted to validate its long‑term efficacy.
43047062:
BACKGROUND: Microfocused ultrasound with visualization (MFU-V) is a widely used noninvasive modality for skin tightening and lifting. Despite its favorable safety profile, transient and occasionally severe complications necessitate evidence-based management protocols, which remain underdeveloped in current literature.
OBJECTIVE: This narrative review synthesizes existing evidence to develop stepwise recommendations for managing MFU-V-related complications, emphasizing rapid recognition, severity stratification, and targeted interventions.
METHODS: Following PRISMA guidelines, a systematic search of PubMed and Scopus (January 2015-April 2025) was conducted. A reproducible search strategy was employed. A total of 133 articles were identified, and after screening, 26 studies met the inclusion criteria. Data extraction focused on complication types, anatomical variations, and management strategies. A risk-of-bias assessment was performed using the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) checklist.
RESULTS: Adverse events were predominantly mild and transient, including erythema (48-h resolution), edema (8-day resolution), and bruising (20-day resolution). Facial and neck regions exhibited higher rates of self-limiting urticarial reactions and dysesthesia, while nonfacial areas (abdomen, knees) reported rare cases of scarring or burns linked to technical errors. Severe complications, such as motor neuropraxia (4-6-week resolution) and postinflammatory dyspigmentation (Fitzpatrick IV-VI skin types), were infrequent but clinically significant. Key risk factors included improper transducer coupling, operator ergonomics, and pulse stacking. It is also critical to have correct training in visualization.
RECOMMENDATIONS FORMULATION: A severity-based management framework was formulated, integrating multidisciplinary consensus and retrospective clinical case analysis. For mild complications (e.g., erythema), topical steroids and sun protection were prioritized. Moderate-severe events (e.g., neuropraxia) required physical therapy, steroids, or adjunctive procedures. Preventive strategies emphasized standardized approaches, real-time ultrasound imaging, and adherence to "no-go zones" near critical nerves.
CONCLUSION: We present stepwise recommendations intended to support the management of MFU-V complications at the point of care. The framework draws on published evidence and on retrospective cases reviewed by the author group and is offered as a working reference that can be refined as further prospective data become available.
43047298:
BACKGROUND: The rs58542926 variant in transmembrane 6 superfamily member 2 (TM6SF2) has been linked to metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), but its associations with disease risk, histological severity, metabolic traits, and outcomes remain unclear. We evaluated these associations in adults.
METHODS: PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library were searched for observational studies published up to 11 November 2025. Pooled estimates were calculated for MASLD susceptibility, histological features, metabolic and liver injury markers, and long-term outcomes. The protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251273179).
RESULTS: Data from 368,852 participants across 55 studies were included in the meta-analysis. Under a dominant genetic model, rs58542926 was associated with higher MASLD susceptibility (odds ratio [OR] = 1.40, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.27-1.55), including in ultrasound-, biopsy-, and elastography-based subgroups. The T allele was associated with moderate-to-severe steatosis (OR = 1.42, 95% CI: 1.11-1.80) and significant fibrosis (OR = 1.34, 95% CI: 1.07-1.68). Carriers showed lower triglyceride, total cholesterol, and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol levels, slightly higher high-density lipoprotein cholesterol levels, and modestly higher fasting glucose, insulin, AST, and ALT levels. For long-term outcomes, the dominant model showed a potential association with increased liver-related event risk (HR = 2.20, 95% CI 1.22-3.95), and CT vs. CC was associated with lower cardiovascular mortality in one study (HR = 0.35, 95% CI 0.13-0.97).
CONCLUSION: TM6SF2 rs58542926 is associated with increased MASLD susceptibility, greater steatosis and fibrosis severity, a lipid-lowering phenotype accompanied by modest alterations in liver injury markers, and a potential increase in liver-related events. These findings support its potential value in genetic risk stratification, although clinical utility requires validation.
43047656:
BACKGROUND: Vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) has been investigated as a potential therapy for obesity because of the vagus nerve's role in satiety, gastrointestinal signaling, autonomic regulation, and metabolic homeostasis. However, studies vary substantially in stimulation site, interface, parameters, species, diet condition, and reported outcomes.
METHODS: PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched from inception through May 6, 2026. Eligible studies evaluated chronic electrical stimulation of the vagus nerve or a defined vagal branch, included a comparator, and reported quantitative body weight data. Random-effects meta-analyses using Hedges' g evaluated final body weight and weekly body weight change, while food intake, adiposity, metabolic outcomes, and safety were summarized narratively.
RESULTS: Of 629 records identified, 23 publications met the inclusion criteria, yielding 25 experimental comparisons. Across 22 comparisons, VNS was associated with lower final body weight than control conditions (Hedges' g = -1.07, 95% CI -1.43 to -0.72; I 2 = 55.5%; P < 0.001). Across 14 comparisons, VNS was associated with lower weekly body weight gain or greater weekly body weight reduction (Hedges' g = -2.82, 95% CI -4.23 to -1.41; I 2 = 93.3%; P < 0.001). In animal studies, modality-specific final body weight estimates favored conventional implanted electrical VNS (g = -0.84), transcutaneous auricular VNS (g = -1.54), and self-powered triboelectric VNS (g = -8.36), although the triboelectric subgroup comprised two comparisons from one publication. Excluding the triboelectric comparisons, VNS remained associated with lower final body weight (g = -0.93, 95% CI -1.23 to -0.63, I 2 = 39.4%). Food intake was commonly reduced after VNS, and adiposity outcomes generally favored stimulation, whereas metabolic and safety outcomes were reported inconsistently.
CONCLUSION: Chronic, anatomically specific VNS was associated with lower body weight across predominantly preclinical studies. The final body weight estimate showed moderate heterogeneity, whereas the weekly body weight change estimate was highly heterogeneous and should be interpreted as supportive rather than as a precise estimate of effect magnitude. Translation to obesity treatment remains limited by sparse human evidence, potential small-study effects, and inconsistent reporting of metabolic and safety outcomes.
43047868:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the long-term immunological, oncological, and clinical consequences of adult thymectomy by synthesizing recent basic, translational, and real-world clinical evidence.
BACKGROUND: Historical surgical paradigms regarded the post-pubertal adult thymus as an immunologically redundant, fatty involuted organ, justifying routine "incidental" resection during cardiac procedures. A high-profile 2023 cohort study in The New England Journal of Medicine (NEJM) challenged this concept, reporting that adult thymectomy significantly increased 5-year all-cause mortality and cancer risk. Subsequent population-level studies (US SEER/NCDB, French PMSI) and deep-learning imaging cohorts have sparked debate, offering both corroborating and conflicting insights into adult thymic function.
METHODS AND SYNTHESIS: This review synthesizes cellular mechanisms (TREC dynamics, TCR repertoire contraction, senescence-associated T cells, Treg lineage stability) and endocrine factors (thymulin-mediated myeloid regulation) with clinical data stratified by age at surgery, indication, resection extent, and follow-up duration.
CONCLUSIONS: The adult thymus remains functionally active, exporting naïve T cells and humoral immunomodulators like thymulin that maintain peripheral immune tolerance and restrain inflammaging. Clinical evaluation must differentiate between incidental resection (which induces avoidable iatrogenic immunosenescence) and therapeutic resection (e.g., for thymic epithelial tumors or myasthenia gravis), where removing a diseased, immunosuppressive microenvironment can reduce secondary cancer risk. Partial thymectomy (PT) is emerging as an option to preserve immunocompetence when oncologically feasible.
43048918:
OBJECTIVE: Diastolic dysfunction (DD) and elevated left ventricular filling pressure (LVFP) commonly occur after acute myocardial infarction (MI) and are associated with adverse clinical outcomes. This study aimed to compare the 2016 American Society of Echocardiography/European Association of Cardiovascular Imaging (ASE/EACVI) guideline and the 2025 American Society of Echocardiography (ASE) recommendations for assessing diastolic function (DF) in patients with acute MI.
METHOD: This prospective, single-center, observational study included consecutive patients admitted with acute MI between November 2025 and April 2026. Comprehensive transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) was performed during hospitalization in the coronary intensive care unit (CICU). The presence of DD, LVFP categorization, and DD grading were evaluated according to both the 2016 ASE/EACVI guideline and the 2025 ASE recommendations. Agreement between the two algorithms was assessed using Cohen's kappa analysis.
RESULTS: A total of 99 patients were included (mean age, 59.3+-12.2 years; 82.8% male). According to the 2016 guideline, DD status remained indeterminate in 3 patients and LVFP categorization remained indeterminate in 13 patients, whereas all patients could be classified using the 2025 recommendations. Among the patients who could be classified using both algorithms, 18 patients classified as having DD according to the 2016 guideline were reclassified as having normal diastolic function according to the 2025 recommendations (P < 0.001). Agreement between the two approaches was substantial for LVFP categorization (Cohen's kappa=0.721, P < 0.001) and moderate for DD grading (weighted Cohen's kappa=0.606, P < 0.001).
CONCLUSION: In patients with acute MI, the 2025 ASE recommendations reduced the number of indeterminate DF classifications and resulted in lower DD grades than the 2016 ASE/EACVI guideline while maintaining substantial agreement for LVFP categorization.
43049183: Autosomal Dominant Osteopetrosis (ADO) is a disorder of mineral metabolism caused by gene defects that impair osteoclast-mediated bone resorption and result in diffuse skeletal sclerosis and increased bone mineral density. There is no approved medical therapy for ADO; however, therapies are being developed that hasten the need for clinical trial readiness. A key part of this process is the development of a core set of endpoints for inclusion in both natural history and interventional studies for ADO. To identify these endpoints, we used a modified Delphi approach to reach consensus among panelists on prioritization of 92 candidate endpoints developed from a detailed literature search and panelist nomination. The international panel was comprised of 11 physicians from four countries (Canada, Finland, France, and the United States) with expertise in ADO plus clinical trials in metabolic bone diseases. After three rounds of anonymous voting, with a structured discussion prior to the final vote, complete consensus (100% agreement) was reached for prioritization of 1) imaging using dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry and plain radiographs, 2) patient-reported outcome measures of pain and global impression of change, 3) blood-based biomarkers of bone metabolism, and 4) clinical outcomes such as fracture and osteomyelitis. We recommend that the prioritized endpoints described in more detail in this manuscript be uniformly incorporated into therapeutic clinical trials and natural history studies in ADO. Consistent evaluation of endpoints in both natural history studies and investigational therapies, with appropriate standardization of the underlying methodologies, will facilitate comparison among therapeutic approaches and support the use of historical control data, ultimately leading to acceleration of therapeutic development for patients with ADO.
43049212:
BACKGROUND: There are no international consensus guidelines on IPNB.
METHOD: An international-multidisciplinary panel performed a critical appraisal of the literature and used a two-round Delphi process to evaluate 24 critical clinical questions, incorporating community feedback from a dedicated 2025 A-PHPBA meeting session in Bangkok.
RESULTS: Salient aspects of the recommendations: (1) IPNB is analogous to intracholecystic papillary neoplasm (ICPNs)/intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm (IPMNs), ranging from innocuous cystic lesions to papillary in situ carcinomas to invasive carcinomas. (2) Possible etiologic factors like stones, parasites, PSC, and PBM/choledochal cysts should be assessed in every case. (3) All nonmetastatic IPNBs are candidates for oncologic resection, preferably along with lymph node dissection. (4) Pre- and intraoperative assessment for multifocality is important. (5) Liver transplant is a consideration in selected cases. (6) Individualized IPNB-focused synoptic pathology reports were devised for use. (7) For invasive IPNBs, adjuvant treatment should follow standard cholangiocarcinoma protocols. (8) Follow-up should mirror main-duct IPMN protocols, adjusted for invasion and margin status. (9) For isolated IPNB recurrence, resection or transplant is advisable; if infeasible or metastatic, consider ablative and systemic therapies. (10) These recommendations are also applicable to IOPN/ITPN but with subtle differences.
CONCLUSION: These recommendations should aid in cross-national standardized classification, diagnosis, reporting, and management of IPNBs, and serve as a launching pad for further studies.
43049228:
OBJECTIVE: To update the RECOVER CPR Preparedness and Prevention Domain's recommendations on education through a systematic review of relevant evidence and the creation and presentation of recommendations, and to identify and present critical knowledge gaps.
DESIGN: Standardized, systematic evaluation of literature pertinent to didactic, simulated, and in-clinic education regarding CPR following Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation methodology. Identified literature regarding prioritized questions in the Population-Intervention-Comparator-Outcome (PICO) format was reviewed independently by Evidence Evaluators, and findings were reconciled by Domain Chairs and Reassessment Campaign on Veterinary Resuscitation (RECOVER) Co-Chairs to arrive at recommendations. This process used a standardized Evidence Profile Worksheet for each PICO question including introduction, consensus on science, recommendations, justification of recommendations, and knowledge gaps sections. Recommendations underwent a 4-week comment period among international veterinary stakeholders prior to finalization. This 2026 RECOVER CPR Guidelines: Preparedness and Prevention-Education paper summarizes recommendations for CPR education of veterinary professionals.
SETTING: Transdisciplinary, international collaboration in university, specialty, and emergency practice.
RESULTS: Seven PICO questions pertaining to CPR education were addressed in this section of the RECOVER CPR Preparedness and Prevention Domain. These seven PICO questions resulted in 14 recommendations. All recommendations are supported by very low-certainty evidence (11) or based on expert opinion (3).
CONCLUSIONS: This 2026 RECOVER CPR Guidelines: Preparedness and Prevention-Education update presents recommendations for individual and team CPR training to optimize veterinary resuscitation team readiness and, hopefully, improve patient outcomes. However, uncertainty remains regarding specific, ideal educational methods to optimize resuscitation team readiness, and high-priority knowledge gaps are presented to guide collaborative research in this area.
43049448:
BACKGROUND: Accurate preoperative risk stratification for lymph node metastasis (LNM) in papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) remains difficult. We developed and validated ThyLNT, a Transformer-based 2.5D deep learning model using preoperative computed tomography (CT), and explored related biological features in multi-omics analyses.
METHODS: A total of 1560 patients with PTC from six hospitals were retrospectively included. The Tongji Hospital cohort was divided into training and internal validation sets, and five external cohorts were used for independent testing. Seven 2.5D tumor slices were extracted per patient, encoded with a DenseNet201 backbone, and fused by a Transformer. Model performance was compared with radiomics, ensemble learning, and multi-instance learning using AUC, calibration, decision curve, and precision-recall analyses. Bulk RNA-seq, single-cell RNA-seq, spatial transcriptomics, and spatial metabolomics were used to explore related biological features.
RESULTS: ThyLNT achieved an AUC of 0.882 (CI, 0.858-0.905) in the training cohort, 0.787 (CI, 0.738-0.835) in the internal validation cohort, and 0.772 (CI, 0.662-0.878) to 0.827 (CI, 0.763-0.885) across the five external cohorts. It showed multicenter discrimination, whereas calibration and threshold-dependent operating characteristics varied across cohorts. Multi-omics analyses provided exploratory biological context, including candidate associations with vascular endothelial growth factor A-related signaling and lipid metabolism.
CONCLUSIONS: ThyLNT demonstrated multicenter performance for preoperative LNM prediction in PTC and may support risk stratification, although calibration, threshold use, and clinical utility require prospective validation.
43049475:
BACKGROUND/METHODS: Levothyroxine (LT4) monotherapy fails to fully normalize thyroid hormone levels or relieve symptoms in 10-20% of hypothyroid patients, prompting interest in combination therapy with added liothyronine (LT3). Existing dosing guidance is largely qualitative. Using the p-THYROSIM mechanistic model-previously fitted and validated against data from 655 patients-we developed computational algorithms from ∼400 simulations to generate individualized residual thyroid function (RTF) values and combination LT4/LT3 dosing recommendations based on a patient's sex, height (H), weight (W), and measured hormone values [TSH, free thyroxine (fT4), and free triiodothyronine (fT3) or total T3 (TT3)]. We implemented these in a user-friendly clinical software package as an app called LT43DOSING.
RESULTS: Simulated temporal plots of fT4, fT3, and TSH for combined dosages in available pill sizes are computed and reported as outputs of LT43DOSING, along with RTFs, separately for both sexes, with body mass indexes (BMIs) ranging from ∼15 to 40. Computed RTFs and dosages are based on patient H, W, and serum hormone concentrations provided as input data. Our findings show that both W and H affect dosing in a nonlinear manner, especially at BMI extremes, whereas sex made little difference. Only combination therapy was able to normalize fT3 levels.
CONCLUSIONS: In simulated identical BMI patients, different H and W combinations produced markedly different RTF values, leading to more accurate dosing predictions based on body size. Simulated combination therapy normalized fT3 levels whereas monotherapy did not, particularly for overtly hypothyroid patients.
43049552: Alzheimer's disease (AD), the commonest neurodegenerative disorder, is characterized by progressive cognitive decline. However, much remains unclear about brain morphological alterations in AD and the underlying molecular mechanisms. We conducted a whole-brain voxel-wise meta-analysis using Seed-based d Mapping with Permutation of Subject Images to identify consistent gray matter volume (GMV) alterations in AD. Significant clusters were assigned to AAL regions and Yeo 7 functional networks and further annotated via Neurosynth. Spatial correspondence between the meta-analysis results and 29 neurotransmitter maps was assessed with JuSpace. Transcriptional associations were assessed using Allen Human Brain Atlas data with partial least squares regression and gene enrichment analysis. The meta-analysis included 70 voxel-based morphometry studies, reporting 2628 AD patients and 2508 healthy controls. AD patients had lower GMV than controls in the bilateral hippocampus, bilateral parahippocampal gyrus and bilateral amygdala (p < 0.05, FWE corrected), regions mainly involved in the default mode network, ventral attention network and the limbic network. Sensitivity analyses indicated high robustness, with low heterogeneity. Neurosynth decoding found the regions of lower GMV to be related to emotional processing and facial expression recognition. Neurotransmitter mapping revealed multiple spatial correlations, notably with the dopaminergic and serotonergic systems (p < 0.001, FDR corrected). Genes associated with the lower-GMV regions were enriched mainly in cytoplasmic translation, ribosomal subunits, cadherin-mediated cell adhesion, and ligand-gated ion channel activity. These findings suggest that GMV alterations in AD predominantly affect temporal regions within specific functional networks and are associated with neurotransmitter systems and molecular pathways.
43049769:
OBJECTIVES: The central vein sign (CVS) is a novel diagnostic imaging biomarker that improves differentiation of white matter lesions (WMLs) caused by multiple sclerosis (MS) and radiological mimics. While susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI) is widely available for visualizing venous structures, standard SWI protocols are not optimized for standalone CVS detection and require T2-FLAIR images to co-localize T2-hyperintense WMLs. This study evaluated whether an optimized SWI protocol improves CVS detection and reader confidence at 3 T.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: Seventeen patients with a clinical diagnosis of MS were scanned on a 3 T MRI scanner using a standard SWI and an optimized SWI acquired with a lower flip angle (FA = 5°). Two radiologists, blinded to the SWI imaging protocols, evaluated the presence of CVS and their confidence levels. Subsequent subject-level analysis was performed to assess the positive detection rate for MS using the "Select-6" rule.
RESULTS: Optimized SWI detected all CVS+ lesions identified by standard SWI plus 33 additional lesions (105 vs. 72). Optimized SWI detected more CVS+ lesions than standard SWI in 14/17 participants, with a higher median number of CVS+ lesions detected per participant (7.0 vs. 4.0; p < 0.001). Optimized SWI also increased high-confidence CVS+ classification compared with standard SWI (p = 0.006). Positive detection rate for MS using Select-6 increased from 41.2% with standard SWI to 82.4% with optimized SWI (p = 0.016).
CONCLUSION: This feasibility study demonstrates that acquiring SWI with a lower FA at 3 T significantly improves CVS detection, reader confidence, and positive detection rate for MS.
KEY POINTS: Question Standard SWI can visualize venous structures at 3 T, but provides limited lesion conspicuity, which prevents standalone detection of the central vein sign (CVS). Findings Optimized SWI with a low flip angle detects more CVS-positive lesions, increases high-confidence CVS classification, and improves MS detection rate using the Select-6 rule. Clinical relevance Optimized SWI improves CVS visibility and rater confidence without increasing scan time, providing a simple technical optimization for assessment of CVS at 3 T.
43049875: Congenital sensorineural hearing loss (cSNHL) has been increasingly recognized given improvements in prenatal and childhood screening efforts. Etiologies vary widely with a growing body of literature continuing to uncover underlying risk factors and associated syndromes. cSNHL results in significant morbidity with the potential to impair language and social development. Imaging is an integral part of the clinical and potential presurgical assessment for these children. Thus, it is essential for radiologists to be familiar with normal inner ear anatomy, inner ear malformations, and syndromic/genetic etiologies of sensorineural hearing loss.
43049877: Pediatric acquired hearing loss represents a clinical challenge, requiring prompt diagnosis in order to optimize normal language and psychosocial development. This review outlines a practical imaging framework categorizing acquired hearing loss etiologies into opacified and aerated middle ears. High-resolution computed tomography (CT) is the gold standard for delineating osseous anatomy, including ossicular discontinuity, fractures, and congenital or acquired bone erosion. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) provides soft-tissue characterization, and can evaluate labyrinth contents, cranial nerves, and for intracranial complications; non-echo-planar diffusion-weighted imaging (non-EPI DWI) can help to identify cholesteatomas. By leveraging these complementary modalities, radiologists can establish a precise diagnostic roadmap to guide clinical management and surgical intervention.
43049891:
PURPOSE: Prostate MRI is shifting toward biparametric protocols that omit the gadolinium-based dynamic contrast-enhanced (DCE) sequence - a decision validated entirely on cancer detection. Whether these protocols preserve the ability to estimate tumor grade, the quantity that drives management, has rarely been tested. Using unsupervised MRI "habitats" as a transferable probe, we asked whether the diagnostic contribution of MRI dissociates between detecting and grading prostate cancer.
METHODS: Unsupervised k-means habitats of within-patient-normalized T2 and apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC), plus semi-quantitative DCE maps where available, were defined on PROSTATEx (training), frozen, and transferred unchanged to Prostate-MRI-US-Biopsy (external; 614 MRI targets and 12,809 biopsy cores with per-core Gleason) and QIN-Repeatability (test-retest). Under patient-grouped nested cross-validation we compared habitat, whole-lesion and clinical models, benchmarked habitats against ADC, validated habitat-pathology concordance against these cores, and tested whether the contribution of MRI dissociated between detection and grading.
RESULTS: Low-ADC habitats localized clinically significant cancer across the gland (odds ratio up to 3.05; two lowest-ADC habitats captured significant cancer at twice the random-sampling rate) - but did not exceed whole-lesion radiomics or the ADC value itself (area under the curve 0.69 versus 0.69, cross-validated in the external cohort; cores 0.58 versus 0.62). In 107 MRI-detected lesions, ADC no longer separated grade groups (p = 0.79), whereas DCE time-to-peak did, remaining associated with grade after adjustment for ADC, zone and volume (adjusted p = 0.006; likelihood-ratio p = 0.026), although out-of-sample prediction was weak (cross-validated κ 0.05).
CONCLUSION: Diffusion localized significant cancer, but mean ADC did not separate grade in detected lesions; perfusion timing was associated with grade, yet predicted it poorly and has not been externally validated. Whether omitting contrast forfeits clinically useful grading information therefore remains an open question, to be tested before contrast-free protocols are adopted where grade estimation matters.
43049893: It is important to understand the surgical steps involved in the creation of the external genitalia to effectively evaluate pelvic imaging in transgender individuals after penile inversion vaginoplasty (PIV). This review provides an overview of PIV, correlates neoanatomy with imaging, and discusses imaging evaluation of postoperative complications to guide clinical practice. During embryonic development of external genitalia, the genital tubercle differentiates into the glans penis and the clitoris in the male and female, respectively. The urogenital sinus differentiates into the lining of the male urethra and the lining of the vestibule in females. Importantly, embryologic homology provides a framework for understanding postoperative neoanatomy. Our institutional approach to PIV surgery utilizes the glans penis to construct the neoclitoris, the lining of the urethra to construct the neovestibule, and the penile and scrotal skin to line the neovagina. After surgery, contrast-enhanced CT is generally the first-line imaging modality for suspected acute deep postoperative complications, while MRI is preferred for detailed evaluation of neoanatomy and chronic postoperative complications. Correlating embryologic development, surgical technique, and imaging may improve clinician understanding of neoanatomy after PIV. This may facilitate accurate imaging evaluation of pelvic pathology in transgender individuals after PIV and promote timely diagnosis.
43050083:
OBJECTIVE: This study compares the diagnostic performance of US and 3-T MRIin diagnosing placenta accreta spectrum (PAS) disorder using final histopathological and surgical findings and explores the benefit of using a combined MRI and US approach to diagnose PAS.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed electronic medical records of all patients undergoing 3-T MRIplacenta at our institution between January 2020 and November 2023. The gold standard for PAS outcome was histopathology, and where unavailable, we referred to the operative notes. Patients without surgical or histopathologic data, and non-diagnostic MRI studies were excluded. Sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), confidence intervals, and p-values were generated for MRI, US, and combined MRI + US to detect PAS with subgroup analysis for placenta accreta/increta and percreta.
RESULTS: Eighty-eight patients met the inclusion criteria. The sensitivity and specificity of MRI for all PAS was 100.0% and 80.0% (p < 0.001), compared to US 89.5% and 62.0% (p < 0.001), and combined MRI + US 100.0% and 56.0% (p < 0.001), respectively. For diagnosing placenta percreta, MRI had a sensitivity and specificity of 83.3% and 94.3% (p < 0.001), compared to US 55.6% and 94.3% (p < 0.001) and combined MRI + US 83.3% and 92.9% (p < 0.001).
CONCLUSION: Both US and 3-T MRIdemonstrated strong diagnostic performances for detecting PAS, with 3-T MRIdemonstrating stronger performance in this selective cohort, and not further improved by including US data. The continued use of US, MRI and clinical data for evaluating PAS disorder treatment options is recommended.
KEY POINTS: Question No dedicated study has evaluated the diagnostic performance of 3-T MRIor the combined use of MRI with US in PAS. Findings 3-T MRIdemonstrates high sensitivity and specificity for diagnosing PAS. The combined MRI and US assessment does not further improve diagnostic performance for PAS. Critical relevance statement 3-T MRImay be particularly useful as an adjunct in selected high-risk patients, equivocal ultrasound cases, or cases requiring assessment of myoinvasive disease and multidisciplinary surgical planning.
43050191:
IMPORTANCE: A pooled baseline prevalence of chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) in populations without repetitive head impact (RHI) exposure is needed to contextualize prevalence in other cohorts.
OBJECTIVE: To estimate the pooled prevalence of CTE in populations without documented contact sport-based RHI exposure.
DATA SOURCES: PubMed and Embase were searched from inception through February 23, 2026, using terms for CTE, prevalence, epidemiology, and neuropathology.
STUDY SELECTION: Studies reporting CTE prevalence in cohorts without documented contact sport RHI history were included and classified by ascertainment rigor into a primary group with verified absence of contact sport RHI or a secondary unscreened reference cohort. Studies were excluded for cohort overlap or for RHI-linked comorbid conditions (eg, epilepsy).
DATA EXTRACTION AND SYNTHESIS: Data were independently extracted by 2 authors, with discrepancy resolved by a third. Risk of bias and quality were assessed using the Joanna Briggs Institute checklist. Pooled prevalence was calculated using a random-effects model with restricted maximum likelihood estimation. Heterogeneity (I2 and τ2) and robustness (leave-one-out sensitivity analysis) were assessed.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: Confirmed CTE in individuals without documented contact sport RHI history was estimated using pooled prevalence and 95% CIs.
RESULTS: Twelve cohort studies (4421 individuals; weighted mean age at death, 75.1 years; 2481 male [56.1%]) were identified. In the primary analysis of 7 cohorts with verified absence of contact sport RHI (1604 individuals), 12 cases of CTE were identified (crude prevalence, 0.75% [95% CI, 0.43%-1.30%]); pooled prevalence was 1.06% (95% CI, 0.10%-10.79%), reflecting substantial heterogeneity (I2 = 87.0%) and limited precision from few cases and presence of an outlier with 5 of 7 individuals with CTE. Excluding the outlier yielded a pooled prevalence of 0.70% (95% CI, 0.28%-1.74%) and reduced heterogeneity (I2 = 6.6%). In the 5 unscreened reference cohorts (2817 individuals), 17 cases of CTE were identified (crude prevalence, 0.60% [95% CI, 0.38%-0.96%]). Across all 12 cohorts, the crude prevalence was 0.66% (95% CI, 0.46%-0.94%), and the pooled prevalence was 0.85% (95% CI, 0.24%-2.89%).
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: This systematic review and meta-analysis of 12 cohort studies not selected for contact sport-based RHI exposure found that CTE pathology was rare, with a baseline prevalence of approximately 1%. These findings provide a reference point for interpreting CTE prevalence in other populations, including cohorts with contact sport exposure.
43050347:
BACKGROUND: Oesophageal perforations are life-threatening emergencies, necessitating prompt diagnosis and intervention. Currently, no standardized approach exists regarding initial diagnosis and management strategies before tertiary care centre transfer within the UK. In the present study, the aim was to establish consensus on the optimal investigations and management strategies required before referral for definitive treatment.
METHODS: A systematic search of databases (PubMed and Ovid) was conducted from inception until July 2026 for studies that detailed the initial management and investigation of oesophageal perforation. Appraisal of the quality of evidence was performed using the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluation framework. These findings informed the two-stage consensus method, with consensus defined as ≥ 75% agreement between respondents.
RESULTS: Forty-nine studies met the inclusion criteria, and the quality of evidence was low. Consensus was achieved among experts on the need to perform a computed tomography scan with oral +/- intravenous contrast, keeping the patient nil by mouth, initiating intravenous fluids, proton pump inhibitors, antibiotics, antifungal therapy, and insertion of a chest drain if suspecting oesophageal perforation with concurrent hydro/pneumothorax. The following did not reach consensus: repeating a computed tomography scan with oral contrast if features suggestive of perforation, initiation of intravenous antiemetics, and the suitability of nutritional support before definitive management.
CONCLUSION: The new guidelines give a framework for referring centres regarding the initial investigation and management strategies of suspected oesophageal perforations before referral. Future studies are needed to validate these guidelines and further improve outcomes.
43050674:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the association between fetal growth restriction (FGR) and adverse maternal cardiovascular outcomes within 5 years postpartum.
METHODS: This was a retrospective study that used a global federated health research network (TriNetX) in which diagnoses are coded using the International Classification of Diseases, tenth revision, Clinical Modification system (ICD-10-CM). Nulliparous women aged ≥ 18 years, without prior cardiovascular disease and with a singleton pregnancy delivered between April 2006 and December 2020, were categorized by the presence or absence of FGR (ICD-10-CM: O36.5). 1:1 propensity-score matching (PSM) was applied using two models: Model 1, matching for pre-existing cardiovascular risk factors; and Model 2, matching for both pre-existing and other pregnancy-related cardiovascular risk factors. Cox regression proportional hazard models were used to estimate hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% CI for a maternal composite cardiovascular outcome including heart failure, acute myocardial infarction and cerebral infarction/ischemic stroke within 5 years postpartum, and for each of these components individually.
RESULTS: After PSM, 84 863 women per group were analyzed in Model 1 and 84 861 per group in Model 2. FGR was associated with an increased risk of the composite cardiovascular outcome (Model 1: HR, 1.33 (95% CI, 1.16-1.52); Model 2: HR, 1.31 (95% CI, 1.15-1.50)), as well as with an increased risk of each of the components of the composite outcome individually: heart failure (Model 1: HR, 1.29 (95% CI, 1.08-1.54); Model 2: HR, 1.30 (95% CI, 1.09-1.56)), acute myocardial infarction (Model 1: HR, 1.55 (95% CI, 1.16-2.08); Model 2: HR, 1.53 (95% CI, 1.15-2.05)) and cerebral infarction/ischemic stroke (Model 1: HR, 1.38 (95% CI, 1.09-1.74); Model 2: HR, 1.33 (95% CI, 1.06-1.68)) within 5 years postpartum.
CONCLUSIONS: FGR in a first pregnancy is associated with increased maternal composite cardiovascular risk, including heart failure, acute myocardial infarction and cerebral infarction/ischemic stroke, within 5 years postpartum. These findings suggest that FGR may be a marker of early cardiovascular vulnerability. However, residual confounding, particularly by unmeasured timing or severity of pre-eclampsia, cannot be excluded. Also, FGR was identified using coding constructs based on electronic health records, which may include overlap with broader 'suspected poor growth' phenotypes such as small-for-gestational age, hence potentially diluting the observed associations. Earlier risk assessment and preventive strategies may help to reduce the risk of long-term morbidity and mortality in this population. © 2026 The Author(s). 43050853:
INTRODUCTION: Despite the availability of recommendations regarding post-urinary tract infection (UTI) diagnostics in infants, clinical practice remains heterogeneous. Observations suggest that vesicoureteral reflux (VUR) is diagnosed in a relatively small proportion of voiding cystourethrography (VCUG) examinations, which may reflect either limited precision of the guidelines or suboptimal concordance with them.
AIM: The aim of the study was to assess familiarity and concordance with current diagnostic recommendations regarding the use of VCUG after UTI in infants among Polish clinicians.
MATERIAL AND METHODS: A nationwide anonymous online survey was conducted among physicians working in centres performing VCUG. A total of 86 responses were obtained; 21% of respondents were paediatric urologists, and 79% were paediatricians and nephrologists/paediatric nephrologists. The participants were asked to comment on different clinical scenarios and to complete a structured questionnaire.
RESULTS: Knowledge of indications for VCUG was declared by 92% of respondents. Concordance varied substantially between individual clinical scenarios (39.5-98.8%): it was nearly complete (98.8%) in cases with a clear clinical picture (impaired renal function, hydronephrosis with ureteric dilatation), but only 48.8% of respondents referred an infant with recurrent febrile UTIs and normal US findings for VCUG. VCUG was most commonly postponed for ≥2 weeks after resolution of infection (90%). Across the clinical scenarios, physicians in training most consistently selected guideline-concordant responses (64.7-100%). Routine antibiotic prophylaxis prior to VCUG was used by 68.6% of physicians. Ultrasound was most commonly recommended twice-during the acute phase of UTI and after its resolution (43%). Renal pelvic dilatation with anteroposterior (AP) diameter of ≥10 to <15 mm was most commonly considered an indication for VCUG, regardless of UTI history. Multicystic dysplastic kidney (MCDK) with a history of UTI was considered an indication for VCUG by 50% of respondents, with urologists being the least likely to recommend the procedure in such cases. Isolated ureteric dilatation and a hypodysplastic kidney with urinary tract dilatation were considered the most suggestive US findings for VUR (56% and 77%, respectively).
CONCLUSIONS: Despite good awareness of current recommendations, responses varied substantially across clinical scenarios, particularly in areas where recommendations were less specific or differed between societies. The greatest uncertainty concerns US findings suggestive of VUR, timing of VCUG and antimicrobial prophylaxis. More unified, explicit and clinically applicable recommendations are needed.
43051238:
AIMS: Whether frequent night-shift work is associated with a distinct subclinical cardiac phenotype and accompanying molecular alterations remains uncertain.
METHODS AND RESULTS: We analysed 42 671 UK Biobank participants without baseline cardiovascular disease who underwent cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR). Night-shift frequency was classified into four categories, and 15 CMR measures were assessed using multivariable regression. Compared with day workers, frequent night-shift workers showed greater left ventricular global wall thickness [standardized β = 0.092, 95% CI 0.050-0.135; false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.001] and left ventricular mass-to-volume ratio (β = 0.072, 95% CI 0.021-0.123; FDR = 0.019), with lower left ventricular end-diastolic volume index, right ventricular end-diastolic volume index, right ventricular stroke volume index, and maximal right atrial volume index (all FDR < 0.05). Left ventricular global circumferential strain was less favourable (β = 0.092, 95% CI 0.040-0.144; FDR = 0.002), whereas left ventricular ejection fraction and global longitudinal strain were not significantly associated. Proteomic (n = 4889) and metabolomic (n = 42 671) analyses identified exploratory inflammatory, vascular, and lipid-related correlates. Mediation analyses identified FDR-significant indirect-effect estimates involving left ventricular end-diastolic volume index for three proteins and four metabolites. Two-sample Mendelian randomization identified associations between selected molecular features and CMR traits, although directions were not uniformly concordant with the observational estimates.
CONCLUSION: Frequent night shift work was associated with greater concentric left ventricular geometry, lower cardiac chamber volumes, and less favourable circumferential strain, together with inflammatory and lipid-related molecular correlates. Prospective studies are required to determine temporal relationships and long-term clinical relevance.
43051248: In 2014 the National Association of EMS Physicians (NAEMSP), American College of Surgeons Committee on Trauma (ACS-COT), American College of Emergency Physicians (ACEP), and American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) published the first joint position statement discussing withholding and discontinuing resuscitation attempts for pediatric traumatic out-of-hospital circulatory arrest (TOHCA). Since then, the body of literature addressing pediatric TOHCA has evolved and evidence has grown that demonstrates the nearly uniformly poor prognosis of children who suffer circulatory arrest in the prehospital setting as a result of trauma. To support emergency medical services (EMS) clinicians in their approach to these high-acuity, low-frequency, and challenging cases, this project aimed to update guidance regarding decisions to withhold or discontinue resuscitation efforts for pediatric traumatic circulatory arrest. NAEMSP, ACEP, ACS-COT, and AAP recommend: EMS resuscitation of pediatric TOHCA should: ○ Prioritize prompt identification of patients who may benefit from transport to definitive care at trauma centers when safe and appropriate. On-scene resuscitation should be balanced against the potential benefit of transfer to a proximate trauma center.○ Emphasize the identification of reversible causes of traumatic circulatory arrest and timely use of clinically indicated life-saving interventions (LSIs) within the EMS clinician's scope of practice. These include: ▪ External hemorrhage control with direct pressure, wound packing, and tourniquets▪ Airway management using the least-invasive airway interventions required to achieve and maintain airway patency, oxygenation, and adequate ventilation.▪ Chest decompression if clinical concern for tension pneumothorax. Empirical bilateral decompression is not recommended in the absence of suspected thoracic trauma.▪ External chest compressions and ventilations have a larger role in pediatric TOHCA resuscitation than in adult TOHCA resuscitation, with children frequently having TOHCA secondary to head injury, hypoxia and other non-hemorrhagic mechanisms. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) should be provided when the cause of circulatory arrest is unclear.▪ Epinephrine is of lower priority than other LSIs.○ Consider point of care ultrasound (POCUS) to guide decisions to withhold or discontinue resuscitation efforts.Resuscitation attempts may be withheld in pediatric TOHCA patients with: ○ Injuries that are incompatible with life (eg, decapitation, hemi-corpectomy, incineration).○ Evidence of prolonged circulatory arrest (eg, rigor mortis, dependent lividity, decomposition).○ Advanced care planning documents that indicate Do Not Resuscitate (DNR)/ Do Not Attempt Resuscitation (DNAR)/Allow Natural Death medical orders.
43051336:
BACKGROUND: Pulmonary nodules may be missed on chest radiographs despite their clinical relevance for early lung cancer detection. Commercial artificial intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly available for chest radiograph interpretation, but evidence for their standalone performance remains fragmented across products, datasets, operating thresholds, and comparator designs.
PURPOSE: To systematically evaluate the standalone diagnostic performance of commercially available AI software for pulmonary nodule detection on chest radiographs compared with radiologists reading alone, and to identify methodological factors shaping interpretation of the evidence.
