METHODS: A systematic review was conducted according to PRISMA 2020 guidelines and registered with PROSPERO (CRD420261383905). PubMed, PubMed Central, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched. Eligible studies evaluated commercially available AI systems as standalone detectors for pulmonary nodules on chest radiographs and directly compared their performance with radiologists reading alone using an accepted clinical reference standard. Risk of bias was assessed using an adapted QUADAS-2 framework. Findings were synthesized narratively because of heterogeneity in study design, populations, reference standards, operating thresholds, and outcome measures.
RESULTS: Six studies met the inclusion criteria, comprising 12 product-level evaluations across 10 commercial AI systems. Standalone AI performance varied: some evaluations showed AI exceeding radiologist-level performance, others showed no significant difference, and one showed AI below individual reader performance with approximately twice the false-positive rate. In the only standardized within-study comparison of multiple commercial products on the same dataset, four of seven systems significantly exceeded mean radiologist AUC. Standalone AI AUC ranged from 0.79 to 0.93 against a mean reader AUC of 0.81 (95% CI 0.77-0.85), indicating that performance varied among cleared products even when tested under identical conditions. Interpretation was limited by differences in operating thresholds, comparator design, reference standards, study populations, and outcome reporting. Risk-of-bias concerns were common, particularly in patient selection.
CONCLUSIONS: In the available peer-reviewed evidence, standalone commercial AI systems for chest radiograph pulmonary nodule detection show variable performance. Evidence remains insufficient to support class-wide standalone deployment because all studies were retrospective or reader-study based, thresholds were inconsistently reported, and real-world false-positive burden remains uncertain. Prospective real world evaluation with clearly reported operating thresholds, standardized comparator designs and complete diagnostic performance are needed.
43051418:
BACKGROUND: Imaging evidence of vasculitis is mandatory for classification of Takayasu arteritis (TA) in children, yet the ability of a negative study to exclude the diagnosis has not been evaluated. We aimed to determine the negative predictive value (NPV) of cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) for excluding TA in children, to describe the imaging phenotype at diagnosis, and to characterise interval change on serial imaging.
METHODS: This retrospective study included all children who underwent CMR for suspected or established large vessel vasculitis at a single tertiary centre between May 2018 and November 2025. The protocol comprised contrast-enhanced angiography, 3D balanced steady-state free precession (bSSFP) imaging, black-blood imaging and late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) of vessel walls. TA was classified by the EULAR/PRINTO/PRES paediatric criteria. A true negative was defined as a negative baseline CMR with no emergence of TA over at least 6 months of documented follow-up. Interval change on serial CMR was classified per scan pair as improved, unchanged or worsened, recording wall findings (thickening, LGE) and luminal findings (stenosis, dilation) separately, by two readers.
RESULTS: 161 children underwent 222 CMR studies. Of 156 initial diagnostic studies, 10 (6%) showed TA and 146 were negative. No child with a negative baseline CMR developed TA during a median follow-up of 3.6 years (IQR 2.1 to 4.7), corresponding to an observed NPV of 100% (95% CI 97.5 to 100). Positive initial studies were characterised by aortic wall thickening and LGE in 7 of 10 children (70%), these were concordant in every child; extra-aortic involvement was present in 7 (70%). Fifteen children with TA underwent serial CMR (51 interval comparisons; inter-reader agreement 90%, weighted κ 0.86, 95% CI 0.71 to 0.96): 11 intervals (22%) showed improvement, 20 (39%) no change and 20 (39%) worsening. Two children had a previously undescribed imaging finding of focal 3D bSSFP signal abnormalities at sites of disease, consistent with a local susceptibility effect that improved or resolved with treatment.
CONCLUSIONS: In a tertiary referral population, no child with a negative CMR developed TA during follow-up. Serial CMR detected interval change with high agreement between readers. These findings support CMR as a reliable investigation for both the exclusion and longitudinal monitoring of TA in children.
43051603: Oligometastatic non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is increasingly encountered in clinical practice, owing to advances in imaging techniques and the emergence of new therapeutic options. This manuscript presents the outcomes of a meeting of experts from Hong Kong, convened to review the evidence and provide guidance on the use of local ablative therapies (LATs) for patients with oligometastatic NSCLC harboring actionable mutations. The discussion addressed key topics, including the definitions of oligometastatic and oligoprogressive disease, criteria for selecting patients for radiotherapy and other LAT modalities, optimal radiotherapy dosage, and the sequencing and timing of LATs in conjunction with targeted molecular therapies. Guidance was also developed regarding whether to pause or continue systemic treatments during LAT, and the evidence supporting emerging biomarkers in this context was reviewed. Consensus statements were formulated using a modified Delphi approach, and several case examples were presented to illustrate the application of these recommendations in clinical management. The consensus statements from this meeting could provide an important basis for tailoring treatment for patients with NSCLC who have actionable mutations, as well as pointing out key areas to explore in upcoming research.
43051666:
BACKGROUND: Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) species are the leading causes of nontuberculous mycobacterial pulmonary disease worldwide. However, the clinical relevance and species-specific manifestations of MAC pulmonary disease (MAC-PD) caused by M. avium, M. intracellulare and M. chimaera remain incompletely understood.
OBJECTIVE: To compare the clinical relevance, radiological manifestations and treatment outcomes associated with M. avium, M. intracellulare and M. chimaera pulmonary disease.
METHODS: We performed a systematic review and meta-analysis of studies published between 2006 and 2 March 2026, identified through PubMed, Embase and Web of Science. Studies reporting adult patients with pulmonary isolates of M. avium, M. intracellulare or M. chimaera were included. Random-effects meta-analyses were conducted to estimate pooled proportions for clinical relevance, radiological manifestations, treatment success, culture conversion, relapse and mortality.
RESULTS: A total of 134 studies comprising 46 980 patients were included, of whom 28 858 had M. avium, 17 540 had M. intracellulare and 582 had M. chimaera. Clinical relevance was comparable for M. avium and M. intracellulare (53.8% versus 54.7%) but lower for M. chimaera (17.8%). Nodular bronchiectatic disease predominated across all species. Treatment success (63.0-67.5%), culture conversion (70.8-71.9%), relapse (27.9-29.1%) and mortality (14.2-19.3%) were similar between M. avium and M. intracellulare. However, patients with M. chimaera were less frequently treated.
CONCLUSIONS: M. avium and M. intracellulare were associated with comparable clinical relevance, disease manifestations and treatment outcomes across geographic regions, whereas M. chimaera was associated with less clinically relevant disease. Improved molecular species differentiation may further clarify species-specific pathogenicity and clinical implications in MAC-PD.
43051704:
OBJECTIVE: The Cancer Committee of the French Association of Urology (CCAFU) proposes an update of the recommendations for the management of recurrent and/or metastatic prostate cancer (PCa).
METHODS: A systematic review of the literature from 2024 to 2026 was conducted by the CCAFU to examine the elements of therapeutic management of recurrent prostate cancer after local or metastatic treatment, evaluating the references and their level of evidence.
RESULTS: Molecular imaging is the standard assessment for recurrence after local treatment. Its use should not delay early salvage therapy. Androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) is the cornerstone of treatment for metastatic prostate cancer (PCa). Intensification of ADT, combined with at least one androgen receptor pathway inhibitor (ARPI), is now a standard of care for metastatic PCa. Other agents may be added depending on tumor characteristics and patient eligibility. Radiation therapy of the primary tumor is standard for patients with low tumor volume or fewer than 5 metastases on conventional imaging. For patients with castration-resistant PCa (CRPC), PARP inhibitors and PSMA-guided internal radiotherapy are newer treatment options. The combination and sequencing of treatments depend on numerous factors (patient and disease characteristics, prior lines of therapy, genomic status, and molecular imaging).
CONCLUSION: This update of the French recommendations should contribute to improving the management of patients with recurrent or metastatic prostate cancer.
43051705:
OBJECTIVE: To update recommendations for the management of kidney cancer.
METHODS: A systematic review of the literature published between 2014 and 2026 was performed to identify relevant evidence on diagnosis, classification, treatment, and follow-up. Recommendations were graded as strong or weak.
RESULTS: Contrast-enhanced thoraco-abdominal CT remains the reference for diagnosis and staging, while PET/CT is not routinely indicated. Percutaneous biopsy is recommended when it may influence therapeutic decision-making and reduce unnecessary surgery for benign tumors. Tumors are classified according to the 2017 pTNM classification (revised in 2025), the 2022 WHO classification, and ISUP grade; metastatic disease is stratified by IMDC risk group. For T1 tumors, minimally invasive robot-assisted partial nephrectomy is the reference surgical treatment. Active surveillance should be offered for masses≤2cm regardless of age and may be considered for selected tumors up to 4cm. Ablative therapies and stereotactic radiotherapy are alternatives for patients unsuitable for surgery. Radical nephrectomy remains the standard for locally advanced disease, and adjuvant pembrolizumab is recommended for patients at high risk of recurrence. Immediate cytoreductive nephrectomy is not recommended in poor-risk metastatic disease. First-line treatment of metastatic clear cell RCC relies on immune checkpoint inhibitor-based combinations according to IMDC risk. Clinical trial enrollment should be prioritized after progression on adjuvant pembrolizumab and in later treatment lines. Patients with non-clear cell RCC should undergo expert multidisciplinary review, with priority given to clinical trials. Appropriate use of healthcare resources and environmental sustainability are integrated throughout the recommendations.
CONCLUSIONS: These updated recommendations incorporate recent advances in diagnosis, surgery, systemic therapy, and disease monitoring, providing a contemporary evidence-based framework for the management of kidney cancer across disease stages.
43051708:
OBJECTIVE: The aim of the Cancer Committee of the French Association of Urology is to propose an update of the recommendations for the diagnosis and management of localized prostate cancer (PCa).
METHODS: A systematic review of the literature from 2024 to 2026 concerning the diagnosis and therapeutic management of localized PCa was conducted by the CCAFU, and the references and their level of evidence were evaluated.
RESULTS: The recommendations specify the genetics, epidemiology, and diagnostic methods of prostate cancer, as well as screening and early detection approaches. Disease staging is performed on the basis of clinical and biological data, MRI, and molecular imaging. Therapeutic options are detailed and recommended according to clinical situations, along with posttreatment monitoring.
CONCLUSION: This update of the French recommendations should contribute to improving the management of localized prostate cancer.
43051709:
OBJECTIVE: To update the CCAFU guidelines for the management of muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC).
METHODS: A systematic review (Medline) of the literature from 2024 to 2026 was performed, considering the diagnostic work-up, treatment options, and NMIBC and MIBC follow-up, with references graded according to their level of evidence.
RESULTS: The diagnosis of muscle-invasive bladder cancer relies on transurethral resection of the bladder. The staging work-up includes CT urography combined with chest CT. Multiparametric bladder MRI may be proposed to refine locoregional assessment without delaying management. For nonmetastatic disease, radical cystectomy with standard pelvic lymph node dissection remains the reference treatment. In cisplatin-eligible patients, a perioperative strategy based on cisplatin-based neoadjuvant chemotherapy should be discussed, with consideration of integrating immunotherapy and perioperative systemic treatment according to available indications. The combination of enfortumab vedotin and pembrolizumab (EVP) is also recommended. In cisplatin-ineligible patients, EVP represents a major therapeutic option when available. A bladder-sparing strategy using trimodal therapy-combining maximal transurethral resection, external beam radiotherapy, and concomitant radiosensitizing chemotherapy-should be discussed and offered to selected, well-informed patients who are compliant with rigorous follow-up. Urinary diversion by enterocystoplasty may be offered to both men and women in the absence of oncologic, functional, or general contraindications; otherwise, ileal conduit urinary diversion remains the reference diversion. Enrollment in an enhanced recovery program after surgery is recommended for all surgical patients. For metastatic disease, the EVP combination is the recommended first-line treatment. After disease progression, subsequent therapeutic options should be tailored according to previously received treatments, patient profiles, potential molecular alterations, and access to clinical trials.
CONCLUSION: This update of the CCAFU guidelines aims to harmonize and optimize the management of patients with muscle-invasive bladder cancer, incorporating recent developments in diagnostic work-up, perioperative treatments, bladder-preservation strategies, and the management of metastatic disease.
43051710:
INTRODUCTION: The purpose of this article is to propose an update of the French guidelines from the national committee ccAFU on upper tract urothelial carcinomas (UTUC).
METHODS: A systematic Medline search for epidemiology, risk factors, diagnosis, prognosis, treatment options and follow-up of UTUC was performed between 2024 and 2026 to evaluate the available references and their levels of evidence.
RESULTS: UTUC is a rare malignancy with specific risk factors, including exposure to aristolochic acid and Lynch syndrome. Its diagnosis is based on the use of computed tomography urography and ureterorenoscopy with biopsies. A prognostic classification has been proposed to discriminate low- and high-risk lesions mainly on the basis of tumor grade (low/high) and imaging aspect (noninfiltrative/infiltrative). Tumor size (<2/≥2cm), focality (uni/multifocal), and hydronephrosis (absent/present) are more relative risk factors. The standard of care for low-risk patients is currently conservative treatment involving mainly ureterorenoscopy laser ablation, whereas radical nephroureterectomy (RNU) is advised for those with high-risk disease. Adjuvant treatments after RNU include the intravesical instillation of chemotherapy to decrease the risk of bladder recurrence and the delivery of platinum-based chemotherapy in pT2-T4 and/or pN+ patients. First-line treatment for metastatic UTUC is based on the use of a combination of enfortumab vedotin plus pembrolizumab. For unfit patients, platinum-based chemotherapy plus nivolumab followed by maintenance nivolumab in those with at least stable disease or platinum-based chemotherapy followed by maintenance avelumab in those with at least stable disease can be proposed. The surveillance regimen and schedule depend on the disease stage.
CONCLUSION: These updated guidelines will contribute to improving the management of patients diagnosed with UTUC.
43051711:
OBJECTIVE: To update the guidelines for the management of testicular germ cell tumors.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: A comprehensive literature review in PubMed was conducted for articles published from 2024 through July 2026 that addressed the diagnosis, treatment, follow-up, and treatment-related toxicity of testicular germ cell tumors (TGCTs). The level of evidence of the selected articles was assessed.
RESULTS: The initial evaluation of a patient with a testicular germ cell tumor is based on clinical examination, serum tumor marker assessment including Alpha-foetoprotein (AFP), total human Chorionic Gonadotrophin (hCG), and lactate deshydrogenase (LDH) levels, and imaging, including scrotal ultrasonography and contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis. Radical inguinal orchiectomy is the first therapeutic step. It provides the histologic diagnosis, establishes the local stage, and identifies prognostic risk factors in patients with stage I nonseminomatous germ cell tumors (NSGCTs). In patients with stage I pure seminoma, the risk of relapse is 15-20%; active surveillance is therefore preferred in compliant patients. Adjuvant chemotherapy with one cycle of carboplatin at an area under the curve of 7 is an option, whereas indications for lombo-aortic radiotherapy are limited. For patients with stage I NSGCT, a risk-adapted strategy - active surveillance or one cycle of BEP chemotherapy (bleomycin, etoposide, and cisplatin), according to the absence or presence of lymphovascular invasion - is preferred over universal surveillance. Staging based on retroperitoneal lymph node dissection has a limited role. Metastatic TGCTs are most commonly treated with BEP chemotherapy, provided that bleomycin is not contraindicated. The number of cycles is determined according to the International Germ Cell Cancer Collaborative Group prognostic classification. Lombo-aortic radiotherapy and chemotherapy are both standard options for stage IIA seminomatous germ cell tumors (SGCTs) and selected low-volume stage IIB tumors. Treatment de-escalation protocols may be considered at expert centers for selected patients with metastatic stage IIA SGCT. Nerve-sparing retroperitoneal lymph node dissection at an expert center may be offered to patients with marker-negative stage IIA NSGCTs. When chemotherapy is indicated, the residual mass size must be assessed at the end of treatment by CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis in patients with NSGCTs. The resection of residual masses is recommended for any residual NSGCT mass larger than 1cm. In patients with SGCTs, reassessment with 18F-FDG PET is recommended for residual masses larger than 3cm to guide the indication for surgery. Surgery remains uncommon in these settings. Guideline-based follow-up should be offered to all patients, together with education on testicular self-examination.
CONCLUSIONS: Adherence to TGCT management guidelines results in excellent cancer-specific survival rates of 99% for patients with stage I disease and more than 85% for patients with metastatic disease.
43051712:
INTRODUCTION: Although the majority of adrenal masses are benign and nonfunctional, it is important to investigate them because of their serious endocrine potential and because of the presence of certain cancers. Malignant adrenal tumors (MATs) mainly include adrenocortical carcinomas (ACCs), malignant pheochromocytomas (MPCs), and adrenal metastases (AMs). This article updates guidelines for the management of adrenal incidentalomas (AIs) and, where appropriate, the oncological management of MATs.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: The multidisciplinary working group updated the CCAFU 2024 guidelines for the management of benign or malignant adrenal incidentalomas on the basis of a comprehensive Pubmed review in 2026.
RESULTS: The work-up for the malignancy of an adrenal incidentaloma includes a full history, physical examination, and a biochemical/hormonal assessment to look for subclinical hormone secretion. Diagnostic hypotheses are sometimes available at this stage, but morphological and functional imaging and histological analysis enable the malignancy assessment to be completed and a carcinological diagnosis to be made. Subsequent management decisions, such as the frequency and modality of surveillance or the surgical approach, depend on the findings of this initial assessment. ACC and MPC are mostly sporadic in origin, but a hereditary origin is possible. ACC can be suspected preoperatively, but only a histological examination enables a definitive diagnosis. The diagnosis of PCM is more complex and is based on clinical, biological, and imaging findings. A definitive diagnosis of MS requires a percutaneous biopsy.
CONCLUSIONS: AIs are common but rarely malignant. The highly specific management of malignant adrenal tumors justifies their referral to the COMETE network in France. A management error is a significant factor in life-threatening situations. Therefore, all patients with MATs should be referred to an expert center.
43051713:
OBJECTIVE: To update the French guidelines of the Cancer Committee of the French Association of Urology on the epidemiology, prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and follow-up of penile tumors for the 2026-2028 period.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: A comprehensive review of the literature published since the previous update, up to 2026, was performed. Recent international classifications and guidelines were incorporated. The available literature was assessed according to its level of evidence to formulate recommendations applicable to clinical practice.
RESULTS: Squamous cell carcinomas account for 95% of invasive penile cancers. Two carcinogenic pathways are recognized, HPV dependent and HPV independent, the latter being notably associated with lichen sclerosus and chronic inflammation. Prevention is based on HPV vaccination, patient information regarding risk factors, and the management of chronic inflammatory conditions. Any persistent penile lesion should prompt biopsy without delay. Clinical examination remains essential for local staging and may be supplemented by magnetic resonance imaging when an organ-preserving strategy is considered. Treatment should favor organ preservation whenever oncologically feasible, with negative surgical margins being mandatory. Lymph node assessment is a major prognostic determinant. In clinically node-negative patients with intermediate- or high-risk tumors, bilateral sentinel lymph node biopsy is recommended. In clinically node-positive patients, 18-FDG PET contributes to staging, although histological confirmation remains necessary. Radical inguinal lymph node dissection is indicated in patients with proven nodal involvement. For cN3 disease, neoadjuvant chemotherapy is recommended, followed by surgery in responders. In the metastatic setting, chemotherapy remains the standard treatment. Data concerning immunotherapy are encouraging but remain insufficient to support its use outside clinical trials. Intensive follow-up should be performed during the first 2 years and should include local and inguinal examinations, patient self-examination, quality-of-life assessments, and psychosexual support.
CONCLUSION: The management of penile cancer relies on early diagnosis, organ preservation whenever feasible, and prompt risk-adapted lymph node management. Centralization of care within expert multidisciplinary teams is essential for optimizing oncological, functional, and psychosexual outcomes.
43052075:
BACKGROUND: Invasive myocardial perfusion normalizes absolute coronary flow to subtended myocardial mass. Coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) assigns vessel-specific mass using a Voronoi algorithm, whereas echocardiography incorporates wall thickness into total left ventricular (LV) mass. Their impact in left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) is uncertain.
METHODS: We included 219 patients undergoing continuous thermodilution assessment in the left anterior descending artery (LAD) with available transthoracic echocardiography and CCTA. Absolute coronary flow (Q, mL/min) was measured at rest and during hyperaemia. The LAD territorial percentage was derived from CCTA using the Voronoi algorithm. LAD-subtended mass was calculated as this percentage multiplied by total LV mass obtained from either CCTA or echocardiography. Myocardial perfusion (MP mL/min/g) was calculated as Q divided by LAD-subtended mass, generating MPLAD,CT and MPLAD, Echo, and compared across LV geometry phenotypes.
RESULTS: Echocardiographic and CCTA-derived total LV mass correlated moderately (r = 0.65, p < 0.001), but echocardiography yielded higher values (mean bias 30 g), with greater divergence in LVH. Concentric and eccentric LVH independently predicted discrepancy. In patients without LVH, perfusion was similar (rest: 1.12 vs 1.05 mL/min/g, p = 0.137; hyperaemia: 3.03 vs 2.62 mL/min/g, p = 0.057). In concentric LVH, MPLAD,CT was higher than MPLAD, Echo (rest: 1.14 vs 0.71; hyperaemia: 2.55 vs 1.46 mL/min/g; both p < 0.001). Similar differences occurred in eccentric LVH (rest: 0.81 vs 0.63; hyperaemia: 2.00 vs 1.54 mL/min/g; both p < 0.001).
CONCLUSIONS: Myocardial mass methodology significantly influences invasive perfusion. In LVH, particularly concentric hypertrophy, CCTA- and echocardiography-based mass estimation diverge, resulting in substantial differences in calculated perfusion. Mass-independent indices may provide more robust assessment.
43052469: Generative artificial intelligence is reshaping HPE by changing how learners access knowledge, judge information, demonstrate competence, and develop professional judgment. This Perspective argues that GenAI does not replace existing educational commitments but intensifies the need for coaching, critical appraisal, self-regulation, trustworthy assessment, and institutional standards that prepare learners for responsible participation in digital medicine.
43052519:
BACKGROUND: Ping-pong skull fractures, although rare, represent a distinctive form of depressed skull fracture that primarily affects newborns and infants following traumatic brain injury, birth-related trauma, or compression during delivery. Due to the high malleability of the cranial vault at this age, the application of negative pressure over the depressed area has emerged as a minimally invasive therapeutic alternative capable of promoting bone elevation through local suction. The present study aims to evaluate the efficacy and safety of this technique in the treatment of ping-pong skull fractures.
METHODS: A systematic search of publications was conducted in databases including PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library, covering studies published up to April 2026. The methodological quality of the included studies was assessed using the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) Critical Appraisal Checklist for Case Series. Data analysis was performed using RStudio (version 2026.01.1).
RESULTS: Among the included studies, comprising a total of 81 patients, complete elevation of the ping-pong skull fracture was achieved in 86.52% of cases (95% CI 71.81-94.17; I2 = 25.0%). General complications were reported in 9.82% of patients (95% CI 4.84-18.90; I2 = 0%). The pooled rate of patients requiring a subsequent surgical approach after vacuum-assisted treatment was 10.58% (95% CI 3.95-25.40; I2 = 0%).
CONCLUSION: The vacuum-assisted elevation represents a therapeutic option for PPF, showing encouraging results across clinical, radiological and safety outcomes. However, more and larger studies are needed to confirm its efficacy and safety.
43052641: The past decade has witnessed the emergence of multiple arterial spin labeling (ASL)-based imaging techniques, with growing evidence supporting their utility across diverse neurological diseases. ASL represents a paradigm shift in perfusion imaging as a noninvasive, contrast-free MRI technique that provides both cerebral perfusion quantification and detection of arterial stenosis or occlusion, offering diagnostic capabilities comparable to the established dynamic susceptibility contrast (DSC) technique while avoiding contrast-related risks. This review article provides a focused clinically oriented overview of Pseudo-continuous arterial spin labeling (pCASL) technique in stroke imaging, discusses the fundamental physical principles of arterial spin labeling, examines various acquisition and optimization strategies, and evaluates clinical applications with primary emphasis on acute ischemic stroke and steno-occlusive cerebrovascular disease, the predominant risk factor for recurrent stroke.
43052702:
PURPOSE: To improve magnetic resonance fingerprinting (MRF) T2 encoding by combining phase-based T2 encoding with optimal experiment design.
METHODS: Six hundred-timepoint MRF sequences with jointly optimized flip angle (FA) and quadratic RF phase increment schedules were generated by minimizing their Cramér-Rao Lower Bound for tissue dependent sets of T1 and T2. Sequences were optimized for 3T and 0.55T brain MRF and 0.55T prostate MRF and compared against FA-only optimized and unoptimized (600- and 1000-timepoint) sequences. Accuracy and precision were first evaluated using Monte-Carlo Bloch simulations in a digital phantom. Additional simulations identified a spiral interleaf ordering which minimized aliasing artifacts under phase modulation. A T1/T2 phantom was then used to validate simulation results. In vivo performance was assessed in nine healthy subjects, where precision was measured using bootstrap Monte-Carlo experiments with 50 pseudo-replicas.
RESULTS: Jointly optimized sequences were found to produce T2 maps with significantly greater accuracy and precision than unoptimized and FA-only optimized sequences in simulation and phantom experiments (p < 0.001). A Step 5 (37.5° between timepoints) spiral interleaf ordering minimized aliasing under phase modulation, while maintaining comparable performance without. In vivo testing in the brain and prostate revealed higher T2 values, reduced T2 coefficients of variation, and lower B1 + sensitivity than unoptimized and FA-only optimized sequence variants.
CONCLUSION: Simulation, phantom, and in vivo studies demonstrate that optimized RF phase modulation improves MRF T2 encoding compared to unoptimized and FA-only optimized sequences, enabling shorter exams and greater T2 precision in the brain and pelvis at 3T and 0.55T.
43053177:
PURPOSE: To develop a computationally viable autofocus method for estimating 3D rigid motion in MR imaging.
THEORY AND METHODS: The proposed method, REACT, assumes a piecewise-constant motion trajectory and estimates the rigid motion parameters of individual temporal segments by optimizing an image-quality metric. Coordinate descent is adopted to decompose the high-dimensional optimization problem into a series of subproblems, each updating the motion parameters of a single temporal segment. The cost function of each subproblem is assumed to be approximately locally convex under suitable acquisition conditions. Each subproblem is then solved using a derivative-free solver, thereby avoiding an exhaustive grid search. Numerical simulations investigated the local convexity assumption and data acquisition requirements. REACT was evaluated for respiratory motion correction on in vivo free-breathing coronary MR angiography datasets. Coronary artery sharpness was quantified using unbounded image edge profile acutance (u-IEPA).
RESULTS: In numerical simulations, the objective surfaces of the subproblems were approximately locally convex when the current motion estimate was sufficiently close to the desired solution, and REACT required the data collected within each temporal segment to be sufficiently distributed across k -space. In the in vivo study, REACT yielded higher u-IEPA for both the left anterior descending artery (LAD) and the right coronary artery than did a conventional translational motion-estimation method using image-based navigators. REACT also yielded higher u-IEPA for the LAD than did a conventional autofocus nonrigid motion correction method.
CONCLUSION: This study demonstrates the feasibility of coordinate descent for autofocus motion correction in MR imaging.
43053180:
PURPOSE: To develop a fast, general-purpose framework for voxelwise noise characterization in iterative MRI reconstructions, recovering the image-domain noise variance, the primary quantity from which SNR, g -factor, and related image-quality metrics are derived. The framework addresses both the intractability of closed-form formulas beyond Cartesian sampling and the long runtime of pseudo multiple replica (PMR).
METHODS: A stochastic noise estimator is proposed that operates in the image domain by Probing the Image-space noise COvariance matrix (PICO) with random probe images. Complex random-phase probes attain minimum kurtosis and reduce estimator variance in the tested reconstruction. PICO was validated against analytical benchmarks and PMR references using Cartesian knee data ( R = 2 ), physical brain phantom data ( R = 2 , 3 , 4 ), in vivo non-Cartesian brain data ( R = 2 ), and compressed-sensing knee reconstructions ( R = 2 ).
RESULTS: In Cartesian reconstructions, PICO accurately reproduced analytical SENSE g -factor maps. In non-Cartesian reconstructions, it achieved 1 % g -factor NRMSE ≈ 11 . 9 × faster than PMR in a phantom and ≈ 2 . 81 × faster in vivo, with the efficiency advantage persisting at higher acceleration. For compressed sensing, the Jacobian-based estimator produced noise maps consistent with PMR and computed them 1 . 84 × faster at equal sample counts. Agreement worsened at large added-noise amplitudes and moderate TV strengths.
CONCLUSION: PICO targets the exact covariance of fixed linear reconstructions and a first-order covariance for nonlinear reconstructions, providing a computationally efficient alternative to PMR. By reusing existing reconstruction primitives, it could help incorporate voxelwise noise maps into reconstruction workflows.
43053601:
OBJECTIVE: Chorioamniotic membrane separation (CAS) is a recognized iatrogenic complication of fetoscopic laser photocoagulation (FLP), the standard treatment for twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome (TTTS). We compared the incidence of CAS between two different means of uterine entry for FLP: the sharp-trocar and Seldinger techniques.
METHODS: This was a retrospective cohort study of monochorionic diamniotic twin pregnancies complicated by TTTS undergoing FLP between 16 + 0 and 26 + 0 weeks' gestation at two tertiary fetal centers in the USA from January 2012 to August 2025. The uterine-entry technique was center-specific: one center used the Seldinger technique exclusively, while the other used sharp-trocar entry exclusively. All patients at both centers underwent routine short-interval postoperative fetal ultrasound examination, with particular attention paid to membrane integrity at the entry sites. The primary outcome was CAS diagnosed intraoperatively or during postoperative ultrasound performed within 48 h after surgery. Secondary outcomes included gestational age at delivery, latency from FLP to delivery, preterm birth < 32 and < 34 weeks, and survival 48 h after FLP, at birth and at 30 days postnatally. Univariable and multivariable logistic regression analysis evaluated associations between clinically relevant anatomical and procedural variables and the occurrence of CAS.
RESULTS: In total, 889 pregnancies that underwent a FLP procedure for TTTS were included (591 using Seldinger entry, 298 using sharp-trocar entry). Sharp-trocar entry was associated with a lower rate of CAS (8.1% vs 14.4%; P = 0.01) and lower rates of delivery before 32 weeks (42% vs 59%; P < 0.001) and delivery before 34 weeks (61% vs 77%; P < 0.001). Among cases with complete data, after adjusting for clinically relevant anatomical and procedural variables, sharp-trocar entry was independently associated with lower odds of CAS (adjusted odds ratio, 0.46 (95% CI, 0.24-0.82); P = 0.01). Delivery was later in the sharp-trocar entry group (median gestational age, 32 + 4 (interquartile range (IQR), 29 + 1 to 34 + 4) weeks vs 31 + 0 (IQR, 28 + 1 to 33 + 5) weeks; P < 0.001), and the median interval from procedure to delivery was longer (82 (IQR, 58-105) days vs 74 (IQR, 48-96) days; P = 0.002). Survival of donor and recipient twins 48 h after FLP, at birth and at 30 days postnatally, was similar between the two groups.
CONCLUSIONS: Sharp-trocar entry during FLP for TTTS was associated with a lower incidence of CAS, longer latency from procedure to delivery and later gestational age at delivery compared with the Seldinger technique. Because the entry technique was center-specific, these differences cannot be attributed exclusively to the technique. Survival was similar between the two groups. Prospective studies in which both entry techniques are used in the same center are needed to confirm these findings. © 2026 International Society of Ultrasound in Obstetrics and Gynecology.
43053827:
BACKGROUND: The evolving landscape of the pre-clinical evaluation of transcatheter aortic valve replacement technologies, emphasizing on long-term durability as the field evolves into a lower-risk and younger patient population. The rapid advancement of transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) technologies requires a comprehensive pre-clinical evaluation strategy addressing not only device performance but also long-term durability.
AIMS: The document aims to discuss the biological mechanisms of bioprosthetic valve failure, current approches to pre-clinical testing, future TAVI technologies, and regulatory considerations related to the development and clinical evaluation of TAVI devices.
METHODS AND RESULTS: The document delves into the biological mechanism of bioprosthetic valve failure, focusing on the differences between xenogenic pericardial tissue and native leaflet tissue. Also, the document highlights the importance of testing tailored to study technical and procedural performance. However, the treatment of younger patients and future need for reintervention has forced a paradigm shift from a technology driven assessment to a more lifetime management focused approach. The paper also discusses the future of TAVI, primarily focusing on polymeric and tissue-engineered heart valves, and emphasizes the need for the development of more specific test methods applicable to their unique properties and biological interactions. Finally, details of specific testing methods such as computational, in vitro, and in vivo models in predicting the long-term performance of TAVI technologies are also discussed. The document concludes by presenting a discussion of regulatory considerations, including perspectives from the European Union Medical Device Regulation and the US Food and Drug Administration regarding the requirements for the development and clinical evaluation of TAVI technologies.
CONCLUSION: Reconciling scientific needs, clinical research, and regulatory guidelines ensures the safe and effective introduction of innovative TAVI technologies.
43054115:
BACKGROUND: Multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (MIS-C) associated with SARS-CoV-2 frequently involves acute myocardial dysfunction. However, the prevalence of persistent left ventricular (LV) systolic dysfunction at longer-term follow-up remains uncertain. We therefore performed a systematic review and meta-analysis to estimate the prevalence of persistent LV systolic dysfunction at ≥6 months after MIS-C.
METHODS: We included observational cohort studies reporting longitudinal echocardiographic follow-up in children and adolescents aged <21 years with SARS-CoV-2-associated MIS-C. The prespecified primary outcome was persistent LV systolic dysfunction, defined as left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) < 55% at ≥6 months. Study-level events and denominators were extracted and harmonized using the number of children who underwent ≥6-month echocardiography as the endpoint-specific denominator. Pooled prevalence was estimated using an intercept-only binomial logistic-normal generalized linear mixed model (GLMM) fitted directly to study-level event counts and denominators without continuity correction. The originally prespecified random-effects logit model with restricted maximum likelihood estimation and Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman confidence intervals, together with alternative continuity corrections and transformation-based approaches, was retained as sensitivity analysis under sparse-event conditions.
RESULTS: Ten cohorts met the inclusion criteria and contributed to quantitative synthesis, comprising 432 children with echocardiography at ≥6 months. Persistent LV systolic dysfunction occurred in 3 children, corresponding to a crude observed proportion of 0.69% (3/432). In the revised primary continuity-correction-free binomial logistic-normal GLMM, the pooled prevalence was 0.69% (95% CI, 0.22%-2.13%). Given that only three events were observed, this model-based estimate should not be interpreted as a precise estimate of the underlying population prevalence. Continuity-corrected sensitivity models yielded pooled estimates from 1.62% to 2.23%, further demonstrating numerical sensitivity to the treatment of zero-event cohorts.
CONCLUSION: Persistent LV systolic dysfunction was infrequently observed among children with MIS-C reassessed by echocardiography at ≥6 months. However, only three events were identified, so the available evidence is insufficient to determine the exact population prevalence with precision. Inference is further limited by heterogeneous follow-up and potential selection bias from nonuniform late imaging. Larger prospective cohorts with standardized long-term surveillance are needed.
43054178:
BACKGROUND: Marfan syndrome is an autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder caused primarily by pathogenic FBN1 variants, with aortic dissection a leading cause of mortality. Improved surgical thresholds have reduced Type A dissection mortality, but Type B dissection remains poorly predicted. This review maps current human evidence on molecular, genetic, and pharmacogenomic biomarkers for Type B aortic dissection risk stratification in Marfan syndrome and identifies gaps that inform a future research agenda.
METHODS: A scoping review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) and the framework of Arksey and O'Malley. PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library were searched for articles published between January 2010 and October 2025. Two reviewers independently screened records, extracted data, and scored each study for evidence certainty across six domains.
RESULTS: Twenty-four studies met criteria, derived from 14 independent source populations; eight came from a single Dutch cohort network. Only two studies reported Type B dissection as a specified outcome; the remainder addressed dissection of unspecified type, aortic diameter or growth, or mechanistic endpoints. Four thematic evidence streams emerged. TGF-β pathway biomarkers show associations with aortic phenotype and disease severity across several cohorts, but their value for prospective prediction of Type B dissection remains unvalidated. Variants in TGFBR2 and TGFB2, and FBN1 cysteine-loss variants, are associated with severe aortic phenotypes yet are not integrated into the Ghent nosology. Losartan shows heterogeneous efficacy, and a predefined randomized trial substudy suggests that benefit may depend on FBN1 variant class, although no trial has stratified outcomes by dissection type. No tool exists to stratify Type B risk in the 5 to 10 percent of clinically diagnosed patients without an identifiable FBN1 variant. Evidence certainty was moderate for the pharmacologic stream and low to very low for the other three, and the biomarker evidence is associational rather than causal.
CONCLUSIONS: A competing-risks multimodal model integrating imaging, genotype, and treatment-adjusted biomarker trajectory, developed and externally validated in multicentre prospective cohorts, represents the next research frontier.
43054196:
OBJECTIVE: To review the biochemical and inflammatory markers implicated in chronic pain and peripheral nerve entrapment, and to evaluate the biochemical rationale, proposed injectate mechanisms, and current clinical applications of ultrasound-guided nerve hydrodissection (US-HD) as they relate to these markers.
METHODS: This structured narrative review was conducted using a literature search strategy across PubMed/MEDLINE-indexed and major publisher-hosted literature. Structured searches using eleven pre-specified query strings were run against PubMed/MEDLINE-indexed and major publisher-hosted literature (Frontiers, MDPI, Nature Portfolio, Wolters Kluwer, Springer Nature, Cureus), combining "hydrodissection", "perineural injection" and "nerve entrapment" with "biochemical marker", "biomarker", "inflammatory cytokine" and named mediators (IL-6, TNF-α, VEGF, substance P, CGRP, NGF, kynurenine, TRPV1). Of 81 records identified, 64 remained after de-duplication; following title/abstract screening and full-text assessment against pre-defined eligibility criteria, 13 studies were included in the qualitative synthesis.
RESULTS: Elevated pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α), angiogenic mediators (VEGF) and fibrotic markers (TGF-β1, BMP-7) are associated with nerve entrapment syndromes such as carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS). Neuropeptide and neurotrophic markers, including substance P, CGRP and nerve growth factor (NGF), alongside kynurenine pathway metabolites, are implicated in the maintenance of chronic and neuropathic pain. Mechanistically, dextrose-based hydrodissection injectate is proposed to downregulate TRPV1 receptor activity, while platelet lysate/platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injectate delivers growth factors and may modulate local cytokine profiles. Clinical studies report improvements with US-HD across CTS, myofascial pain syndrome, ulnar neuropathy and knee osteoarthritis, however, the evidence base is small and heterogeneous; no included study measured biochemical markers before and after hydrodissection.
CONCLUSION: Biochemical markers provide a plausible mechanistic framework for US-HD, but direct evidence linking biomarker change to hydrodissection or clinical improvement is absent. Proposed injectate mechanisms therefore remain theoretical. Prospective studies incorporating pre- and post-procedural biomarker sampling are needed to bridge this gap.
43054462:
BACKGROUND: Management of biopsy-diagnosed intraductal papilloma, particularly lesions without atypia, remains controversial. This umbrella review synthesized evidence on malignant upgrade, malignancy underestimation, predictors, and management strategies.
METHODS: PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library were searched from inception to May 30, 2026. Eligible systematic reviews and meta-analyses reported papillary lesion-specific outcomes after percutaneous biopsy. Two reviewers independently performed study selection, data extraction, and AMSTAR 2 appraisal. Estimates were synthesized narratively without additional meta-analysis; primary-study overlap was assessed using the corrected covered area. The protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261417131).
RESULTS: Six reviews were included from 304 records. The citation matrix comprised 181 occurrences representing 123 primary studies, with moderate overlap (corrected covered area, 9.43%; sensitivity analysis, 9.67%). All reviews received critically low AMSTAR 2 ratings. Malignant upgrade estimates were 1.4% for radiologic-pathologic concordant intraductal papilloma without atypia and 2.82%-5.0% for broader benign populations. Malignant upgrade or malignancy underestimation estimates were 32%-36% for lesions with atypia. Overall malignancy underestimation estimates were 12%-15.7% in broader nonmalignant papillary lesion populations. Outcome definitions, denominators, and verification methods varied across reviews, and composite upgrade outcomes were distinguished from carcinoma-specific outcomes. Atypia was the strongest indication for surgery; discordance, suspicious imaging, inadequate sampling, suspicious residual abnormalities, and concurrent breast cancer supported further individualized assessment.
CONCLUSIONS: Evidence supports risk-stratified rather than routine surgical management. Papillomas with atypia generally warrant surgical excision, although selected cases may benefit from additional preoperative vacuum-assisted diagnostic sampling when clarification could alter treatment planning. For papillomas without atypia, diagnostic vacuum-assisted sampling may improve tissue assessment without requiring complete lesion removal. Imaging surveillance should be restricted to carefully selected radiologic-pathologic concordant lesions with adequate representative benign sampling, no major adverse features, and reliable follow-up; complete removal may provide additional reassurance. The proposed management framework is not clinically validated, and confidence remains limited by critically low review quality and primary-study overlap.
SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: PROSPERO CRD420261417131.
43054757:
INTRODUCTION: White matter hyperintensity (WMH) burden is a common marker of cerebral small vessel disease and may identify stroke survivors with reduced cognitive reserve. Published estimates, however, use different imaging thresholds, cognitive definitions, follow-up periods, and effect measures.
METHODS: We searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science Core Collection, and the Cochrane Library from database inception through 13 August 2026. We defined a principal clinically comparable estimand as an adjusted odds ratio comparing high/pathological WMH or white matter lesion burden with lower/normal burden for categorical post-stroke cognitive impairment. Ordinal, volumetric, regional, dementia-specific, and time-to-event estimates were retained in separate evidence strata. The protocol was registered on 16 April 2026 in PROSPERO (CRD420261367226).
RESULTS: Twenty-one studies were included. Four studies contributed to the principal synthesis, which yielded an adjusted odds ratio of 2.87 (95% confidence interval 2.10-3.92; I2 = 0%; τ2 = 0; Q = 0.85). The modified Hartung-Knapp 95% confidence interval was 1.73-4.75, and leave-one-out estimates ranged from 2.72 to 3.10. Broader dichotomous, score-based, volumetric, vascular-dementia-specific, and time-to-event findings were directionally supportive but were not pooled with the principal estimand.
CONCLUSION: High/pathological WMH burden was associated with higher odds of post-stroke cognitive impairment in a small set of clinically comparable adjusted studies. WMH may help identify cognitive vulnerability after stroke, but current evidence does not support WMH as a causal factor or stand-alone prognostic test.
SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: PROSPERO, CRD420261367226.
43054943:
Mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI) is a neurological event caused by external mechanical force to the head. Athletes in contact sports are at particular risk for repeated mTBI, which may result in cognitive symptoms and long-term adverse health outcomes. So far, neither diagnostic, prognostic, nor predictive biomarkers have been validated, and conventionally used radiological methods such as computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) have limited sensitivity to the subtle functional, metabolic, and microstructural abnormalities following mTBI. Moreover, research is challenged by the heterogeneous nature of mTBI and comorbid psychiatric conditions. To address these limitations, multimodal brain imaging studies appear promising. This study systematically reviewed multimodal imaging studies of athletes and narratively synthesized key neuroimaging findings. The databases Web of Science and PubMed (MEDLINE) were searched between January and August 2026 (all years). Studies were eligible if they included athletes with mTBI and acquired two or more complementary imaging modalities within the same participants using cross-sectional or longitudinal designs. Fourteen studies were included in the systematic review with a narrative synthesis. Risk of bias was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. The main modalities used were functional MRI, arterial spin labeling, diffusion tensor imaging, and magnetic resonance spectroscopy, assessing changes in functional connectivity, cerebral blood flow (CBF), diffusion metrics, and brain metabolites, respectively. No study, however, combined MRI-based and electrophysiological methods. Significant alterations in functional connectivity, diffusion metrics, CBF, and brain metabolites were reported at assessment time points beyond the acute phase. Nonetheless, no consistent neuroimaging pattern emerged due to clinical and methodological heterogeneity. To strengthen biomarker research, future studies should aim to implement standardized, longitudinal study designs that include baseline assessments followed by multimodal data fusion analyses.
SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: The details of the OSF project are: doi: 10.17605/OSF.IO/R5B6S, https://osf.io/r5b6s/overview?view_only=9c2267f359474efc93a9ca67cf99ed57.
43055207: Intrauterine insemination (IUI) is a widely used fertility treatment with numerous add-ons and protocol variations, many of which are offered empirically. This guideline systematically reviews the available evidence to provide evidence-based recommendations for their clinical use, aiming to optimise treatment outcomes, standardise practice and facilitate future research. A total of 25 interventions were evaluated, including follicular monitoring, LH surge detection, catheter type, bladder filling, insemination technique, operator experience, cervical mucus aspiration, endometrial scratching, hydrotubation, ovarian stimulation, ovulation triggering and timing, intrauterine infusions, medications affecting endometrial receptivity or uterine contractility, double insemination, ultrasound guidance, bed rest and luteal phase support. A systematic literature search identified 154 randomised controlled trials involving 34,825 participants. Meta-analyses were conducted where feasible. However, the limited availability of adequately powered trials and the predominantly low-quality evidence restrict the certainty of most recommendations. These limitations should be clearly communicated during patient counselling. Future research should prioritise high-quality trials evaluating the effectiveness of IUI add-ons in specific patient populations, considering underlying infertility diagnoses.
43055381: Choline is an essential nutrient in canine and feline diets with physiological roles in lipid metabolism, hepatic function, one-carbon metabolism, neurotransmission, growth, and overall health. Current published dietary recommendations by the National Research Council establish recommended allowances of 425 mg choline/1,000 kcal metabolizable energy in dogs and 637 mg choline/1,000 kcal metabolizable energy in cats. However, these recommendations are largely derived from a limited number of studies in growing puppies and kittens, in which choline deficiency resulted in impaired growth, anorexia, hepatic lipid accumulation, and/or death. In comparison, little is known about the dietary choline requirements of adult, senior, gestating, lactating, overweight, obese, or working animals, or how dietary composition may alter the need for choline. Factors such as dietary fat concentration, methionine, folate, vitamin B12, betaine, choline source, life stage, body condition, and hepatic health may influence choline utilization and dietary requirements. Emerging evidence in companion animals, together with findings from other species, suggests that dietary choline intake above current published recommended allowances may be beneficial for hepatic lipid metabolism, growth and development, cognitive health, aging, and obesity management. However, species-specific research in dogs and cats remains limited, and targeted research is needed to refine dietary recommendations according to life stage, health status, and/or diet composition. This review summarizes current knowledge of choline metabolism, published dietary recommendations, factors influencing dietary requirements, the implications of dietary deficiency and excess, and considerations for choline intake in canine and feline nutrition.
43055436:
IMPORTANCE: Postpartum sexual dysfunction is common, but long-term outcomes beyond the early puerperium remain insufficiently integrated into routine postpartum and gynecologic care.
OBJECTIVE: The objective was to systematically review dyspareunia and sexual dysfunction beyond 6 months postpartum, including associated factors and rehabilitation interventions.
STUDY DESIGN: We searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, PsycINFO, and CENTRAL from inception to January 31, 2026. Eligible primary studies included postpartum women with at least 1 relevant sexual outcome assessed at or beyond 6 months after childbirth. Prevalence and associated-factor findings were synthesized descriptively. Quantitative synthesis was restricted to randomized rehabilitation trials reporting validated sexual-function outcomes at eligible postpartum time points with extractable numerical data.
RESULTS: Twenty-two eligible reports representing 21 unique studies or cohorts were included; 2 randomized rehabilitation studies contributed to quantitative synthesis. Dyspareunia and broader sexual dysfunction remained clinically relevant beyond 6 months postpartum, with incomplete recovery persisting in a substantial subset of women. Persistent morbidity was most consistently associated with severe perineal trauma, including obstetric anal sphincter injury; associations with operative delivery were less consistent. Breastfeeding-related symptoms, depressive symptoms, pelvic floor morbidity, and genital or body image concerns were also reported. The pooled rehabilitation estimate favored intervention but was imprecise and highly heterogeneous (standardized mean difference: 1.19; 95% CI, -0.18 to 2.57; I²=91.7%), with very-low-certainty evidence.
CONCLUSIONS: Persistent dyspareunia and broader sexual dysfunction remain clinically relevant beyond 6 months postpartum and warrant proactive assessment within routine postpartum and gynecologic follow-up, with multidisciplinary management and referral for pelvic floor rehabilitation or urogynecologic evaluation when indicated.
43055619: Purpose To evaluate ventilation and perfusion in control participants and individuals with lung disease using 0.55-T phase-resolved functional lung (PREFUL) MRI. Materials and Methods In this prospective study at a single academic institution, multisection free-breathing hydrogen 1 MRI was performed with a 0.55-T scanner with a balanced steady-state free precession sequence. PREFUL analysis was used to quantify the ventilation-defect-percentage (VDP), perfusion-defect-percentage (QDP), and ventilation-perfusion-mismatch (VQM) defects. Scan-rescan repeatability was assessed in 42 participants. Statistical analyses included nonparametric group comparisons and correlations with pulmonary function test (PFT) parameters. Results A total of 67 participants (mean age ± SD: 51 years ± 19; 32 female) were enrolled between November 2022 and March 2024, including 38 with different lung diseases, some with multiple underlying diagnoses (obstructive = 20, vascular = 9, fibrotic = 14, cancer = 34 and other = 23), and 29 control participants. Compared with control participants, individuals with lung disease had greater QDP (17% vs 11%; P = .02), VDP (30% vs 22%; P = .003), and VQM defects (7% vs 3%; P = .002). VDP and VQM defects were correlated with PFT measurements, including forced expiratory volume in 1 second (ρ = -0.59, P < .001; ρ = -0.50, P = .001), forced vital capacity (ρ = -0.53, P = .005; ρ = -0.49, P = .01), and diffusing capacity of the lung for carbon monoxide (ρ = -0.53, P = .02; ρ = -0.52, P = .02). Scan-rescan analysis revealed minimal bias (P = .06-0.3), coefficients of variation between 10.1% and 37.8%, and intraclass correlation coefficients of 0.64-0.90 for the three MRI metrics. Conclusion 0.55-T PREFUL MRI provides a reproducible, noninvasive method for quantifying ventilation and perfusion defects and effectively distinguishes individuals with lung disease from control participants. Keywords: MR-Functional Lung Imaging, Thorax, Lung Supplemental material is available for this article. © RSNA, 2026.
43055664: Objective: Combination psychopharmacology is common but understudied. Expert guidance is needed to help practitioners follow rationale-based principles when devising and maintaining polydrug regimens. Participants: The American Society of Clinical Psychopharmacology (ASCP) convened an expert Task Force composed of 60 academic clinical psychiatrists and psychiatric pharmacists from 16 countries. Members developed and completed a 2-round Delphi survey on the use of combination psychopharmacology. Evidence: Survey content focused on experts' opinions regarding pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic interactions, efficacy vs tolerability risk-benefit analyses, and clinical decision-making. Gaps were identified between evidence-based literature, personal experience, and pharmacologic rationales. Consensus Process: Consensus (defined as ≥75% agreement [or disagreement] with "strong" or "moderate" ratings) was achieved on 62/66 items (94%). Findings encompassed several principles: (1) General: (a) reserve combination psychopharmacology for complex, comorbidly ill, treatment-resistant presentations; (b) favor complementary/nonredundant drug mechanisms; (c) recognize drug-drug interactions; (d) focus on the mechanistic coherence of polydrug regimens rather than sheer number of components; (e) proactively address cumulative adverse effects; (f) prioritize patient preference via shared decision-making. (2) Specific: (a) avoid nonclozapine antipsychotic combinations; (b) favor switching over augmenting after minimal improvement. (3) Strategic: (a) before augmenting, assure/update diagnoses, dose optimization, adherence, and alignment to therapeutic targets; (b) individualized decisions should govern sequential versus simultaneous pharmacotherapies for comorbidities; (c) consider when adjunctive psychotherapies are preferable to polypharmacotherapies. Conclusions: In the context of limited research, the consensus recommendations from this Task Force can help practitioners identify clinically driven principles that shape coherent multidrug regimens and identify issues in need of further empirical investigation.
43055685: In 2014 the National Association of EMS Physicians (NAEMSP), American College of Surgeons Committee on Trauma (ACS-COT), American College of Emergency Physicians (ACEP), and American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) published the first joint position statement discussing withholding and discontinuing resuscitation attempts for pediatric traumatic out-of-hospital circulatory arrest (TOHCA). Since then, the body of literature addressing pediatric TOHCA has evolved and evidence has grown that demonstrates the nearly uniformly poor prognosis of children who suffer circulatory arrest in the prehospital setting as a result of trauma. To support emergency medical services (EMS) clinicians in their approach to these high-acuity, low-frequency, and challenging cases, this project aimed to update guidance regarding decisions to withhold or discontinue resuscitation efforts for pediatric traumatic circulatory arrest. NAEMSP, ACEP, ACS-COT, and AAP recommend:EMS resuscitation of pediatric TOHCA should:Prioritize prompt identification of patients who may benefit from transport to definitive care at trauma centers when safe and appropriate. On-scene resuscitation should be balanced against the potential benefit of transfer to a proximate trauma center.Emphasize the identification of reversible causes of traumatic circulatory arrest and timely use of clinically indicated life-saving interventions (LSIs) within the EMS clinician's scope of practice. These include:External hemorrhage control with direct pressure, wound packing, and tourniquetsAirway management using the least-invasive airway interventions required to achieve and maintain airway patency, oxygenation, and adequate ventilation.Chest decompression if clinical concern for tension pneumothorax. Empiric bilateral decompression is not recommended in the absence of suspected thoracic trauma.External chest compressions and ventilations have a larger role in pediatric TOHCA resuscitation than in adult TOHCA resuscitation, with children frequently having TOHCA secondary to head injury, hypoxia and other non-hemorrhagic mechanisms. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) should be provided when the cause of circulatory arrest is unclear.Epinephrine is of lower priority than other LSIs.Consider point of care ultrasound (POCUS) to guide decisions to withhold or discontinue resuscitation efforts.Resuscitation attempts may be withheld in pediatric TOHCA patients with:Injuries that are incompatible with life (e.g., decapitation, hemi-corpectomy, incineration).Evidence of prolonged circulatory arrest (e.g., rigor mortis, dependent lividity, decomposition).Advanced care planning documents that indicate Do Not Resuscitate (DNR)/ Do Not Attempt Resuscitation (DNAR)/Allow Natural Death medical orders.Resuscitation attempts may be discontinued in pediatric TOHCA patients who:Have no return of spontaneous circulation after provision of at least 15 minutes of high-quality CPR in addition to performance of other lifesaving interventions directed at treating potentially reversible causes of pediatric TOHCA. Longer durations of CPR, up to 30 minutes, may be considered for patients with positive predictors of survival such as organized rhythm, witnessed arrest, bystander CPR, or with proximate access to a trauma center.Have known predictors of very low probability of survival such as penetrating trauma without proximate access to a trauma center, asystole, unwitnessed arrest, or lack of bystander CPR.Protocols guiding decisions to withhold or discontinue resuscitation of pediatric TOHCA benefit from oversight by EMS physicians in collaboration with pediatric experts and local or regional trauma system stakeholders. Implementation of such protocols for pediatric patients benefits from involvement of community stakeholders including family representatives, law enforcement, medical examiner, and child fatality review committees.Considerations for protocol implementation include local resource availability, EMS clinician and public safety, psychosocial support to surviving family members and emergency responders, and dignified handling of the deceased patient.Training needs for EMS clinicians include techniques to communicate with family members regarding the death of a child and understanding the clinician's own response to this low-frequency, high-emotion experience.
43055695: Chronic liver disease, caused by a range of etiologies, can lead to progressive liver function deterioration, hepatic fibrosis, cirrhosis, and, ultimately, end-stage liver disease. With cirrhosis and end-stage liver disease, complications include portal hypertension, gastrointestinal hemorrhage, refractory ascites, hepatic encephalopathy, and primary hepatocellular carcinoma. Imaging plays an important role in the diagnosis, treatment response assessment, and surveillance of chronic liver disease, specifically of hepatic hemochromatosis, steatosis, and fibrosis, in an effort to prevent progression to cirrhosis. This document reviews the imaging modalities best suited for these clinical scenarios, and a summary of current evidence is provided to support the use of various modalities for each of the clinical contexts. The American College of Radiology Appropriateness Criteria are evidence-based guidelines for specific clinical conditions that are reviewed annually by a multidisciplinary expert panel. The guideline development and revision include an extensive analysis of current medical literature from peer reviewed journals and the application of well-established methodologies (RAND/UCLA Appropriateness Method and Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation or GRADE) to rate the appropriateness of imaging and treatment procedures for specific clinical scenarios. In those instances where evidence is lacking or equivocal, expert opinion may supplement the available evidence to recommend imaging or treatment.
43055778:
OBJECTIVES: To evaluate 24-month clinical, biochemical, ultrasonographic, and safety outcomes after ultrasound-guided microwave ablation (MWA) for persistent or recurrent Graves' disease (GD) and to explore baseline factors associated with recurrence.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: Twenty-four consecutive patients with persistent or recurrent GD despite at least 18 months of antithyroid drug (ATD) therapy were retrospectively analyzed. All patients underwent ultrasound-guided bilateral MWA. The primary outcome was complete remission at 24 months, defined as euthyroidism or hypothyroidism without ATDs. Secondary outcomes included thyroid function, thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor antibodies (TRAb), thyroid volume reduction, vascularity, and complications. Associations between baseline variables and recurrence were explored using univariable Cox regression.
RESULTS: At 24 months, 20 patients (83.3%) achieved complete remission; 18 remained euthyroid and two developed subclinical hypothyroidism. Median thyroid volume reduction was 41.5%, and thyroid vascularity markedly improved. No transient or permanent recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy or other major complications occurred. Higher baseline free thyroxine (FT4) was associated with recurrence (HR: 1.07, 95% CI: 1.01-1.14, p = 0.028). A preliminary FT4 threshold of 39.11 pmol/L yielded an area under the curve of 0.71, but this estimate was based on four recurrence events and was not validated.
CONCLUSIONS: Ultrasound-guided MWA was associated with favorable 24-month outcomes and an acceptable safety profile in selected patients with persistent or recurrent GD. The association between baseline FT4 and recurrence requires validation in larger controlled cohorts.
KEY POINTS: Question Patients with persistent or recurrent Graves' disease need nonradiative, minimally invasive treatment options when antithyroid drugs fail and definitive therapies are declined. Findings Among 24 patients, microwave ablation achieved 83.3% complete remission at 24 months, reduced thyroid volume, improved vascularity, and caused no major complications. Clinical relevance Ultrasound-guided microwave ablation provided durable remission while preserving thyroid function in most selected patients who declined surgery or radioactive iodine.
43055821: This study aims to compare the effects of early and late pharmacological thromboprophylaxis (PTP) on venous thromboembolism (VTE) in patients with traumatic intracranial hemorrhage (ICH). A comprehensive retrieval for literature up to October 2026 was conducted across the PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, and Cochrane Library databases. Early PTP was defined as administration within 72 h post-admission. The analysis encompassed thirteen cohort studies, including a total of 18, 554 patients with traumatic ICH. The primary outcome measures were the occurrence of VTE, progression of ICH, cranial surgery, and in-hospital mortality. Early PTP was associated with a significantly lower incidence of VTE (OR, 0.51; 95% CI, 0.39-0.67), whereas no statistically significant differences were observed between the groups for ICH progression (OR, 0.91; 95% CI, 0.64-1.29), cranial surgery (OR, 1.15; 95% CI, 0.79-1.69), or in-hospital mortality (OR, 0.99; 95% CI, 0.83-1.18). Initiating PTP within 72 h of hospital admission may reduce the incidence of VTE without significantly increasing the rates of ICH progression, cranial surgery, or in-hospital mortality in patients with traumatic ICH. Nevertheless, given the observational design of the included studies and the potential for residual confounding, these findings should be interpreted as associations and require confirmation in prospective, randomized controlled trials.
43055828:
OBJECTIVES: To evaluate diagnostic performance, radiation dose, and quantitative spectral characteristics of dual-phase photon-counting CT (PCD-CT) for parathyroid adenoma localization after inconclusive first-line imaging.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: Consecutive patients with primary hyperparathyroidism and negative, discordant, or inconclusive first-line imaging underwent paired [18F]FECh PET/CT and dual-phase PCD-CT with arterial and venous acquisitions. Three radiologists, blinded to clinical and reference-standard information, retrospectively assessed arterial and portal-venous 40- and 70-keV images and VNC reconstructions. The reference standard comprised surgery/histopathology with biochemical confirmation, concordant PET/CT with persistent biochemical disease in nonsurgical positive patients, or clinical/biochemical resolution in negative patients. Lesion-level sensitivity, positive predictive value (PPV), and interreader intraclass correlation (ICC) were calculated. Aorta-normalized attenuation and wash-in and wash-out metrics were compared among adenomas, thyroid tissue, and lymph nodes.
RESULTS: Forty-nine patients (mean age, 64.2 ± 10.9 years; 42 women) were included, with 45 patients having 49 reference-standard-positive lesions. PCD-CT lesion-level sensitivity was 67.3%-83.7%, and PPV 67.3%-90.0%, with an interreader agreement of 0.506. Aorta-adjusted wash-out was greater in adenomas (27.2%) than in thyroid (20.2%) and lymph nodes (-3.1%; both p < 0.001). Arterial adenoma-thyroid attenuation and wash-in overlapped between adenomas did not differ significantly (arterial p = 0.615 and thyroid tissue. 0.945 at 40 and 70 keV; wash-in p = 0.363). Mean estimated effective dose was 1.23 ± 0.47 mSv.
CONCLUSION: Dual-phase PCD-CT provided reader-dependent parathyroid localization at low radiation dose in a difficult second-line cohort. Quantitative wash-out may aid differentiation from thyroid and lymph-node mimics but requires prospective threshold validation.
KEY POINTS: Question Inconclusive first-line imaging complicates parathyroid lesion localization. Findings Reader sensitivity ranged from 67.3% to 83.7% at 1.23 mSv. Critical relevance statement Aorta-adjusted wash-out differed among parathyroid lesions, thyroid tissue, and lymph nodes.
43056042:
BACKGROUND: Postoperative chylothorax is an uncommon but potentially life-threatening complication after thoracic surgery. Conventional iodized oil-based lymphangiography (CL) and percutaneous lymphatic interventions (PLIs) are increasingly used as minimally invasive diagnostic and therapeutic tools, but standardized, imaging-guided management strategies remain limited. This systematic review synthesizes current evidence and provides a practical treatment algorithm with illustrative cases. Main body Following PRISMA 2020, PubMed and Embase databases (1999-2025) were searched for clinical series (≥ 15 patients) reporting CL and/or PLIs in postoperative chylothorax. Data on imaging findings, procedural techniques, technical and clinical success, time to resolution, complications, and salvage approaches were qualitatively analyzed. As a result, 16 retrospective cohorts were included. CL (transpedal or intranodal) achieved high technical success (88-100%) and leak detection rates (58-90%), with variable therapeutic effect (38-83%) and delayed sealing (≤ 2 weeks). Among the various PLIs, TDE was the predominant technique, which demonstrated high per-protocol clinical success (> 90%) and rapid resolution (≤ 1 week), although technical success averaged 68% (44-100%). Salvage techniques included thoracic duct disruption, afferent lymphatic embolization/sclerotherapy, and direct lymphocele embolization. Overall effectiveness of a TDE-based strategy was 68.2%, with low complication rates (5.3%, mostly minor). A chyle output-based, imaging-guided management algorithm is proposed.
CONCLUSION: CL plays a central role in both leak localization and treatment planning. When leakage is identified, sequential TDE enables rapid resolution, while alternative PLIs and surgery serve as complementary salvage options.
43056214:
BACKGROUND: Complete revascularization is recommended in haemodynamically stable patients with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) and multivessel disease, but the optimal timing of nonculprit percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) remains uncertain, and recent meta-analyses have reached conflicting conclusions.
AIMS: We compared immediate versus staged complete revascularization, assessed whether the accumulated randomized evidence is sufficient to guide practice, and described the methodological differences that may have contributed to the divergent conclusions of previous meta-analyses.
METHODS: PubMed, Scopus, Embase and CINAHL were searched through June 2026 for randomized controlled trials comparing immediate versus staged complete revascularization in STEMI with multivessel disease. The primary outcome was all-cause mortality; secondary outcomes included major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), cardiovascular mortality, recurrent myocardial infarction, unplanned ischaemia-driven revascularization, stroke, major bleeding and stent thrombosis. Certainty of evidence was assessed using GRADE, alongside an information-size analysis with a sequential-monitoring illustration for the primary outcome.
RESULTS: Eleven randomized trials were retained for the evidence map (4430 randomized patients). The primary direct-timing analysis excluded iMODERN and included 10 trials involving 3287 patients (1646 immediate; 1641 staged). Immediate revascularization had a higher all-cause mortality estimate [relative risk (RR) 1.41, 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.02-1.97; P = 0.040; I2 = 0%], with low-certainty evidence and a fragility index of 1; the accumulated information remained substantially below the required information size of 15 352 patients based on a clinically selected 25% relative-risk increase. MACE was similar (RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.76-1.28; P = 0.91; I2 = 39%), while recurrent myocardial infarction was lower with immediate treatment (RR 0.66, 95% CI 0.46-0.94; P = 0.02), subject to outcome-ascertainment limitations. iMODERN was reanalysed separately as an exploratory analysis using the corrected 1143-patient report.
