43081791: Mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI) may lead to a buildup of neurotoxic metabolites in the brain that require clearance by the glymphatic system. Non-invasive magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) methods such as the diffusion tensor imaging along the perivascular space (DTI-ALPS) index and enlarged perivascular space (ePVS) quantification post-mTBI are being increasingly adopted despite an incomplete understanding of the biological limitations and methodological considerations of these techniques. To synthesize the current literature and identify knowledge gaps, a comprehensive search was performed using PubMed, Embase, Web of Science Core Collection, and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials. Human studies written in English between 2000 and 2025 were included, resulting in 18 studies in the final sample. Extracted data included: study design and population, number of participants, time from injury, MRI method, and results. PRISMA reporting guidelines for scoping reviews were followed. Included studies were heterogeneous in study design, choice of study population, time from injury to MRI scan, confounders controlled for, and study results. Decreases in the DTI-ALPS index were reported in studies including mixed injury severities and, in some studies limited to mTBI, while other mTBI-only studies reported increases or no change. ePVS findings were also heterogeneous, with studies reporting either no group differences or higher ePVS measures in injured participants. This scoping review identified three studies that included both DTI-ALPS index and ePVS quantification and determined that these measures may assess distinct biological processes. These results highlight the need for multiparametric, standardized MRI investigations of the glymphatic system post-mTBI.
43082028:
BACKGROUND: Procedural anxiety in pediatric oncology patients can negatively affect outcomes.
AIM: To compare the efficacy of virtual reality (VR) versus standard Child Life (non-VR) distraction in reducing preoperative anxiety.
METHODS: In a randomized crossover design, 52 pediatric oncology patients aged 5-18 years undergoing port access procedures received both VR and non-VR interventions in randomized order. Anxiety was assessed using the modified Yale Preoperative Anxiety Scale (mYPAS) before and during port access. Parental perceptions were collected via surveys.
RESULTS: VR significantly reduced anxiety during the induction phase compared to non-VR interventions (p = 0.0001). No carryover or sequence effects were observed. Most parents reported VR helped reduce their child's anxiety (92.16%) and would prefer VR for future procedures (94.12%).
CONCLUSION: VR is an effective nonpharmacologic tool for reducing procedural anxiety in pediatric oncology patients.
43082029:
BACKGROUND: Standardized assessment to identify and address family financial hardship is recommended in pediatric oncology clinical settings. In an observational study of financial distress among parents of children with newly diagnosed acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), conducted through the Children's Oncology Group (COG) National Cancer Institute Community (NCI) Oncology Research Programs (NCORP), we describe the practices of financial assessments and available resources within participating COG NCORP practices to inform future interventional research to address financial hardship.
METHODS: Among 50 eligible COG NCORP practices, 28 activated and enrolled at least one parent participant in the study (COG ACCL20N1CD) and thereafter were prompted to complete a practice-level survey using the Research Electronic Database Capture (REDCap) platform. The survey assessed each practice's current conduct of financial assessments as well as resources available within and external to the practice to address financial concerns of parents whose children are treated at the practice. Survey responses are reported descriptively.
RESULTS: Twenty (71%) of the 28 practices reported conducting routine financial assessments; among these, most (80%) reported that social workers were responsible for conducting financial assessments. Twenty-nine percent of practices reported having financial navigators available within their clinical care setting. The processes for responding to financial assessments varied; among the 20 practices reporting routine assessment, three (15%) indicated using a standardized review process. Regarding resources available, most practices reported access to at least some internal (institutional, hospital-based) or external (community-based) financial resources to support families of children with cancer.
CONCLUSION: Though most COG NCORP practices enrolling in a study of parental financial distress in pediatric ALL report conducting routine financial assessments, there is notable variability in assessment tools used, response to family-reported financial concerns, and human or system-level resources available. These findings offer insights to improving the ability to identify and address financial hardship within pediatric cancer settings.
43082050:
BACKGROUND: Relapsed pediatric acute myeloid leukemia (AML) has poor outcomes. Molecular relapse provides a window for pre-emptive therapy. This study evaluated azacitidine as a bridge-to-transplant strategy to avoid reinduction and improve hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) outcomes.
METHODS: AMoRe2017 was a prospective, international, multicenter, open-label phase II trial (EudraCT: 2017-003422-32). Patients aged 3 months to <21 years after first complete remission (CR1) with molecular relapse received azacitidine 75 mg/m2 intravenously on Days 1-7 of a 28-day cycle, for up to six cycles. The primary endpoint was molecular response; secondary endpoints included safety, HSCT rate, overall survival (OS), and event-free survival (EFS).
RESULTS: Between May 25, 2018, and February 4, 2023, 20 patients were enrolled; 19 patients were evaluable (median age 11.0 years; 11 male). Five (26.3%; 95% CI 11.8-48.8) patients achieved a molecular response. All responders underwent HSCT without intensive reinduction. HSCT was performed in 18 patients (95%). Ten patients (53%) developed hematological relapse. At median follow-up of 24 months, the OS was 69% (95% CI 47.6-100) and EFS was 30% (95% CI 13.3-66.9). Of the 152 adverse events, 76% were Grade 1 or 2, 19% were Grade 3, and only 5% were Grade 4; no treatment-related deaths occurred.
CONCLUSIONS: Azacitidine controlled molecular relapse in selected pediatric AML subgroups, allowing direct HSCT without reinduction and with manageable toxicity. Efficacy was greatest in favorable genetic subtypes (e.g., RUNX1::RUNX1T1) and limited in highly proliferative disease (e.g., KMT2A rearrangements; KMT2A-r). Results support pre-emptive intervention at molecular relapse and allow further risk-adapted trials.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: EudraCT number: 2017-003422-32.
43082139:
BACKGROUND: Clinically significant cancer-related cognitive changes are well documented in survivorship, but findings on neurocognitive outcomes in pediatric populations remain inconclusive and often rely on broad normative classifications or subjective report. Identifying subtle cognitive changes is particularly important in children, where even mild inefficiencies may negatively affect academic performance and psychosocial functioning.
OBJECTIVES: To evaluate cognitive functioning in pediatric acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) survivors 1-3 years after completing chemotherapy compared to healthy peers using standardized neuropsychological measures and to compare objective performance with self-reported cognition.
METHODS: Seventeen pediatric ALL survivors and 47 age-matched children without history of disease (CTL) between 5 and 17 years of age completed a self-report measure of cognitive functioning and NIH Toolbox objective sensory and cognitive subtests. Group differences were compared using t-tests and regression analyses adjusted for age and biological sex.
RESULTS: Self-report did not differentiate groups; both groups scored within the norm. In contrast, objective testing revealed inefficiencies in attentional control among ALL survivors even when mean scores remained within normative limits, whereas measures of memory and auditory sensory processing did not distinguish groups.
CONCLUSIONS: Findings suggest that pediatric ALL survivors experience subtle but measurable attentional deficiencies following chemotherapy, even when performance falls within normative ranges. These results indicate that reliance on normative cutoffs or self-report measures alone may underestimate cognitive difficulties associated with childhood cancer treatment. More sensitive approaches for detecting attentional difficulties may improve identification of treatment-related cognitive changes during survivorship.
43082233: We describe a neonate with foetal hydrops, blueberry muffin syndrome, hepatosplenomegaly, severe hepatic injury, persistent hyperferritinaemia and widespread extramedullary haematopoiesis who died at 30 days. A previously affected foetus died in utero at 24 weeks and showed overlapping pathological features. Whole-exome sequencing identified a novel homozygous NCKAP1L nonsense variant, c.843G>A, p.(Trp281*), predicted to cause loss of HEM1 expression. The absence of neonatal anaemia contrasts with the erythrocyte phenotype of Hem1-deficient mice. These findings extend HEM1 deficiency to a severe foetal-neonatal phenotype and support NCKAP1L testing in unexplained neonatal cutaneous extramedullary haematopoiesis.
43082257:
BACKGROUND: We evaluated long-term outcomes (median follow-up >12.5 years) of pediatric T-ALL treated via the CCLG-ALL 2008 protocol. Although D33 MRD is an established response marker, it may not fully capture the heterogeneity of early treatment response. We therefore evaluated whether D15 FCM-MRD provides additional prognostic information in children with T-ALL.
METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed 140 T-ALL patients (124 with evaluable flow-cytometric MRD). The optimal D15 MRD cutoff was identified via maximally selected rank statistics. Analyses incorporated multivariable Cox regression, bootstrapping, and competing risk models.
RESULTS: Ten-year event-free (EFS) and overall survival (n = 140) were 69.5% and 83.2%, respectively. The optimal cutoff, D15 MRD ≥ 20%, refined the conventional ≥ 10% high-risk category, predicting inferior 10-year EFS (45.4% vs. 76.8%, p = 0.002). Crucially, among patients achieving D33 MRD < 1%, D15 ≥ 20% still conferred poor outcomes (10-year EFS: 50.0% vs. 77.9%, p = 0.014), whereas D15 10%-19.9% outcomes mirrored those of D15 < 10%. D15 ≥ 20% remained an independent prognosticator (HR = 2.85; 95% CI: 1.38-5.90; p = 0.005) across internal validations. Additionally, D15 ≥ 20% predicted disproportionate treatment-related mortality (TRM; cause-specific HR = 5.49; p = 0.006), with a 10-year incidence of 25.0%. Dual D15 ≥ 20%/D33 ≥ 1% positivity identified extreme risk (HR = 4.41; p = 0.008).
CONCLUSIONS: D15 FCM-MRD ≥ 20% identified a small subgroup of patients with an increased risk of relapse and inferior survival, including patients who subsequently achieved D33 MRD < 1%. These findings require validation in a larger independent cohort.
43082408: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) is the most common subtype of non-Hodgkin lymphoma and remains curable for many patients with frontline immunochemotherapy; however, optimal treatment continues to evolve. The Canadian Hematology Consensus Group convened a national panel of lymphoma experts to develop evidence-informed recommendations for the first-line management of adults with DLBCL in Canada. Recommendations were developed using a modified Delphi process and address frontline regimen selection, treatment intensity, central nervous system (CNS) risk assessment and prophylaxis, interim response assessment, and end of treatment management. The panel recommends Pola-R-CHP for patients with international prognostic index 2-5 and activated B-cell subtype by gene expression profiling (or if unavailable, non-germinal centre B-cell subtype by immunohistochemistry). All patients should be assessed for fitness to receive full-dose therapy, with dose attenuation considered when clinically appropriate. Routine high-dose methotrexate prophylaxis is not recommended, and CNS screening should be individualized. Interim imaging may be used to confirm response, but treatment escalation should not be based on PET positivity alone. Patients achieving complete metabolic response at end of treatment require no further therapy, and routine surveillance imaging is not recommended. These recommendations support consistent, evidence-informed, and equitable care for patients with newly diagnosed DLBCL across Canada.
43082481: Multidisciplinary team meetings (MDTMs) support coordinated lung cancer care, but Canada lacks national lung-cancer-specific guidance on their structure and processes. We conducted a quality-improvement initiative in which an expert panel adapted international good practices for lung cancer MDTMs to the Canadian context. Fourteen purposively selected healthcare professionals completed an electronic questionnaire describing 14 MDTMs and participated in semi-structured interviews, while one patient representative provided a separate perspective. Findings informed draft recommendations, which were rated electronically before an in-person workshop, refined at the workshop, and approved by all 15 participants. Key variations observed included that only 7 of 14 respondents reported mechanisms to promote participation by every profession, and MDT coordinators always or often attended meetings in 4 of 14 MDTMs. Identified shared challenges include inconsistent representation of core disciplines, variable access to unified electronic patient records, and non-standardized documentation. The panel agreed on 13 recommendations and four statements on the perceived value of MDTMs. The recommendations are deliberately kept general and flexible, to allow adaptation to provincial and local resources, organization, and culture. These recommendations and statements can support MDT consistency, communication, and patient-centred care.
43083529: Aortic stenosis is characterized by progressive fibrocalcific remodeling driven by inflammation, fibrosis, and calcification. Although echocardiography and noncontrast computed tomographic calcium scoring (aortic valve calcium score) remain the clinical standards for hemodynamic and structural assessment, computed tomographic angiography, already routinely performed for transcatheter aortic valve replacement planning, provides complementary tissue-level characterization of fibrotic and calcific valve remodeling. Artificial intelligence is increasingly being applied to facilitate the quantitative assessment of fibrocalcific burden and periaortic adipose tissue inflammation. This review examines emerging applications of computed tomographic angiography for fibrocalcific tissue characterization, inflammatory phenotyping, and artificial intelligence-enabled risk assessment in aortic stenosis and discusses their potential role in complementing conventional hemodynamic assessment.
43083652:
BACKGROUND: This review examined whether within-device exposure-setting or nominal voxel-size changes in cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) affect linear alveolar bone measurements for implant planning, separating accuracy from agreement.
METHODS: Database-specific search strategies and retrieval counts are reported for PubMed/MEDLINE, Ovid Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science Core Collection. Study selection is presented in the updated PRISMA flow diagram. The reported International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO) identifier is CRD420261361509. Studies were grouped by outcome, protocol contrast, and experimental model. The Quality Assessment Tool for In Vitro Studies (QUIN) appraisal was performed by one reviewer. A revision-stage source and analysis-unit audit led to withdrawal of the planned inverse-variance meta-analyses and their ±0.5 mm equivalence claims; structured study-level synthesis was used instead.
RESULTS: Eight studies addressed linear measurements; two additional reports were retained only as methodological context. Seven linear-measurement studies compared protocols within a device, and one compared different devices. All were experimental. In one five-skull study, mean absolute errors were 0.50, 0.46, and 0.51 mm at 40, 20, and 7 s, respectively. A cadaver study reported mean absolute errors of approximately 1.10-1.20 mm. Small mean between-protocol differences sometimes coexisted with impaired anatomical visibility. Repeated observations were not equivalent to independent specimens, and several required sampling variances could not be reconstructed.
CONCLUSIONS: Selected within-device protocol changes may preserve average measurements under controlled experimental conditions. The evidence does not establish statistical equivalence, interchangeability of protocol classes, or clinical safety near critical anatomy. Validation in living patients is needed before broad implementation.
43083656: Background/Objectives: Computed tomography (CT) and CT angiography (CTA) are central to assessing aortic aneurysm and dissection, but manual segmentation and geometric analysis remain time-consuming and operator-dependent, while evidence on artificial intelligence (AI) is fragmented. This task-based systematic review synthesised AI applications to CT/CTA of the thoracic and abdominal aorta by primary task: segmentation, measurement, or detection and classification. Methods: PubMed/MEDLINE and Europe PMC were searched from 2015 to September 2026 following PRISMA 2020; the protocol was registered retrospectively (INPLASY2026110004). Segmentation and measurement studies were appraised with CLAIM and detection studies with QUADAS-2/QUADAS-AI, and results were synthesised without meta-analysis. Results: Of 118 included studies (42 segmentation, 38 measurement, 38 detection), half were published since 2024. Median Dice similarity coefficient was 0.90 or higher for the outer wall, lumen and true and false lumina, but 0.86 for intraluminal thrombus and 0.63 for false lumen thrombus. Automated maximum diameter showed a median absolute bias of 0.26 mm (95% limits of agreement about ±5 mm). Detection of aortic dissection reached a median AUC of 0.96-0.97, mostly in enriched samples. External validation was reported in 14%, 34% and 55% of segmentation, measurement and detection studies, 33 of 38 detection studies were at high risk of bias, and only two systems were evaluated prospectively. Conclusions: AI supports technical automation of aortic CT/CTA segmentation and measurement and is progressing toward multistructure geometric phenotyping and clinical decision support, but independent multicentre validation, consecutive cohorts and prospective reader-in-the-loop studies are required before clinical integration. Detection/classification tools require independent diagnostic and workflow validation.
43083875:
PURPOSE: Immune-related response patterns may complicate interim FDG PET assessment in Hodgkin lymphoma (HL). We evaluated whether quantitative residual metabolic burden adds prognostic information beyond Lugano/LYRIC-based assessment during PD-1-based therapy.
METHODS: This retrospective single-center landmark study included 63 patients with HL who underwent baseline and interim FDG PET/CT during PD-1-based therapy. Interim PET was categorized using a Lugano/LYRIC-based three-level classification. Interim total lesion glycolysis (TLG) was designated as the principal residual-burden metric, with interim metabolic tumor volume (MTV) evaluated as a closely related alternative volumetric measure. Landmark progression-free survival (PFS) was calculated from the interim PET date. Associations were assessed using Kaplan-Meier analysis, Cox models, incremental model performance, and sensitivity analyses.
RESULTS: Fifteen PFS events occurred during a median follow-up of 34.2 months. Categorical Lugano/LYRIC assessment, Deauville grouping, and percentage change in SUVmax were not statistically associated with PFS. Higher log-transformed interim TLG (HR per 1-SD increase, 1.97; 95% CI, 1.10-3.55; P = 0.023) and interim MTV (HR, 1.86; 95% CI, 1.14-3.04; P = 0.013) were associated with higher PFS event hazards. Among 54 patients without definite progression, PFS events occurred in 8 of 25 patients with high interim TLG and 3 of 29 with low interim TLG. Models incorporating quantitative residual burden yielded higher apparent and optimism-corrected C-index point estimates than categorical assessment alone, but internal performance estimates remained variable.
CONCLUSION: Higher interim residual FDG-avid burden was associated with less favorable PFS and may complement categorical response assessment, particularly by revealing prognostic heterogeneity among patients without definite progression. The observed improvement in discrimination was exploratory and requires prospective multicenter validation.
43083897:
PURPOSE: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) can induce immune-related adverse events (irAEs), including subclinical inflammatory toxicities detectable by 18F-FDG PET/CT. This systematic review aimed to synthesize current evidence on the organ distribution, diagnostic utility, and prognostic significance of PET-detected irAEs (PET-irAEs) in patients with cancer.
METHODS: A systematic search of PubMed, Web of Science and Embase was conducted through September 2026. Studies reporting on PET-detected irAEs and clinical outcomes in human participants treated with ICIs were included. Data were summarized via narrative synthesis. No formal meta-analysis was performed; organ-site events were aggregated descriptively by cancer type.
RESULTS: PET-irAEs displayed cancer-specific organ profiles: bladder cancer showed thyroid (34%) and gastrointestinal (28.3%) enrichment; non-small-cell lung carcinoma (NSCLC) was characterized by gastrointestinal (50%) and pulmonary (19.5%) involvement and melanoma exhibited a heterogeneous multisystem distribution. Evidence regarding the predictive and prognostic significance of PET-irAEs remains inconsistent. Although several studies have demonstrated associations between PET-irAEs and favorable treatment responses or survival outcomes, others have reported no statistically significant relationships. Interpretation of the available evidence is limited by small sample sizes, the lack of adjusted analyses, and susceptibility to selection bias, residual confounding, and time-dependent bias.
CONCLUSION: 18F-FDG PET/CT shows promise as an important tool for the early detection and monitoring of immune-related toxicities. However, the utility of PET-irAEs as imaging biomarkers for predicting treatment response and prognosis requires further validation in large-scale prospective studies.
43083903:
PURPOSE: Accurate preoperative localisation of hyperfunctioning parathyroid glands enables minimally invasive parathyroidectomy (MIP) in primary hyperparathyroidism (pHPT). This umbrella review summarises more than a decade of meta-analytic evidence on preoperative localisation imaging.
METHODS: Twenty-eight systematic reviews (published 2012-2025) were identified through a PubMed search and assessed within a predefined inclusion period (2011-2026). The analysis covered ultrasonography (US), [99mTc]Tc-methoxyisobutylisonitrile ([99mTc]Tc-MIBI) scintigraphy with single-photon emission computed tomography/computed tomography (SPECT/CT), four-dimensional CT (4D-CT), and [11C]methionine and [18F]fluorocholine positron emission tomography/CT (PET/CT). Pooled sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), and detection rate (DR) were extracted, using histopathology and, where available, postoperative biochemical cure as reference standard.
RESULTS: Pooled sensitivity/specificity was 80%/77% for US and 84%/87% for [99mTc]Tc-MIBI scintigraphy. Detection rates were 84-88% for SPECT/CT, 74% for SPECT alone, and 70% for planar scintigraphy. Multiphase CT achieved 73% per-quadrant and 81% per-side sensitivity; after negative or inconclusive scintigraphy, 4D-CT reached 71% sensitivity and 81% PPV. [11C]methionine PET/CT sensitivities ranged from 77 to 86%. Radiolabelled choline ([11C]choline and [18F]fluorocholine) PET performed best (pooled sensitivity 95%, PPV 97%, DR 91%). [18F]fluorocholine outperformed [99mTc]Tc-MIBI scintigraphy (96% vs. 54% per patient), [11C]methionine (92% vs. 80% per lesion, indirect comparison) and 4D-CT (92% vs. 85% per patient). In the largest choline meta-analysis (1,716 patients), pooled sensitivity was 93.8% and the surgical cure rate 92.8%.
CONCLUSION: Among currently available techniques, [18F]fluorocholine PET/CT provides the highest diagnostic accuracy for preoperative localisation of hyperfunctioning parathyroid glands. It consistently surpasses conventional scintigraphy and 4D-CT in sensitivity while entailing lower radiation exposure.
43083904:
PURPOSE: Subcutaneous U87MG xenografts are widely employed for the evaluation of FAP-targeted radiopharmaceuticals, despite limited insight into the regulation of FAP expression. In this study, we investigated the temporal changes of FAP using longitudinal PET/CT imaging, biodistribution studies, autoradiography, immunohistochemistry, in vitro co-cultures, pharmacological and theranostic interventions.
METHODS: Subcutaneous U87MG xenografts were longitudinally imaged using [68Ga]Ga-DATA5m.SA.FAPI and [68Ga]Ga-DOTAGA.Glu.(FAPI)2 PET/CT. Ex vivo biodistribution, autoradiography, and species-specific immunohistochemistry were performed across tumor development. Soluble FAP (sFAP) levels were quantified in plasma and conditioned media. Paracrine U87MG-fibroblast communication was investigated in normal and cancer-associated fibroblasts (NF and CAF) co-cultures with or without galunisertib or UAMC1110. The potential involvement of TGF-β signaling was examined in vivo using galunisertib, and exploratory radionuclide therapy was performed using [177Lu]Lu-DOTAGA.Glu.(FAPI)2.
RESULTS: [68Ga]Ga-DOTAGA.Glu.(FAPI)2 PET uptake increased from day 7 to 15 (3.2 ± 0.2 to 9.1 ± 0.9%ID/mL) followed by a decline at day 21 (6.7 ± 1.8%ID/mL). Ex vivo biodistribution supported this increase (13.5 ± 2.5 to 27.8 ± 1.3%IA/g) but showed only a modest decline by day 21 (24.3 ± 1.8%IA/g). Descriptive immunohistochemical analyses showed an apparent increase in human and murine FAP staining across the examined tumor specimens at early and intermediate time points. Galunisertib-treated mice showed numerically lower radiotracer uptake at day 15 (7.5 ± 1.6 vs. 10.5 ± 1.3%ID/mL) (p = 0.0652). In vitro, U87MG-fibroblast interactions induced fibroblast activation, with a 6-fold increase in FAP expression, up to 900-fold IL-6 upregulation and increased sFAP release (472 ± 149 pg/mL), while galunisertib treatment reduced these responses. Radionuclide therapy reduced tumor growth but did not abolish [68Ga]Ga-DOTAGA.Glu.(FAPI)2 uptake at day 29.
CONCLUSION: FAPI uptake varies as subcutaneous U87MG xenografts progress, and complementary biological analyses provide additional context for interpreting these changes. These results highlight the importance of tumor stage and biological context when evaluating FAP-targeted radiopharmaceuticals in this preclinical model.
43083980: This narrative review summarizes the clinical potential and current challenges of magnetic particle imaging (MPI) for cardiovascular imaging and endovascular interventions. As an emerging tracer-based imaging modality, MPI offers radiation-free imaging, high temporal resolution, and quantitative signal properties, facilitating radiation-free real-time intravascular tracking and hemodynamic assessment without nephrotoxic contrast exposure. Numerous preclinical studies and recent first-in-human examinations highlight its translational promise and mark the beginning of clinical evaluation. Despite these advances, significant challenges remain, including the availability of clinically approved dedicated MPI tracers and technical limitations associated with scanner up-scaling. Regulatory approval and robust clinical evidence from RCTs will be essential to establish MPI as a future modality for image-guided interventions.
43084013:
OBJECTIVES: Drowning is a challenging forensic diagnosis, and postmortem computed tomography (PMCT) is increasingly used as an adjunct. This systematic review synthesizes PMCT findings in drowning and evaluates the diagnostic usefulness of individual imaging signs.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched through July 2026 following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines. Original studies reporting PMCT findings in human drowning cases were included. A study-family approach was used to address cohort overlap, and quality was assessed using a modified Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies 2 (QUADAS-2) tool. Data were synthesized narratively (Synthesis Without Meta-analysis).
RESULTS: Thirty-two studies (2007-2026) met the inclusion criteria, encompassing approximately 1400 drowning cases. Cohort overlap reduced unique individuals to approximately 900. Paranasal sinus fluid (88-100%) and pulmonary ground-glass opacity (89-100%) were the most frequent findings, but specificity varied with the comparator (0-100% and 0-38%). High-attenuation airway sediment and a three-layer stomach pattern were absent in controls in single studies, whereas frothy airway fluid also occurred in asphyxiation controls. Quantitative approaches showed inconsistent discriminatory ability. Artificial intelligence (AI)-based classification achieved high internal performance but markedly reduced accuracy on external validation.
CONCLUSION: PMCT identifies a constellation of supportive findings, but no single sign has validated accuracy sufficient to establish drowning on its own. Discrimination depends on the comparator cause of death. A multi-parametric approach combining qualitative and quantitative assessment is promising, but its superiority over single findings remains unproven and requires external validation.
KEY POINTS: Question Which postmortem CT findings are reproducibly reported in drowning, and which of them reliably distinguish drowning from other causes of death in forensic practice? Findings Across 32 studies, sinus fluid and ground-glass opacity were sensitive but non-specific, whereas airway sediment and a three-layer stomach pattern were specific but infrequent. Critical relevance statement Postmortem CT supports but cannot independently establish the diagnosis of drowning; this review gives radiologists a comparator-dependent hierarchy of signs to interpret findings within the autopsy-based investigation rather than relying on any single feature.
43084061:
OBJECTIVES: To benchmark commercial breast cancer detection algorithms for standalone reading, paired reading, and triage in a UK cohort.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: Digital mammograms were retrospectively collected from two UK Breast Screening Programme sites (Cambridge and Norwich; 2017), excluding mammograms without two-view images, 3-year follow-up, or algorithm scores. Eight algorithms from five companies were assessed at single-reader specificity as a standalone reader or paired with the first human reader, and in low- and high-suspicion triage scenarios. The reference standard was histopathologically confirmed cancer (screen-detected, interval, or next-round). Performance metrics included AUC, sensitivity, specificity, recall rate, and arbitration rate; noninferiority was assessed at a 5% margin.
RESULTS: Of 22,778 mammograms (median age: 59 years; IQR: 54-63), 294 were screen-detected, 151 were interval, and 209 were next-round cancers. AUCs ranged 0.82-0.91; one algorithm was inferior to all others (p < 0.001). As a standalone reader, four algorithms had noninferior sensitivity (range: 47.2-64.5%) versus single reading (62.9%). Paired with the first reader, sensitivities were 64.7-67.4% (all but one noninferior to double reading: 67.9%) and specificities 97.5% (all superior to double reading: 97.1%; all p < 0.001). Low-suspicion triage ruled out 37.4-65.7% of mammograms, missing ≤ 1.0% of screen-detected cancers; high-suspicion triage ruled in 3.6-12.2% of interval and next-round cancers. In combined triage, sensitivity (68.8-71.2%) was superior to double reading for five algorithms and noninferior for the remainder.
CONCLUSIONS: Algorithms demonstrated variable standalone performance. When paired with a human reader, all but one were noninferior to double reading; in a combined triage workflow, all were noninferior and several had superior sensitivity.
KEY POINTS: Question How do eight commercial deep learning algorithms from five vendors compare as standalone readers, paired with a single reader, and for triage in a UK breast screening cohort? Findings Most algorithms performed comparably and were noninferior in sensitivity to double reading when paired with a single reader, with one consistent underperformer; combined triage was noninferior or superior in sensitivity while maintaining specificity, at the cost of increased arbitration. Clinical relevance Commercial algorithms differ in performance, and newer versions are not necessarily better, supporting independent, head-to-head evaluation before prospective evaluation.
43084062:
OBJECTIVES: To compare the diagnostic performance of ultra-low-dose CT (ULD-CT) and conventional radiography (CR) for fracture detection in trauma patients, using standard-dose CT (STD-CT) as the reference.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: This prospective study on diagnostic accuracy was conducted at five centers from October 2019 to September 2023 and included adult participants with suspected fractures of the extremities, pelvis/hip, or thoracolumbar spine. All participants underwent CR, ULD-CT, and STD-CT during the same visit. Blinded radiologists independently assessed fractures and associated abnormalities. Sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, radiation dose, image quality, and interpretation time were evaluated.
RESULTS: Five hundred and thirty-three participants (mean age, 52 ± 22 years; 283 women) were evaluated, including 282 (53%) with fractures. For fracture detection, CR yielded 201 out of 282 true positives (sensitivity: 71% [65-76%]) and 81 out of 282 false negatives (29%), compared with 269 out of 282 true positives (sensitivity: 95% [92-98%]) and 13 out of 282 false negatives (5%) with ULD-CT (p < 0.01). Specificity was 242 out of 251 (96% [93-98%]) for CR and 245 out of 251 (98% [95-99%]) for ULD-CT (p = 0.58). ULD-CT showed higher sensitivity for both articular (154 of 171 (90%) vs. 93 of 171 (54%); p < 0.001) and soft-tissue abnormalities related to trauma (287 of 315 (91%) vs. 184 of 315 (58%); p < 0.001). Effective dose (E) was lower with ULD-CT than with STD-CT (p < 0.01) but higher than with CR, except for distal extremities (p = 0.33).
CONCLUSION: ULD-CT demonstrated higher sensitivity than CR for fracture detection, with similar specificity, using standard-dose CT as the reference.
KEY POINTS: Question Can ultra-low-dose CT (ULD-CT) improve detection of fractures and associated traumatic abnormalities compared with conventional radiography (CR) while maintaining high diagnostic confidence? Findings ULD-CT showed significantly higher sensitivity than CR for fractures, articular injuries, and soft-tissue abnormalities, with similar specificity. Clinical relevance ULD-CT increased diagnostic confidence and improved detection of fractures and associated traumatic abnormalities compared with CR, potentially reducing missed injuries and the need for additional imaging examinations despite slightly longer interpretation times.
43084063:
OBJECTIVES: To develop and validate a semi-automated method for segmenting 2DT1-weighted (T1w) spin-echo (SE)-defined black holes (BHs) on 3DT1w gradient-echo (GRE) images in people with multiple sclerosis (pwMS), accounting for the increased sensitivity of the GRE protocol.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: Eighty-eight pwMS with 2DT1w SE, 3DT1w GRE, and 3D-FLAIR scans were selected from the Amsterdam MS cohort. A semi-automated 3DT1w BH method (3DBHSeg) was developed in an optimization set (n = 20) using cortical gray matter (cGM)-based intensity thresholding, optimized against manually segmented 2DT1w-defined BHs. Performance was evaluated in a validation set (n = 68) using a hybrid score, incorporating voxel-wise, lesion-wise, and volumetric agreement metrics. Associations between BH volume and EDSS score were assessed using adjusted linear regression models.
RESULTS: The optimal threshold for BH segmentation was 0.95 × median(cGM) intensity. In the validation set, median BH volume was 1.54 mL (IQR: 0.80-2.57 mL) for 3DBHSeg and 1.24 mL (IQR: 0.65-2.47 mL) for the 2DT1w reference, with a hybrid score of 0.76, an ICC (absolute agreement) of 0.92 (95% CI [0.87-0.95]), and a mean DSC of 0.59 ± 0.10. The median BH/FLAIR lesion volume ratio was 24.3%. Log-transformed 3DBHSeg volume was associated with EDSS score (B = 0.33, p = 0.04), whereas FLAIR lesion volume was not (B = 0.19, p = 0.30).
CONCLUSION: 3DBHSeg enables segmentation of BHs on heavily T1-weighted 3D GRE images in accordance with their definition on mildly T1-weighted 2D SE images, allowing quantification of severe tissue damage in MS.
KEY POINTS: Question Black holes reflect areas of severe tissue damage in multiple sclerosis, yet no validated segmentation method exists for contemporary 3D T1-weighted gradient-echo acquisitions. Findings Our method, 3DBHSeg, segmented black holes on 3D T1-weighted images, achieving an ICC of 0.92 and DSC of 0.59 relative to a 2D T1-weighted reference. Clinical relevance 3DBHSeg enables identification of black holes, as originally defined on 2D T1-weighted images, directly on 3D gradient-echo acquisitions, allowing quantification of severe tissue damage associated with clinical disability in multiple sclerosis in the absence of 2D T1 images.
43084064:
OBJECTIVES: To identify postoperative MRI features associated with knee stiffness and residual posterior laxity in symptomatic patients after posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) reconstruction.
MATERIAL AND METHODS: This retrospective study reviewed postoperative knee MRI examinations in patients after PCL reconstruction. Two radiologists graded arthrofibrosis severity (none-mild-moderate-severe) and assessed graft morphology and tunnel positioning. In a subset, posterior translation was quantified on stress radiographs (> 8 mm = increased laxity). Associations between imaging findings and relevant knee stiffness requiring arthrolysis/manipulation under anesthesia or increased posterior laxity were analyzed using Firth's penalized logistic regression. Inter- and intrareader agreements were evaluated with Cohen's kappa (κ) and intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC).
RESULTS: Fifty-three patients (mean age 33.1 ± 11.1 years, 15 females) were evaluated; stress radiographs were available for 43 (81.1%). Arthrofibrosis was present in 25 patients (total 47.1% [mild 26.4%; moderate 9.4%; severe 11.3%]), with nodular cyclops-like lesions in 35.8%. Seventeen patients (32.1%) required arthrolysis or manipulation under anesthesia. Higher arthrofibrosis grade was associated with an increased likelihood of secondary intervention for stiffness (OR 2.67; 95% CI: 1.45, 5.63; p < 0.01). An S-curved graft configuration (24.5%) was significantly associated with increased posterior laxity (OR 6.83; 95% CI: 1.71, 46.9; p < 0.01), but not with patient-reported subjective instability (p = 0.98). Inter- and intra-reader agreements were substantial to almost perfect (κ/ICC 0.71-0.98).
CONCLUSION: Higher arthrofibrosis grades on postoperative MRI, including nodular cyclops-like lesions along the intercondylar PCL graft, are associated with clinically relevant stiffness requiring re-intervention. S-curved graft morphology correlates with objective residual posterior knee laxity on stress radiography.
KEY POINTS: Question What postoperative MRI features after PCL reconstruction are associated with clinically relevant knee stiffness and residual posterior laxity in symptomatic patients? Findings Higher arthrofibrosis grades were linked to stiffness requiring arthrolysis or manipulation under anesthesia, while S-curved graft morphology correlated with residual posterior laxity on stress radiographs. Clinical relevance Postoperative MRI assessment of arthrofibrosis severity and graft morphology in symptomatic patients after PCL reconstruction revealed distinct imaging features associated with knee stiffness and residual posterior laxity, which may aid clinical evaluation and management.
43084065:
OBJECTIVES: To evaluate whether lesion conspicuity remains consistent between diagnostic and biopsy acquisitions in recombined-only lesions undergoing contrast-enhanced mammography (CEM)-guided biopsy, and to identify determinants of reduced procedural conspicuity.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: This retrospective single-centre study included 169 consecutive recombined-only lesions undergoing CEM-guided biopsy between October 2019 and September 2025. Lesion conspicuity (LC) was assessed on diagnostic and projection-matched stereotactic scout recombined images using a three-level ordinal scale (low, moderate, or high). Reduced procedural conspicuity was defined as a decrease in LC category. Continuous perceptual variation was assessed using a visual analogue scale (VAS). Associations between ordinal LC change (ΔLC) and median VAS were evaluated using Spearman correlation. Multivariable logistic regression using Firth's penalized likelihood method was performed to identify predictors of reduced conspicuity.
RESULTS: Procedural LC was maintained or increased in 136/169 lesions (80.5%), whereas reduced conspicuity occurred in 33/169 lesions (19.5%). The same diagnostic and procedural LC category was observed in 111/169 lesions (65.7%). ΔLC correlated with median VAS (Spearman ρ = 0.665; p < 0.001). In multivariable analysis, non-mass enhancement morphology (adjusted OR 5.10, 95% CI: 1.94-14.06; p < 0.001) was independently associated with reduced conspicuity, whereas marked background parenchymal enhancement demonstrated a positive but statistically non-significant trend (adjusted OR 3.49, 95% CI: 0.97-12.55; p = 0.055). Technical variables were not independently associated.
CONCLUSIONS: LC remained largely consistent between diagnostic and procedural acquisitions in most lesions undergoing CEM-guided biopsy. Reduced conspicuity was primarily associated with non-mass enhancement morphology rather than acquisition-related factors.
KEY POINTS: Question Does LC remain consistent between diagnostic and biopsy acquisitions during CEM-guided biopsy, and which factors are associated with reduced procedural conspicuity? Findings LC remained stable or increased in most lesions undergoing CEM-guided biopsy, with reduced conspicuity primarily associated with non-mass enhancement morphology. Clinical relevance LC is generally preserved at the CEM-guided biopsy scout acquisition, supporting consistent procedural visualisation of recombined-only lesions.
43084066:
BACKGROUND: Imaging is central to diagnosing giant cell arteritis (GCA). Ultrasound (US) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) are widely used, but prospective head-to-head comparisons are limited.
OBJECTIVES: To compare extended MRI with routine US for suspected giant cell arteritis and to assess the influence of US expertise.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: Ninety-three consecutive patients with suspected GCA underwent US and MRI (median interval 0 days). US assessed the superficial temporal, carotid, subclavian and axillary arteries. MRI additionally evaluated the superficial occipital and vertebral arteries, the thoracic and suprarenal abdominal aorta, and the abdominal aorta. MRI was analyzed (1) restricted to the same vessels as US and (2) including all MRI-assessed vessels (MRI-all). Readers were blinded to clinical data. The reference standard was the final clinical diagnosis after 12 weeks.
RESULTS: GCA was confirmed in 45/93 patients. MRI-all vessels showed higher sensitivity than routine US (80% vs. 44%, p < 0.001), with similar specificity (96% vs. 94%). MRI restricted to US-matched vessels also showed higher sensitivity (60% vs. 44%, p = 0.04). Expert US detected 12/15 cases (80%). MRI identified vasculitis in non-US-accessible territories in 9/45 patients (20%). Predictive values reflected the prevalence of the enriched fast-track.
CONCLUSIONS: Extended MRI was more sensitive than routine US in this fast-track cohort, whereas expert US achieved comparable sensitivity. Ultrasound remains appropriate when expertise is available; MRI is useful for atypical, large-vessel, or inconclusive cases.
KEY POINTS: Question In suspected giant cell arteritis, the diagnostic impact of extended MRI versus routine ultrasound, and the role of ultrasound expertise, remain uncertain. Findings Extended MRI had higher sensitivity than routine ultrasound, but expert ultrasound reached comparable sensitivity; both modalities maintained high overall specificity. Clinical relevance Ultrasound should remain the first line when local expertise is available, while MRI can support atypical, large-vessel, or inconclusive cases.
43084067:
OBJECTIVES: To quantitatively characterize plaque heterogeneity using high-resolution vessel wall imaging (HR-VWI) and to investigate the value of this heterogeneity marker in identifying vulnerable carotid atherosclerotic plaques associated with stroke.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: This multicenter retrospective study analyzed 423 carotid plaques in 341 patients from three medical centers between June 2018 and June 2024 using contrast-enhanced T1-weighted HR-VWI. Plaque voxels were clustered via a Gaussian mixture model, and the spatial distribution patterns of subregions were integrated to compute the plaque heterogeneity score (PHS). A multivariable discriminative model was developed to identify stroke-associated plaques. An age-stratified analysis was further performed to assess the consistency of model performance across age subgroups.
RESULTS: Plaques from Center 1 were divided into training (n = 168) and internal validation (n = 72) sets, while Centers 2 (n = 73) and 3 (n = 110) served as external validation cohorts. The integrated model (graphically represented as a nomogram) demonstrated excellent discriminative performance across all datasets, with areas under the curve (AUCs) of 0.849-0.865. The model maintained robust discriminative accuracy across age subgroups, with a maximum intergroup AUC difference of 0.041. PHS showed significant incremental discriminative ability (ΔAUC: 0.080-0.112; IDI: 0.089-0.138; all p < 0.05) beyond conventional vulnerability and burden assessments. In external validation set 1, adding PHS to Plaque-RADS improved discrimination (ΔAUC: 0.134; IDI: 0.143; both p < 0.05).
CONCLUSIONS: The PHS effectively quantifies carotid plaque heterogeneity and provides significant incremental value for identifying stroke-associated plaques when integrated with conventional metrics. This interpretable framework holds promise for future clinical translation.
KEY POINTS: Question Current identification of stroke-associated carotid plaques relies on qualitative plaque assessment, which is operator-dependent and lacks quantitative measures of plaque heterogeneity. Findings The plaque heterogeneity score independently identified stroke-associated carotid plaques; combined with conventional metrics, it achieved areas under the curve of 0.849-0.865 across multicenter cohorts. Clinical relevance Integrating the plaque heterogeneity score with conventional assessment improves identification of stroke-associated vulnerable carotid plaques, supporting individualized risk stratification and timely preventive decisions in patients with carotid atherosclerosis.
43084068:
OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to investigate the association between reperfusion status assessed by expanded Thrombolysis in Cerebral Infarction (eTICI) grade and clinical outcomes in patients with middle cerebral artery (MCA) M2 occlusion undergoing endovascular treatment (EVT).
MATERIALS AND METHODS: Patient data were pooled from five randomized controlled trials and a cohort study. Patients with MCA M2 occlusion undergoing EVT were stratified into 3 groups (eTICI 0-2a, eTICI 2b-2c, and eTICI 3). The primary effectiveness outcome was modified Rankin Scale (mRS) score 0-2 at 90 days. Secondary effectiveness outcomes included 90-day mRS score 0-1, 0-3, and ordinal mRS score distribution. Safety outcomes were 90-day mortality and symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage (sICH) within 48 h. Multivariable logistic regression and inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) were performed.
RESULTS: Among 599 patients, 308 achieved eTICI 3 reperfusion. Compared with eTICI 0-2a, eTICI 3 was significantly associated with 90-day mRS 0-2 in both the adjusted (aOR, 2.94; 95% CI, 1.54-5.60; p = 0.001) and the IPTW model (aOR, 3.49; 95% CI, 2.30-5.30; p < 0.001). eTICI 2b-2c was also associated with higher odds of 90-day mRS 0-2. Similar trends were observed for secondary effectiveness outcomes. After IPTW, eTICI 3 was associated with lower rates of mortality (p < 0.001) and sICH within 48 h (p = 0.002).
CONCLUSIONS: In patients with MCA M2 occlusion undergoing EVT, eTICI 3 reperfusion was associated with better functional outcomes. However, the safety of achieving eTICI 3 reperfusion in this population needs further validation.
KEY POINTS: Question How is the degree of reperfusion achieved after endovascular treatment associated with 90-day functional outcomes in patients with middle cerebral artery M2 occlusion? Findings In 599 patients with middle cerebral artery M2 occlusion, eTICI 3 was associated with functional independence, whereas associations with mortality and intracranial hemorrhage were less consistent across analytical models. Clinical relevance Among patients with middle cerebral artery M2 occlusion undergoing endovascular treatment, eTICI 3 reperfusion was associated with better functional outcome. The association may inform postprocedural assessment, but the benefit of an additional attempt to achieve eTICI 3 reperfusion needs further study.
43084069:
OBJECTIVES: Breast cancers have diverse biologic features associated with variable prognoses, treatment selection, and eligibility for targeted therapies. We evaluated the discriminatory performance of an image-only deep learning (DL) breast cancer risk model across diverse tumor phenotypes, including histologic subtypes, grades, molecular profiles, and disease stages.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: This retrospective, multisite study included consecutive women 30 years or older undergoing screening mammography across six sites from 2009 to 2022. A previously validated image-only DL model (Mirai) was used to generate risk scores from screening mammograms. Demographic data were retrieved from electronic health records, and cancers diagnosed within 1 year were identified through linkage to regional and state tumor registries. Discrimination across histologic subtypes, grades, molecular profiles, and stage was evaluated using areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUCs), with DeLong comparisons.
RESULTS: Among 341,921 examinations in 104,472 patients (median age, 59 years [IQR, 51-68]), 1991 cancers were diagnosed, including 1543 (77.5%) invasive cancers and 448 (22.5%) ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS). Discrimination was similar for invasive cancer (AUC 0.81; 95% CI: 0.80-0.82) and DCIS (AUC 0.81; 95% CI: 0.79-0.83; p = 0.88) and did not differ between invasive ductal and lobular carcinomas (AUC 0.81 vs 0.78; p = 0.08). Discrimination was robust across grades for both invasive cancer and DCIS (AUC range, 0.79-0.83), molecular profiles (AUC range, 0.77-0.88), and stages (AUC range, 0.71-0.82).
CONCLUSION: Screening mammograms contain imaging biomarkers associated with diverse breast cancer phenotypes. An image-only DL risk model demonstrated robust discrimination across histologic subtypes, grades, molecular profiles, and disease stages.
KEY POINTS: Question Does an image-only mammography-based deep learning breast cancer risk model (Mirai) demonstrate similar performance across breast cancers with different phenotypes? Findings In a multisite cohort of 341,921 screening mammograms, Mirai demonstrated similar discrimination across invasive cancer and ductal carcinoma in situ and maintained robust performance across histologic subtypes, tumor grades, molecular profiles, and stages at diagnosis (AUC range, 0.71-0.88). Clinical relevance A deep learning breast cancer risk model applied to screening mammography demonstrates robust discriminatory performance across cancers with diverse phenotypes, supporting risk-stratified screening and prevention strategies.
43084070:
PURPOSE: This first-in-human study investigated whether scintigraphy with a 99mTc-labelled KN035-derived anti-PD-L1 nanobody could visualise PD-L1-associated uptake in hypofunctional thyroid nodules and whether uptake patterns were related to the predominant PD-L1-positive cell population identified histopathologically.
METHODS: Eight patients with scintigraphically hypofunctional thyroid nodules scheduled for thyroidectomy underwent planar scintigraphy and SPECT/CT after intravenous administration of the radiotracer. Tracer uptake was assessed visually and semi-quantitatively using L/T and L/B uptake ratios and was compared with postoperative histopathological findings and qualitative PD-L1 immunohistochemistry.
RESULTS: Tracer administration was well tolerated. Intense focal uptake was observed in oncocytic thyroid tumours with predominant tumour-cell PD-L1 staining, whereas intermediate uptake occurred in lesions with predominant macrophage-like PD-L1-positive cells. Absent or minimal uptake was observed in lesions without identifiable PD-L1 staining. Diffuse thyroid uptake was observed in the patient with Hashimoto thyroiditis, with predominant lymphocyte-like PD-L1-positive inflammatory cells on histopathology. L/T uptake ratios differed across the three predefined histopathological categories (Kruskal-Wallis H = 6.25; P = 0.044), although this exploratory finding requires cautious interpretation given the very small group sizes. No diagnostic threshold or screening algorithm was derived from the observed uptake ratios.
CONCLUSION: In this exploratory first-in-human study, 99mTc-labelled KN035-derived anti-PD-L1 nanobody scintigraphy was feasible and demonstrated distinct uptake patterns associated with different histopathological PD-L1 staining patterns. These findings are hypothesis-generating and support further prospective investigation of PD-L1-targeted molecular imaging to assess the spatial and cellular distribution of PD-L1 in thyroid tissue.
43084071:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the incremental value of computed tomography (CT)-derived body composition indices for preoperative prediction of lymphovascular invasion (LVI) in clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC).
METHODS: This single-center retrospective study included 315 patients with pathologically confirmed ccRCC who underwent preoperative multiphasic CT between May 2020 and December 2024. Patients were randomly divided (7:3) into training (n = 223; 81 LVI-positive) and internal validation (n = 92; 28 LVI-positive) cohorts. Postoperative histopathology served as the reference standard for LVI. Clinical characteristics, conventional CT features, and body composition indices were collected. Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression and multivariable logistic regression were used for predictor selection and model construction. Model performance was assessed using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves, calibration curves, and decision curve analysis (DCA).
RESULTS: The clinicoradiological model included body mass index (BMI; odds ratio [OR], 0.758; p < 0.001), neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR; OR, 1.765; p = 0.010), and size (OR, 1.629; p < 0.001). The body composition model included skeletal muscle index (SMI; OR, 0.951; p = 0.005) and total adipose tissue index (TATI; OR, 0.977; p < 0.001); the combined model included all five predictors. In the training cohort, areas under the ROC curve (AUCs) were 0.852, 0.730, and 0.851 for the clinicoradiological, body composition, and combined models, respectively. The combined model did not significantly outperform the clinicoradiological model (p = 0.917). In the internal validation cohort, the clinicoradiological and combined models had AUCs of 0.778 and 0.774, respectively (p = 0.609). In both cohorts, confidence intervals for Brier score differences included zero, indicating no apparent improvement in calibration with the addition of body composition indices. DCA showed no consistent advantage in net benefit.
CONCLUSION: Although SMI and TATI are associated with LVI in the standalone body composition model, they provide no clear incremental predictive value beyond the clinicoradiological model. Findings from this cohort support prioritizing multicenter external validation and clinical impact assessment of the more parsimonious clinicoradiological model.
43084072: PI-RADS v2.1 category 3 on prostate MRI (Magnetic Resonance Imaging) represents an intermediate risk category imaging phenotype rather than a uniform clinical risk category contributing to the dilemma in biopsy decision-making. Clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa) is found in a minority of PI-RADS 3 lesions, yet interobserver agreement is moderate and benign mimics, such as stromal BPH nodules and focal prostatitis are common, so a simple binary interpretation of biopsy versus no biopsy (biopsy avoidance) is inadequate. This review proposes a two-step approach. Step 1 is to confirm that the lesion is truly PI-RADS 3 by addressing image quality (PI-QUAL v2), interpretative variability, and overcall or undercall. Step 2 is to apply clinical risk stratification, in which PSA density (PSAD), treated as a continuum rather than a single cutoff is the most validated modifier, supplemented by biopsy history, PSA kinetics, family history and lesion-level imaging features. Selected low-risk patients can safely avoid immediate biopsy under a structured safety-net surveillance pathway, whereas patients with higher post-MRI risk should undergo targeted sampling with perilesional or systematic cores as appropriate. Population-specific baseline risk, including the higher csPCa prevalence and lower MRI negative predictive value reported in Black men, may alter pathway performance, although validated race-specific thresholds remain uncertain. Emerging tools, including serum and urine biomarkers, quantitative MRI and artificial intelligence, and PSMA PET with the PRIMARY score, may refine this pathway but require different levels of validation before routine use.
43084073:
PURPOSE: To assess the diagnostic performance of LI-RADS version 2018 in patients at high risk for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) presenting with locally advanced intrahepatic tumor burden on CT or MRI.
METHODS: This retrospective study included consecutive CT and MRI exams containing liver lesions from January 1, 2013-December 30, 2022, of patients at high risk for HCC. CT and MRI exams were reviewed independently by eight radiologists who assigned a LI-RADS category to the largest lesion. Pathology served as the exam-level reference standard for HCC diagnosis. Positive predictive value (PPV), sensitivity, and specificity of the LR-5 (definitely HCC) category and combined LR-5 and LR-TIV (tumor in vein) "definitely due to HCC" categories to determine HCC diagnosis were calculated.
RESULTS: In 408 patients (340 [83%] men, mean age, 66 years ± 9.6) with 472 exams, 328 (80%) patients had HCC. The PPV for LR-5 alone was 95% (95% CI: 92-99%), with high specificity of 90% (95% CI: 84-97%) and low sensitivity of 48% (95% CI: 43-54%). The PPV of the combined categories was 96% (95% CI: 93-98%), with moderate specificity of 86% (95% CI: 78-94%) and moderate sensitivity of 77% (95% CI: 73-82%). Inter-reader agreement was substantial for LR-5 alone (κ = 0.71 [95% CI: 0.57-0.84]) and moderate for the combined categories (κ = 0.58 [95% CI: 0.40-0.73]).
CONCLUSION: Findings in this selected pathology-confirmed cohort support the potential role of imaging-based diagnosis in this setting. Further research in broader, unselected clinical populations is warranted.
43084083:
PURPOSE: This study aimed to assess the potential of abbreviated dynamic [18F]FDG PET imaging using a long axial field-of-view (LAFOV) scanner for non-invasive characterization of tumor subtypes and prediction of programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) status in treatment-naïve patients with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC).
METHODS: 51 treatment-naïve patients with histologically confirmed NSCLC (34 adenocarcinomas [LUAD], 17 squamous cell carcinomas [LUSC]) underwent a 20-min dynamic [18F]FDG PET/CT acquisition starting 45-min post-injection on an LAFOV system. Parametric images of net influx rate (Ki) and distribution volume (DV) were reconstructed using a direct Patlak approach with patient-specific scaled population-based input functions. PD-L1 tumor proportion score was determined from one histopathologically sampled lesion per patient.
RESULTS: PD-L1 positive lesions demonstrated higher SUVmax (16.9 ± 9.6 vs. 11.6 ± 5.7; p = 0.04), Kimax (0.077 ± 0.04 vs. 0.054 ± 0.02; p = 0.03), and DVmax (428.7 ± 253.5 vs. 278.7 ± 145.2; p = 0.02) than PD-L1 negative lesions. LUSC lesions showed higher SUVmax (18.7 ± 8.5 vs. 12.9 ± 8.2; p = 0.008) and Kimax (0.08 ± 0.02 vs. 0.06 ± 0.04; p = 0.02) than LUAD lesions, whereas DVmax did not differ (p = 0.69). In the histopathology-matched LUAD analysis, apparent/optimism-corrected AUCs were 0.74/0.70 for SUVmax/Kimax, 0.71/0.67 for Kimax/DVmax, and 0.75/0.71 for SUVmax/SUVpeak, without evidence of superior discrimination by any model.
CONCLUSION: PD-L1 prediction using both static and kinetic [18F]FDG PET parameters was feasible in NSCLC, with comparable performance between SUV- and parametric-based metrics, without evidence of superior discrimination by any model. These preliminary findings require validation in larger independent cohorts. Abbreviated dynamic LAFOV PET/CT enables whole-body assessment of tumor glucose kinetics in a clinically practical protocol.
43084153:
OBJECTIVES: To evaluate paraspinal muscle degeneration using proton density fat fraction (PDFF) and T2 mapping and to investigate their associations with degenerative spine features and clinical outcomes in low back pain (LBP).
MATERIALS AND METHODS: This prospectively recruited cross-sectional study included 86 participants with LBP and 86 controls who underwent q-Dixon and T2 mapping at L4/5. PDFF and T2 values were measured in the multifidus (MF) and erector spinae (ES). Degenerative spine features were assessed. Group comparisons, Spearman correlations, and multivariable linear regression analyses were performed, adjusting for age, body mass index, and sex, with additional sensitivity analyses incorporating structural variables.
RESULTS: After correction for multiple comparisons, PDFF and T2 values in the superficial and whole MF and ES were higher in the LBP group. PDFF and T2 values showed moderate-to-strong correlations within the same muscle (ρ = 0.571-0.743, all q < 0.001). However, pain status was not independently associated with imaging parameters after adjustment, whereas age showed consistent positive associations. Additional multivariable analyses showed that T2 values, but not PDFF, were associated with selected degenerative spine features after adjustment for covariates. Inter-reader reliability was excellent for PDFF and T2, with ICCs of 0.98 and 0.97, respectively.
CONCLUSION: After adjustment, LBP status was not independently associated with PDFF or T2 values, whereas age was associated with both and selected degenerative spine features were associated with T2 values in exploratory analyses. Given the cross-sectional design, causal relationships among muscle alterations, structural degeneration, and pain cannot be determined.
KEY POINTS: Question Do paraspinal muscle proton density fat fraction and T2 values reflect low back pain independently of demographic and lumbar degenerative features? Findings After demographic adjustment, low back pain status was not independently associated with paraspinal muscle proton density fat fraction or T2 values. Critical relevance statement Radiologists should interpret paraspinal muscle proton density fat fraction and T2 values alongside patient demographics, lumbar degenerative findings, and clinical measures rather than as direct imaging markers of low back pain.
43084169:
OBJECTIVES: To characterize radiology residents' training experience and reporting practices in rectal MRI staging in Romania, an Eastern European training environment.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: A multicenter, cross-sectional survey with nationwide dissemination was conducted in late 2025. A pretested questionnaire developed by a three-member panel was distributed through the Romanian Society of Radiology and Medical Imaging and residency coordinators. Items addressed demographics, rectal MRI exposure, self-assessed difficulty and confidence, practice context, learning methods, and structured reporting. Spearman's rank correlation assessed the association between residency year and self-reported rectal MRI exposure.
RESULTS: Of 160 respondents (estimated survey uptake: 16.0%, 24.7%, or 23.4%, depending on denominator), 142 with prior general MRI experience formed the main analytic cohort. Higher residency year was associated with greater reported rectal MRI exposure (Spearman's rho = 0.527, p < 0.001), although exposure remained limited: approximately 70% of fifth-year residents reported ≤ 30 cases. Confidence was lowest for T4a and EMVI. Practice-context barriers included limited case volume (33.1%) and restricted resident involvement in interpretation (9.2-11.3%). Internet-based platforms (90.1%) and peer-to-peer learning (57.7%) were the dominant learning methods; only 10.6% attended dedicated workshops. Local training activities were rated useful or very useful by 87.3% of respondents. Prior use of structured reporting for rectal MRI was reported by 21.8%.
CONCLUSIONS: This multicenter survey suggests a potential training gap in rectal MRI staging during radiology residency in Romania. Reported exposure remained limited even in later residency years, learning was predominantly self-directed, and a minority of respondents reported prior use of structured reporting.
KEY POINTS: Question Rectal MRI staging is complex and clinically important, but residents' actual exposure, learning pathways, and structured reporting use during training remain poorly described. Findings A Romanian multicenter survey identified limited rectal MRI exposure, variable confidence across staging tasks, and prior structured reporting use among 21.8% of respondents. Critical relevance statement Identifying limited resident exposure, self-directed learning, and limited prior use of structured reporting supports targeted residency training and more consistent rectal MRI staging practice.
43084267: Background: Prior studies have documented increasing utilization of emergency department (ED) CT and MRI but have generally focused on restricted populations or on individual modalities, anatomic regions, or clinical indications. Purpose: To characterize temporal trends in utilization of CT and MRI across radiology subspecialties in U.S. EDs and to project future such utilization shifts. Methods: This retrospective study used deidentified aggregate EHR data from U.S. healthcare organizations participating in the Epic Cosmos platform. The platform was queried from 2016 to 2025 to identify annual counts for ED encounters and associated CT and MRI events, stratified by subspecialty, age group, and U.S. census region. Utilization was expressed per 100 ED encounters. Quasi-Poisson regression models were used to determine annual percentage change and to project utilization through 2030. Results: The analysis included 431,876,897 ED encounters during the study period. Utilization per 100 encounters for CT increased from 27.3 to 53.9 (annual percentage change, 7.4%), for MRI from 3.6 to 5.4 (4.3%) and for CT and MRI combined from 30.9 to 59.3 (7.1%). The proportion of ED encounters without CT or MRI decreased from 80.0% in 2016 to 66.8% in 2025. Utilization per 100 encounters increased for all subspecialties (6.2-9.1%), age groups (5.0-6.2%), and census regions (5.6-7.6%). Among subspecialties, the contribution to the absolute increase in utilization was greatest for neuroradiology (36.3%) and body imaging (29.0%). Assuming that the trend from 2016 through 2025 remained unchanged through 2030, utilization per 100 encounters was projected to increase further for CT to 78.4, for MRI to 6.7, and for CT and MRI combined to 84.8. In sensitivity analyses, projected utilization per 100 encounters for CT and MRI combined in 2030 was 85.5 when excluding calender years 2020 and 2021 (relating to the COVID-19 pandemic) and 80.6 when modeling based on only years 2022 through 2025. Conclusion: Per-encounter ED utilization of CT and MRI increased substantially from 2016 to 2025; the growth occurred broadly across subspecialties, age groups, and census regions. Clinical Impact: These findings may inform targeted workforce allocation, scanner capacity planning, workflow redesign, and imaging stewardship strategies, to help address evolving ED imaging demands.
43084399:
BACKGROUND: High-volume hospitals are associated with better outcomes in some surgical fields, including emergency general surgery (EGS). However, the association of hospital volume with outcomes in after-hours EGS remains unclear. This study aimed to evaluate the association between hospital-year volume of after-hours EGS and in-hospital mortality and total healthcare costs.
METHODS: We conducted a nationwide retrospective cohort study using the Japanese Diagnosis Procedure Combination database. We included patients aged ≥16 years who were directly admitted from outpatient settings and underwent after-hours EGS on or the day after admission between April 2014 and March 2023. The primary outcome was in-hospital mortality; the secondary outcome was total healthcare costs during hospitalization. Associations were evaluated using mixed-effects models. Hospital-year volume was analyzed continuously using natural cubic splines and categorically (1-19, 20-49, 50-99, and ≥100 cases/year).
RESULTS: Overall, 235,465 patients were included. In the mixed-effects logistic regression model, each 10-case increase in hospital-year volume was associated with lower in-hospital mortality (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 0.97; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.96-0.98; p<0.001). Spline analyses showed that the adjusted odds of in-hospital mortality generally decreased with increasing hospital-year volume, although this decline became less pronounced at higher-volume levels. Adjusted healthcare costs decreased across most of the volume range before increasing slightly at the highest levels. Compared with 1 to 19 cases/year, the aORs for in-hospital mortality were 0.77 (95% CI, 0.71-0.83), 0.72 (95% CI, 0.66-0.78), and 0.66 (95% CI, 0.59-0.74) for 20-49, 50-99, and ≥100 cases/year, respectively (all p<0.001). The corresponding adjusted relative costs were 0.99 (95% CI, 0.99-1.00; p=0.205), 0.98 (95% CI, 0.97-0.99; p=0.001), and 0.97 (95% CI, 0.96-0.99; p<0.001).
CONCLUSIONS: Higher hospital-year after-hours EGS volume was associated with lower in-hospital mortality and modestly lower healthcare costs. These associations varied across the volume range.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Prognostic/epidemiological; Level III.
43084405:
BACKGROUND: Alterations in neutrophil receptors provide valuable insights into the immune response after polytrauma. Point-of-care (POC) technologies enable rapid on-site analysis of neutrophils. Previous studies demonstrated individual neutrophil surface patterns after trauma, depending on injury severity and metabolic status. We hypothesized that infectious complications after polytrauma are preceded by specific neutrophil cell surface receptor alterations.
METHODS: A POC neutrophil analysis system (AQUIOS® Flow Cytometer) was implemented at a Level 1 trauma center. Polytrauma patients with an Injury Severity Score (ISS)≥25 were prospectively included. Neutrophil cell surface expression of CD10, CD11b, CD64, CD62L, and CD16 was analyzed immediately after admission and after 8 hours, 24 hours, 48 hours, and 5 days. Patients were grouped according to the occurrence or absence of infectious complications.
RESULTS: Thirty-two polytrauma patients with a median ISS of 34.5 were included in this study. Trauma sequelae included spine fractures, long bone fractures, and traumatic brain injury. During hospitalization, 13 out of 32 patients developed infectious complications. Patients who subsequently developed infectious complications showed significantly higher CD64 expression throughout the observation period, and CD62L demonstrated a trend toward higher expression. In addition, CD11b expression was elevated 8 hours after trauma.
CONCLUSIONS: Longitudinal assessment of multiple selected neutrophil markers draws an individual neutrophil surface profile, with specific patterns associated with the development of infectious complications. This offers a promising tool for early risk stratification and identification of trauma patients vulnerable to post-traumatic infectious complications and allows for future immune-protective trauma surgery.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Prognostic and Epidemiological; Level III.
43084431: Pancreatic disease in pediatric patients includes a diverse range of congenital, inflammatory, traumatic, and neoplastic conditions. In this article, the authors provide a comprehensive overview of the imaging features of a broad range of pancreatic diseases in children, highlighting the roles of conventional and advanced imaging techniques while addressing pediatric-specific challenges. A structured review of pediatric pancreatic abnormalities, including the findings of US, CT, MRI with MR cholangiopancreatography, and nuclear medicine studies is presented. In addition, the benefits and limitations of these diagnostic imaging methods, as well as the necessity of a tailored, multimodality imaging paradigm for accurate diagnosis and management of pediatric pancreatic disease, are outlined. Emerging quantitative imaging methods have recently enabled objective evaluation of the pancreas at the cellular and molecular levels by means of assessment of the parenchymal volume, fat fraction, tissue stiffness, and microvascular architecture. In addition, radiomics and artificial intelligence models may enhance diagnostic accuracy by extracting large volumes of quantitative data from medical images to characterize tissue dimensions, morphology, and tissue heterogeneity. The authors provide a comprehensive review of the imaging findings of the most common neoplastic and non-neoplastic pediatric pancreatic diseases and their mimics. Finally, they outline the most common pediatric pancreatic surgical procedures, expected postoperative changes, and potential postsurgical complications to facilitate communication between the surgeon and the radiologist.
43084432: Breast cancer treatment has progressively evolved toward less invasive, more personalized therapeutic strategies that maintain oncologic efficacy while minimizing morbidity. Cryoablation, a percutaneous image-guided technique, has emerged as a promising alternative to surgery in selected patients with breast cancer. Initially explored in patients unfit for surgery or those declining operative management, cryoablation is now supported by growing evidence demonstrating favorable local control rates for older women with low-risk, early-stage breast cancer. Ongoing trials are further investigating these findings and evaluating whether cryoablation may exert immunomodulatory effects that enhance systemic antitumor immunity. If so, this may provide a rationale for combination strategies with immune checkpoint inhibitors and cancer vaccines. The authors examine the technical principles of cryoablation, summarize clinical outcomes from key studies, and explore its role in special populations including elderly patients and those declining surgery. Ongoing research will determine how cryoablation can be integrated into standard breast cancer treatment as part of a broader movement toward therapeutic de-escalation. ©RSNA, 2026 See the invited commentary by Mitchum and Ward in this issue.
43084433: Diagnosis and management of lower genitourinary trauma presents substantial challenges to the complex anatomy and functional diversity of the affected organs. Imaging plays a critical role in accurately assessing the injury location and severity, guiding clinical decisions, and improving patient outcomes. US, CT, and conventional urethrography and cystography are commonly used for the initial assessment of patients with lower genitourinary trauma. MRI, with its superior soft-tissue contrast resolution and direct multiplanar imaging capability, is invaluable in selected cases of lower genitourinary trauma. MRI has a complementary role in diagnosis of acute penile fractures and testicular injuries when US findings are inconclusive, as MRI effectively delineates the tunica albuginea of the corpora of the penis as well as the testicles. Disruption of the tunica albuginea is an indication for immediate surgical repair. Traumatic urethral injuries can lead to strictures and disruptions, which often necessitate delayed reconstructive surgery. MRI has an adjunctive role in conventional urethrography and provides detailed anatomic information about the urethra and periurethral structures such as urethral stumps, urethral gap length, periurethral fibrosis, displacement of the prostate and rectum, fistulas, false channels, fractures and avulsions of the corporal bodies, and fluid collections such as hematoma, urinoma, and abscess. Bladder rupture with surrounding fluid collection can be identified at MRI, although confirmatory CT or conventional cystography may be necessary. Furthermore, MRI with and without intravenous contrast material is helpful for diagnosis of suspected partial segmental thrombosis of the corpus cavernosum. © The Author(s) 2026.
